Fun fact: prospecting is more important than outreach!!! *gasp*

I hate to break this to you, but if your list is bad then there is a 0% chance your outreach works 🙂 

The rule of thumb here is: thou shalt only reach out to thy prospects with a real reason 

And, in case you were curious, "X title in X vertical in X territory" is not a real reason!! That is a generic filter!! Use your brain and go deeper!! 

Here's 3 steps to make a legit list: 

1. Ditch your bulk-exported lists- ✨ these are trash ✨ 

This is a good starting point, but not the final product- it's too generic 

2. Actually THINK: why am I reaching out to this person? What makes them a good fit for my solution? How did I find this reason? 

Some reasons could be: mergers, ads in market, office locations, services they use, competitors, expansion/downsize- honestly, anything!! 

3. Add prospects to lists based on reason, then you can easily customize outreach based on specific reasons 

The more specific the better since you can get very personalized with your messaging without having to go person by person 

That's it!! And remember, without the list- you are nothing!!!!!

Being remarkable isn’t enough. 

Seth Godin ‘Purple Cow’ is a lie. Here’s my take: 

Seth Godin famously said that the key to growth is creating something remarkable—something so unique that people can’t help but talk about it. But here’s the problem:

Most “Purple Cows” die in obscurity.

Countless startups have built innovative, remarkable products that never took off. 

Why? Because being interesting doesn’t mean you’ll be discovered.

The Truth:

Growth isn’t just about being different. It’s about:

- Getting in front of the right people (distribution > uniqueness)

-Solving a painful problem (people talk about what impacts them, not just what’s cool)

-Creating a movement, not a gimmick (Figma wasn’t just ‘better design software’—it built a tribe)

Takeaway:

Don’t just be a Purple Cow. Be a cow in the middle of the highway, causing a traffic jam—undeniable, unavoidable, impossible to ignore.

What do you think? Is being “remarkable” overrated?

The 9-Step Blog Traffic Revival Plan:

1️⃣ Dive into GSC – Analyze 28-day, 3-month, 6-month, and 1-year data for organic clicks, position, impressions, and CTR. Patterns don’t lie.

2️⃣ Upgrade your keyword research – Identify new long-tail keywords and update your primary/secondary focus.

3️⃣ Check search intent shifts – If Google redefined what users expect, your blog needs to follow. Write a 1-2 paragraph analysis.

4️⃣ Level up your content – The gap between good and great is expert insight. Tap a subject matter expert (SME) to refine it.

5️⃣ Optimize for AI Overview – If Google’s AI feature is ranking at the top, match its format and answer the same query upfront.

6️⃣ Revamp your metadata – Craft a high-CTR title and meta description based on updated keyword research.

7️⃣ Add schema markup – Use ChatGPT to generate FAQ schema in seconds and boost your chances of a rich snippet.

8️⃣ Internal linking overhaul – Find related content, update anchor texts, and link strategically.

9️⃣ Check keyword density – Ensure 1-2% coverage of your target keywords without stuffing.

When someone responds "no thanks" to your cold email- throw a hail mary!!!! you have nothing to lose!!!! they already declined you!!! YOLO!! 

Here's what I do when someone says no, it works sometimes... not all the time... but it's turned a no to a yes before 🤷‍♀️

First: acknowledge their no

Say something like "completely understand", "got it, no problem", etc. This way, you are not being pushy and convincing them that they are wrong. They owe you nothing! 

Second: reiterate WHY you reached out to THEM specifically

"The reason I reached out is...." Make this relevant- remember you have a solution to their problem!!! This is a real human reaching out with a real solution! If you do this correctly, the recipient may put 2 + 2 together!

Third: acknowledge their no again... but leave things open ended

Sign off with something like "totally get this may not be of interest right now, but if that changes let me know"- this way, you are respecting their "no" but you are leaving the door open in case they changed their mind

Again, this is not a magic solution... BUT I am a firm believer in shooting your shot- you have nothing to lose!

Most people write cold outreach selling their solution... bad!!! that's about you!!! You need to make it about THEM!

Here are some lines I've received recently that have not landed b/c they are selfish-"I", "we", "company".....

⚫️ "I never heard back on my last email? "
⚫️ "Well, we are still waiting to hear from you..."

⚫️ "I wanted to take a moment to share a personal recommendation with you."
⚫️ "Would love to know what you think of our COMPANY tool?"

I hate to break it to you, but your prospects ✨don't remotely care about you or your company ✨- so none of these will land, ever 😗✌️

What they DO care about are themselves, their job, and their company. So.... write your copy reflecting the same!

It's actually extremely easy to change your copy from 'you' to 'them'- I like to think of it as inverting your messaging

Some ways you can do that:
1.  Be a helpful consultant vs an annoying sales rep: copy should reflect
2. Remove you: I, we, our, your company, etc.
3. Replace with them: you, their company, their problem
4. Re-organize: include observations/challenges upfront 

Now.... go rewrite your messaging and go get em!!!!!

Your Marketing Isn’t Working (Hint: It’s Not Your Ads)

Most real estate tech startups have a positioning problem. Here's why 👇 

I see it all the time:
🚀 A startup pours money into LinkedIn ads, Google Ads, and outbound campaigns… but the leads don’t convert.
📉 The team blames the marketer, who blames the ad creative, the targeting, or the budget.
🔄 They keep tweaking tactics, yet nothing changes.

Here’s the truth: No amount of paid spend will fix bad positioning.

What’s happening?
	•	Your messaging is too generic (e.g., “We streamline real estate workflows” – so what?)
	•	You sound like every other proptech startup. What is differentiating you?
	•	Your ICP isn’t clear or specific enough, so your ads are speaking to no one.

💡 Positioning should come BEFORE ads. If your startup can’t answer these three questions, you have a positioning problem:
1. Who is your most profitable, fastest-closing customer? (Not “anyone in real estate.”)
2. What urgent pain are you solving for them?
3. Why are you the only company that solves it this way?

Fix your positioning, and your marketing will start working.

How to win clients on LinkedIn in 2025:

(from awareness → closing offer)

Data: We’re working on 40+ LinkedIn accounts. These range from CEOs, to Founders to even a couple meme accounts across a huge range of industries. Marketing, Sales, AI, Paid, SEO.

From that... here are 3 things, that you should be thinking about:

1. Competency statements.

Having a good hook isn’t enough. There is so much content on the internet. For a user to choose to read your LinkedIn post. They have to believe two things:

 - This will benefit me
 - This author is legitimate

The latter is solved by competency statements. Before or after your hook, say a statement that proves your an expert. (some examples in the video)


2. Prove your hook

This one's simple. Use media that proves your hook. If in your hook, you make a claim. Use the visual asset to prove that you did it.

So if you said you increase conversion rates by 20%
 -> Show a graph of that

If you said in your hook you spoke to 20 CEOs in the last 6 months.
-> Show blurred out meeting notes.

Typically, a raw screenshot is enough to prove out the hook.


3. Micro offers

This is a slightly new one.

(watch the video for where I start using the whiteboard)

Instead of pitching the big retainer. Earn trust and win a micro transaction.

What that means, in that every market - for every complex solution sold. There are micro offers.

So if you’re an agency selling a retainer service for lead generation ($5-10k p/m).

You can sell many micro offers

-> List building ($1k)
-> Data validation ($1k)
-> Tech set ups ($5k)

The benefit of selling micro offers is that they're typically more profitable and they're things you're already doing as part of your complex offer.

And there are more leads in-market for micro offers vs fully baked retainers.

Now you have micro offers you have

a) more products to pitch on a sales call
b) more price points to pitch on a sales call
c) more potential closed customers

In other words: you can make more profit per sales call

Note: You don’t need sell this outright on the front end. You can just talk about it. And then people will come inbound. On the sales call you can route the lead to the best solution for them.

Harsh truth about LinkedIn:

Your best performing posts are getting you LESS clients.

Most people think more likes = more leads.

Likes do not equal clients.

In fact -

Most of my best-performing posts (tons of likes, comments, and engagement) didn’t bring in a single dollar of revenue.

So, what’s the disconnect?

It all comes down to Content Strategy.

Here’s what actually works:


1 - Focus on Your Ideal Client

Your audience should be specific and targeted.

Creating viral content for the sake of engagement often attracts a diluted audience who will never buy from you.


2 - Master the Funnel

Divide your posts into two types:

Top of Funnel

Personal and opinion posts that build connection and brand awareness.

Bottom of Funnel

Social proof, testimonials, and case studies that drive action.

Here’s a framework we’ve used to generate consistent leads:

→ 1 TOF post per week (Share personal insights or market opinions)
→ 3 BOF posts per week (Showcase client results, testimonials, and case studies)
→ 1 Lead Magnet post (Offer a free, high-value resource to collect leads)


3 - Use Proven Formats

Every successful post on LinkedIn falls under one of these categories:

Social Proof
Education
Personal Stories
Trending Topics

If you write a post, and it doesn’t fit any of those 4:

It’s not going to perform.

And it’s not getting you more leads.

The takeaway:

If you’re constantly chasing likes, you’re setting yourself up for failure.

The goal of LinkedIn isn’t to spike your dopamine with:

→ Likes
→ Followers
→ Engagements

It’s to:

→ Write specifically for your ICP
→ Filter out everyone else
→ Sign clients

Lead gen from cold email in 2025 is tough...

But this LinkedIn post can 2-4x your pipeline.

Especially when we use lead magnets (valuable giveaways in exchange for engagement).

Here’s are 3 reasons why lead magnets are better than sending cold emails for booking calls:


1) 1:1 versus 1-to-many

Cold email is a 1-to-1 tool.

You send a message from yourself, to another business.

Lead magnets are 1-to-many.

You create 1 lead magnet, and loads of businesses come to it.


2) Low authority

When you’re cold emailing, you’re inherently coming from a low authority.

You’re going out into the market asking people to buy your stuff.

With lead magnets, you’re saying:

“Hey, look how amazing my stuff is. Who wants to hear about it?”

The frame is completely different.


3) Collecting vs Spraying

With cold email, you’re spraying the entire market.

You actively have to go out and find the 3% of people who are in-market for your business.

When you’re doing a lead magnet -

- You’re chucking something out as bait
- Collecting a bunch of leads
- Qualifying them on the back end

Would you rather be the business that goes out and sprays the market?

Or the one that passively collects them?

All in all -

- Lead mags are incredible assets.
- You position yourself better.
- They’re lower effort.

And you’ll book higher quality calls simply because people will feel like you’ve done them a solid.

P.S. Am I saying cold email will never work? No. There’s a time and place…  

But there’s a reason why even the cold email agencies are posting on LinkedIn…

This is classic “demand capture versus demand generation”.

Demand capture is looking to sign clients that are actively looking for solutions.

The issue with demand capture is that:

 - Your competitors are all targeting the same buyers
 - Prospects compare deliverables instead of value
 - It’s difficult to charge prices that you’re worth.

Prospects have no reason to choose you over your competitors.

Demand generation fixes this.

Which is when you create demand by educating prospects“before” they need your service.

They’re not actively looking for a solution now but when they are?

You’ll be top of mind.

There’s a number of ways you can generate demand through LinkedIn content.

You could post top of funnel content that educates your prospects on solving a pain point.

For example - a post could be “Why your LinkedIn strategy isn’t generating leads despite you posting daily”.

Another would be using micro-offers to give prospects a low-risk way of getting value.

For example - this could be workshops, courses, or an audit.

Another would be using trust assets regularly in your content.

For example - screenshots of case studies, client wins, and testimonials.

Demand generation is the easiest way to charge premium prices and land premium deals.

You top competing with other agencies for the same leads. Instead you educate prospects about your company which makes closing them easier.

You might book fewer sales calls this way.

But your closing rate and number of deals signed would go way up.

They lied about how “repurposing” is supposed to work.

And it’s quietly wrecking your marketing

THE WAY YOU'VE BEEN TOLD: "REPURPOSE" 

We, marketers & founders, have been fed the same formula: 
a) start with a piece of long form content, a blog post, a podcast episode, or a webinar
b) and slice it up into dozens of short form pieces. 

The idea sounds simple enough. One big piece magically becomes 10 LinkedIn posts, 5 Reels, and a month of content in one afternoon.

But the reality is very different. When you try to pull clips from a 45 minute video or rip lines from a 2,000 word blog, things fall apart: 

1. The hook doesn’t land.
2. The flow feels broken. 
3. There’s no emotional pull or natural context left
4. The style no longer fits the platform / audience it's posted for. 

Truth is unless you are willing to spend massive amounts of extra time and creative energy reshaping each short form piece from scratch, this “easy” repurposing strategy ends up being harder and far less effective than anyone admits.

THE BETTER WAY: "REUSE"

Reusing doesn’t mean changing formats. It means amplifying what is already working. The better way is simple: start with a post that already hit, one that got real engagement, real reactions, or real conversions, and replicate it smartly.

Instead of slicing apart different types of content you... 

1. Keep the format the same.
2. Keep the platform the same.
3. Change the hook. 
4. Tweak the emotional stakes. 
5. Adjust the angle to resonate with slightly different ICPs. 

Here you are not creating an orange from an apple. You are testing Granny Smith versus Pink Lady. Same fruit, different flavor.

This approach is faster, easier, and dramatically more effective. You are building momentum, not burning energy reinventing the wheel. And because you are anchoring every version to a proven post, your odds of winning go way up without doubling your effort.


Personally, I wasted WAY too much time with the long form to short form myth. I have to be so PARTICULAR about what I repurpose from long form.

If you want real leverage from your content, stop trying to reinvent.

Start by doubling down on what already resonated, and tune it, amplify it, and repeat it.

Just told a $3m ARR+ consulting co they'll see ZERO new leads from LinkedIn for the next 3 months. They said "Let's start!". Here's what's going on & why you should slow down. 

1/ We will likely see leads in the first 90 days. Unsurprisingly, most good founders already have a decent connection base. I've run too many accounts to see the same pattern every single time. 2/ Cold leads can come fast, but it’s less predictable at the beginning. We can crank things up with lead magnets, outreach, aggressive copy. For our 90 day consulting clients we want to push ROI fast so we run certain tactics (e.g. Micro Offers) that get new inbound quickly. Most of the time it rips. But when you’re selling into bigger companies doing $1M, $10M, $50M+ in revenue, you’re dealing with fewer accounts and longer cycles.

3/ LinkedIn ROI isn’t always measured by leads. I work with a SaaS founder and although he's made $100k+ with LinkedIn, his main ROI is brand, hiring, ability to raise, getting noticed at conferences. You won’t always see it immediately, but that doesn’t mean it’s not working.

4/ This is a layer on channel. They’ve already got a sales engine and have predictable playbooks that bring net new leads. Those didn't get spun up in 90 days. We’re not here to save the business. We’re here to build brand and add leverage. And if I do say so myself, turn on the channel with the richest possible prospects all consuming information. 

5/ Could we get results faster? Of course. But only if we're willing to reduce constraints. In other words, more aggressive / irresistible offer. Lower requirements on what a good client is. Going harder on outreach. Running rage bait style hook and running more lead magnets.

What’s working right now on LinkedIn? 

(Based on 40+ LinkedIn client accounts, 100s of posts & 1000s of DMs we're managing monthly)

We've got eyes on a lot of data on LinkedIn. 

Here's 3 things we're seeing. 


1/ Hook Strength 

Hooks make or break your post. Last year, sub-par hooks would work. But, the last couple of months we've seen the bar increase.

Before you hit post, ask yourself: 
"How could I increase the strength of this hook?" 

Easy ways:
- Add numbers / data 
- Remove words / shorten hooks 

A more interesting way... what words/ideas can we use to pull the post to a more emotional extreme

E.g. 
Changing → Shifting 
Slowing → Flatlining
Bad → Brutal

(We want to do this without becoming overly dramatic / clickbaity - just enough to increase the stakes ever so slightly higher) 


2/ Resonant Ideas

Every niche has a resonant idea that works right now: 

For example:
- B2B marketing -> Anything about attribution 
- LinkedIn -> Anything about the em-dash
- SEO -> Anything about traffic drops 

Once you identify a resonant idea (by seeing it get outized engagement / appear a lot) you use it in your own content.

Essentially, you already know what your audience wants to engage with. You're now just fitting yourself into that story. 


3/ Raw Media

Best media posts seem to always be screenshots, taking head, looms and lifestyle shots. Nothing crazy here.

You do not need to invest in lots of production, effects, editing etc. 

Minimal / raw is almost always better, provided it's supporting the emotional angle / idea of the hook.

This is a good thing. You don't have to heavily invest into editing / design etc 

(unless you want to be one of those engagement pod influencers punching out dense cheat sheets with 1000s of likes that we all know no one is reading) 


--- 

TLDR: Ask these 3 questions before you hit post. 

1. Can I increase my hook strength with less words, more numbers, more emotion?
2. Can I tap into a resonant idea which my audience already engages with? 
3. Can I post a supporting raw media asset to support my hook?

What's working in B2B marketing? 

Quick list of 'easy' tactics I'm seeing: 


1. B2B Facebook Retargeting Ads

Set up a custom audience in Facebook with users that are leads at the bottom of your funnel. Maybe trial sign ups, booked a call, high intent leads. You can upload a csv list or set it up dynamically. Serve them ads from $5 per day. Probably the highest ROI ads you'll ever spend on.

2. Founder Led LinkedIn Content 

No brainer. It's so easy to pick up 1,000 to 3,000 impressions on a single post and get in front of your target customers. Lots of attributable pipeline. Buyers trust personal content > company content. 

3. Video Explainers

Add a video walkthrough of your product / service / consultancy towards the top of your page. Can be an interactive demo or just walking through slides. Even Salesforce are doing it. 

4. Publishing Original Data 

Databox do this really well. They'll survey existing customers, experts, and surface interesting data insights no one else can, and publish in to regular reports. If it wasn't for these, I wouldn't be aware they exist. 

5. Email Nurture

Buyers buy when they want to buy. Not when you want to sell. Once they're on your list enter them into a 'new lead' flow that tries to get them to take the next step in 10 days. If it doesn't convert, push into a 'nurture newsletter' flow for the rest of eternity. 

6. Tighter Targeting 

Get super specific on the ICP you're selling to. Competition has increased. If you're speaking to everyone, you're speaking to no one. You can dramatically cut down who your customers perceive are your competitive solutions just by narrowing niche. 

7. LinkedIn Thought Leader Ads

Ads that don't look like ads on LinkedIn. Super high CTRs / engagement rates and lower CPLs and CACs. One of the most effective ad units.

8. AI Sales Transcripts

Finally mentioning AI. Get your most qualified sales calls transcripts. Push through AI and identify ideas / pains / desires / words. Use this back into marketing to attract similar personas. Comment AI below and I'll send you a killer prompt I use. 

9. 3-Multi Attribution

This is a free way to properly attribute where customers are coming from. a) free field on your booking forms that asks "where did you hear about us" - let the user write whatever they want. b) ask on sales calls "how did you find us". c) UTM codes. That's 3 different attribution angles you can use that typically reveal 2-3 different marketing sources.

I speak to a lot of founders who want to start on LinkedIn, but don't know where to start. Here's 10 post stories I suggest to get them going.

1. “Why I Started My Business”
Tell the real reason behind launching your company. What was the itch you had to scratch. What was the problem you couldn't ignore (or the opportunity you saw before others) 

2. “The Moment I Knew I Had to Quit My Job”
Share the turning point that pushed you to leave the safety of a job / degree etc. People relate risk you take and it sets you up to create stakes for your journey. 

3. “I Thought This Would Work. I Was Wrong.”
Reveal a bet you made that you were convinced would pay out - but ultimately flopped. Why did you have such conviction? What actually happened? What was the consequences of that? What did you learn. 

4. “How I Got My First Customer”
Give the insider tea. Who was that first customer. How did you acquire them? Break down the scrappy tactics, outreach (or luck lol) that landed your first paying client.

5. “The Advice I Ignored (And Regret)”
All founders are swimming in advice. And we all ignore good advice sometimes. Share one that cost you (and you regret not listening to). Who said it? Why did you ignore it? What do you recommend others do? 

6. “What I Learned in Year One”
Reveal 10+ lessons from your first year in business. Make it punchy and honest. Run it as a listicle - not to dissimilar to this post.

7. “A Hard Conversation I Had to Have”
Turn the vulnerability dial up here. Whether it was firing someone, breaking up with a cofounder, or walking away from a bad deal. Create stakes, and then show how you handled it.

8. “Our First $100k ( or $10k, etc) Month”
Share the milestone, how you got there, and what changed to hit that number. Typically tying back to growth works reallllyyy well on LinkedIn. 

9. “Why We Turned Down Investment/Partnership.”
LinkedIn loves the bootstrapper vs VC story. Or if that doesn't fit - adjust for partnerships / tempting opportunities. Explain why you turned it down, what it means for your business. 

10. “This Team That Got Us Here”
Show off your team and their personal achievements. They're characters in your story, highlight them, be publicly proud of them and give them their chance in the light.

Using data to create signals in outbound campaigns is great and should be done but isn't your silver bullet to a repeatable outbound machine. Refining the offer you use to a cold audience is much more impactful. 

As access to data becomes cheaper and cheaper (remember when you were a genius for automating targeting companies when they raised money) folks on LinkedIn and companies are talking/asking more about how to do outbound campaigns with better signals. 

Which is great, I think everyone should be doing that, but off the top of my head there's two places that signals fail. 

1. If you need more meetings than the signals can find for you in your market.
2. You're chasing a signal that isn't actually public information and you throw away good companies when you look for roundabout ways to get the data.

Just raised funding, new hires enroll, hiring for new team members or company news about a new product launch, etc, are very common signals that I see on LinkedIn and that our customers ask us for. 

Let's say your target market has 100,000 people in it that you can reasonably contact. How many of them at any given point are starting a new job or just got a promotion? 10%? 20%?

No where near enough that you can build a full outbound motion just off of signals. 

Same with point 2. We have one customer that has asked us in the past, "we want to target companies spending $40k+ per month on marketing."

Ok so there's no public way to get that information but I can tell you who has 5 people on their marketing team, is actively running Meta/Google/and LinkedIn ads. 

But what about the company that has 1 marketing person because they use a lot of contractors and is only running Meta ads but under the hood they are spending $100k a month on ads. 

Maybe the argument could be made that some kind of site traffic number should then be used as a proxy but isn't perfect yet again. 

1 thing that we have seen fix both issues is taking the time to figure out a front end offer that your audience resonates with. 

For us, our first campaign is free as a pilot. So we can tell everyone that before they pay us anything, we will prove we can get leads. 

For Clay, to a cold audience, finding case studies or the kinds of customers they sell to based on their website content and showing people how to easily build lookalike lists is the best performing outbound campaign hook.  

A video content agency we work with makes the first 10 videos and payments is collected only after the customer is satisfied. 

Of course, there's lots of ways to skin this cat. And I think more people should be talking about refining their offer to a dead cold audience vs. the next triple double backflip equivalent of an outbound workflow.

Open tracking has one really important benefit that we use it for and it's not knowing who actually opened our email.

Recently, we made the decision to start testing a couple of campaigns with open tracking turned on only on Thursdays and Fridays, and honestly, it's been a great decision. 

If you didn't know, open tracking is essentially a vanity metric. After an Apple iOS update, if somebody has the Mail app on their phone, every email that they receive that lands in their inbox pings the open pixel. 

Sometimes teams will tell us, "Can you get a list of all the people who open the email," and we always tell them, "Hey, let's score them on other things like their website content and other intent signals" because just because there's an open doesn't mean they actually opened the email. 

But what it does give us is data on whether or not our emails are landing in inbox for spam. 

Now I won't say open tracking is perfect, but you can be sure that if one of your inboxes is getting a 10% open rate and another inbox is getting a 75% open rate, that inbox with a 10% open rate can be tossed to the side and not used in any other campaigns. 

No other metric (such as watching for replies on the campaign or out of office replies) gives you enough of an inbox-level guide on this. They can tell you if the overall campaign is going well but not the immediate warning on the inbox.

Inbox spam placement tests are okay, but due to the nature of the test, if you start sending too many of them, the spam test is going to recognize the email it's being sent from and then keep it in the primary box. 

Some of the built-in spam testing tools are repairing your inbox health, and if they detect it going to spam, they're moving to the inbox which would negate the test the next time you try.

The New York Times paraphrased me saying Clay is a "powerful but unwieldy tool". That's not what I said and this post is for anyone that thinks it's "unwieldy."

When people get started with Clay, I recommend a crawl, walk, run framework because it's not that Clay is difficult to use. 

There are only 4 things you can do in Clay. 

Import Data, Enrich Data, Use Formulas, and Export Data. 

This isn't the unwieldy part. The fact that you have to onboard on to Clay and ALL the other integrations is where it gets confusing. 

So I tell everyone that they should Crawl, Walk, and then Run with Clay. 

Crawl looks like what I talk about in the video. 

There are workflows that I know you must be doing every day that can be easily automated like pulling leads, validating their emails, and cleaning the company names to be uploaded into a campaign. 

A manual workflow of the past now thanks to Clay. 

"Walk" is to add in some level of AI or if/then segmentation into your campaigns. 

"If VP of finance vs. head of finance, then change messaging this way" type workflows.

"Run" workflows are the workflows that you create when you watch yourself manually reach out to 20 people and think about how to automate the work you did when you were manually reaching out to people and capturing that into your workflow. 

Don't worry about doing workflows with triple double backflips or anything when getting started. Just automate away the low hanging fruit first.

I've got a $250k/mo client. They never post selfies and still make 7-figures from LinkedIn with simple text posts. Yes, pics of yourself help, but 3 things are MORE important for driving inbound clients. 

I've also seen this across ALL the 200+ accounts I've worked on and the 100s of posts we're publishing monthly. 

1) OPINIONS

Impressions come from attention.
Attention comes from contrast.
Contrast comes from opinions.

See, opinions are a KEY part of getting impressions on LinkedIn. Create a 1 pager. Write down everything you stand for (and against). 

Now the best lead generating opinions? They're the ones that your ICP is thinking about and can rally behind. Don't be afraid to turn OFF segments of your ICP.

I'm doing it in this post right now. If you don't have a strong opinion and are unwilling to stand for something... we're probably not a fit. 


2) RECENT EXPERIENCES

This $250k/mo client is CONSTANTLY sending us new/interesting stories. Ok yes, we're prompting for them... BUT this is key.

Stuff like: new client wins, new conversations with ICP, recent personal experiences. 

This stuff adds a 'newness' to the content. It makes it feel fresh. You might not feel like the stuff you're doing on a day to day would make interesting content, but I almost can guarantee it does! Throw your AI note taker into AI and ask what interesting moments could make for a LinkedIn post - I don't guarantee the AI will do a great job, but it'll get you going.

Ok needs to be said. If you're not exceptional at what you do, or willing to be opinionated. You're going to really struggle on LinkedIn.

If you want to play on the highest level here, you better be able to open your post with competency statements. Stuff like "I did [BIG THING]".  The bigger the claim. The faster you'll grow.

I had the opportunity to teach a Pavilion cohort with Yash Tekriwal 🤔 and here are 11 outbound tips we went over when automating your workflows!

I hit the character limit on this post so if you have any questions about the nuance, don't hesitate to comment as there's for sure a lot here. 

1. "Personalization" should = 10 minutes of what you would manually research
 
The most common mistake is asking “What are other companies doing with AI?” Instead, ask “What should we be doing with AI?”

Think about how you’d research a company for 10 minutes: what you’d check, how those checks change your message (hook, value, CTA), and then how to automate that same research.

Rule of thumb: Claygent can usually handle most of the research you need.

2. Generate AI snippets, not AI emails

Long, “all-in-one” prompts rarely nail everything. It’s much easier to create strong outputs in small pieces (e.g., 2–7 words or one short sentence at a time) and assemble the final message.

3. Don’t ever tell the model you’re writing a “cold email”

Describe the persona and tone you want instead. This avoids the generic “sales-blog” style many models default to.

4. One job per prompt

Every AI in your workflow should do one task at a time. Claygent does one research task. Your writing prompt does one writing task. Combining tasks creates errors and cost creep.

5. Feed actual data into the prompt

Don’t say “This is salesforce.com, write an email.” Give the model the specific facts you’d use yourself.

The more grounded the inputs, the less guessing.

6. Examples are the most important input for your prompts.

Great examples can turn an okay prompt—and an okay system prompt—into something excellent. Curate 2–3 gold-standard input→output examples and keep them fresh. Remove weak ones. Examples anchor style, brevity, and relevance.

7. Always use conditional formulas/run-conditions to protect spend

Only run research when required inputs exist; only run writing when research fields are filled. Guardrails reduce wasted credits and noisy outputs.

8. Dictate your prompts

If typing slows you down, speak your prompt, then ask the model to tighten and clarify it. You’ll capture more nuance, faster.

9. Ask AI to critique your prompt

Paste your draft prompt + goal and ask: “Do you have any follow-up questions to help make this more accurate?” Answer them, then have the model rewrite the prompt with fewer tokens.

10. Model + cost hygiene

We use GPT-4o mini for most tasks, and we lock our API key to that model so the team can’t accidentally run expensive ones. 

Keep prompts short and examples essential to control token spend.

11. Ban filler/jargon with a general system prompt

Keep a fifth-grade reading level, short sentences, and concrete verbs.

Ask ChatGPT to draft a reusable system prompt that bans words like “leverage,” “synergy,” “innovate,” etc., and apply that system prompt to any AI 
that writes email snippets.

Here are all the mistakes I made on my first outbound campaign that I thought sent 50,000 emails but no way it sent more than 2,000. 

Back in 2019, I was getting into outbound automation for the first time. 

As many people do, I was compiling a list of all of my target accounts and thought I was doing a great job. 

As soon as I finished, the hospitals reached out to the non-profit that I was working at and asked if there were any way to get the word out to get donations for N95 masks. 

We said we could help and it turned out that we solicited over 100 bulk donations of masks, but in doing so I made every mistake in the book. 

1) I thought I was sending 50,000 emails from my individual inbox on my main domain. 

If you look up the settings on outlook back in 2019, no way I got past 2,000 emails sent. 

2) I didn't validate my list so the bounces on my account were insane. 

For this reason and reason number 1, I couldn't actually email anyone for about a week because all my emails were going to spam. 

3) I had no idea who I was emailing so even though we were comparatively successful to the effort we put in, I emailed a ton of irrelevant people. 

Of course this was all for a good cause and I was only working in a non-profit. 

Funny to look back on this campaign with what I thought I had accomplished and now with what I know today, how much I could have improved and maybe even gotten more donations for the hospitals.

The only rule we have for buying domains is we only buy .com and .co domains and don't mess with any of the other riff raff of the TLDs. 

From our experience, as long as the domain forwards your main domain, you're going to be all set.

some lil tips and tricks to show your outreach was sent by you, not a robot 🤖

you can write the best outreach in the world, but the default today is sequences, so here are some ways ways to prove "I am in fact a person trying to contact you" not "you are in step 1 of my sequence". 

(this is obvi assuming you have good relevant messaging, if your messaging is bad this will not help you haha)

1. lower case names: sequencers pull names as written, I know "julia" isn't proper grammar, but sequencers pull names or capitalize them, so lower case it is!

1A --> this also goes for company name, competitor names, etc. 

2. Quick connection requests after an email or inmail: connect with a note like "hey just sent you an email about X, putting a face to the name!" --> sequencers force a buffer between automated steps, if there's little to no buffer it means you sent it, + putting a face to an email is always a good thing!

3. Quick follow ups: similar concept to before, but if you send a follow up quickly (5-45 min after message 1) like "only asking b/c" or "oh also meant to send X", it shows you are not sending some automated follow up days later 

4. Go for the convo, not the pitch: I am working on this as my brain is wired to "book meetings" but I am trying to pivot from "meetings" to "convos", and they key here is REAL convos, not with an agenda to book a meeting- they often can point you in the right direction

+ bonus hot take: voice notes/videos don't mean you're not a robot, sooo many tools today can scale "personalized" videos/voice notes across groups of ppl.... if you're going to do it, do it right!!

By no means is this a magic pill, but just some subtle ways to standout as a person vs. a sequencer

Whenever I post about the average reply rate that we see, agency owners I'm close with message me and tell me to stop because their customers then ask about getting that average reply. But often people are asking the wrong question. 

We get asked all the time, "What's a response rate that we can expect?"

The real answer is: If you were to take all of our customers and divide the amount of positive responses we get by how many emails we have to send out, the number right now is about 1 positive response out of 425 contacts that we enroll. (Up from 1 in 300 2 years ago I might add). 

But there's so much nuance underneath this. We have some people that get one positive response for every 78 people that they reach out to. 

Their LTV is $2,000.

Another customer, (who has happily worked with us for a year I might add) gets 1 positive response for every 2,000 leads.

Their LTV is $200k

 Asking what the average is fine, so that you can have an expectation of performance. But you also need to consider:

How many experiments have you run?
Have you truly thought through a lot of ideas and tested them?
How many times have you changed your copywriting and framing?

As long as you're constantly experimenting and trying new things, your response rate eventually is just what your response rate is in your market. And you have to make sure that that math works out for your business in particular.

If you were helping someone get started on Clay, what's a piece of *niche* advice you would give that most people don't talk about? Here's some of mine. 

1. Make it a rule across your team that no paid columns can run without a conditional formula. 

2. Replace your templates with their new functions feature. Functions allow you to run a workflow outside of your main Clay table so that if you ever need to change it, you don't need to change 300 Clay tables, you just change the function.

3. Save all paid data to our Supabase (or pick another tool/CRM) so that when you enrich data about a company or contact, you can keep it.

4. Everyone on the team is given practice assignments to scrape and integrate with Apify and ZenRows. These tools give you access to so many different ways of getting new data. 

5. Always have fallback campaigns or lines when we are creating outbound campaigns. Signals and intense filtering are great but outbound still is a numbers game. Keep great campaigns in your back pocket when people don't qualify for your signal campaigns. 

6. You can keep a campaign automatically turned on with a $15/month Hubspot account automatically syncing to Clay so you don't have to think about refilling the campaign as often. 

7. We have a whole set of other niche AI rules that the team has to follow when they do any kind of AI prompting as well which might be better for another post.

Nurture cadences= the worst way to re-engage a lost lead

"checking in", "here's what's new!", "is now a better time?", "here's a case study", "are you still interested?", "we upgraded X feature", etc.

would you respond to that? 😐

Lost deals= a gold mine, orgs recognize this, but strategy is lazy. Reps follow up at their leisure, auto cadences get sent. They *think* they are being tailored using things like CRM lost reasons, rep notes, and call transcripts, but these campaigns fall flat as they rely on vague inputs (what does "timing" even mean??) or selfish inputs (company updates, not prospect needs)

The best engagement campaigns are structured as so: 
1. Find out why you lost 
2. Identify who you can win back 
3. Re-engage with relevance
4. Evaluate and Improve 

To execute this: 
1. Understand from the *buyers* POV (not the rep) why the deal was lost --> this rarely matches up with CRM reason. If you go off the CRM reason that does not match with the buyer, the campaign will not land 

2. Ask buyers if they are open to re-engagement--> they voluntarily say yes/no and when. Usually ~50% are open to it, don't waste time on the other half

3. Use buyers own words + other data (public signals, transcripts, etc.) to say the right thing at the right time --> messages like these can be automated with Clay workflows 

4. Track this religiously just like inbound/outbound: call it "rebound" --> total lost deals, total feedback collected, total deals interested again, total back in pipeline, total won back 

Lost deals *can* be a consistent revenue channel, but it requires a true system + measurement, not just random check ins or nurtures

We build systems like these for orgs: turning "lost" into repeatable revenue, more info here: https://lnkd.in/efJUDNHF

sales teams have 3 revenue channels: outbound, inbound, and rebound 

🔥 outbound= reps getting leads 
🔥 inbound= leads coming to reps 
🔥 rebound= former opportunities who want to re-engage

Everyone tracks outbound + inbound, few track rebound 

Rebound provides: quick wins (educated buyers who are willing to re-engage) and clear metrics to measure + improve upon that you weren't looking at before

To create a rebound funnel you need to:
⭐️ Find out why you lost 
⭐️ Identify who can be won back 
⭐️ Reach out with relevance 
⭐️ Evaluate and improve

Most orgs have a re-engagement strategy, but typically it's adhoc (reps follow up when they feel like it, nurture sequences sent) + does not adhere to a true measurable funnel

When measuring rebound funnel, we track these metrics:
# deals lost
# of feedback collected
# of deals who want to re-engage 
# of deals back in the pipeline
# of deals closed-won 

Rebound funnels identify recoverable revenue + help teams win it back in a consistent and repeatable manner. Instead of relying on "wake the dead" campaigns or hoping "it's a better time", take control + make a system out of it

I'm posting on 30+ LinkedIn accounts. Every month I'm co-writing 100s of posts and they MUST perform. Yesterday, a $5m ARR founder asked how do I know that a post will do well before it's been published and the LinkedIn Overlords have made their judgement? 

First, the truth: 

1. I'm not an oracle.
2. And I'm not alone (team of content strategists / writers)

BUT, after enough  posts you begin to see patterns. 

Here's the checklist. Save this for your next post.

1. Do I care?

Does the hook make me care enough to click 'See More'. I'll throw the post into AuthoredUp and use their free 'Text Formatter' to make the post truncates where we want it to. It's free, anyone can do it ^ 

2. Who are you? 

(This is especially true for new accounts). You have to fight for every impression. You have to scream why you're relevant through quick competency statements that prove you're good at what you do and your opinion is worth listening to. E.g's 'We're at $Xm ARR' / 'We send XX,XXX cold emails'. The hook of this post is a clear example. 

3. Is it digestible? 

Can I quickly skim through the main points. Where is my eye drawn back to after the hook. Typically best done through listicles, clear formatting, white space. This post is an ovbious example and is one of my favourite formats. A clear point with a small-ish paragraph. The goal is here is to increase dwell time on the post (one of the more important LinkedIn algo factors)

4. Can I comment? 

Is there a reason for me to comment? Is there a debate to be had, a conversation to engage with? You can make this happen by talking about interesting topics. You can also make this happen by just asking the reader. You see this all the time 'Agree?' - but you can do better... "Anyone else seen this?", "What am I missing?", or end on a 'feel good' platitude that people can identify with. 

Save this checklist for the next time you post.

It's quick and easy.

One way we closed 6 deals in 3 months with 90 minutes of work was to use cold email to expand traditionally inbound channels. Here’s our playbook. 

Admittedly, I’m not the biggest fan of talking to dead cold prospects for our offerings.

Too many people are sending the same “I’m so desperate we will work for free until we get results” kind of message that changes the expectations for prospects when they talk to us and they expect everything to be free. 

I thought, “If we could just get more people into watching my YouTube (where our best customers come from) I could warm them up there and then they’ll reach out when ready.”

So the question is, how do we get a dead cold prospect to see my YouTube. 

It starts with what does everyone who would be serious customers want? 

They could want a number of things, but our best customers want some kind of signal to know they should be reaching out. 

By far the broadest and most useful signal for any b2b company is knowing when a new department leader joins a new company or gets a promotion.
 
So we made a list with Clay of every person new in their role in the past 30 days and included their job title, industry, company headcount, etc. so we could send an email that looked like. 

"Hey, our customers love to target people new in their role. Here’s a list of all of the new people in the United States with a director and above position. I also included the company industry, headcount, description, and state so you could filter for what you want. Just request access to the list so that I know you got it."

Then anyone that would request access to the list we would follow up saying “Hey we actually give this list away every other Monday. Want to be added to the newsletter so you always get this list?”

4/5 people say yes to this in which we add them to the newsletter and send the list as well as sending one of my YouTube videos to get them into our content. 

We used beehiiv to keep the newsletter pumping and of course Clay to get the new hire data on repeat. 

If you have the ability to wait for really great leads to warm themselves up in your other channels, using outbound to get them there can be a great way to leverage cold email.

I had a gun to my head. It was pressed into my temple. And then he spoke: "How do I get more leads from LinkedIn"

Not wanting to anger the assailant, I got straight into 5 tips.

And not wanting to waste a good content opportunity. 

I'll share it here too. 

1. Use 'I' more

Linked has changed. Generic content is falling flat. Almost always, across all the accounts we're working on - we see the same common theme. Using the word 'I' dramatically increases content performance. Instead of '6 ways to grow' - lean into 'here's 6 ways I grew' or, somewhat worse but can work, 'I've seen 6 ways to grow' 

2. Speak in symptoms

I'm beginning to avoid the phrase 'pain points' - and instead leaning into symptoms. Think about your ideal customer, and think like a Doctor. If they were a patient, what symptoms, that they can feel and are aware of, do they display. Now speak to that. For example, don't speak to their 'PAIN' of being unable to scale, but their 'SYMPTOM' of seeing high CACs. 

3. More proof 

You need to convince your market that you're genuinely good at what you do. That means you need to post proof. If you do not post proof, you cannot expect leads. As plain and simple as that. Proof can take many forms. It can be results, dashboards, screenshots. It can also be competency statements / micro case study lines. For example "Just helped a client add $90k in the last month from LinkedIn. This is what we did". That's enough to begin to show your audience you're an authority. 

He interrupted me. "But what about Ads?"

Good point. 

4. Upload TAM

Use a tool like Clay. Create a stupidly clean list of every company you want to target. Don't be lazy now. Open that CSV of 1000, 2000, 20,000 companies. Whatever that number is. And read through every single one. Make sure it's clean. Then upload that list to LinkedIn Ads. This is the cleanest way to make sure you can force impressions into your ICP

5. Graduate organic performers

Take your top 10% of organic posts. Boost them as ads. Run them into the job titles at your target account list. Use the formula AudienceSize*50%*5-7x*CPM to work out your monthly budget. You'll want to run them as thought leader ads, and ideally be boosting posts that have already generated you leads via organic distribution.

Unpopular opinion: the best outbound campaigns that we have seen usually work right away. If they don’t, something needs to change drastically. Here’s what we look at first in all cases:

1. Is our list as correct as we thought it was?

 We do a lot of checks internally: inclusion/exclusion keywords, AI checks, job title matching. Did something slip through the cracks?

2. Is our list correct but our decision to target them with this messaging wrong?

 We talk to our customer and use ChatGPT for deeper analysis. We even look at open job postings to understand what roles are being asked to do.

3. How can we change the messaging of what’s in it for the prospect?

 The overarching value prop isn’t always the best outbound message. Break down individual features and test what resonates.

For example, Clay’s main value prop is connecting to 150+ integrations. That doesn’t resonate in outbound. The best campaign we ran focused on name-dropping customer case studies and showing how to find more companies like them automatically.

4. Are there other buying signals we can add?

 Signals reduce list size and add complexity but they sharpen targeting. Think: what would we research for 10 minutes if we were reaching out manually, and how does it change the message?

5. Have we tried lookalike campaigns?

 They add two benefits:

Messaging comes directly from a case study, so it’s less hypothesis and more storytelling.

Prospects always react better when they know something has already worked for a peer.

From there, it comes down to the biggest insight from Facebook ads: the companies making the most money were doing the most split testing.

Different channel, same principle, keep split testing between lists, messaging, and lead magnets until you find what works.

There are 2 reasons to hire an outbound agency. If you don’t know which one you are, that’s where problems occur.

Reason 1: To learn about the channel faster and experiment with new ideas. You want to get started quickly, tap into expertise, and have someone take care of everything while you learn.

Reason 2: You already have something working and want to scale. An agency can give you better economies of scale, automation, error fixes, time savings, and insights from the broader market.

Every company at one point needs to learn about the channel whether they use an agency or not — but not every company is ready to scale it.

The biggest problem in agency relationships? Customers not understanding what they’re paying for if they’ve never done outbound or marketing before. (Founder-led sales transitions are often the scariest).

If you haven’t run campaigns before and think “This company is just going to fix our pipeline issues,” maybe they will, maybe they won’t. You might not know your ICP as well as you think, or you might not have communicated your messaging clearly enough.

If you’re looking to work with any agency and you don’t have the learning mindset first, the relationship could be doomed from the beginning.

After running millions of outbound emails, these are the patterns I see that kill meeting rates.

1. Using a calendar link as your CTA.

 Calendar links feel convenient, but security filters + human behavior both work against them. People are more likely to reply “Sure, let’s chat” than click a random link. Earn the reply first, then offer booking options.

2. Not following up fast enough.

 Speed is leverage. The longer you wait, the colder the lead gets. Reply the same day if you can — it signals you’re paying attention.

3. Not following up enough.

 There’s a balance: don’t spam, but if someone raised their hand once, don’t stop until they book or say no. I positively responded to Rippling and it took that poor soul 8 follow ups for me to book. I'm still sorry but it wasn't my biggest priority. 

4. Not adding value in follow-ups.

 Repeating “just checking in” is lazy. Each touch should reinforce why the call matters: ROI, risk avoidance, case study, new idea. After a few tries, you can even add a kicker (we’ve seen success offering a gift card to qualified prospects at this stage).

5. Not giving booking options.

 Don’t force a link or a back-and-forth. Do both.
 “Would Tuesday at 9am ET or Thursday at 2pm ET work? Or if it’s easier, here’s my calendar.”

 You’re reducing friction while respecting preferences. Some people like booking with a calendly, others are offended by it. I don't get it but appease both people. 

6. Not following up across channels.

 A reply rate isn’t the same as a meeting rate. Sometimes an extra LinkedIn DM or quick phone call takes a warm response over the finish line. People book with people, not just with inboxes.

How do you prioritize which lost deals to come back to?

CRM lost reasons= generic
CRM notes= rely on AE input
Signals= messy 
Reminders= manual 

All of these are a recipe for why so much pipeline remains untouched- there is no real rhyme or reason to reach back out outside of discretion

You *should* have an evergreen process to revive lost deals that isn't a nurture cadence (generic) or manual task reminder (inconsistent)

We've created "the rebound funnel" a way to consistently identify in-market buyers and reach out to them at the right time with the right thing to say, measured to improve 

How we do this: 
1. Don't rely on signals, rely on the actual buyer: website visits and clicks don't mean much, actual buyer feedback tells you really why they didn't buy (often does not align with CRM notes) 

2. Identify winnable deals: in the feedback survey, buyers are asked if they want to be re-engaged, they can answer yes, wait 3 months, no, or other (open text)

3. Winnable deals get routed to AEs with survey + deal context + what to say based on their answers 

4. Now, what happens when they don't answer a survey? Then we analyze call transcripts and identify deals who have urgency to buy that quarter, same process: route to reps w/ context + what to say 

5. Measure as a funnel: # lost, # who want to re-engage, # back in pipe, # won back 

Now, you have 3 revenue sources: inbound, outbound, and rebound- check out the rebound funnel here https://lnkd.in/efJUDNHF

This is how can are trying to make landing in the inbox inevitable for our customers at Growth Engine X.

Some first principles that guide me in this process decision making. 

1) no matter how good your campaign is, people are going to mark you as spam and keeping back up infrastructure is necessary. 

2) Some providers like proofpoint and outlook can't be beat with just 2 weeks of warmup. Longer warmup times for these inboxes are necessary. 

3) We need to be catching bad domains as they happen so that we can cycle in our back up infrastructure, cancel those bad domains, and reorder new ones to keep a healthy stack of domains. 

What we do about each below.

Every customer that joins us gets an infrastructure that can send 5,000 emails per day off the bat. Most of our customers start by sending 500-1500 emails per day. Setting up more than necessary from the beginning allows us to 

- Scale volume immediately if a successful campaign is found
- Always have back up infrastructure in case the first batch of inboxes goes wrong. 
- Allow for inboxes to reach a 4 week warming to have a higher chance of breaking into Outlook/Proofpoint inboxes. Some inboxes even get 2 months of warming before we ever use them. 

This investment early on allows us to be prepared for 1 and 2. 

If a customer does ramp up to 5,000 a day, we buy another batch of inboxes capable of sending 2,500 emails per day and start that warmup. 

Hypertide.io is our main partner here.

We leverage the Smartlead API and Supabase to catch bad domains. 

Every Friday, we pull a report of the last 3 weeks of sending per domain. The bottom 10% of domains based on reply rate are cancelled and reordered with fresh domains from Hypertide. 

If we think a customer is having more deliverability issues than just the bottom 10% of domains, we will go even further. 

Basically, investing early, keeping inboxes in reserve, and weekly reply rate monitoring are some recent things we have implemented to try to stay ahead of deliverability issues. 

And because Hypertide makes it so easy to order inboxes, anyone of any size can follow this with an automated system or just a weekly manual report.

3 things we have changed in our Email Deliverability workflow at Growth Engine X and 2 things we are keeping the same that I think everyone should think about doing. 

1) Cleaning up bad domains with Smartlead API and reordering on Hypertide.io

Smartlead upgraded their API. Now we can get the exact reply rate statistics on a domain level for any time period that we want. 

We're sending this data to Supabase and then writing SQL queries to figure out which domains we should be canceling and which domains we should be keeping. 

2) Sending to Google first and then harder to reach inboxes when campaigns are falling flat. Leadmagic just made a tool called inboxriskscore(.)com you can use to identify easy vs. hard domains to send emails to. 

We've also been seeing that Outlook/Proof Point is harder to break into. Nick Abraham released a report that 10% of his replies at his agency are coming from Outlook. 

The only thing that we've seen consistently combat these low inbox placements on these harder-to-reach inboxes is letting the domains age for a longer time.

 But customers can't usually wait for 4-8 weeks to start an email campaign.

Start with a regular 2-week warmup, sending to Google inboxes, and then start bringing in the Outlook proof point inboxes if necessary. 

3) Auto batching inboxes into campaigns to keep within domain rate limit threshold. Smartlead implemented a domain rate limit threshold to protect Azure sending accounts but it messed up our sending volume. 

We easily use Cursor now to plug into our Supabase to find relevant accounts and divide them appropriately across campaigns so that ever hypertide domain is dedicated to one campaign and one campaign only. 

Things that are staying the same. 

1) Continue to keep open tracking off. Cancelling open tracking test and moving to just reply tracking. 

I'm still not completely against open tracking, but for the past four to six weeks that we've been trying the experiment, we saw positive responses go down on the days that we were tracking opens, and reply rate was just as good of a metric to be watching. 

So we'll cancel using this test as a systemic thing that we automatically do every week and only turn it on as needed. 

2) Buying capacity with Hypertide to send 5,000 emails per day even if a client needs 1,000 per day just to make sure we always have reserve and they age much longer. 

Still keeping 50% of sending capacity in warming reserve at full volume.

Always keep more than you need in reserve so you can try as best as possible to not get caught with no warmed up healthy inboxes.

As Clay's largest user, we've learned a ton about scaling with the platform.
Here are the 5 lessons I talked about on stage at Sculpt in San Francisco recently. (Link to video at the end). 

Clay Rules & Best Practices

1. Always Always Always Use Conditional Formulas on Paid Integrations.

Seems super simple and obvious but getting your team in this habit helps to prevent unnecessary API calls and only trigger paid integrations when data truly needs enrichment.


2. Save Paid Data Externally

Store enriched data in CRM or Supabase, not inside Clay only.
I pay $30 a month for Supabase and just one of our databases amongst over 20 has 11.4M records.

3. Leverage Scheduled Sources

Automate evergreen campaigns that continuously refresh and send new leads into workflows without manual input. This features is still under used by people that have cracked an outbound campaign for themselves and need to keep it on all the time without forgetting. 

4. The formula generator can really do a lot. If you want the same thing to happen every time it sees an input, try this before using AI. 

Use formulas for:

Cleaning and combining data
If/Then logic
Lead scoring
State abbreviation

Reminder: Clay formulas run on JavaScript, so almost any data transformation is possible.

5. The GEX AI Prompting Framework

Prompting Rules

The 10-Minute Manual Research Rule:
Don't steal other people's playbooks. Think about when you are manually researching a company. What are you looking for if you had 10 minutes to research them? And how does that change your message? 

One Thing at a Time:
Give AI a single, focused task, avoid multitasking prompts.

Safeguards:
Build filters for low-context outputs (e.g., return “purple” when uncertain).

Use Examples:
 Always include examples in prompts for better accuracy.

Meta Prompting:
 Ask ChatGPT “What questions do you have to improve this prompt?” before finalizing.

Reasoning First:
 For high-stakes tasks (like industry classification), ask AI to output reasoning before its final answer.

Handle Edge Cases:
 Be ready to prompt around specific constraints (e.g., tone, banned words, output format, length).

Mindset Takeaway
“AI is the smartest thing in the world built to solve Calculus problems.
 I promise it can write your emails, you just need to give it some TLC.”

Overall: 
 → Think like a system designer, not a button clicker.
 → Use Clay, Supabase, and AI together to build repeatable, data-rich workflows that scale outbound.

Last week, I explained to the Sell Better audience that I think AI generated emails fit into 4 tiers. Use these buckets to brainstorm how it could apply to your business. 

We all want the perfect AI generated email but not every offer is capable of getting the best email. 

Top Tier - the famous Jordan Crawford Permissionless Value Prop email. An email so good, they would pay to receive it. Using your own internal data, data you scrape publicly, and AI to make a message that shows you did your research, uncovered a problem, and gave them a taste of the solution, while explaining how you can help more in the future. 

Second Tier - an email based on what you would research about a company for 10 minutes manually and using AI to change your messaging based on that. 

Not as in depth as Jordan's best following similar principles. Think about what you were to research manually about someone, keep track of what sources you check, and how it helps you make decisions on what to say. 

Use the literal messages you sent manually as the training data for your AI. 

Third Tier - Using AI to help someone imagine what it would be like if you were to work together. Simple, but still wildly effective. Basically a liner adding specificity about what you do and how it could specifically help them. 

Fourth Tier - Attention Hacking. Bottom of the barrel you probably stole it from someone on LinkedIn but everyone has to put food on the table so I get it. Especially in industries that don't receive very many sophisticated emails, these can still work. 

We've seen emailing local businesses and name dropping the top steakhouse in the area still increases replies over not doing it. 

So when making AI outbound workflows in Clay or other places. 

First think - is there anything I can send them that's inherently valuable and custom to their business without having to speak to them that I can automate. 

Second - what would I say if I were reaching out manually anyway?

Third - use AI to make the email more specific to their situation and business from information you can easily find on their website. 

Fourth - do what you gotta do haha

Any other ideas for tiers?

This is what I wish I knew about bounce rates when I first started. When I first started, I thought all bounces happened because the email address didn't exist. 

But there are so many other reasons for bounce issues and all can help you understand if email deliverability is a problem for your campaigns. 

1) Erol Toker and I talk about this all the time that people marking your email as spam is by far the worst thing for your sender reputation. Repeated bounces is second worst BUT Erol and I in different experiments purposely bounced a ton of emails and landed in inbox the next day. 

So still goes to show that getting marked as spam is by far the worst. 

2) Bounces happen from hard bounces and soft bounces. Hard bounces are those bounces where the email is incorrect. Soft bounces can happen for a number of reasons. But if you see status code 550, that means your inboxes are being flagged as spam and the recipients aren't letting it come through (even to land in spam). 

3) another reason you could be getting bounces (that can get up to literally 100%) is if you're sending from outlook and they throttle your sending because they think as an email sender that you're sending spam. 

So in your email sending platform like Instantly or Smartlead, the bounces will sky rocket which is why you want to keep the sender bounce protection and domain threshold rate limit turned on to avoid this. 

Bounces aren't just incorrect emails, they help you know which domains are fried and which are still healthy.

Our client braces for their worst month every September. But this year they hit 10.01 ROAS over Labor Day weekend and turned their slowest month into a record breaker.

Here's how we did it:


THE SITUATION:

Our client makes decorative covers and snow shields for outdoor HVAC units. Their products protect the units while making backyards and patios look polished. Spring and summer were strong. September was their Achilles' heel.

Every year, sales consistently dipped in September. Even with Labor Day promotions running, the month felt like a dead zone. For a brand built on seasonal outdoor supplies, fall became the month they braced for instead of leaned into.


WHAT WE CHANGED:

We reframed September from a slow month to a launchpad for Q4. The strategy had three components: repositioning the Labor Day creative, launching winter products earlier than expected, and shifting the entire brand tone from utility to luxury.

We rolled out Labor Day creative that highlighted both discounts and design beauty. The focus shifted from functionality to aesthetics. HVAC covers weren't positioned as protective utility products anymore. They were positioned as luxury design upgrades for outdoor spaces.

We also started pushing snow shields in early September to colder states before winter hit. Historically, winter products didn't move until November. We tested early demand in cold-weather markets and it worked. The tone shifted across all creative to make HVAC covers aspirational instead of functional.


THE RESULTS:

September went from their worst month to a record month. Labor Day weekend hit 10.01 blended ROAS. Net sales jumped 28% year-over-year for the holiday. September overall delivered 5.59 ROAS.

The early winter product push worked. Airdeko recorded their first-ever early September snow shield sales at 2.69 ROAS. Products that historically sat dormant until November started moving two months early in cold-weather states.

Airdeko stopped bracing for the September slump. Now they treat it as momentum heading into Q4.


THE TAKEAWAY:

Our client’s September problem wasn't seasonality. It was positioning and timing. We repositioned HVAC covers from utility to luxury and pushed winter products earlier than the market expected demand.

Labor Day promotions had always been there. The creative messaging hadn't been. If your brand has a slow month that repeats every year, the issue might not be the calendar. It might be how you're framing your product during that window.

Here’s my 2-hour process for building winning ad concepts (stop waiting for inspiration):

1. Build your swipe file before you need it (ongoing).

If you're in the creative space, you should be adding to your creative swipe file every single day.

We save concepts, formats, hooks, and frameworks as we see them.

By the time we need creative inspiration, we have thousands of references organized by industry, format, and performance metrics.


2. Study what's been running longest (20-30 minutes).

Look at competitor ads and adjacent ads. See what concepts, formats, and styles they're using repeatedly.

If an ad has been running for months with spend behind it, it's working.

We don't copy the ad, but we identify the underlying patterns.

We might ask ourselves, is the ad testimonial-driven? Problem-agitation? Before-and-after?

The format that runs longest reveals what resonates with your market.


3. Mine customer data from 5 specific sources (30-40 minutes).

 - Customer surveys (what problem led you here?)
 - Review mining on Google, Yelp, Reddit, Trust Pilot
 - Sales call transcripts
 - Customer support tickets
 - Competitor reviews (what are their customers complaining about?)

We extract pains, desires, triggers, failed attempts, transformations, and golden nugget phrases.


4. Map pain points to specific audiences (20-30 minutes).

Take notes of the pain points, triggers, and audiences competitors are targeting. Then map it all out.

Which pain points hit hardest for which segment?

For a healthcare brand, we mapped PTSD treatment concerns to different demographics.

The ads that spoke to specific pain-audience combinations dropped CAC from $5,000 to $3,000.


5. Feed everything to AI for rapid ideation (20-30 minutes).

Add all your research into AI.

Literally everything including your swipe files, customer insights, competitor patterns, pain-audience maps.

Then use AI to generate different concepts, formats, styles, and scripts specific to your business.

To be clear, we're not using AI to write final copy but we are using it to rapidly explore creative territories we might have missed. It's pattern recognition at scale.


6. Turn research into structured creative briefs (20-30 minutes).

From the Full-Stack Ads doc: Create briefs that specify angle + format for each concept. 

Map out 4-6 variations per concept before any designer touches it.

This is specific creative direction like "hook with integration objection, testimonial format, customer transformation focus, enterprise social proof throughout.

Now we can produce banger ad briefs in a couple hours tops.

Another search that uses the keyword matching in case that's broad enough.

The best performing ad types right now:

1. Start with static ads to validate messaging.
Before we touch video production, we launch static creative first. Static ads let us test messaging and concepts fast without burning budget on video that might not convert. We use comparative positioning ads, high-clarity explanatory visuals, charts, social proof screenshots, and customer testimonials talking about results. Once we find the messaging that performs, we move to video.

2. Short-form video with a person talking to camera.
Live-action, face-to-camera content is dominating performance right now. This isn't scripted agency production. It's authentic, visually distinct content that drives emotional connection. The format works because it feels real, not manufactured.

3. UGC-style testimonials.
Customer testimonials shot in UGC style consistently outperform polished case study videos. We're talking about real customers, real environments, real reactions. Not studio lighting and scripted talking points. Authenticity wins over production value.

4. Face-to-camera mixed with product demos.
Combine a person explaining the product on camera with actual product demo footage. This hybrid format gives you the trust of face-to-camera content with the clarity of seeing the product in action. It works especially well for software and tech products where showing the interface matters.

5. UGC mashups.
Layer different formats together. Start with a UGC hook from a customer, transition to a founder explanation in the middle, then close with another UGC testimonial. This mashup format builds credibility through multiple voices while keeping the founder's authority in the mix.

6. Problem-agitate-solve videos
Use quick-cut storytelling to walk through the problem your customer faces, agitate that pain point, then show your solution. This structure works after you've validated the messaging with static ads. The format creates emotional momentum that drives conversions.

7. High-clarity static ads
Don't abandon static creative once you move to video. High-clarity static ads with explanatory visuals, comparison charts, social proof screenshots, and review graphics still convert. They're cheaper to produce, faster to test, and perform well across platforms.

--

The sequence matters:

1. validate messaging with static ads first
2. scale the winning concepts into video formats that feel authentic and visually distinct.

Here’s our in-house funnel checklist we use across 55+ ad accounts spending $5.6M/mo to prevent budget waste:

1. Start with numbers and expectations.
Pull forecast versus actuals. What's your cost per SQL? What's your SQL to customer conversion rate? What's your CAC across different channels? Is all your pipeline coming from one channel or multiple? Compare your metrics against industry benchmarks. If your numbers are off, you need to know which stage is broken before you pour more budget in.

2. Audit conversion tracking first.
If your tracking is broken, every decision you make is based on bad data. Check if your finance data matches your CRM data. Check if your CRM data matches your ad platform data. All three need to align. We've seen brands optimize campaigns for months based on tracking that was reporting 40% fewer conversions than actually happened.

3. Review account structure.
Are your campaigns and ad groups structured to maximize performance? Are you following best practices for spend level and platform? Most accounts we inherit have campaign structures built for $10k/month when they're now spending $100k/month. Structure that worked at lower spend breaks at scale.

4. Evaluate targeting strategy.
Are you using the right keywords? Are you targeting the right audiences? What's your targeting strategy across awareness, consideration, and conversion stages? We see brands targeting the same audience with the same message across all stages. That's spray and pray.

5. Assess creative performance.
Is there creative variety or are you running the same three ads for six months? Does your creative hit on benefit, positioning, emotional response, and clarity? We tested hundreds of creatives for B2B clients. The accounts with 10+ active creatives outperform accounts with 3 creatives every single time.

6. Analyze landing pages and funnel alignment.
Are your landing pages optimized for conversion? Is there message continuity from ad to landing page to email sequence? Most brands send traffic to generic homepage URLs and wonder why conversion rates are low. Your landing page needs to continue the conversation your ad started.

7. Review post-click experience.
What happens after someone converts? Is your email marketing moving them through the funnel? Does each touchpoint provide sales momentum? B2B buyers hit 7-12 touchpoints before converting. If any of those touchpoints create friction, you'll lose customers.

--

What we've found auditing 55+ accounts:

Conversion tracking issues cost brands 20-300% into true performance. Poor campaign structure wastes 10-30% of budget on the wrong audiences. Landing pages that don't match ad messaging kill 50-200% of potential conversions.

Before you scale spend:

 - Fix tracking
 - Fix structure
 - Fix targeting
 - Fix creative variety
 - Fix message match
 - Fix post-click experience

If these don’t get dealt with? 

Good luck scaling a funnel that’s riddled with holes.
