The difference between $100k/month and $1M/month ad accounts isn't the budget. It's how they test creatives. I manage $5.8M/month in ad spend. Here are the 6 mistakes smaller accounts make that keep them stuck:

(1) Testing tweaks instead of concepts.

$100k accounts test headline swaps and button colors. Meta's Andromeda algorithm sees these as the same ad and deprioritizes them. $1M accounts test completely different concepts, formats, creators, and angles. Each test is visually and conceptually distinct.


(2) Not isolating what you're testing.

$100k accounts change five things at once. $1M accounts isolate variables systematically. Test the hook separately from the offer. Test the creator separately from the script. When something wins, you know exactly why. We helped a B2B finance brand realize their hook was perfect but their offer was killing conversions. Fixed just the offer and we went from 1 to 7 leads per week.


(3) Making micro-edits to winners instead of major iterations.

$100k accounts find a winner and make tiny adjustments. $1M accounts treat iterations like completely new launches. Keep the winning element (benefit, positioning, or emotional trigger) but express it in a visually unique way. Take that winning testimonial and reshape it as an animated explainer, founder story, or case study breakdown.


(4) Surface-level creative research.

$100k accounts rely on intuition or quick competitor scans. $1M accounts mine customer reviews on Google, Reddit, Trust Pilot, and forums. They analyze competitor and adjacent market ads. We discovered through Reddit mining that one partner's prospects were failing with three specific solutions before finding them. Built our entire creative strategy around that insight. CAC dropped from $5,000 to $3,000.


(5) Over-indexing on one creative type.

$100k accounts find UGC works and go all-in on UGC. $1M accounts build diverse portfolios hitting different angles, emotions, and stages of awareness. We run testimonials, demonstrations, educational content, transformation stories, and data-driven creatives simultaneously.


(6) Tracking vanity metrics instead of money metrics.

$100k accounts obsess over CTR and CPM. $1M accounts track creative hit rate (how often do new creatives beat existing winners?) and cost per hit (how much does it cost to find a winner?). If you're launching 50 creatives but only 2% become winners, you're wasting resources.

--

It comes down to this:

$100k/mo accounts think more volume equals better results.

$1M/mo accounts know systematic testing beats random volume.

Every test needs to be distinct enough to produce valuable data.

This is how you profitably scale ad campaigns.

The brands winning in 2025 aren't the ones with the biggest ad budgets. They're the ones orchestrating paid, earned, and owned channels while their competitors pour everything into Google Ads.

Here’s how SaaS, tech, and healthcare brands spending $50k+/month on ads dominate the rest of 2025:


1) Set funnel targets by time decay.

Cost per MQL on day 7 after spend. Cost per SQL on day 30. Cost per customer on day 60. Most B2B brands track final CAC after 90 days and wonder why they can't optimize faster. We helped a SaaS client discover their day-7 MQL costs predicted 85% of their final CAC. Now they iterate weekly, not quarterly.


2) Win across paid, earned, and owned channels simultaneously.

Paid means your ad campaigns. Earned means PR, organic SEO, and word-of-mouth. Owned means your website, email, and content hub. The brands scaling past $10M aren't winning on Google Ads alone. They're orchestrating all three.


3) Make the messaging across the entire funnel congruent.

You need different messages for each stage of the buyer journey. During awareness, prospects don't even know you exist. During consideration, they're comparing multiple solutions. During conversion, they're ready to buy. Most B2B brands use conversion messaging everywhere then wonder why their CAC goes up.


4) Use creative variety that breaks the "corporate" mold.

This means founder-led thought leadership, real client testimonials (not polished case studies), partner co-marketing content, industry-specific messaging by role, and UGC from actual users. We tested hundreds of creatives for our B2B partners. Less polished content consistently outperforms agency-produced assets.


5) Balance fuel versus engine.

Fuel equals your content and creative assets. Engine equals your distribution systems and ad budget. Too much content without distribution channels means your best assets collect dust. Too much budget without enough creative means ad fatigue in 2 weeks.


6) Build measurement discipline into your CRM.

Track every touchpoint. First touch, last touch, and everything between. B2B buyers interact with 7-12 touchpoints before converting. If you're only tracking last-click in Google Ads, you'll lack visibility on your customer journey.


7) Execute a robust paid strategy for rapid testing.

Paid ads aren't just for scale. They're your testing laboratory. Organic takes months to validate. Paid gives you answers in days. Test messaging, test audiences, test offers. Then roll winners into all channels.

Meta learned the difference between someone who books a call and someone who actually buys.

literally following the breadcrumbs from first touch to closed-won.

Back at Salesforce, I managed a $25M ad budget. The marketing ops team installed a non-functional attribution system that claimed my ads weren’t performing. It nearly cost me my job.

--

It wrongly told us that our ads had a negative ROAS which made leadership panic.

The CMO almost cut my budget and told me to kick rocks… here’s the full story:

(1) Everything “looked” ok to us (the marketing team).

We were driving leads successfully according to all our platform metrics.

This was the weirdest part… everything looked fine to the marketing team.

But apparently our ads were performing horribly according to the model.

We were genuinely considering cutting all ads that day.


(2) We get pulled into emergency meetings

The director of online marketing got pulled into meeting after meeting with the VP and CMO.

The conversation kept circling back to cutting the ad budget since the model showed ROAS below 1.

Years of proven performance were about to get thrown out because of one faulty model.


(3) We pushed back hard

My team and I kept pushing back that all our metrics looked fine in the actual ad platforms.

This was the first time we'd ever heard that ads weren't working, and it contradicted everything we'd been seeing for months.

We insisted the model had to be wrong.


(4) The model WAS wrong

We launch 500+ creatives per month across 55+ clients. It’s easy when you’ve got a brain-dead simple process that’s replicable EVEN when things get chaotic… here’s that process:

(1) Testing doesn't mean flooding meta with incoherent angles and creatives.

Rapid testing sounds sexy, but in practice it usually means constant creative churn, inconsistent learning environments, and no clarity on why something worked.

You end up confusing Meta's delivery system and your team. The result? No creative compounds long enough to scale.


(2) The anti-chaos framework (our 3-tier testing system):

Tier 1: Concept test - find the storyline or emotional hook that resonates. This is what drives performance on paid social. Examples: Founder vs. UGC angle, benefit-led vs. transformation-led.
Tier 2: Iteration test - optimize a winning concept through structure and tone. Change the hook, order, or framing, but keep the message the same.
Tier 3: validation & scaling - verify these are hit ads at scale before cloning across other channels. We run 3-5 versions to confirm algorithmic stability.

Each level builds on the last.

There’s no random rapid testing that drops new variables mid-cycle.


(3) The pre-launch metrics that actually matter.

We score creative across The Big 4 before we launch:

Clear benefit - "what's in it for me?"
Strong positioning - "why you, not them?"
Emotional response - "do I feel something?"
Clarity - "I want that" vs. "what is that?"

If it doesn't hit all four, we don't scale it. We fix it.


(4) Systems before sprints.

Every creative is tagged and categorized inside a shared system (visual hook, angle, offer type, creator style).

That allows us to pull winning patterns across brands, identify underperforming emotional tones, and eliminate redundant testing.

--

Rapid testing fails because it assumes that volume equals insight.

But platforms like Meta reward consistency and data density.

When you reset learning every 3 days, you're not actually helping the ad platform.

There’s no space for it to provide iterations and valuable data because variables keep changing.

What works instead:

 - Iteration loops every 7-10 days
 - Minimum $1K-$1.5K per concept before judgment (3x your target CPA per creative)
 - Cut based on trendlines as opposed to 48-hour snapshots
 - Focus on creative diversity

I’ve audited 1,000 ad accounts in the last 10 years. I’ve literally seen it all… slow websites that ruin conversions, tech not set up properly, typos in ad headlines. But there’s one thing that drags performance down the most:

Lack of creativity in the ads.

Recent example of this happening:

In August, I audited an account spending over $500,000 per month on Meta ads.

They were getting decent results, but the client was convinced he was being shadow banned or taken over by spam because performance started tanking.

Here's what I actually found:

--

They had a strong offer and a strong funnel from the beginning. The offer was carrying the entire account.

But there was zero creative iteration. They'd launch ads and just let them run. The media buyer was stretched thin across other parts of the business and couldn't actually optimize. The creative team would get a request like "I need a new ad this month" with no direction.

No learning from prior results. No specific briefs. No data-driven requests like "launch three statics, two UGCs, two talking heads with these hooks because this is what the data shows."

--

The account was being carried by two top-performing creatives. When I looked at the trends on those ads, the CTR was dropping and cost per click was skyrocketing. Classic creative fatigue.

Worse, because all the ads were running in the same ad set, the top performer was cannibalizing the majority of traffic. Older ads that performed well in the past stopped getting any spend at all.

--

I told the client to break out some of the better older ads into new ad sets to see if they could capture more traffic.

He did it.

Two days later, he saw a huge increase in qualified booked calls (his main KPI).

--

Obviously, the real issue wasn’t “shadow bans” or “spam”.

It was a disconnect between functions. The media buyer and creative team weren't coordinating. There was no process connecting data to creative decisions. The entire funnel (conversion tracking, bid strategy, campaign structure, targeting, ads, landing page) needs to be in alignment.

When departmental teams don’t work together or share results, you’ll waste budget no matter how much you’re spending.

I took a consultant through the PPP framework in 90 minutes. They closed just over $100k in the following 12 weeks. 

PPP = Person, Pain, Problem
Why = To get the exact client you want INBOUND. 

Here's the framework (save it down) 

P1: Person
- Define the person you're selling to firmographically
- What are the attributes you would put into a lead database
- Job Title
- Company Size
- Location 
- Revenue 

P2: Pain 
- What are the things that the Person says out loud as complains
- If you were unwell, this would be the symptoms you were suffering from
- E.g. "Runny nose" --> "My clients churn fast" 
- E.g. "Headache" --> "CPMs are really high this quarter" 
- The more 'present' and 'symptomatic' these are, the more you should reference them early in your posts 
- This is what your Person understands. 

P3: Problem
- What are the root causes of the Person's Pain
- This is what the Doctor diagnoses because of all your Symptoms
- E.g. "Runny nose + Headache + Winter" = Flu? 
- E.g. "High Client Churn + Team Churn + Can't Delegate" = Culture Issue? 
- You'll find your clients have many Problems for their Pains.
- You need to choose the Problem you can solve, how fast you can alleviate their Pain, depending on your Solutions 

This framework is general enough it works for any niche

Example = 3000/15000 * 100% = 20% Penetration Rate

LOW PENETRATION RATE

FLAT PENETRATION RATE

If Penetration Rate = not increasing AND you're bidding & spending more
--> Likely you've hit your full LinkedIn active audience

HIGH PENETRATION RATE

If Penetration Rate = high AND no conversions 
--> Likely your audience is seeing your ads, but somethings wrong. The messaging isn't landing / offer isn't converting / marketing cycle is longer than you think 

If you know:

- Your offer is converting / getting traction
- You've got a few grand in ad budget

I've been completely wrong about AI prompting, and it's cost me thousands of dollars and it might be costing you money too. 

For months, I've been telling my team (and all of you) to structure prompts like this:

1. Tell the AI what you want it to do
2. Give it the data to analyze and reference
3. Provide examples of good outputs

I didn't realize that this approach wastes tokens. Especially when you're running outbound campaigns at scale.

I know this may seem obvious to technical people out there but I didn't even consider making a change. 

I had a call with my enterprise rep from OpenAI last week and they asked me why I wasn't using cached inputs based on my use case. 

I didn't even consider it because we use the Clay OpenAI integration.

Cached inputs save 50% on input tokens for GPT-4o mini, and 90% on GPT-4 when the input stays the same.

For those of us using AI for outbound messaging, this is exactly what we're doing. Running the same prompt structure over and over with different prospect data.

But the prompt needs to stay the same for as long as possible for the inputs to cache.

My old approach was mixing up the prompt by putting variable data (company descriptions, prospect info) in the middle.

The correct way:

Put everything that changes at the very bottom of your prompt.

Keep the instructions, examples, and framework identical at the top.

Only vary the prospect-specific data at the end.

I met with Jeff Barg on the Clay team directly about this and you shouldn't have to change all your integrations. The prompt will cache automatically with how they have the integration set up. 

This might seem obvious to technical people, but this is the ignorance debt you pay when you're not technical.

I'm sorry I made the wrong suggestion for so long.

Any serious company should be using it: 

One of Google’s most gated features is its incrementality testing

Historically, it’s only been available if you’re spending $100,000

Now the threshold’s been lowered 20x to $5,000 - making it FAR easier for advertisers to know where the incremental gain is in their advertising.

We run regular incrementality tests across our clients. You can save this framework for when you’re ready to test. 

STAGE 1: Brand search incrementality.
 - Pause brand search for one week or lower it by 50% (or double it)
 - Compare organic traffic and paid traffic during the week brand was running versus not running
 - Calculate the lift from having brand run and figure out how many incremental clicks you got
 - Run this multiple weeks in a row: one week on, one week off, repeat
 - Example: 100 incremental clicks at a 5% brand conversion rate gives us 5 incremental conversions. If we're paying $5,000 for those 5 conversions, that's $1,000 per incremental conversion.

STAGE 2: Geo holdout tests.
 - Run ads in specific geographies and compare them to similar fit geographies that you’re not running ads to
 - Measure the lift from running ads versus not running them
 - Use this for Meta ads or out-of-home campaigns
 - Validates impact beyond what the platform reports, especially for view-based channels

STAGE 3: ABM Incrementality (if going upmarket).
 - Take 10,000 target companies and only run ads to 5,000 of them
 - Evaluate pipeline velocity and lead volume on companies you're targeting versus not targeting
 - Use the holdout group as the baseline
 - Upload a customer list to Google for this, or use LinkedIn and Meta for more precise ABM targeting

STAGE 4: LTV model testing.
 - Tie the Google Click ID to the user and identify which variables predict accurate LTV
 - Include variables like: onboarding speed, source, enriched form data, probability of conversion, expected upsell, estimated months before churn
 - Run an experiment: half the traffic optimizes towards the LTV model, half towards SQLs
 - When we did this, the LTV model delivered a 73% lift in ROAS


In order to use incrementality testing in forecasting we:

 - Bake incremental data into quarterly forecasting
 - If Meta has a 1.2x halo effect and Meta CAC is $1,000, we show actual Meta CAC is $833 after the halo effect
 - This helps us make smarter budget decisions when clients ask where to spend an extra $100K

I think it’s super important to do these sorts of tests - because if you're spending six figures per month on ads without running incrementality tests…

You don't know which channels are driving incremental conversions versus which ones that take credit for conversions that were already coming.

It's almost 2026 and marketers are STILL launching 10 creatives per ad set with $300/day budgets, wondering why CPMs keep climbing and CTR keeps dropping... expecting Meta's algorithm to find winners with $70/week per creative, then acting surprised when campaigns stay stuck in learning for 3+ weeks

One of our new partners came to us with exactly this problem.

Here's the math on why their ads weren’t scaling.


The setup:

B2B SaaS campaign with $300 per day total budget. Three ad sets, each $100 per day. They decided to test 10 creatives per ad set because more tests equals faster learnings, right? Let's break that down: $100 ÷ 10 = $10 per day per creative. That’s $70 per week per creative in spend.


What happens under Meta's Andromeda system:

Meta's Andromeda delivery model doesn't require 50 conversions per ad anymore in a 7-day period, but it still needs enough data density per signal cluster (modeled conversions).

The system now optimizes across ad sets, not just individual ads. It looks for shared creative patterns like similar hooks, visuals, or emotional tones. It still needs 20-30 modeled conversion signals per ad set before it stabilizes. 

If your B2B lead costs $80, that's $80 × 25 = $2,000 per ad set minimum for stable learning.But you're spending just $700 per week per ad set. You're feeding the algorithm only a third of what it needs to understand performance.


This results in budget dilution:

Instead of gathering 2,000 data points on one or two strong creatives, you've split the same signal across 10. That means none of them exit learning. CPMs climb as Meta keeps retesting. CTR drops because relevance never compounds. In other words, Meta can't find a winner because you never gave enough data to crown one.


Real account example:

Account A: B2B SaaS, $300 per day, testing 10 creatives per audience. All ads stuck in learning for 3+ weeks. CPM increased 18%. CTR dropped 24%. No stable winner.

Account B: Same spend, $300 per day, testing 3 creatives per audience. Learning stabilized in 8 days. Two ads hit 4x spend-to-revenue ratio within 2 weeks.

The difference was data concentration because Meta recognized creative-level engagement trends faster when there were fewer ads fighting for attention.

--

My rule of thumb for rapidly improving every launch:

 - Run fewer ads per ad set.
 - Give each ad time and budget.
 - Iterate and change one variable at a time (hook, format, or emotion).

I’ve audited over 115 brands over the last 24 months. Sounds freaky but I can predict which ones will scale to 9-figures and which ones will die based on 1 question:

"Where is performance breaking in your funnel?"

And it plays out in 1 of 2 ways:


1. Founders have no idea where their funnel is breaking.

They don't understand the click-to-lead conversion rate. They don't understand the lead-to-sales call conversion rate. They don't understand the sales call-to-customer conversion rate.

They can't tell me where the bottleneck is.

So when I ask, "Where is performance breaking?" they say things like:

"Our ads aren't working."
"Meta's algorithm changed."
"Our CPCs are too high."

These are symptoms, not diagnoses. If you don't know whether the bottleneck is cost per click being higher than expected or conversion rate to lead being lower than expected, you can't fix it.

You’d just be guessing… which wastes budget.


2. Founders can pinpoint the exact step where their funnel breaks.

They'll say something like:

"We're getting solid click-through rates, but our landing page conversion is 2.3% when it should be 4%."

Or:
"Our lead-to-call show rate is 68%, but our call-to-close rate dropped from 32% to 19% last month because our sales team is underwater."

Or:
"Cost per lead is fine, but 80% of our leads are unqualified because we're optimizing for form submits instead of qualified opportunities."

When someone can answer that question with specifics, I know they're going to scale fast and effectively.

How am I so certain? Because here’s what I've learned after spending $200M+ on ads:

You can only be as strong as your entire funnel. If your sales process sucks or your product sucks, marketing isn't going to be successful.

At the beginning of every month, we forecast performance for every account. Then we look at pacing during the month. We look at how actual performance is pacing against those forecasts.

And that allows us to spot the bottleneck. Sometimes the bottleneck is cost per click is higher than expected, or conversion rate to lead is lower than expected.

From there we can dive in and really pinpoint the main reason why we aren't getting the returns we want.

This allows us to consistently drive better performance. So if you can't answer "Where is performance breaking?" with pinpoint detail and precision? That's your first problem to fix.

Screw it - 10 B2B ad opinions I have after spending $200M+ that'll probably p*ss people off:

1. Gated content creates cheap leads, not qualified ones. Conversion rate from visit to form fill is low. From form fill to qualified meeting is even lower. 90%+ of leads from gated PDFs never open a nurture email. I'm a big fan of ungating content or using quiz funnels that show value upfront and give users that aha moment before they give their information.

2. Professional polish doesn't build credibility the way you think. Some professional ads perform well, but overproduced ads repel decision-makers. Lo-fi founder or UGC-style videos outperform cinematic explainers across Meta and LinkedIn. It all comes down to having a strong value prop and messaging that matches your ICP.

3. Meta works incredibly well for B2B, even in boring industries. We have an IT software client where Meta ads is one of their best performing channels. Who would think an IT person becomes a qualified lead from an Instagram ad? But employees are people, and Meta reaches so many people on the platform and does well at targeting the right ones. Meta CPMs are 3-5x cheaper and reach the same ICPs before they're actively shopping.

4. B2B buyers justify with logic but decide with emotion. Emotional storytelling improves watch time and conversion from the testing we've run. Ads that say "This tool saved me 6 hours a week" beat "Automate your workflows efficiently."

5. Facebook's Lead Gen objective optimizes for form fillers, not pipeline builders. Running lead gen campaigns on Meta gets you volume, but lead quality is typically poor. Use Traffic or Video View objectives to pre-qualify through engagement, then retarget with demo CTAs.

6. Founder-led content drives trust. When we have founders as talking heads in the ads, those are typically our top performers. They don't always have to be in the ad, but especially when scaling, get them in there.

7. Algorithms fatigue faster in 2025. Winning creative dies in weeks. We're big fans of iterating on top performers, and we spend 80% of our time and budget on iteration. New openers, emotional reframes, and fresh voiceovers extend lifespan 3-4x. Meta deprioritizes lookalike ads, so make every iteration visually unique.

8. The problem should be the hero, not the product. The product is the resolution. Ads that dramatize the pain outperform pure feature demos by up to 4x CTR from our testing.

9. Most B2B marketers track metrics that don't move pipeline. We focus on hit rate, hold rate, and SQL-to-opportunity conversion. Too many companies optimize for lead volume when those leads aren't qualified. Optimize as far down funnel as you can without sacrificing conversion volume.

10. B2B targeting has shifted from who they are to what they do online. Rely on behavior (video views, comments) over job title targeting. Accounts using behavioral lookalikes hit 32% higher ROAS vs. job title filters.

5 marketing ROI metrics every CEO must know. 

LTV to CAC Ratio 
↳ Shows if your customer acquisition costs are worth it. 
↳ A ratio above 3:1 means you’re scaling right. 
↳ Anything less? You’re burning cash, not building value.

Lead to Customer Conversion Rate 
↳ Measures how well you turn leads into paying customers. 
↳ High conversion = efficient marketing. 
↳ Low conversion? Time to fix your funnel, not just throw more money at ads.

CAC Payback Period 
↳ Tells you how fast you recover what you spent to get a customer. 
↳ Short payback = more capital to reinvest. 
↳ Long payback? You’re stuck waiting for your own money. 

Return on Ad Spend (ROAS) 
↳ Tracks how much revenue you get for every dollar spent on ads. 
↳ Channel by channel, campaign by campaign. 
↳ If it’s not profitable, cut it. No mercy.

Customer Lifetime Value (CLV or LTV) 
↳ Predicts the total revenue a customer brings over their time with you. 
↳ The north star for subscription and SaaS models. 
↳ High LTV means you can outspend your competition and win.

Why these matter: 
• They show if your marketing is a money-maker or a money-pit. 
• They reveal if your growth is real or just a mirage. 
• They help you scale without running out of cash.

Benchmarks to remember: 
• LTV:CAC should be 3:1 or higher. 
• CAC payback under 12 months is gold. 
• ROAS above 4x means your ads are working. 
• High conversion rates mean your team is dialed in.

Every CEO needs these numbers on speed dial - and their CMO needs to provide them, weekly. 

They’re not just metrics. 

They’re your business’s health check. 

Ignore them, and you’re flying blind. 

Master them, and you’re building a machine that prints money.

There's only 2 rules you need to follow to be able to save anywhere from 50%-90% on your OpenAI input tokens by using cached inputs. 

I made a post recently about how you could save on your OpenAI calls with cached inputs and I did some testing to make sure it works.

Jeff Barg explained to me that the integration in Clay with OpenAI is ready to do cached inputs. We were prompting wrong (and so is the Clay metaprompter). 

The 2 rules you need to follow to have the highest chance of hitting cached inputs is to 

1. Make sure your prompt is over ~1,024 tokens. You can just ask chatgpt how many tokens a prompt is and it'll tell you. This is nothing for most of our prompts. 

2. As much of your prompt needs to be the same from the beginning of the prompt to whenever you make a change. 

That's what the caching of the input is. They already computed the beginning of the prompt and stored it. They recognize that it's been computed before and pass that saving to you. 

We were messing it up with putting custom parts of the prompt in the second or third sentence. 

Put all that custom stuff at the end and you will have a really high chance of hitting cached inputs. 

It feels like a black box because the Clay API at the point of this post doesn't tell you if you used cached inputs but they'll add that in soon!

Most companies waste half their marketing budget.

They just don’t know which half.

But the best CMOs do things differently.

They know exactly where every dollar goes and why.

Here’s how world-class marketing leaders allocate their budgets for maximum impact:

The marketing budget is split into three main buckets:

→ Advertising & Media (40-50%)
→ Content & Creative (15-25%)
→ Technology & Tools (15-20%)

Let’s break down what this really means:.

1/ Advertising & Media (40-50%)

This is the biggest slice. It covers digital ads, offline media, paid social, and influencers.

→ Digital ads and paid social drive fast results. You can see what works, double down, and cut what doesn’t.
→ Offline media, TV, radio, print—still matters. It builds trust and reaches people who aren’t glued to their phones.
→ Influencers bridge the gap. They bring credibility and reach new audiences.

The smartest CMOs don’t pick just one. They blend digital and traditional, so their message hits everywhere.

2/ Content & Creative (15-25%)

This is the engine behind every campaign.

→ Content production means videos, blogs, and graphics that grab attention.
→ SEO and organic search are the long game. They cost less over time and keep bringing in new customers.
→ Creative agency fees pay for the big ideas that set brands apart.

Great content is a force multiplier. It makes every ad, every post, and every campaign work harder.

3/ Technology & Tools (15-20%)

This is where the magic happens behind the scenes.

→ MarTech stacks connect all your tools, so nothing falls through the cracks.
→ Analytics and data tools show what’s working and what’s not.
→ AI productivity tools save time and boost results.

The best teams use data to make every decision. They don’t guess. They know.

But here’s the twist:

The marketing budget does NOT cover everything.

→ Product development, sales salaries, and capital expenses are separate.
→ This keeps marketing focused on what it does best: driving growth and building the brand.

The real secret: 

The best CMOs treat their budget like a living thing. They adjust fast. They cut what’s not working. They double down on what is.

They know that every dollar has a job.

And they make sure it delivers.

If you want to win, stop guessing.

Start allocating with purpose.

Your bottom line will thank you.

“There are NO shortcuts to building effective Meta Ads campaigns that profitably spend millions.” Actually, there are. And it comes from tracking 5 metrics that most marketers ignore:

These metrics aren't really popular yet.

But I'm sure they'll get the recognition they deserve in the next one or two years:

1. Creative Hit.
We look at data for the last 30 days and find the ads that have spent 25x the target CPA and have an actual CPA that's better than the target CPA. For example, if your target CPA was $100, a creative hit would be an ad that's spending at least $2,500 and has a CPA below $100.

2. Hit Rate.
What percentage of the launched ads turn into hits? This measures the quality of our ideas and execution. Hit rate = number of hits created ÷ total number of ads launched. The goal is a strong enough hit rate to sustain profitable scaling. Typically 10-30%.

3. Cost Per Creative.
How much it costs to produce each individual ad, including design fees, copywriting, video production, talent, etc. Every dollar we sink into creative is a non-working dollar that isn't fueling ads in the market. If our creative is too expensive, we'll test fewer variants, leaving missed opportunities.

4. Cost Per Hit.
This all-in metric combines the two sides of the creative equation: production cost and success rates. It shows how expensive it is to unlock each new winning ad. We also track creative velocity (how many new ads are produced over a given time period).

5. Creative Velocity
This is the number of new ads produced over a given time period. We produce 500+ creatives per month across our accounts. The more we test and the more informed we are in our tests, the faster we can reduce portfolio risk. In practice: If a client has a $100K budget, target CPA of $100, and needs 1,000 conversions per month, they need at least 20-30 fresh ads per month. A hit rate of 20% means 4-6 new winners per month, which ensures consistent scaling. Without this, one fatigued creative could ruin performance.

Here's what's wild:

There are definitely tons of accounts where we see ads that don't perform as well on the CTR side of things, but they have a much better CPA. An ad can be really appealing to people to click on, but if you're not targeting the right person with the right messaging, they'll click on it but they won't convert.

Too often, marketers fixate on vanity stats like thumbstop ratio, CTR, and hook rate as the top drivers of performance. These are valuable metrics, don't get me wrong. But they aren't directly correlated to what businesses actually want, which is profitability.

My advice? Just track what increases profit.

We spent $5.6M/mo on ads.

I always use these 7 ad types: 

1. Start with static ads to validate messaging.
Before we touch video production, we launch static creative first. Static ads let us test messaging and concepts fast without burning budget on video that might not convert. We use comparative positioning ads, high-clarity explanatory visuals, charts, social proof screenshots, and customer testimonials talking about results. Once we find the messaging that performs, we move to video.

2. Short-form video with a person talking to camera.
Live-action, face-to-camera content is dominating performance right now. This isn't scripted agency production. It's authentic, visually distinct content that drives emotional connection. The format works because it feels real, not manufactured.

3. UGC-style testimonials.
Customer testimonials shot in UGC style consistently outperform polished case study videos. We're talking about real customers, real environments, real reactions. Not studio lighting and scripted talking points. Authenticity wins over production value.

4. Face-to-camera mixed with product demos.
Combine a person explaining the product on camera with actual product demo footage. This hybrid format gives you the trust of face-to-camera content with the clarity of seeing the product in action. It works especially well for software and tech products where showing the interface matters.

5. UGC mashups.
Layer different formats together. Start with a UGC hook from a customer, transition to a founder explanation in the middle, then close with another UGC testimonial. This mashup format builds credibility through multiple voices while keeping the founder's authority in the mix.

6. Problem-agitate-solve videos
Use quick-cut storytelling to walk through the problem your customer faces, agitate that pain point, then show your solution. This structure works after you've validated the messaging with static ads. The format creates emotional momentum that drives conversions.

7. High-clarity static ads
Don't abandon static creative once you move to video. High-clarity static ads with explanatory visuals, comparison charts, social proof screenshots, and review graphics still convert. They're cheaper to produce, faster to test, and perform well across platforms.

--

Here's how to use them in the right order. 

1. Start with ad type 1: static
2. Validate messaging works
3. Choose easiest video format for your business (e.g. if you have someone internally who can speak to camera, go to ad type 2. If you have customers that are willing to do UGC, go to ad type 3)
4. Start video with same hook as step 1. 
5. Try in a new video format 
6. Make sure each new video looks 'different' (Andromeda likes this) 
7. Scale (easier said than done)

Is your Google Ads setup or keywords the problem?

These graphs & checklist will tell you: 

1. Check device CPA separately. Go to Campaigns > Segment > Device. I've seen Desktop CPA at $1,375 and Mobile at $7,355. Same leads. 5x difference. Adjust bid modifiers accordingly.
2. Verify conversion actions are set to Secondary, not Primary. When you reactivate old conversions, they default to Primary. Google will optimize toward them immediately. Set all but one to Secondary.
3. Click every site link and make sure it loads. Site links pointing to dead pages means you're paying for clicks that go nowhere.
4. Search your negative keyword list for "free," "trial," "demo." Broad match negatives can block high-intent queries like "free trial." One bad negative can kill your best traffic.
5. Confirm conversion count is set to "One" not "Every." If a lead gets uploaded twice, Google counts two conversions. The algorithm thinks performance is 2x better than reality.
6. Segment Search Partners separately. Go to Campaigns > Segment > Network. Search Partners are usually 2x worse than Google Search. If CPA is bad, turn them off.
7. Verify your negative keyword list is still applied. Shared lists can disappear during account transitions. Check it's attached to all campaigns.
8. Switch from Max Conversions to Target CPA if efficiency is bad. Max Conversions spends your entire budget no matter what. Set Target CPA 30-40% below current to stabilize.
9. Check when negative keywords were last added. Go to Change History > last 90 days. If none added in 60+ days, no one is reviewing search terms.
10. Check if RSA headlines are over-pinned. If every headline is pinned, Google can't test combinations. Only pin Headline 1 if you need brand name first.
11. Make sure RSAs have all 15 headlines and 4 descriptions filled. Fewer headlines means fewer combinations means less chance of finding winners.
12. Add dynamic keyword insertion to headlines. Use {KeyWord:Fallback Text} to match the search query. Relevance up. CTR up. CPC down.
13. Check match type distribution. If Broad match is 80% of spend and CPA is bad, move keywords to Phrase or Exact. Tighten before you scale.
14. Set audiences to Observation, not Targeting. Targeting limits reach. Observation gathers data without restricting. Adjust bids on winners later.

Rippling is the only SaaS I’ve seen do this:

(it’s not normal) 

They run 1 landing page for every 15 ads:

This is what's going on: 
- They’re called a ‘Compound Startup’ SaaS
- They are building 20+ businesses/products at once
- They can amortize their CAC across 20 products.
- When they acquire a customer for Payroll, they have 19 other products to cross-sell and increase LTV
- They can afford a higher CAC because their LTV is higher

So they were forced to maximize offer and creative diversity:
- "Gift Card" offers for HR
- "Corporate Card" angles for Finance
- “SaaS Growth” reports for C-Suite

Thing is, this playbook is replicable even if you're not Rippling

(save this down) 

1. Build a "SaaS Offer Portfolio"

Most SaaS brands rely on one offer: "Book a Demo."
This saturates fast & prospects tune out.

Instead, map offers to intent levels: 
→ Cold (Awareness): ChatGPT prompts, salary reports, templates 
→ Warm (Consideration): Webinars, ROI calculators, comparison guides
→ Hot (Conversion): Incentivized demos ($100 Amazon card, AirPods, Apple Watch)

E.g.: Rippling has run the "gift card for demo" offer for 12+ months. 
If it wasn't working, they'd have killed it.


2. More landing pages

Rippling has ~1 landing page for every 15 live ads. 

Every offer gets its own destination:
→ Resource Ad → Resource LP (
→ Webinar Ad → Webinar LP
→ Gift Card Demo Ad → Gift Card Demo LP

CPMs fall and CACs fall because ad promise = landing page reality = higher conversion rates.

3. Remix Formats: 

Some segments of your audience only watch Reels vs Statics.

So, you need to create a range of formats to target the full audience and funnel when scaling. This is crucial for Meta's Andromeda and GEM updates. It's not only about creative velocity anymore. Creative DIVERSITY is just as important these days:

We use these 12 formats: 
- iPhone screenshot, Apple Notes list (Lo-fi Static)
- Selfie-style talking head, Loom-style walkthrough (Lo-fi Video)
- Professional photography, branded templates (Polished Static)
- Studio-lit demos, motion graphics (Polished Video)
- Quote cards, "I was struggling with..." testimonials (Emotional Static)
- Customer story arc, PAS narrative (Emotional Video)
- Feature comparison charts, spec breakdowns (Functional Static)
- Step-by-step explainer, before/after demo (Functional Video)
- UI screenshots, dashboard views (Product Static)
- Product demo, click-through tour (Product Video)
- Person at desk using tool (Lifestyle Static) 
- Workplace context, "day in the life" frame (Lifestyle Video)

4. Hook matching

Match hooks to where your customer is:
→ Top (Cold): "Problem & Solution" — "Stop wasting 5 hours on payroll" 
→ Middle (Warm): "Features & Benefits" — "Run payroll in 90 seconds" 
→ Bottom (Hot): "Promotion & Incentive" — "Get AirPods when you switch"

Rippling is rotating all 3. This lowers ad fatigue at high spends. 

Turns out - you don't need 20 products to run the Rippling playbook.

I'm posting on 30+ LinkedIn accounts. Every month I'm co-writing 100s of posts and they MUST perform. I (kinda) know that a post will do well before it's been published and the LinkedIn Overlords have made their judgement.

First, the truth: 

1. I'm not an oracle.
2. And I'm not alone (team of content strategists / writers)

BUT, after enough posts you begin to see patterns. 

Here's the checklist. Save this for your next post.

1. Do I care?

Does the hook make me care enough to click 'See More'. I'll throw the post into AuthoredUp and use their free 'Text Formatter' to make the post truncates where we want it to. It's free, anyone can do it ^ 

2. Who are you? 

(This is especially true for new accounts). You have to fight for every impression. You have to scream why you're relevant through quick competency statements that prove you're good at what you do and your opinion is worth listening to. E.g's 'We're at $Xm ARR' / 'We send XX,XXX cold emails'. The hook of this post is a clear example. 

3. Is it digestible? 

Can I quickly skim through the main points. Where is my eye drawn back to after the hook. Typically best done through listicles, clear formatting, white space. This post is an ovbious example and is one of my favourite formats. A clear point with a small-ish paragraph. The goal is here is to increase dwell time on the post (one of the more important LinkedIn algo factors)

4. Can I comment? 

Is there a reason for me to comment? Is there a debate to be had, a conversation to engage with? You can make this happen by talking about interesting topics. You can also make this happen by just asking the reader. You see this all the time 'Agree?' - but you can do better... "Anyone else seen this?", "What am I missing?", or end on a 'feel good' platitude that people can identify with. 

Save this checklist for the next time you post.

It's quick and easy.

To run an aggressive promotion strategy you need to:  

1. Diversify across 4 formats

Static Images
- Cheap, fast to test.
- Create in 1-2 hours per variation.
- Motion/animated.
- Good for complex products.
- Hook in first 3 seconds.
- Show product immediately.
- Under 30 seconds for cold traffic.
- Create in 4-8 hours (simple) to 2-3 days (complex).

UGC
- Best for emotional hooks and objection handling.
- Let creators use their own words. Imperfection signals authenticity.

Talking Head
- Often top performer for B2B/high-ticket.
- Direct eye contact. Speak to one person.
- Handle biggest objection in first 10 seconds. Be specific (numbers, timelines, outcomes).
- 30 min filming = 5-10 ad variations.

2. Remix winners
Don't make "new" ads. Remix winners into other formats. The winning element is usually the messaging. The hook, pain point, or claim.

Static headline wins?
- UGC creator opens with that line.
- Founder explains why it's true.
- Motion graphic visualizes the claim.

UGC wins?
- Transcribe it.
- Turn best line into static quote ad.
- Create motion version with key stats.

Motion explainer wins?
- Key frame becomes static.
- Talking head does walkthrough version.
- UGC creator reacts to demo.

3. Track Creative KPIs

Identify Hits in last 30 days
- Spent 25x the target CPA (cost per acquisition).
- Maintained an actual CPA lower than the Target CPA .
- If target CPA is $100, a "Hit" must spend $2,500+ and maintain a <$100 CPA.

Hit Index
- Hit Index = Hit Conversions / Total Conversions.
- < 0.6: Lack enough winning ads; need more/better creative tests.
- 0.9: Overdependence on very few ads; if a top performer fatigues ad account is in trouble.

Hit Rate:
- Hit Rate = No. of Hits Created ÷ Total No. of Ads Launched.

How to forecast marketing for 2026: 
 
1. Build baseline.
 
-> Pull 12-24 months of full-funnel data 
-> Segment by brand vs non-brand, geography, and product line 
-> You need enough history to see how cohorts actually convert over time
 
2. Map the full funnel with conversion rates at each stage.
 
-> Upper funnel: Spend, Clicks, CPC 
-> Mid funnel: MQLs, SQLs, cost and conversion rate at each stage 
-> Lower funnel: Opportunities, Customers, CAC, cost and conversion rate at each stage 
-> Revenue: ROAS, LTV 
-> Most teams stop at Cost/MQL.
 
3. Run cohort bake analysis.
 
-> Use historical conversion patterns to forecast how current leads will convert over time 
-> Track actual MQL/SQL counts this month 
-> Apply expected CVR from past cohort behavior 
-> If your historical MQL→SQL rate is 30% at 60 days, you can project March leads forward before waiting until June
 
4. Monitor pacing to plan.
 
-> Compare MTD vs Forecast, 7-day rolling averages, and daily actuals 
-> Prioritize upper-funnel metrics like CPC and Cost/MQL that reach full bake quickly 
-> These give you early warning signals while lower-funnel metrics are still cooking
 
5. Build scenario models.
 
-> Run Conservative, Base, and Aggressive forecasts 
-> Factor in seasonality curves, competitive intelligence, planned optimizations, and market dynamics 
-> When historical data is strong, build regression models for tighter predictions
 
6. Make scaling decisions with both signals.
 
-> Only increase spend when upper-funnel pacing is on track AND bake forecast aligns with targets 
-> If metrics underpace or quality signals deteriorate: pause, diagnose, then fix 
-> More effective than bidding on upper-funnel events alone for long revenue cycles
 
Main takeaway:
 
-> CPL and MQL volume are lagging indicators 
-> Cohort bake analysis lets you forecast downstream performance today -
-> Combine upper-funnel pacing with bake projections before scaling
-> (Save this for later)

How to convince a CFO to 5x ad budget

CFOs don't care about ROAS.

What actually matters is payback period.

Which is when they can expect the money to come back.

I’ve had this conversation at-least 15+ times in the last year with various clients. 

Use this framework to convince your CFO to increase budget:

1. Calculate actual payback period

-> Map the real cash timeline
-> Ad spend: $50K
-> Leads generated: 100
-> SQLs: 20
-> Closed deals: 5
-> Contract value: $250K ARR
-> Billing: Quarterly
-> Q1 cash collected: $62.5K
-> Q2 cash collected: $62.5K
-> Total: $125K
-> Real payback: 4 months
-> This is the number your CFO wants to see

2. Show the cash flow forecast

-> Build a simple model
-> January spend → April cash
-> February spend → May cash
-> March spend → June cash
-> Show when dollars go out and when they come back
-> CFOs think in cash flow, not attribution windows

3. Request increases in increments

-> Use the 20-30% rule
-> Month 1: $50K → $65K (30% increase)
-> Month 2: $65K → $85K (30% increase)
-> Month 3: $85K → $110K (30% increase)
-> Prove incrementality at each step
-> Show that added spend drives added revenue, not cannibalized organic

4. Show the competitor gap

-> Pull competitor spend data from SEMRush or SimilarWeb
-> "Competitor X spends $200K/month on paid search"
-> "We're at $50K"
-> "We're getting outspent 4:1 in channels where our buyers make decisions"
-> Frame it as market share risk, not a marketing request

Bottom line:

Give your CFO two things: 

1. When the cash comes back 
2. What happens if you don't invest.

This is all it takes to get more budget approved.

There are only 3 ways to scale Meta ads

Increasing budget is the worst one. 

You find some winning ads and started increasing budgets

But eventually it loses effectiveness because:

-> The same people start seeing your ad 5, 6, 7 times
-> Cost per customer goes up 
-> Your winner ads burn out
-> The Meta algorithm runs out of new people to find

You can combat against this. 

There are 3 ways to scale:

(1) Vertical - increase spend on what's working. This is the default and the first to break. Use it until frequency starts climbing, then stop.

(2) Horizontal - change the message angle to increase creative diversity. The way I like to think of this is "motivator mapping". Different people have different motivations. For instance, if you’re running an efficiency angle ("Save 10 hours a week"), it’ll only reach efficiency buyers. Status buyers will scroll past no matter how much you spend. So, launch a status angle ("Look like a genius to your boss") or an enemy angle ("Stop letting [Competitor] win") and you reach a different segment. You can spend $50K/month on each without them competing.

(3) Diagonal - change the format to increase creative diversity. Some people skip videos. Some only watch Reels. If you only run statics, you're invisible to half the audience. Take your winning angle and produce it in static, motion, UGC, and founder-led. Take the same message and push it into new ad inventory.

Quick scaling checklist: 
→ Vertical: Can you increase budget and control CPA?
→ Horizontal: What motivator could reach a new buyer?
→ Diagonal: Which format is missing from your account?

How much should you spend on branded keywords?
 
We spent $40.4k over the last 6 weeks to find out brand search incrementality:
 
We wanted to figure out
 
• What is the optimal amount to spend on ads?
• Is Google Ads taking more credit than it should?
• Could we spend more on Google Ads and drive incremental revenue?
 
So we ran a 6 week, 3-stage test 
 
BASELINE:
 
→ Week 1: $2.2k ad spend
→ Week 2: $1.5k ad spend
 
TEST 1: (~3x BASELINE)
 
→ Week 3: $6.6k ad spend
→ Week 4: $6.5k ad spend
→ Week 5: $7.5k ad spend
 
TEST 2: (~11x BASELINE)
 
→ Week 6: $16k ad spend
 
Then we measured the results:
 
1. Layered all data
 
• Exported Google Search Console data for branded clicks on a weekly basis
• Exported Google Ads data for branded spend, clicks and conversions on a weekly basis
• Created a table for every week so we could easily see all the data
 
2. Compared time buckets
 
• Created average weekly stats for Baseline, Test 1 and Test 2 periods
• Generally, we saw as paid spend increased organic clicks decreased.
• But we wanted to see exactly how many incremental clicks were driven (after organic decreased) by spending more on ads.
 
When we spent 3x Baseline (Test 1 vs Baseline)
 
• Spent ~$5.5k more every week
• Drove +2,500 more ad clicks
• Lost -5000 organic clicks
• Net lost -2,500 clicks
• That means we paid $5.5k more and got less traffic.
• In other words, incredibly loss making
 
We then ran Test 2 (which was a ~2x increase on Test 1)
 
• Spent ~$9.1k more every week
• Drove +1000 more ad clicks
• Lost -850 organic clicks
• Net gain 150 clicks
• That means we paid 9k for a ~62x worse incremental CPA
 
All in all, it means every time we increased ad spend, we ate into our organic traffic.
 
• Most of the “extra” conversions would’ve happened anyway
• We were paying to intercept traffic we already owned
 
Dropping spend back down from $16k/week to $2k/week seems drastic.
 
• Will competitors steal our traffic if we don’t bid?
• Will our brand keeps lose surface area?
• Does losing brand mean losing customers?
 
But it’s clear from the data that the spend wasn’t incremental.
 
And now we have it and black and white.
 
So now we can add that extra $14k into generating net new demand.
 
Every brand running Google Ads should be running this test every 4 months to make sure they’re not wasting spend. We’ve run this across multiple accounts and the results always vary (spend more or spend less).

"Brand keywords are a waste of ad spend "

Heard this one before?

I just ran a test for one of our long-term clients:

We 2x'd branded ad spend:
- Organic conversions dropped from ~1,000 to ~500
- Paid conversions increased from ~1,800 to ~2,800

No surprise that: 
- Branded search ate into organic conversions.
- We were paying for conversions that were going to happen anyway.

But what was more interesting: 
- Paid drove 1,000 more conversions.
- Subtract the 500 we lost from organic.
- We're up +500 conversions.

In this case, spending on branded keywords is incremental.

But that’s not always true. I've seen increasing branded search be incremental, and not incremental. It just depends. 

For example, last week I posted about how we spent $40k proving that brand search was NOT incremental for another brand.

Here's how we run Google Ads brand incrementality tests:

1. Choose a testing period
- We need to run this test for several weeks.
- Find a time in the calendar where there are minimal brand fluctuations (e.g., promos, brand campaigns, holidays, etc.).

2. Minimize fluctuations
- Run 1 week on, 1 week off campaigns.
- E.g.: Week 1 - Normal Spend, Week 2 - 2x Spend, Week 3 - Normal Spend, Week 4 - 2x Spend (and so on).
- This allows to minimize variation from brand / competitor campaigns

3. Dedicate 2x spend minimum
- To run a clean test you want to at least double your ad spend.
- This will give you enough contrast in the data to see incrementality.

4. Collect all data
- Export Google Search Console data for branded clicks on a weekly basis.
- Export Google Ads data for branded spend, clicks, and conversions on a weekly basis.
- Group all the weeks of normal spend and 2x spend.

5. Run these calculations:

PAID
- Calculate the average number of paid clicks and paid conversions of normal spend. Remove any promo weeks if they happened to fall into your testing campaign.
- Repeat this for your 2x spend time period.
- Calculate the difference. These are your incremental paid conversions. I.e., you spent 1x more to get 1,000 more conversions.

ORGANIC
- Calculate the average number of organic clicks of normal spend vs. 2x spend.
- Calculate the difference. These are the lost organic clicks due to increasing Google ad spend.
- Multiply this by your historical conversion rates. This gives you the lost organic conversions because you increased ad spend.

DIFFERENCE
- Incremental Conversions = Extra Paid Conversions − Lost Organic Conversions
- Incremental CPA = Extra Ad Spend / Incremental Conversions
- If both numbers above are positive, brand search was incremental.

Depending on the Incremental CPA (and the LTV of those conversions), we can decide whether to a) spend more on branded search or v) redirect that spend to demand generation.

We run these tests every few months.

Results are always fascinating.

How to get enterprise leads from Google Ads
 
(Based on $3M spend in Dec):
 
1. Disqualifying keywords
 
- Negative keyword anything that signals self-serve: 'free', 'tool', 'how to', 'template', 'DIY', 'cheap'
- Your ad copy needs to pass the enterprise sanity-check. Use language like 'Enterprise-Grade', 'Security', 'Compliance', 'Certified'
- We ran this for a B2B SaaS client whose CAC was ~75% above target. After tightening keywords and adding ABM-style landing pages, CAC dropped to 1% below target.
 
2. Landing page friction
 
- Test listing high-ticket pricing directly on your landing page. Statements like 'starting from $25K/mo' filters out 80%+ of unqualified leads before they ever fill out a form.
- Send all paid traffic to a dedicated "Strategy Call" or "Request Demo" page. Not "Get Started" / 'Limited Slots' / "Book Now". That language is too short term and attracts SMB buyers.
- Build landing pages that show big logos, reference VP/C-suite job titles, highlight relevant certifications (e.g. SOC2/HIPAA/ISO) and use procurement-friendly language.
 
3. Budgeting cash flow
 
- For Enterprise, invest at least $100k+/month in ad spend to gather meaningful data. Below that threshold, you won't have enough conversions to optimize and the CPCs will feel painful.
- Measure success by "Qualified Meetings per week" (target 3-5) rather than raw leads or cost-per-lead. Lead volume means nothing if 80% are unqualified.
- Track conversion rate from Qualified Meetings to Deal to ensure forecast assumptions are accurate.
- Plan for an 8-12 week sales cycle. Your December Google Ads spend drives Q2 pipeline.
- If cashflow is tight, use financing solutions to bring forward revenue from closed deals and reinvest faster.
 
4. Bidding strategies
 
- Aim for 30+ conversions per month. You don't want to send Google junk conversions, but use upper funnel conversions if needed in order to get sufficient volume. Then work to move your primary conversion action down funnel as quickly as possible.
- High CPCs ($25-50+) and low click volume are expected and a signal you're reaching the right audience.
- Track impression share on high-intent terms (target 70%+), absolute top of page rate (target 50%+), and consistency in visibility over time. Provided you're getting in front of the audience and your messaging is strong, it's just a matter of exposure.
 
This playbook works because enterprise buyers are trying to answer:
 
1. 'Is this brand known & legitimate?'
2. 'Who are the top 3 players in this space?'
3. 'Do they work with other companies like us?'

Cost of Inaction (COI) isn't best used to close a deal. But, it's great for opening one. 

There are two major decisions a buyer needs to make in a buying process:

#1 - Of all the fires we need to fight in our business, is this problem worth solving, and worth solving now?

#2 - Are you the right partner to solve it with? And is this the right solution to solve it?  

If the prospect is eager to solve the problem your solution solves, you probably don't need to use COI with your prospect. They've already decided it's a problem worth solving and solving now. You MIGHT need it when it comes to helping your champion convey the need to act with the rest of the buying group. But, the bigger problem here is usually a lack of decision confidence in the best way to solve it. 

COI is best used when prospects believe how they're solving the problem is "good enough". It's geared at addressing job #1. 

Here's an example to distinguish the two. 

Most of us use shampoo (hopefully). 

If I think my current shampoo is good enough, a "better" shampoo pitch won't make a difference. I perceive what I'm using today as good enough to get the job done. Here, I'd need to illuminate a problem with status quo (my current shampoo) before pitching a solution. That's COI. 

But, if I KNOW I need a new shampoo, I go to the store. I walk down the aisle and see 100 different shampoos. 70% of them sound like they could work for me. Now, I'm stuck. There are so many different options. The prospect is stuck on job #2. That's an indecision problem. 

The JOLT Effect book exposed the difference between the two. It's a phenomenal read for anyone losing deals to no decision. 

The reason I teach COI is because much of my Sales training is focused on how to open deals in an outbound motion. 

I grew up in Sales selling intangible solutions that weren't high-demand. 

No one has ever said "man, are we almost out of functional best practice research?".

To earn a swing at those opportunities, we had to expose a negative consequence of execs making opinion-based decisions. It wasn't an obvious problem.

I spend $5M/mo on Google ads 

And I use 3 attribution models:

1. First Touch Attribution Model
→ Answers: how should I allocate my budget?
→ Use this to decide how much goes to brand vs non-brand vs Performance Max
→ Shows which channels actually introduce new prospects to your funnel
→ If a channel never shows up in first-touch, it's capturing demand created elsewhere

Q: Which ad set/campaign is performing best?

2. Data Driven Attribution Model
→ Answers: Which ad set/campaign is performing best?
→ Use data-driven model to optimize within Google (last touch if you’re on Meta)
→ This is where retargeting performance lives - it won't show up in first-touch
→ Good for comparing ad sets/campaigns, keywords, and audiences within a single platform
→ Bad for comparing across platforms or making budget allocation decisions

3. Holdout Tests
→ Answers: Is this channel driving incremental results?
→ Pause a channel for 2-4 weeks and measure what actually changes
→ If conversions stay flat, that channel was capturing people who would've converted anyway
→ If conversions drop, that channel was actually creating new customers

There’s a time and place for complex models. 

But in the grand scheme of things, whilst they do look cool and impressive - they often don’t help to make better ad decisions. 

Bottom line: 

→ Use first-touch for budget allocation
→ Use data-driven for optimization
→ Use hold out tests for incremental validation

Yesterday, I wrote a post asking what you want to see more & less on your LinkedIn feed this year. 200+ comments later, here is the dominant winner (& loser):

Winner:
Honest lessons from losses/experiments/failures (not thinly veiled humblebrags or overly dramatized stories). 

Loser:
Comment "X" for something

One of the most liked comments came from Jacob Casey. My favorite excerpt from his comment was:

"I’d love to see more people share how they think."

Here's a framework I use in my LI "how-to" posts to do this.

1. Situation: hook should clearly explain the job-to-be-done (so reader can quickly assess if it's relevant to them before hitting 'see more').

2. Old Beliefs & Assumptions: What were my beliefs and assumptions about that job-to-be-done? How did I form those beliefs/assumptions?

3. Flaw: What negative outcome occurred as a result? What showed me my approach was flawed?

4. New Beliefs & Assumptions: What are my new beliefs/assumptions that frame how I'm thinking about the new solution?

5. New Solution: What did I do instead? (written from the POV of - 'so here's what I tried instead", not "so here's what you need to do instead").

6. Outcome: Did it work? Did it create a new problem to be solved? What do I want to keep iterating? 

The best part about posts that share how we think? 

You don't need 20 years of experience. You don't need a fancy title. 

Every single one of us has held a belief we later learned was flawed. And, every single one of us has tried, failed, tried again, failed again, and ultimately found a different way to approach it. 

IMO, the 3 keys of "how-to" posts that stop my scroll are:

- they don't overdramatize the story 
- the don't paint it as THE way to solve the problem. Just A way that's worked for them. 
- they share the thinking behind what they're doing differently (not just what they're doing)

There are only 3 ways to scale Google Ads

Increasing budget is the worst one. 

You find some winning keywords and start cranking spend

But eventually it loses effectiveness because:
→ You hit impression share ceilings
→ Cost per click starts climbing
→ You're paying more for the same searches
→ The algorithm runs out of high-intent queries to show you on

You can combat against this. 

There are 3 ways to scale:

(1) Vertical - increase auctions on what's already working. You can increase budgets (if on Max Conv), and you can also increase target CPA. When costs climb too high, pull target CPA back down to control efficiency. Keep an eye on IS (budget). If it’s a high percentage (10%+) you’ve got more room to scale. But after you’ve maxed out auctions - what’s next?

(2) Horizontal - expand keywords to reach new searches. This happens naturally if you're running broad match or phrase match and vertically scale. But you can also do this deliberately: research new customer pain points, expand your TAM, test different angles. If you're only bidding on "CRM software," you're invisible to someone searching "how to organize customer data." Map out the full buying journey and go after each stage.

(3) Diagonal - launch new campaign types to tap new inventory. Performance Max and Demand Gen unlock YouTube, Display, Discover, Gmail. But be careful - these campaigns love to spend on irrelevant placements. You need heavy negatives and placement exclusions from day one and be optimizing for deeper funnel conversion events. Do not optimize for form fills and data leads. Start at 10% of your Search budget and slowly increase as you validate quality. The traffic looks different, but there is incremental revenue in these campaigns.

Quick scaling checklist:

→ Vertical: Can you increase budget AND control CPA with your target levers?
→ Horizontal: What search terms are your customers using that you're not bidding on?
→ Diagonal: Have you tested PMax or Demand Gen with proper conversions and exclusions in place?

Here's a discovery call mistake I used to make with inbound leads (+ an elementary school math teacher tactic I used to fix it). 

Let's say someone called in with a request for negotiation training. 

I don't offer negotiation training. So, I'd try to convince them that negotiation wasn't the right problem to solve - an earlier stage problem was. 

Problem is - none of us enjoy the experience of being "convinced". It creates an offense vs. defense dynamic between us and the prospect. We end up in a losing battle of who's "right". 

I lost plenty of deals in discovery that way. So, here's the question I started asking instead. 

"How did the team arrive at negotiation as the problem to be solved?"

When we seek to understand how someone got from problem-->solution, it exposes potential flawed beliefs/assumptions. 

Remember when your math teacher had you write out how you arrived at your answer on a math test? 

It's like that. 

They did it so they could identify exactly where our logic derailed.

The difference in Sales calls is we're not their teacher. They're not handing us a test to grade. 

So, instead of us correcting them with a "here's where you're wrong" statement - our job is to ask a question that helps THEM expose the gap. 

Back to that negotiation example. 

Prospect answer: "Well, we're losing deals on price to a much lower-cost competitor. So, we got the regional VPs together and decided our reps need negotiation training." 

Me: "This might be a stupid question - but is there any material difference between your product and your competitor's?"

Prospect: "Yes - their parts are cheaper, but need to be replaced sooner."

Me: "And what's the negative consequence of that?"

Prospect: "More factory downtime. Every min of downtime while they wait for a part to be replaced costs $$". 

Me: "And, does negotiation feel like the right time to bring that up?"

Prospect: "No - that should happen much earlier in the sales process."

Me: silence

Prospect: "We're solving for the wrong thing, aren't we. This is a perceived value issue."

Notice how I didn't tell them they're "wrong". She concluded it on their own. 

There's power in that psychology. It's her idea. Her conclusion. She's more likely to socialize it. 

I beat this dead horse often, but in Sales, nothing always works and nothing never works. 

This approach sounds nice and neat in a LinkedIn post, but there are plenty of times I've run this and the prospect did NOT budge from their original conclusion. 

That's Sales. We don't convince prospects to change. Prospects convince themselves to change, with the information, beliefs, and assumptions they hold. 

But, the more consistent I was in using that approach in discovery, the better my discovery outcomes were. (Even if it meant I was just disqualifying sooner - or recognizing that this person wasn't going to be the ideal change agent inside of the account.)

CEO: Let’s scale brand search. It’s got 4x ROAS!!

CMO: That’s a bad idea.

CEO: Why? It’s 4x on the dashboard. Let’s spend more.

CMO: That 4x ROAS might not be right

CEO: What? We just spent $20k on this dashboard. Should I message the 
support? Or is it our tech?

CMO: No, it’s not the dashboard. It’s working fine. But it's not telling you the whole truth either.

CEO: Ok and what’s that?

CMO: Let me ask you something. If someone types our brand name into Google, what are they about to do?

CEO: ...buy from us.

CMO: Right. They already decided. They're not comparison shopping. They're coming to us. So if we pay to intercept them with an ad, what are we actually paying for?

CEO: The conversion.

CMO: No. We're paying for something that was going to happen anyway.

CEO: But without the ad, a competitor might steal them.

CMO: Maybe. Or maybe they just click the organic link right below and we get them for free. That's what we have to test.

CEO: Test what exactly?

CMO: Whether spending more on branded search actually increases total conversions—paid AND organic combined—or if it just shifts conversions from free to paid.

CEO: How?

CMO: We run alternating weeks. Normal spend, then 2x spend, then normal, then 2x. Compare the total clicks and conversions across both periods.

CEO: And?

CMO: We just did this. Spent $40k over six weeks proving that our branded spend wasn't incremental.

CEO: Wait what?

CMO: When we 3x'd spend, we drove 2,500 more paid clicks but lost 5,000 organic clicks. Net loss of 2,500 clicks. We paid more money to get less traffic.

CEO: That can't be right.

CMO: It was. Every extra dollar we spent cannibalized our organic. The "conversions" Google Ads took credit for? They would've happened anyway through organic.

CEO: So we should cut branded spend to zero?

CMO: Not necessarily. I've seen tests go the other way too. At my last company we 2x'd spend and drove 1,000 incremental conversions after accounting for organic loss. It just depends.

CEO: Depends on what?

CMO: Competitor activity, how much organic real estate we own, the search landscape. That's why we test every few months instead of assuming.

CEO: So that beautiful 4x ROAS...

CMO: Could be a 0x. Or it could be legit incremental. We won't know until we test it. But blindly increasing spend because of a sexy ROAS number? That's how we pay $14k a week for conversions we already owned.

CEO: And if the test shows it's not incremental?

CMO: We take that $14k and put it into generating net new demand instead of intercepting demand we already created.

CEO: This is giving me trust issues with dashboards.

CMO: Good. Attribution is a liar. Incrementality is the truth.

CEO: You should put that on a t-shirt.

CMO: *pans webcam down*

Years 0-4: $5m ARR
Year 5: $10m ARR
Here's how: 

It took 5 years, but here's the shortcut.

One avatar
One channel
Two products**

HERE'S HOW TO BUILD A 2ND PRODUCT FAST

1. Find the pain
-- mine your support tickets + tag feature requests
-- search reddit, LLM's and review sites for problem sets
-- write these pains down and by categorize severity vs ease
-- Choose the one with highest severity + lowest ease of solving

2. Schedule customer calls
-- find 10 customers and 10 prospects who feel the pain
-- ask them what would tools they currently use to solve the pain
-- ask them what the issues are with those tools
-- verify the pain is real

3. Test demand
-- Add a grayed-out menu item for the new product with "Coming Soon" or "Waitlist"
-- make your support email address readily available on the page
-- keep an eye on support emails/tickets related to this feature.
-- when you get interest through support email = you have demand
-- If you get support emails about the product, it means they worked super hard for the solution.
-- if true, you have found demand (aka initial pmf)

4. Test new product demand
-- build/vibe code the new product
-- give your waitlist the new product to test drive
-- have waitlist provide feedback
-- Improve the product
-- repeat feedback loop 3x
-- Get your first testimonials

5. Go to market
-- Translate your identified pains into benefit copy
-- use copy on landing pages and marketing collateral
-- create your dream 100 customers based on successful beta users
-- Start manual outreach
-- find ways to scale your outreach

There are 3 advantages of adding a 2nd product:
- a built-in audience to upsell to
- you have brand trust & loyalty
- an engaged beta test group

Expanding your ICP requires educating a new market. 

Adding another channel has a steep learning curve. 

Both are are possible, but 10x more risky.

Success requires tight partnership between product, sales, and customer success.

Thinking about going off on your own? I sat down with ☁️ Cliff Simon to share the ugly parts of my experience starting a solo business on the Lodestar podcast. 

Some backstory here. 

I was unmarried and kidless until I turned 40. Work was always my #1 priority. Probably because I felt shame re: being "old" and single. So, I measured my self-worth by my % to quota. Doing well at work made me feel like I was worthy. Doing poorly made me feel like shit. So, I worked extra hard to avoid feeling that way.

At 40, I got engaged to my husband and became a stepmom to 4 wonderful kids. It forced me to reflect on how I was spending my time.

My kids couldn't care less if I hit 100% of quota. Lucia wanted to show me her dance routine. Nicky wanted to tell me the stories behind his 5 Nights at Freddy's character drawings.  

I decided that I was tired of giving 1000% to a company. Always teetering on the edge of burnout. It was time to go off on my own. I quit my Sales job of 18 years at Challenger Sales to start DemandJen. 

A month later, I chickened out and took another W2 job at Lavender AI. 

9 months later, I left to go all-in on DemandJen.

6 months later, I realized it was never the company's fault for my burnout. I was doing the exact same thing, except this time, I had no company to blame. 

Going off on my own was messy, mentally. It wasn't the "I left W2 and my life is so much better!!!" story I kept reading on LinkedIn. 

2+ years into DemandJen, I'd love to say I've figured everything out. I haven't. Not even close. 

But, the experience has forced me to confront a lot of my own shortcomings. It's been a great mirror. I spend a lot more time thinking about whether 90 year old Jen would be proud of how I chose to spend my time and energy. 

And that's the stuff I talked about with Cliff. Not my usual sales, cost of inaction, cold email, discovery, enterprise sales stuff :)

Use this metric to find out: 

It’s called Search Lost IS (budget)

It shows the % of auctions you’re losing because either: 
1. Your daily budget is too low
2. Your Target CPA is too high / Target ROAS is too low.

People were actively searching for what you sell, Google was ready to show your ad, but your campaign ran out of money. 

You’ll know this is happening if your Google campaigns spend the majority of their budget in the morning, and then minimal spend in the afternoon and evenings. 

How to analyze: 
- Low number = good. It means you rarely hit your budget cap.
- High number = bad. It means you could be showing way more ads if you simply spent more or had a more effective bit strategy. 

If this metric is 30%:
→ Increasing your daily budget by 30% will unlock 30% more auction volume
→ Reducing your target CPA by 30% will unlock 30% more auction volume

Quick Checklist: 

If Search Lost IS (budget) = High
→ Low budget or high target CPA is your bottleneck
→ Increase budget or lower target CPA

Happy to help in the comments. 

P.S.

Note (1): For brand campaigns, you want to minimize your Search Lost IS (budget) to protect your brand from competitors raiding your own keywords. You can also run incrementality tests to ensure you’re not wasting spend here (did a couple posts on this last week) 

Note (2): If you increase spend, Search Lost IS (rank) will decrease. That’s ok. More spend will push you into more auctions, these aren’t as relevant anymore so your rank will naturally become worse.

“We increased budget… but leads dropped?” 

Google didn't just spend more: 
→ It expanded your audience
→ Introduced irrelevant search terms 
→ Optimized for finding more ‘cheap’ conversions 

I see it on accounts that spend $50k/mo to $1M/mo. 

To mitigate against lead volume and quality dropping: 

1. When a sales rep marks a lead as "Spam" or "Disqualified" in your CRM, automate a retraction signal back to Google via API. Do this within 24 hours. You force the algorithm to un-learn that conversion. It stops optimizing for lookalikes of the bad lead and stops bleeding budget on junk traffic.

2. Switch from Maximize Conversions to Target CPA bidding. Especially useful when you’ve pushed the budget too high, performance is falling and you want to reign it in. Set Target CPA to below actual CPA to force algo to find efficient audience pockets. Based on performance you can increase the target CPA and control how much budget is being spent. 

3. Pull raw search terms via the API. Feed them to AI (Gemini or ChatGPT are fine) with a specific prompt: "Score relevance to [Product] from 0-10." Flag any term scored 0-2 for deletion. This process surfaces 500-700 flagged keywords per run vs around 20 manually. Now manually review the flagged keywords and mark them as Negative inside Google ads so you stop spending budget on them.

4. Capture the GCLID in a hidden form field and pass it into your CRM. Then upload these conversion actions to Google. Move your primary conversion action as far down the funnel as possible, while still maintaining 30-50+ conversions per month in the account. If all conversions are from Brand campaigns, then you'll need to stay up-funnel until more unbranded conversions come in. 

5. Alternatively, upload offline conversions with static values to train Target ROAS bidding. E.g. MQL: $50. SQL: $250. Closed Deal: actual revenue. Now Google moves budget away from keywords that generate cheap MQLs and towards keywords that actually generate SQLs. These might be more expensive keywords, but they’re also higher ROI.

6. If the primary conversion action has to be upper funnel due to volume, add spam filters such as Recaptcha to lead forms. And add more specific qualifying criteria. This will allow for better data to be passed to Google.

7. If you're on Target CPA or Target ROAS, make sure your account doesn't have "Search Lost IS (Budget)". This results in CPCs that are more expensive than they need to be.


The bottom line:

> Send retraction signals within 24 hours
> Remove irrelevant keywords on a weekly basis 
> Implement offline conversion tracking and tell Google which leads closed
