“Competitor brand campaigns don’t work”

This is probably why: 

Competitor brand campaigns can burn your budget - especially if the competitor is running a defensive campaign to increase CPCs.

In 2025 we had to use a more advanced playbook. It made $12.3M. 

1. Cherry pick easiest target
List every competitor in a Google sheet and create a matrix of every dimension you compete on. E.g. pricing, features, support, use cases. Cherry pick the competitors where you have an obvious and clear advantage and you look different. There’s no point trying to compete against a big incumbent who is likely to outprice and/or out-product you. The more selective you are here, the better. We found a huge range in CPAs depending on the competitor we go after.

2. Build dedicated landing pages
Build dedicated pages that directly address "why us vs. them" for each major competitor. List their pain points. Show your advantages. Make the comparison obvious. Conversion rates go up because you're meeting the searcher exactly where they are. It’s important to be as factually correct on this page as possible. There’s no point lying or bending the truth to convert a lead that ultimately doesn’t have the right expectations, and then ultimately churns and has a low LTV. We found a 30% reduction in CPL just with dedicated landing pages.

3. Segment LTV by competitor  

This is where most competitor campaigns fall apart. You need GCLID and UTM parameters flowing all the way through to your CRM, tied to the specific competitor keyword that brought them in. And then from there, you track win rates by competitor, not just leads. You track LTV by competitor. Some competitor traffic converts at lower rates but higher deal sizes. Some converts faster but churns. 

4. Improve Keyword Intent

Not everyone searching a competitor name is in-market. Some are job seekers looking to work there. Some are existing customers searching for support or login pages. We aggressively remove terms from the start, things like "careers," "jobs," "login," "support," "help desk." (You should already have these in your NKL anyways!) Otherwise you're paying for clicks that were never going to convert. It seems obvious, but we see this mistake in almost every competitor campaign audit we run. When budgets get large enough we use Negative Nancy. It’s our AI agent that runs every week on client accounts and ingests every keyword that drove clicks. If the intent of the keyword is poor, we add it to negative keywords inside Google ads (this by itself can lower CPLs by 30% in 24-48 hours).

SUMMARY: 

→ Cherry pick weakest competitors 
→ Build dedicated landers 
→ Full funnel tracking from ad click to closed deal 
→ Negative keywords 

If you're running competitor campaigns and not seeing pipeline like this, the issue is usually one of these four things.

My favourite content framework 

1. What [10%]
2. Why [20%]
3. How [70%] 

What = Hook

Why = Context / Agitation

Most ABM fails in the data layer.
Not in the ads.

ABM is not a campaign.
It’s a system.

A system that turns messy account data into:
target accounts, buying groups, intent signals, and revenue.

If you want ABM to work, build it like an engineer 👇

1. Define the account universe
Lock your ICP with firmographics, technographics, and exclusion rules.
Hard filters > vibes.

Output: a versioned account universe with an owner + refresh cadence.

2. Normalize account identity
One account key across CRM, MAP, ads, and intent tools.
Domain > company name.
Parent / subsidiary logic matters.

Output: a clean account table (account_id, domain, parent_id, segment, owner).

3. Model buying groups, not leads
Deals close via committees.
Map 6–10 roles per product and track role coverage per account.

Output: buying-group coverage score per account.

4. Instrument intent correctly
Most intent = noise.
Use 3 layers:
• 1P (pricing, product, docs)
• 2P (partners, reviews)
• 3P (topic surges)

Weight by proximity to purchase.
Add fast decay.

Output: intent score with topic, strength, source, timestamp.

5. Create account stages with rules
Target → Engaged → MQ → SQ → Pipeline → Won.
Each stage has explicit entry criteria.
Log every transition.

Output: full account stage history.

6. Orchestrate plays, not blasts
Signals trigger coordinated actions:
ads + email + SDR + sales talk track.
Timing > volume.

Output: playbook with triggers, SLAs, and stop conditions.

7. Fix ABM attribution
Measure at the account + buying group level.
Track:
• Coverage
• Engagement
• Stage progression

Separate sourced vs influenced pipeline.

Output: a weekly ABM dashboard sales trusts.

8. Close the loop with revenue
Won/lost deals train the system.
Update ICP rules quarterly.
Kill plays that don’t move stages.

ABM isn’t creative first.
It’s data integrity, identity resolution, buying-group logic, and signal-driven execution.

Build the system.
Then scale the spend.

On mature LinkedIn accounts

I post content like Meta ads: 

Testing
- 30% of post volume 
- Speaking to a new point 
- Trying a completely new hook 
- Imitating a post from a different niche 

I'll typically see 40% of these posts 'underperform', 40% do average, and then 20% absolutely go viral. 

Iteration
- 70% of post volume 
- Speak to winning pain point 
- Reuse similar winning features (e.g. hook, image, format, style) 
- Imitate yourself 

Goal is to maintain impressions and/or beat them by working out what was throttling growth before. 

Very important if the post was low impressions but got leads. More leads = more impressions here. 

How to repeat posts (without it getting dry)

1. Take a winning post
2. Copy and paste it exactly 
3. Copy the body and image, change the hook
4. Copy the hook and body, change the image
5. Keep the same format, change the hook, body, image 
6. Take the same idea, change the format completely 

I've found I can do the same post 10-20 times and the audience loves it.

How to scale Google Ads to $3.2M/mo spend

→ Brand

- Always use manual bidding here. We find Google drops CPCs $2-3 during tests (probably to entice us in) but after a few weeks it creeps up. Much safer to control manually.

→ Competitors
- Typically ~10% of budget
- Sometimes higher in ‘urgent’ verticals like rehab, finance and legal.

→ Non-Brand
- Non-Brand gets the majority of spend. We split campaigns by intent level (high vs low), then by service line. Each gets its own ad group theme.
- If you have regional variation, geo-segment campaigns into state clusters and use dynamic keyword insertion for local relevance e.g. "Now Serving {Location}."
- Match type hierarchy: Exact → Phrase → Broad. Tighten when efficiency drops, broaden when scaling.
- Run 2-3 RSAs per ad group with maxed headlines (6 keyword-focused, 7 features/benefits, 3 CTAs).
- Our winning lever here is negative keywords. We maintain master negative keyword lists at the MCC level with 30,000+ negatives in industries we have big spend in. These get applied immediately to every new account and block known waste.

2. PERFORMANCE MAX

- Launch after non-brand search gets 30 quality conversions per month
- We run 1-3 PMax campaigns per business line.
- Ensure all optimization is for down funnel events (do not optimize for form fills ends up bringing junk leads)
- Asset groups are structured like ad groups with tight, coherent intent per persona. 
- We use 15 headlines pulled from top-performing Search ads, 5 long headlines, 5 descriptions, 20 images in all aspect ratios, and videos in multiple lengths. The top 25 converting Search keywords become "Search Themes."
- Audience signals include Customer Match, remarketing lists, and in-market segments.
- PMax channel performance varies month to month, but on average its 33% Search, 33% Display, 33% Youtube
- We’re currently getting some clicks for $0.10 to $0.15 through URL expansion with solid intent, which would have been atleast $4-$5 from Search. Big opportunity. 

3. DEMAND GEN

- Launch when PMax gets to 50 quality conversions per month
- Split into two campaigns: prospecting (new audiences) and retargeting (engaged audiences)
- Avoid over segmentation and group relevant audiences in same ad group to speed up learning and give algo more data
- DemandGen does really well at retargeting. PMax retargeting is signal based, it includes lookalikes.
- Copy over best performing video and static assets from Meta and launch without edits
- Set daily budget to 15x CPA for optimal learning

Bottom Line:
→ If you skip Search, PMax wastes money.
→ If you skip PMax, Search caps growth.
→ If you skip Demand Gen, you’re missing out on the next big thing.

Harsh Google ads truth:

There is no such thing as “bad keywords”

Just bad bids. 

Example: 

- Your target CPA is $50. Google spends $5 per click and it converts at $80
- You think the keyword just has bad intent, so you pause the keyword 

But what if you dropped your max CPC bid by 30-40% (via smart bidding)? 

- Google is forced to find cheaper auctions (that still convert)
- You spend $3 per click, it converts at same rate, but now at $48 CPA

Yes - you’ll get less volume at this bid…

But you’re within your CPA targets. 

This is because every keyword has a value threshold (a CPC where the math works out)

You can go through all your old keywords and do this exercise:

1. Pull your "paused for performance" keywords
2. Calculate actual CPA vs target CPA
3. For keywords within 2x your target, test reactivating at 40-50% lower bids
4. Give it 2-3 weeks of data before judging

I've seen "bad" keywords become good performers once the bid matched their true value.

Bottom line:

Before you pause a keywords make sure you've tested it at multiple bid levels.

How much should you spend on branded keywords?

Run this test:

1. Choose a testing period
- We need to run this test for several weeks.
- Find a time in the calendar where there are minimal brand fluctuations (e.g., promos, brand campaigns, holidays, etc.).

2. Minimize fluctuations
- Run 1 week on, 1 week off campaigns.
- E.g.: Week 1 - Normal Spend, Week 2 - 2x Spend, Week 3 - Normal Spend, Week 4 - 2x Spend (and so on).
- This allows to minimize variation from brand / competitor campaigns

3. Dedicate 2x spend minimum
- To run a clean test you want to at least double your ad spend.
- This will give you enough contrast in the data to see incrementality.

4. Collect all data
- Export Google Search Console data for branded clicks on a weekly basis.
- Export Google Ads data for branded spend, clicks, and conversions on a weekly basis.
- Group all the weeks of normal spend and 2x spend.

5. Run these calculations:

PAID
- Calculate the average number of paid clicks and paid conversions of normal spend. Remove any promo weeks if they happened to fall into your testing campaign.
- Repeat this for your 2x spend time period.
- Calculate the difference. These are your incremental paid conversions. I.e., you spent 1x more to get 1,000 more conversions.

ORGANIC
- Calculate the average number of organic clicks of normal spend vs. 2x spend.
- Calculate the difference. These are the lost organic clicks due to increasing Google ad spend.
- Multiply this by your historical conversion rates. This gives you the lost organic conversions because you increased ad spend.

DIFFERENCE
- Incremental Conversions = Extra Paid Conversions − Lost Organic Conversions
- Incremental CPA = Extra Ad Spend / Incremental Conversions
- If both numbers above are positive, brand search was incremental.

Depending on the Incremental CPA (and the LTV of those conversions), we can decide whether to a) spend more on branded search or v) redirect that spend to demand generation.

Just ran a test for a client:

We 2x'd branded ad spend:
- Organic conversions dropped from ~1,000 to ~500
- Paid conversions increased from ~1,800 to ~2,800

No surprise that: 
- Branded search ate into organic conversions.
- We were paying for conversions that were going to happen anyway.

But what was more interesting: 
- Paid drove 1,000 more conversions.
- Subtract the 500 we lost from organic.
- We're up +500 conversions.

In this case, spending on branded keywords is incremental.

But that’s not always true. I've seen increasing branded search be incremental, and not incremental. It just depends. 

We run these tests every few months.

Results are always fascinating.

Is your Healthcare Google Ads under-optimized?

This 37 point checklist will tell you: 

1. Check device CPA separately. Go to Campaigns > Segment > Device. I've seen Desktop CPA at $1,375 and Mobile at $7,355. Same exact leads. Adjust bid modifiers accordingly.

2. Verify conversion actions are set to Secondary, not Primary. When you reactivate old conversions, they default to Primary. Google will optimize toward them immediately. Set all but one to Secondary.

3. Click every site link and make sure it loads. I often see site links accidently pointing to dead pages. Even big accounts ($500k+ /mo spend sometimes make this mistake) 

4. Search your negative keyword list for "free," "trial," "demo." Broad match negatives can block high-intent queries like "free trial." 

5. Confirm conversion count is set to "One" not "Every." If a lead gets uploaded twice, Google counts two conversions. The algorithm thinks performance is 2x better than reality.

6. Segment Search Partners separately. Go to Campaigns > Segment > Network. Search Partners are usually 2x worse than Google Search. If CPA is bad, turn them off.

7. Verify your negative keyword list is still applied. Shared lists can disappear during account transitions. Check it's attached to all campaigns.

8. Switch from Max Conversions to Target CPA if efficiency is bad. Max Conversions spends your entire budget no matter what. Set Target CPA 30-40% below current to stabilize.

9. Check when negative keywords were last added. Go to Change History > last 90 days. If none added in 60+ days - you're likely burning budget. 

10. Check if RSA headlines are over-pinned. If every headline is pinned, Google can't test combinations. Only pin Headline 1 if you need brand name first.

11. Make sure RSAs have all 15 headlines and 4 descriptions filled. Fewer headlines = fewer combinations = less chance of finding winners.

12. Add dynamic keyword insertion to headlines. Use {KeyWord:Fallback Text} to match the search query. 

13. Check match type distribution. If Broad match is 80% of spend and CPA is bad, move keywords to Phrase or Exact. 

14. Set audiences to Observation, not Targeting. Targeting limits reach. Observation lets you get data. Adjust bids on winners later.

Saw a 103% brand search lift for $130M SaaS

→ Exposed group: saw ad on YouTube
→ Control group: didn’t see ad

Google then measures how many brand searches happened from the two groups 

Brand Search Lift = Exposed Group Brand Search - Control Group Brand Search 

In this case, it was a 103% increase. 

(Which means Youtube is generating new demand) 

Here’s how we ran the test: 

1. Launch YouTube campaigns (In-Stream or Shorts work best)
2. Enable Brand Lift Study option in campaign settings
3. Select "brand searches" as your measurement goal
4. Run for 7-14 days minimum
5. Wait for clean data (you'll need $5k-$10k spend for statistical reliability)

Google tracks these search types:

→ Direct brand name ("Acme Consulting")
→ Brand + service ("Acme consulting pricing")
→ Misspellings and variations
→ Product names that tie to your brand

And then the metrics we’re measuring are: 

- Incremental searches per impression. Tells us which audience segments performed above or below average. Values above 1.0 = above average performance.
- Incremental searches per cost. Shows cost-effectiveness by segment. Again, above 1.0 = better than your study average.
- Relative lift. This shows the percentage increase in search volume. E.g. 100% means exposed users were twice as likely to search compared to the control group.

What lift benchmarks should you expect?

- 10-50% = solid performance for most brands
- 50%+ = very strong performance (like our 103% result)
- Cost per lifted search below your Search CPA = excellent ROI

We’re seeing highest lifts in: 

→ B2B SaaS
→ High-ticket coaching
→ Founder-led brands
→ Educational or authority-driven videos

one demo request ≠ buying intent

Account 1: champion asks for a demo
Account 2: 4 stakeholders engage across web, ads, and sales

Prioritize Account 2
Most revenue teams are trained to reward hand-raisers.

But in high-ACV B2B, deals don’t close because one person is interested.
They close when an organization is mobilizing.

A single demo request = curiosity
Multi-stakeholder activity = internal alignment forming

That’s why signal scoring should priortize:
- buying-group breadth
- role seniority
- cross-channel reinforcement
- recency + velocity

Not just demo form fills.

Here’s how to make the transition:

1. Collapse contact signals into an account score
Stop treating leads as first-class objects.

Implementation:
Every contact-level event (page view, reply, meeting, ad click) 
→ rolls up to the Account
The Account is the record of truth

Result:
↳ sales stops chasing people.
↳ they prioritize companies.

2. Weight breadth higher than depth
Stop summing engagement. 
Start counting unique humans.

Track:
- # of engaged contacts per account
- # of distinct roles engaged
- Add a multiplier for new stakeholders engaging

Result:
↳ One obsessed champion doesn’t hijack priority.
↳ Buying groups surface naturally.

3. Require multi-role confirmation
Role coverage becomes a gating factor.

Implementation:
Normalize contacts into role buckets:
- Economic buyer
- Champion / user
- Technical / risk

Account score can’t cross “sales ready” unless:
- ≥2 roles are active
- ≥1 is decision maker

Result:
↳ CRM detects internal alignment

4. Reward cross-channel overlap
Single-channel engagement stops mattering.

Implementation:
- Create a rolling time window (e.g. 14–21 days)

- Score increases only when:
>>Web activity
>>AND sales interaction
>>AND/OR paid or event exposure
happen inside that window

Result:
↳ You surface accounts where awareness is spreading internally

5) Decay isolated activity aggressively
Time becomes a first-class variable.

Implementation:
-Apply decay functions to all dynamic signals:
>> Fast decay for content & page views
>> Slower decay for meetings & exec engagement

-If new signals don’t arrive:
>> Account score automatically falls
-No “evergreen” intent signals

Result:
↳ Stale accounts disappear.
↳ Live deals stay visible.

What happens IRL:
↳ Accounts that are truly sales ready (better win rates, happier sales team)

I have a saying in my workshops when it's time for sellers to give peer feedback after a cold email readout or discovery call roleplay.

"Never be nice, never be mean."

"Never be mean" is obvious. Don't be a pompous ass when someone is putting themselves out there.

"Never be nice" is the harder one. Sellers have a hard time giving constructive feedback to peers. But, if you're there to get better (which most sellers are), it's rude to sit on feedback that could help them do that.

Ugly YouTube ads work

Just hit a 4x ROAS

→ No need to pay for any additional creatives
→ Or make anything bespoke for Youtube 
→ And can be done with existing assets

We’re now spending ~$800k across accounts profitably

This is the playbook: 

1. Ads

- Grab your highest performing social/Meta Ads. If you aren't running social, just make some simple animated text-based ads in 16x9, 9x16, and 1x1
- Launch into a PMax / DemandGen campaign 
- Avoid early traps of over-segmenting into YouTube-only campaigns. Let Google figure it out here. 
- Dedicate enough spend for 50 conversions per month (base CPA off search historicals)

We’ve found that production value isn’t a deal breaker for Youtube to work.

Ugly ads have high performance with this structure: 

- First 5 seconds must create pattern interrupt. 
- Then acknowledge the problem directly, mirror what viewers already know. 
- Finally, present simple resolution with clear next steps. 

Ugly = anything you already have motion graphics, founder talking heads, static-to-video conversions, basic screen recordings.

2. Scale on CPA

- Don’t compare Youtube to Meta. Instead, compare it to Search. If using Demand Gen, look at the "platform comparable" columns.
- Scaling = CPA within 20-30% of search + consistent conversion volume 
- Keep an eye on brand search volume, it’s likely Youtube will generate demand that Search will take attribution for. 

3. Creative Upgrade

- Ideally, you’re seeing positive returns from Youtube 
- Now you've earned better production
- YouTube users have longer attention spans and expect education or entertainment.
- Think mini-documentaries, content series and informative assets 
- We bucket creative into 3 different lengths. Length 1 (20% of assets) = 30-60 seconds for fast validation, Length 2 (70% of assets) = 60-120 seconds for core performance, Length 3 (10% of assets) 2-5 minutes for education and high trust. 

Playbook summary: 

1. Validate cheaply (ugly ads)
2. Prove economics (CPA vs Search)
3. Upgrade creatives (structured creative)

Starting 2026 I purged our outbound tech stack (sequencers, list builders, etc.) + went back to a good ole fashioned google sheet 🫠 

The google sheet is 100% a PITA, the tracking is a bit sketchy (human error), BUT in only a short span of time the results have been pretty compelling: 

2025: ~200 emails + ~200 LIs sent per week -> .025% response rate, 1-2 ICP meetings booked /week  -> automations sending a lot (~20% accept rate on LI)

2026: ~50 LIs sent per week -> 26% response rate, 3-4 ICP meetings booked/week -> manually sending everything (~40% accept rate on LI)

I was getting solid acceptances on my cold pitch invites on my ICP LI (tbh my cold pitch was pretty 🔥)  but few were converting into conversations b/c it was still soooo cold 

I have since ditched that + now invest my time in "direct triggers" aka things like specific comments, posts, responsibilities mentioned in a job posting, sending relevant value adds (warm leads, solutions to a problem that don't have to do with me, etc.) + being more curious/ consultative vs trying to just book the meeting 

All my outbound meetings now come from LI -> I connect referencing my relevant piece of information + weave in our solution in a low pressure way, this looks different for each DM b/c each piece of info is unique.

If you're a "hunter" I highly suggest, if you have a rigid set of accounts, I don't think this is for you- assuming you can't go outside of that specific list 

It's a work in progress + my goal is to layer on more 'cold' tier 1 ICP contacts into the mix (there is value in these still!!) + build some more "scalable" plays.... but I am happy w/ how it's going so far + I guess the moral of the story is sometimes the hard route is in fact the best route 🤷‍♀️

Run gametape for every closed-won/lost for 30 days

3. Reshape targeting, messaging & spend
look for repeating combos (3x or more): 
-buying group composition vs proof type
-trigger x segment x message
-channel vs time to close

Create output statements:
(write these down)

"deals missing Z role stalled or died"
"deals with A proof type skipped budget stalls"

4. Convert patters into rules
Update your ICP and target accounts using evidence
- Accounts with [role] actively engaged
- Accounts showing [trigger]
- Include exclusions

Map proof to when it actually mattered in winning deals
-Early-stage proof that created momentum
-Mid-stage proof that reduced risk
-Late-stage proof that removed friction

6. Create named revenue plays
Turn patterns into repeatable motions, not one-off campaigns

Each "play" includes:
- Trigger to watch for
- Target segment + buying group
- Core message angle
- Required proof
- Channels involved

7. Enforce signal thresholds before sales engagement
Stop routing based on form fills or demos

Require:
- Multi-role engagement
- Trigger present
- Proof consumed

Rules to write down:
- “No AE handoff without X signals”
- “Single-contact interest ≠ opportunity”

8. Reallocate spend to assist patterns
Ignore sourced attribution

- Channels that appear before opportunity creation
- Channel combinations that shorten time to close
- Touches that show up in Closed-Won timelines

Rules to write down:
- “Spend follows pre-opportunity signals, not MQL volume”

9. Feed Closed-Won back into campaigns weekly
Every win should change something upstream

Required outputs:
- New targeting rule
- Updated message
- New asset
- Retired campaign

Rules to write down:
- “Closed-Won data updates marketing every 7 days”

Is your Google conversion bid strategy the problem?

This quadrant tells you: 

Ask yourself two questions. 

1. How many conversions do you get per month?
2. How much do your conversion values differ from each other?

E.g. 
- PLG SaaS, $300k/mo ad budget with 2-3 pricing plans = high conversions, low value variance
- Rehab clinic, $3M/mo budget with wildly variant insurance payouts= high conversions, high value variance
- Startup SMB SaaS, $25k/mo ad budget with one subscription = low conversions, low value variance
- Enterprise SaaS, $30k/mo ad budget with F500 ICP = low conversions, high value variance

Top Left:
- High volume of conversions and low value variance
- Every conversion is worth roughly the same
- Google has enough data to hit a target and every lead looks the same
- Go for tCPA

Top Right:
- High volume of conversions and high value variance
- Some conversions are worth 5x or 10x others (and you're tracking that value)
- Google has enough data AND meaningful value signals to chase your best customers
- Go for tROAS

Bottom Left:
- Low volume of conversions and low value variance
- You don't have enough data for Google to reliably hit a target yet
- Let the algorithm learn. Don't constrain it with targets it can't achieve.
- Go for Max Conversions

Bottom Right:
- Low volume of conversions and high value variance
- Still not enough data for targets, but your conversions have different values
- Let Google learn while at least prioritizing higher-value outcomes
- Go for Max Conversion Value. 

Cheatsheet: 
→ High volume + low value variance = tCPA
→ High volume + high value variance = tROAS
→ Low volume + low value variance = Max Conversions
→ Low volume + high value variance = Max Conversion Value

Marketing generates 'crap' leads 
Sales closes non marketing leads
Marketing gets the blame

But the finger-pointing is a distraction.

Your Sales and Marketing misalignment is actually a data issue disguised as a performance problem.

The old model:

Impressions > Clicks > MQLs > SQLs > Close won/lost

But we know:
MQL’s generated does not always = pipeline

The new model is:

Engagement > Prospecting > Close

Each stage has marketing and sales KPIs

What emerges are patterns that kill/improve deal velocity:

↳Speed by Source: Comparing how fast ""High Intent"" closes vs. Outbound (instead of a useless blended average).
↳Signal Density: Do deals with 3+ channels (Web + Event + Sales) move faster than single-channel deals?
↳True Win Rates: Realizing ""Demo Requests"" close at 20% while ""Content Downloads"" close at 0.1% and clog the pipeline.
↳Volatility: Which sources deliver steady, predictable revenue vs. which ones are just random luck?

These correlate to pipeline created, revenue closed, win rate, average deal size, sales cycle length.

Where marketing & Sales are measured on how efficiently accounts move from Engaged to Prospecting to Pipeline…. and then to close.

Instead of a handoff, the funnel is now unified

Here are KPI’s for each stage of the new funnel:

-Engagement-

Marketing: 
↳ # of High-Intent Opportunities"" — hand raisers + demo requests
↳ # of target accounts showing interest (web visits, content downloads, events)

Sales
↳ identifying signal initiated the conversation before opp creation
↳ Account acceptance rate: the % of marketing-engaged accounts accepted by sales for prospecting.

-Prospecting-

Marketing:
↳ what % of pipeline interacted with marketing programs *while* being actively worked by an SDR.
↳ Content effectiveness: identifying which specific assets are consumed during outreach phase that correlate to booked meetings.

Sales
↳ Attempt to Meeting rate: conversion from ""all attempts"" to ""meeting booked"" (e.g., did it take 100 calls or 5,000 calls to get 5 meetings?)
↳ Time-to-Qualify: the average duration from attempted contact to a fully qualified opportunity.

-Close-

Marketing:
↳ active deal influence: the % of open opportunities that interacted with a marketing initiative during the active sales cycle.
↳ Velocity acceleration: specific channels or content pieces that correlate with faster sales cycles and higher win rates.

Sales
↳ DQ context: tracking specific reasons for drop-off (bad timing, no budget, wrong fit) rather than just ""closed lost.""
↳ Win rate stability: measuring the consistency of win rates across specific lead sources rather than a blended average.

If your reporting ends at MQLs, you’re not measuring revenue.

The teams that fix this stop arguing about *who sourced the deal* and start asking:

“What data actually moves an account from engagement → pipeline → close?”

Curious how you’re measuring this today.

👉 Are marketing and sales aligned or still handing leads over a wall?"

I have to admit, six months ago I didn't get the point of MCPs.         
                                         
This post is for people who were like me. Also for my employees who are reluctant to start using these tools.                     
                                         
What is an MCP (Model Context Protocol)?                    
                                         
Think of it as a gateway for an AI agent to understand a tool.         
                                         
Instead of asking an agent to read API documentation (it will miss things),  
you connect it to an MCP. The agent figures out:                
 - What endpoints exist                             
 - What payloads to send                            
 - How to actually accomplish your task                     
                                         
Then you ask it to write the TypeScript or Python to make those API calls   
directly.                                   
                                         
Way more efficient. Way fewer tokens.                     
                                         
 My biggest tip:                                
                                         
 We're not actually doing a lot of work with MCPs as in moving data or doing work with MCP.             
                                         
We use them so agents understand the API documentation better.         
                                         
The MCP helps the agent learn the tool. Then we have Claude write actual code that calls the APIs.                                
                                         
That's the workflow:   
                           
 1. Connect MCP                                 
 2. Agent learns the tool                            
 3. Agent writes the automation code                      
 4. You run the code directly                          
                                        
 If you've been confused about MCPs, hopefully this helps.

PMax is beating Google Search. 

Turn it on ASAP if: 

1. Conversion volume. Don't run PMax until you’re over 50 conversions per month. Stay with Search-only (and maybe manual CPC) until you build volume. Between 50-100? Test PMax at 10-20% of budget. Over 100? PMax can scale. 

2. Tracking. Is GCLID captured on every form submit? Are UTMs applied to all Google campaigns? Does your CRM data reconcile with Google Ads within tolerance? If any of these are missing, PMax will train on incomplete data. We've seen cost per customer rise from $800 to $1,900 in three months because tracking wasn't set up correctly.

3. Conversion actions. Are you optimizing to form submits or to SQLs and opportunities? You must go as bottom funnel as possible. If you optimize to form fills, it finds the cheapest clicks - YouTube pre-roll, Gmail promos, Display placements. Aim for SQLs and opportunities as much as possible.

4. Search. Do you have stable performance from Search campaigns first? Are your keywords, match types, and negatives dialed in? PMax works best as a scaling layer on top of working Search. If Search isn't performing yet, fix that first. (assuming your vertical has search demand)

5. Negative signal process. Do you retract spam leads from Google? Unqualified leads? Test or duplicate submissions? Removing bad conversions teaches PMax what not to look for. If you get bad leads, it’s probably because you’re not retracting. 

Failed any of the above? 
→ Run Search-only with Manual CPC (if very low conv volume) for 30-60 days. 
→ Use Exact Match and Phrase Match only. 
→ Bid on high-intent terms specific to your product.

Passed all five? 
→ Introduce PMax at 10-20% of total Google spend. 
→ Compare cost per qualified lead against Search weekly. 
→ Scale when PMax matches or beats Search on down-funnel metrics.

→ Non Brand Search: $262 CPA
→ PMax: $87 CPA.

Writing like a 'publicist'

Is the hack to AEO ranking: 

- Most people write like a blogger.
- Publicists write like a distribution engine.

AEO rewards the second.

Because AI answers pull from pages that feel:

- clear
- quotable
- credible
- easy to lift

Publicists build that on purpose.

1. Lead with the headline answer
- Put the answer in the first 2 lines, not the last paragraph.
- AI grabs early clarity. Humans stay for the why.

2. Write in “pull quotes”
- Every section needs a line that can stand alone.
- If a sentence cannot be screenshotted, it is too soft.

3. Name the category fast
- Publicists label the thing so others can repeat it.
- “This is a checklist.” “This is a framework.” “This is a 3-step process.”

4. Build a one-sentence definition
- AEO loves clean definitions.
- Use: Term + means + plain English + outcome.

Example pattern:

- “AEO means writing so AI can quote you without rewriting you.”

5. Add proof without flexing
- Publicists use receipts, not ego.
- Use specifics you can defend: process, examples, constraints, sources.

Good proof looks like:
- what you did
- what changed
- what you learned
- what you would do again

6. Create a “press kit” inside the post
Make it easy to cite you.

Include mini assets AI can reuse:
- a definition
- a checklist
- a step-by-step
- a short example
- a common mistake
- a fix

One post. Many extractable parts.

7. Answer the follow-ups before they get asked
- Publicists know the next headline.

So they pre-load the clarifiers:
- who this is for
- when it works
- when it fails
- what to do first

This reduces ambiguity.

Ambiguity kills AEO.

8. Use the “two-layer” structure
- Layer 1 is the simple claim.
- Layer 2 is the mechanism.

Example:

- Claim: “Short intros rank.”
- Mechanism: “AI summaries weight early text and headings.”

Publicists always give the mechanism.

It makes the claim feel true.

9. End with a repeatable script
- Publicists ship language people can reuse.
- Give a fill-in template.

AEO intro script:
- “X is how you get Y.”
- “Here’s the mental model.”
- “Use these steps.”
- “Start with this.”

The core idea stays simple.

AEO is not a writing contest.

It's a quoting contest.

Think like a publicist.

Make your content easy to lift, easy to trust, and hard to misquote.

1. Validate cheaply (ugly ads)
2. Prove economics (CPA vs Search)
3. Upgrade creatives (structured creative)

I think we've cracked a list-building process that gets new customers started with really high-quality lists right after they onboard with us.

Here's the problem:

I'm the best list builder on my team. But when onboarding a new customer,
 we're not trying to build a 100% TAM list.

We need a really good sample, enough data to run campaigns for 1-2 months.

We can always rerun for full coverage later.

Here's the process:

Step 1: Analyze their existing data

Take their do-not-contact list or dream customer list. Enrich in Clay to find:

Industries
Department headcounts
Website keywords
Pricing strategy
Any other data points they claim matter

Clay's derived data points make this analysis deep. I LOVE the data that comes with the enrich company integration (cache it in Supabase for everyone that is going to be in my comments that it's expensive)

Step 2: Use AI to find patterns

Run it through Sculptor or GPT 5.2 to analyze:

Best industries
Most common industries
Key details beyond industry/headcount/location
What actually correlates with being a good fit

Sometimes our customers will say that a signal was important when the company purchased and that might not always be the case.

Someone thought that the ratio of SDRs to AEs on a sales team was the most important signal and all of their buyers actually all had Sales Ops on the team and the ratio of SDRs to AEs was all over the place.

Step 3: Pull companies via Prospeo.io

Now we know: "We're looking for companies in X industry because of Y reasons."

We use Prospeo to pull all companies matching the top level industry, headcount, location criteria.

Why not Clay? They are working on this but I just don't want to be messing around in a UI if I can help it now. Prospeo's search API gets what we need. 

Step 4: Enrich final data points in Clay and AI validates the list

Build a prompt that looks at their actual customers, then checks: "Are these new companies good fits?"

This also builds out the ICP process.

Step 5: OpenAI batch API

For anything custom, run through Claygent. Then batch API through GPT to verify fit.

Cache the input for 90% off. Batch API for 50% off the call.

The result:
When we onboard a customer, we throw as much data and AI cleanup at it as possible to get a really strong starter list. 

Between Clay's derived data points and the Prospeo API, you can get really far, really fast, with really high quality.

What a time to be alive in B2B go-to-market because of the availability of data and the cost of GPT processing going down.

"Brand keywords are a waste of money"
 
We spent $40.4k over 6 weeks to find out.
 
We wanted to figure out
 
• What is the optimal amount to spend on ads?
• Is Google Ads taking more credit than it should?
• Could we spend more on Google Ads and drive incremental revenue?
 
So we ran a 6 week, 3-stage test 
 
BASELINE:
 
→ Week 1: $2.2k ad spend
→ Week 2: $1.5k ad spend
 
TEST 1: (~3x BASELINE)
 
→ Week 3: $6.6k ad spend
→ Week 4: $6.5k ad spend
→ Week 5: $7.5k ad spend
 
TEST 2: (~11x BASELINE)
 
→ Week 6: $16k ad spend
 
Then we measured the results:
 
1. Layered all data
 
• Exported Google Search Console data for branded clicks on a weekly basis
• Exported Google Ads data for branded spend, clicks and conversions on a weekly basis
• Created a table for every week so we could easily see all the data
 
2. Compared time buckets
 
• Created average weekly stats for Baseline, Test 1 and Test 2 periods
• Generally, we saw as paid spend increased organic clicks decreased.
• But we wanted to see exactly how many incremental clicks were driven (after organic decreased) by spending more on ads.
 
When we spent 3x Baseline (Test 1 vs Baseline)
 
• Spent ~$5.5k more every week
• Drove +2,500 more ad clicks
• Lost -5000 organic clicks
• Net lost -2,500 clicks
• That means we paid $5.5k more and got less traffic.
• In other words, incredibly loss making
 
We then ran Test 2 (which was a ~2x increase on Test 1)
 
• Spent ~$9.1k more every week
• Drove +1000 more ad clicks
• Lost -850 organic clicks
• Net gain 150 clicks
• That means we paid 9k for a ~62x worse incremental CPA
 
All in all, it means every time we increased ad spend, we ate into our organic traffic.
 
• Most of the “extra” conversions would’ve happened anyway
• We were paying to intercept traffic we already owned
 
Dropping spend back down from $16k/week to $2k/week seems drastic.
 
• Will competitors steal our traffic if we don’t bid?
• Will our brand keeps lose surface area?
• Does losing brand mean losing customers?
 
But it’s clear from the data that the spend wasn’t incremental.
 
And now we have it and black and white.
 
So now we can add that extra $14k into generating net new demand.
 
Every brand running Google Ads should be running this test every 4 months to make sure they’re not wasting spend. We’ve run this across multiple accounts and the results always vary (spend more or spend less).

In 2025, this Google account spent $24 million 
9,365 SQLs → 6,486 Closed. 
Playbook below:
 
Context - we're targeting expensive leads + selling what is considered an 'Enterprise' service. 
 
1. Disqualifying keywords
 
- Negative keyword anything that signals self-serve: 'free', 'tool', 'how to', 'template', 'DIY', 'cheap'
- Your ad copy needs to pass the enterprise sanity-check. Use language like 'Enterprise-Grade', 'Security', 'Compliance', 'Certified'
- We ran this for a B2B SaaS client whose CAC was ~75% above target. After tightening keywords and adding ABM-style landing pages, CAC dropped to 1% below target.
 
2. Landing page friction
 
- Test listing high-ticket pricing directly on your landing page. Statements like 'starting from $25K/mo' filters out 80%+ of unqualified leads before they ever fill out a form.
- Send all paid traffic to a dedicated "Strategy Call" or "Request Demo" page. Not "Get Started" / 'Limited Slots' / "Book Now". That language is too short term and attracts SMB buyers.
- Build landing pages that show big logos, reference VP/C-suite job titles, highlight relevant certifications (e.g. SOC2/HIPAA/ISO) and use procurement-friendly language.
 
3. Budgeting cash flow
 
- For Enterprise, invest at least $100k+/month in ad spend to gather meaningful data. Below that threshold, you won't have enough conversions to optimize and the CPCs will feel painful.
- Measure success by "Qualified Meetings per week" (target 3-5) rather than raw leads or cost-per-lead. Lead volume means nothing if 80% are unqualified.
- Track conversion rate from Qualified Meetings to Deal to ensure forecast assumptions are accurate.
- Plan for an 8-12 week sales cycle. Your December Google Ads spend drives Q2 pipeline.
- If cashflow is tight, use financing solutions to bring forward revenue from closed deals and reinvest faster.
 
4. Bidding strategies
 
- Aim for 30+ conversions per month. You don't want to send Google junk conversions, but use upper funnel conversions if needed in order to get sufficient volume. Then work to move your primary conversion action down funnel as quickly as possible.
- High CPCs ($25-50+) and low click volume are expected and a signal you're reaching the right audience.
- Track impression share on high-intent terms (target 70%+), absolute top of page rate (target 50%+), and consistency in visibility over time. Provided you're getting in front of the audience and your messaging is strong, it's just a matter of exposure.
 
This playbook works because enterprise buyers are trying to answer:
 
1. 'Is this brand known & legitimate?'
2. 'Who are the top 3 players in this space?'
3. 'Do they work with other companies like us?'

There are only 3 ways to scale Healthcare Google Ads 

Search is usually the first one teams rely on.

You find some winning keywords and start cranking spend.

But eventually it loses effectiveness because:

→ Impression share for your core patient-intent keywords hits a ceiling at ~80%.
→ Cost per click (CPC) climbs 15–25% month over month.
→ You’re paying more to show ads for the same limited high-intent searches.
→ The algorithm runs out of new queries with real patient intent to target.

We see this a lot with Healthcare companies once they start scaling acquisition.

You can combat this.

There are 3 ways to scale:

(1) Search – Use exact and phrase match to capture your core audience. Remember it’s capped in volume. Scale search by expanding match types cautiously or layering in new geographies or services. Expect ~10–30% monthly volume growth before diminishing returns. Increase auctions on what’s already working. You can increase budgets (if on Max Conv) and also increase target CPA. Keep an eye on IS (budget). If it’s a high percentage (10%+) you’ve got more room to scale. But after you’ve maxed out auctions- what’s next?

(2) PMax – Uses Search, Discovery, YouTube, Gmail. Launch after non-brand search gets ~30 quality conversions per month. Ensure optimization is tied to down-funnel events (appointments, qualified calls, patient starts). If you optimize for form fills, you’ll usually bring in junk leads. Use YouTube inventory within PMax- we often see ~30% of conversions coming from YouTube placements inside these campaigns.

(3) Demand Gen – Use when you want to fill the top of the patient acquisition funnel and avoid bid inflation on Search. Launch once PMax reaches ~50 quality conversions per month. Target custom intent audiences, affinity segments, and in-market users on YouTube with a goal of +10–30% funnel volume increase in 3–6 months. Scale by testing different video lengths and creative angles (education, patient outcomes, brand stories, etc.). This also drives stronger view-through rate and watch time, which tends to increase branded search over time. For example, across Healthcare accounts we manage we’ve been able to scale spend from ~$10K/month to ~$95K+/month while maintaining stable CPCs and continuing to generate patients at scale.

Low Google Ads quality score?

That’s bad... Or is it?

A lot of teams tend to obsess over the metric.

Probably because it’s really easy to understand (simple score from 1–10).

But in reality, the quality score metric is not directly correlated with account performance

Even though its derivative metrics are used in the auction:
1. Expected Click-Through Rate (CTR): Google's prediction of how likely someone is to click your ad when it shows (based on historical performance).
2. Ad Relevance: How closely your ad matches the user's search query/keyword.
3. Landing Page Experience: How relevant, useful, and user-friendly the page is after someone clicks (e.g., fast-loading, mobile-friendly, delivers on the ad promise).

So yes, a bad quality score could indicate something is wrong…

But I’ve seen ads for healthcare companies with quality scores of 1–3 achieve a lower cost per conversion than ads with 5 and 7.

In fact, across several healthcare accounts we manage, we’ve still driven strong outcomes like:

~75–80% reduction in cost per call ($900–$1,200 → $206)
~95% reduction in cost per qualified conversion (~$26K → ~$1K)
1000+ patients and 10K+ appointment submits generated at scale

And there are so many more factors that impact Google performance

So instead of looking at quality score, look at the business metrics that matter

- Conversion rate
- Conversion values
- Conversion volume

And quality score will fall in-line.

Or not. Who cares. (:

Is AI Max driving incremental conversions? 

We spent $4.9M to find out: 
- What is the optimal amount to spend on AI Max
- Is Google AI Max taking more credit than it should?
- Could we spend more on AI Max and drive incremental revenue?

TEST: 
- Spent $4.9M on ads overall
- AI Max claimed 4 conversions
- Broad match claimed 1,543 conversions
- Phrase/exact match claimed 3,662 conversions

The issue is that AI Max competes in the same auctions as your broad match campaigns… 

ANALYSIS:
- Check search terms report for every AI Max keyword that drove conversion
- If search term matches an existing keyword (or close variant), subtract the conversion
- This shows incremental AI Max conversions

Incremental = AI Max Conversions - Existing Keywords In The Account

In this case, we only drove 4 incremental conversions at CPA of $3.6k which was 5x above target CPA. 

As Ginny Marvin wrote (will link in comments), AI Max is a repacking of existing features with better controls that help the suite of tools work better together.

ChatGPT ads are rolling out. 

How I see it unfolding (spent $200M on ads): 

1. AI Ads

ChatGPT will likely use their AI to generate your ad copy and targeting. You'll install the pixel, maybe set up server-side conversion tracking, and ChatGPT will do the rest. They’ll reduce knobs and dials for media buyers and lean heavily on automation. Think Performance Max from day one.

Google has been trying to go keywordless and fully automated for the 12+ years But there's still lots of media buying involved. So we'll see if ChatGPT can actually pull it off.

2. Data moat

If ChatGPT controls targeting and creative, the only lever you have is what data you feed it. Conversion tracking will be important: server-side tracking, clean conversion data, proper event hierarchy.

3. SEO & AEO

SEO and AEO will matter a lot. I bet ChatGPT will optimize based on the organic data they have on you as an advertiser. That's your profile, your content, anything you've already used to rank organically.

4. Ad formats

Creative isn't going to be images or videos to start. It's going to be text. Which is interesting because it's a move away from short-form video and back to text ads. Images and video will come later, but not at launch.

5. Low conversion rates

ChatGPT's conversion optimization is brand new. They won't be able to optimize the click-to-conversion path as well. I'm predicting conversion rates lower than Google Search. We'll have to see if it's worth it. 

6. Big opportunity for serious advertisers

Everyone wants to say they're running ChatGPT ads and will be trying to take advantage of the arbitrage. I expect a flood of advertisers rushing in without setting strong foundations.

The advertisers that win will be the ones who:

→ Set proper conversion tracking from day one
→ Understand why people are using ChatGPT (not just that they're using it)
→ Work within the platform's best practices instead of forcing old playbooks

7. Attribution

We see 2 ways to handle

a) Use your current model. UTM source equals chatgpt. Stitch session data together. First touch or data-driven, whatever you're already using. Credit ChatGPT the same way you credit other channels.

b) Give full attribution to ChatGPT for any touch. Then compare to your standard model. The delta between the two shows you how much incrementality ChatGPT is actually driving.

We'll be starting with b) approach to really understand the channel. You can always scale back the attribution later once you understand the true impact.

This is just my predictions + internal playbook based on $200M+ ad spend and having seen Meta, Google, Snap Inc., and TikTok feature roll outs over the last 10 years.

Our plans:

→ We're managing ~$7m+ in ad spend per month across multiple platforms.
→ We'll be allocating 5-10% of total ad spend to start - depending on existing monthly spend.
→ Track, measure, scale what works.

Agencies MUST be held accountable to revenue.

But if they’re missing targets:

They need to:
- Make the gap visible fast
- Identify the constraint
- Bring in new resources

This is how we do it at TNT Growth

1. VISIBILITY
- Have a dashboard tracking actuals vs forecasts
- Growth managers should review it daily 
- Slack reporting should identify any gaps early 
- Track at multiple altitudes: monthly pace, campaign contribution, and 72-hour shifts
- Monitor leading indicators that predict problems before they hit revenue
- Click-to-lead dropping signals landing page or audience issues
- Lead-to-admit dropping signals quality or follow-up issues
- E.g. Reporting shows 0.5x more leads converted over last 3 days = red flag

2. CONSTRAINT
- If a gap is measured, investigation takes priority 
- Constraint is identified, and verified.
- It’s communicated clearly in messaging
- Follow a diagnostic sequence rather than guessing:

→ First, external factors: competition, seasonality, platform updates
→ Second, tracking integrity: broken pixels, attribution drift, CRM sync failures
→ Third, campaign mechanics: bids, budgets, audience fatigue, creative decay
→ Fourth, downstream factors: sales follow-up speed, capacity

3. RESOURCING
- Growth Managers have power to pull in resources on demand
- This allows for promptly fixing the gap and getting back to targets
- Structure the team so growth managers own outcomes, specialists own craft
- Maintain capacity margin so someone is available when things break
- Build clear escalation paths so everyone knows who handles what
- Pre-authorize certain actions: bid increases, pausing underperformers, emergency creative requests
- E.g. Bid is increased without approval need and specialists fixes tracking in 3 hours 

It’s ok to occasionally fall behind target. 
I’m not going to make out that we hit every number perfectly. 
No agency or in-house team can do that

But it’s NOT ok to fall behind target and not see it. 
Or to see it, and then not allocate more resources to fix it

Founders frequently ask me:
“How do we know if ads are working?”

This is a key growing pain under $5m ARR

But the mistake is thinking the answer is:
→ buying expensive/inaccurate attribution software
→ hiring a full time marketing ops person

But the truth is:

If you need complex software to prove your ads work… they probably don’t.

You only need 3 signals:
1. Did pipeline increase after we turned them on?
2. Did sales cycles get shorter?
3. Did deal size or win-rate improve?

If none of those moved,
ads are just generating noise.

Now the practical hack most teams miss:
Account & identity resolution

This is the fastest way to see whether ads are actually touching real buyers.

It’s not perfect but it is a directional truth.

Here’s how:

1. Get Unify and create this audience filter:
a. “high intent” AND
b. page views containing “demo” “trial” etc.
c. 5+ sessions in last 30days
d. utm source = [list ad sources]

This list is the accounts your ads are reaching

You’re looking for an account match = 80%+

2. Get RB2B pixel on your site
RB2B will start finding real people visiting your site
it will also find emails & LinkedIn profiles

3. Cross-reference these two data points
-Export your top 50-100 accounts from Unify
-Export your last 7 days of RB2B identities

Match them using company domain

Track this number: % of RB2B identities that belong to Unify high-intent accounts

That’s your ad contribution score.

How to interpret it

-70–80%+ match:
→ Ads are hitting real buyers at real target accounts

-30–50% match:
→ Targeting is leaky, but salvageable

<20% match:
→ You’re paying to educate the wrong market

Takes less than 20mins/week

And you don’t need expensive attribution dashboards

I think most people are wasting their LinkedIn outreach thinking of it like email instead of it's own channel. Here's the 3 strategies I'd do instead. 

I was speaking to James Winter about some suggestions I had for his portcos with Claude code and such and I brought up how one of their portcos wanted to sync LinkedIn outreach with email. 

"We think if we email them twice, we should move over to LinkedIn."

In my opinion, that's a waste of the channel. 

LinkedIn outreach (especially using voice notes) 99/100 times has higher reply rates than cold email but lacks the ability to scale without fake accounts. 

If you only had 25-50 connection requests to send per day, why would you use the same strategy of email where the channel scales linearly. 

When you're doing LinkedIn outreach, I'd focus on these things first. 

1) Use a tool like Trigify.io or some Rapid API endpoints to find your ICP engaging and connecting with customers you have permission to name drop. 

Find everyone engaging with your customer's employees posts and their company page.

Don't say, "I saw you engaging with my customer's post" but instead send your regular message you usually would but leave a custom variable in your social proof line of your message to reference that customer.

Instead of sending a message saying, "We help companies like {{company they have never heard of}}...." you can name drop that customer case study who they will of course know. 

2) Install every website deanonymization software on your site with a free trial. if they do contact lookup, clean them up and make sure they are ICP. If they do company lookup, use Clay or Prospeo.io to find contacts. 

Target people and companies with a high likelihood of being on your site. 

Again, don't mention anything about being on the site. Just reach out like you normally would and put a little delay on it. 

Track which tools give you the highest reply rates/success and pay for them. 

Probably a whole post can be dedicated on why I suggest you try them all for your niche but it's free, so trust me on this one. 

3) Reach out to people showing intent about your solution/problem/they are doing research/etc by targeting people in your ICP engaging with posts on the topic (or your competitor's post....) 

Same strategy here, just going a little bit more broad and using the last amount of capacity you'll have because of the limits of reaching out from 1 account. 

So instead of thinking about LinkedIn as an extension of email, remember you only get so many shots on goal and the reply rates are so much higher on LinkedIn. Use them to reach out to some of your hottest leads.

How to drive incremental Search revenue

With Microsoft Ads:

I've been running Microsoft ads since 2015 when I managed Search at Salesforce.

Here's the playbook I follow:

1. Budget allocation

- Start with 5-10% of your Google Search budget
- The larger your total budget, the lower the percentage
- You need enough spend to make the test viable - at least $5K/month, ideally $7.5K. This depends on CPA as well - ideally enough to get 10+ unbranded conversions per month

2. What to expect

- CPCs will be 2-3x lower than Google
- Landing page conversion rates will be 2-3x lower too
- Cost per customer should be even with Google (or better)
- If it's not even, you're not spending enough on Microsoft for the algo to learn - increase spend until it levels out
- That typically happens at 10-20% of Google budget
- Caveat: before increasing spend make sure everything is set up correctly and unit economics point to a reason why Microsoft Ads are underperforming

3. Conversion benchmarks

- Need 10+ unbranded conversions to evaluate if the channel has potential
- 30 conversions/month is Microsoft's minimum for smart bidding to keep optimizing
- Run a 30-day test, compare ROAS/CPA, then reallocate based on results

4. Campaign setup

- Mirror your Google campaign structure
- Only launch exact and phrase match keywords
- If you want to be conservative, only launch your highest-converting keywords from Google
- Find the primary conversion action that will give you enough conversion volume while still optimizing for quality. This may need to be more upper funnel than Google when first starting
- Consolidate campaigns to pool conversion data. Microsoft only has 3.6% of search volume vs Google's 91%, so the algorithm needs more help learning
- Make sure search partners are turned off
- For B2B, use LinkedIn profile targeting (company, industry, job function)

Here's the results with one of our clients in 2025:

Google ads:
- Spend: $925K
- CPL: $1,176
- CPA: $12,000

Microsoft ads:
- Spend: $140K
- CPL: $1,105
- CPA: $6,100

Half the acquisition cost on the same lead quality.

Microsoft users convert worse on landing pages (2-3x lower conversion rates), but once they enter the funnel, they close around the same or better. 

We’re observing less comparison shopping. Bing is their default browser, they search something up, click what catches their eye, and move on. 

I am not saying Microsoft will replace Google.

But as a secondary channel?

It's proven to be solid incremental volume at comparable/better unit economics.

Test Microsoft ads ASAP if:

- Your offer has clear search demand
- You've got budget to test ($5K-7.5K/month minimum)
- You're getting 100-200+ conversions/month on Google Search

this 'dumb’ ad beats most saas creative

This is how:

1. It doesn’t say “need a manicure?”. It’s pattern interrupting.

In b2b stop saying “want more leads?”, start saying:

HubSpot: Where go-to-market teams got to grow
Jira: Focus on OUTCOMES, not admin
Calendly: Easy scheduling ahead
ClickUp: maximize human productivity
Zoom: Find out what’s possible when work connects
Customer.io: Say more, more powerfully

2. The hook is nostalgic. It’s the Old Spice “look at your man, now back at me” ad. Instant familiarity and curiosity.

Salesforce ads are shot like movie trailers (some featuring Matthew McConaughey)
-Big tech companies care about embedding inside of culture - follow their lead.

-monday.com: clean, color coded & easy to read workflows
-Salesforce: technical sales dashboards, pipeline views, forecasting screens
-Gong: waveforms, call transcripts; sales leaders instantly know its for them

4. It creates a status gap: distance between reality and dream state.

We market “freedom” as the dream state when marketing to real estate investors.
-Reality: stuck in the grind
-Dream state: live and work passively, here’s “our way” to do it.

Your B2B ad shouldn’t sell “more ROI”.
It should: “look like the smart [ICP] who fixed this before it blew up”. 
Status>features.

The ad is entire about “here’s the difference between you and the ideal.”

Slack: showed teams before vs after
You = email chaos
Ideal = real-time collaboration

Notion: didn’t explain databases, docs, wikis
Instead: “Your thinking is messy. The best structure theirs”
You = scattered notes
Ideal = second brain

HubSpot: never said “we do inbound marketing”
Instead: “some companies grow. The best ones grow better”
You = random tactics
Ideal = systematic growth

6. Doesn’t say “also pedicures, lashes, waxing.” One promise, one visual.
That’s why it hits in under a second.

-Most B2B ads die from trying to communicate 5 benefits at once instead of one sharp angle

It’s raising the creative bar inside your company so your team treats “dumb” local ads like this as mandatory study material for hooks, callouts, and status gaps…

Lovable grew YouTube spend to $26M in 2 months

Here’s their playbook: 

Data:
- Pre-November: Testing a couple ads per month
- Mid-November: Two hit ads launched
- Last 2 months: from $313k to $26M in spend

That's an 83x increase in spend in 60 days.

Their hit ads all follow the same structure

0 to 5 seconds:
→ Open with a random fun fact, akin to organic content.
→E.g. 1: "Americans eat 3 billion slices of pizza every year. Enough to cover Manhattan five times over" ($3.4M all-time spend)
→ E.g. 2: "Humans eat more than 15 billion pounds of chocolate every year" ($2.5M all-time spend)
→ E.g. 3: "A hundred years ago, a man named Michael J. Owens invented a glass factory that could make 240 bottles per minute" ($2M all-time spend)

5 to 25 seconds:
→ They then keep going deeper into the fun fact
→ Viewer learns something genuinely interesting they can share with friends
→ 20 seconds of pure entertainment (before any pitch)
→ Gets their mind engaged and thinking about "how things changed"
→ Pizza E.g.: "So how do we make so much pizza? Industrial ovens cook 200 pizzas per hour. What used to take generations of secret recipes, hand-toasted dough, wood-fried perfection, now uses rolls of conveyor belts."

25 to 30 seconds:
→ Tie back the random fun fact to Lovable's core message
→ It's always going from something that used to be complex and slow to now simple and fast
→ It feels like a natural next line, not a forced pitch
→ E.g. 1: "And that's exactly what's happening with starting an online business"
→ E.g. 2: "The same revolution is happening to app development"

30+ seconds
→ Speed is the core USP, they are immediately showing how fast it is to use
→ Any product with a quick 'aha' moment can do this
→ E.g. 1: "Create an app that rates images of pizza using AI with sharing features"
→ E.g. 2: "Building this literally took 3 minutes"
→ Classic product led growth with the demo selling itself

Lovable's ads fit perfectly for YouTube.

I wouldn't be surprised if Elena Verna is the one pulling the growth levers on this. It's awesome.

YouTube:
- Entertainment first, value for the viewer, then product
- Feels like organic content you'd actually watch
- 20+ seconds of content before the pitch

Vs traditional Meta ads:
- Pattern interrupt and stop the scroll
- Quick hook in first 3 seconds
- Direct response, get to the offer fast

I'm not saying Meta-style ads don't work on YouTube. We run $700K/month on YouTube with repurposed Meta-style ads. They're a great way to start on the platform without additional creative cost.

Bottom line:
1. Understand why people are on the platform (YouTube = entertainment + education)
2. Give them something valuable before you pitch (20+ seconds of pure entertainment)
3. If your product has a quick a-ha moment, show it immediately
4. Make content that fits the platform, not content that interrupts it

How mature SaaS think about customer journey

In 4 stages:

-How do customers discover us? (marketing)
-How do they become a customer? (sales)
-What is the experience after they purchase? (CS)
-How do they interact with the product and expand? (product + cs/sales)

A systems map can clearly lay out the “happy path” for customers.

Here’s how to build one for marketing/sales:

1. Secret shop: audit the current experience by clicking every button and submitting every form.
-pro tip: actually schedule a call/demo with your sales team to ‘feel’ the experience.

2. Map the “current” logic: document the full experience in Miro/Whimsical to establish a baseline.

3. ID the single most important marketing entry point (e.g. demo/trial) - is all traffic ending there?

4. Draw the “Happy Path” from left to right, from traffic source to conversion.

5. Draw subordinate paths - these are usually other lead magnets + content.

How to sign $100k to $1M/year deals with Google Ads

Don't:
→ Turn on Smart Bidding
→ Launch Performance Max
→ Wonder why lead quality tanks.

We've spent $1M+/mo on this high-ticket Google Ads playbook:

1. Start with $20K/month minimum
→ Can work at $10K ad spend but results get volatile
→ You need enough budget to collect data across keywords, ad copy, and landing pages
→ Anything less and you're guessing

2. Use Manual CPC bidding
→ Not Target CPA
→ Not Maximize Conversions
→ Smart Bidding needs data density you don't have at 5 leads a week
→ Stay manual until you hit 50+ conversions per month

3. Only bid on high-intent keywords
→ For e.g. target "[Your service] for large companies" or "Enterprise [solution]"
→ Avoid "[Your service] cheap" or "best [solution] for free" (these attract SMBs)

4. Skip Performance Max
→ PMax mixes YouTube, Gmail, Display, and Search into one campaign
→ It needs massive data to optimize placement mix
→ At 5 leads a week, it'll burn budget on low-quality placements before learning anything

5. Add hard qualifiers to your landing page
→ Before any form fields, ask: Annual budget? Employee count? Timeline?
→ Filter for big budgets and high employee counts
→ Lead volume will likely drop but quality goes up

6. Plan for a 90-day bake period
→ High-ticket B2B has long sales cycles
→ You won't know true ROAS for 60-90 days after a lead comes in
→ Expect $2K-$3K per qualified meeting while the system learns

Bottom line:
→ Google Ads works for high-ticket B2B but needs intentional structure
→ Stay manual, stay focused on high-intent, filter aggressively
→ Give it 90 days before deciding if it's working

Starting a cold email/DM with "Saw your comment on NAME's post" and then pitching their company/product.

Now, in the big picture of stuff to GAF about today, this is item #12127862483. But, I'm writing this because it's clear many sellers are still being told to do it. And this post is to share an alternate POV. 

I'm a big believer in assuming positive intent. I believe most sellers who use this tactic think they're personalizing the email. It's well-intentioned. 

But, there are a couple downsides:

If a reader reads it - they often fwd it to the author of the post, asking "Do you have a relationship with COMPANY? Are you aware of this outreach?". When they're told no, they often come back with, "That's weird".

Further, it unintentionally penalizes the author of the post. If you comment on Mary Smith's post, then receive cold emails with "Saw you commented on Mary's post", you're going to think twice about commenting on Mary's posts again. 

Prospecting is HARD. And, it keeps getting harder. I love when sellers try new ideas. But, IMO, this is a tactic we can retire.

Are your Google ads optimized right? 

This quadrant tells you: 

Ask yourself two questions. 
1. How many conversions do you get per month?
2. How much do your conversion values differ from each other?

E.g. 
- PLG SaaS, $300k/mo ad budget with 2-3 pricing plans = high conversions, low value variance
- Rehab clinic, $3M/mo budget with wildly variant insurance payouts= high conversions, high value variance
- Startup SMB SaaS, $25k/mo ad budget with one subscription = low conversions, low value variance
- Enterprise SaaS, $30k/mo ad budget with F500 ICP = low conversions, high value variance

Top Left:
- High volume of conversions and low value variance
- Every conversion is worth roughly the same
- Google has enough data to hit a target and every lead looks the same
- Go for tCPA

Top Right:
- High volume of conversions and high value variance
- Some conversions are worth 5x or 10x others (and you're tracking that value)
- Google has enough data AND meaningful value signals to chase your best customers
- Go for tROAS

Bottom Left:
- Low volume of conversions and low value variance
- You don't have enough data for Google to reliably hit a target yet
- Let the algorithm learn. Don't constrain it with targets it can't achieve.
- Go for Max Conversions

Bottom Right:
- Low volume of conversions and high value variance
- Still not enough data for targets, but your conversions have different values
- Let Google learn while at least prioritizing higher-value outcomes
- Go for Max Conversion Value. 

Cheatsheet: 
→ High volume + low value variance = tCPA
→ High volume + high value variance = tROAS
→ Low volume + low value variance = Max Conversions
→ Low volume + high value variance = Max Conversion Value

Just helped a $5m saas find 30 ready to buy accounts sitting in their crm

Here’s how:

Every account is scored from 0-100%
- 100% = big deal, short sales cycle
- 0% = no intent, no clear data, out of market, bad fit
- SDR’s attack score 70%+

Score is based on 25 automatically populated variables. e.g. here are the best 5:

1. Competitor presence: ai scrapes case studies on competitor pages, checks press releases & credible news, and a set of universal account urls

2. Financial pressure: clay scrapes official webpages, announcements from past 12 months with keywords: budget freeze, funding cuts, reduced state funding for [industry], reduced federal funding for [industry], hiring freeze, cost containment measures.

3. Account fit signals: score accounts on ICP match level. 100% need to be true to pass ICP match: industry, revenue, tech stack (via builtwith / Theirstack), operational complexity = high/medium/low (low = increase score 10%). Most important: at least 75% of buying committee is identified in CRM.

4. Contract renewal timing: enterprise saas often makes quiet announcements about partnerships.
- We scraped for contract announcements using ai
- Mapped 1 and 3 year contract renewal dates based on announcement date
- Backed out our sales cycle time (5 months)
- *found 11 accounts that were up for renewal in next buying cycle.

5. Buyer committee engagement: map 5 contacts per account, and map social & intent signals. If all 5 buyers are “green flag”, buyer committee category = 100% signal.
- Champion: awarded when contact interacts 7x (in 7 days)
- Decision maker: green flag when has positive engagement (comment/like, lead mag submit, demo submit) 4x in a month.
- Influencer: 3x per week visits
- User: checks help center, product content 3x in set amount of time
- Blocker: no activity in last 7 days = positive signal

Custom weighting logic:
20% → Competitor presence
15% → Financial pressure
15% → Account fit signals
10% → Contract renewal timing
10% → Buying committee engagement
30% → 20 other variables

There’s a version of this for every b2b saas, and the more custom variables, the better your account scoring will be.

In 2025, we launched 1,517 campaigns and generated over 60k positive responses across all of our customers. Here's 9 things we learned from the data. 

We had an AI analyze the offer, the leads in the campaign, and we made an AI summary. 

I threw 30 Claude sub agents at the database to answer a bunch of questions and here's what we learned. 

1. Our success metrics and average success of a campaign looks way different than it was 3 years ago. 

3 years ago, I said a campaign was successful and should be scaled if it was getting 1 positive response for every 300 people you reach out to. 

The numbers have moved for sure. I asked Claude to put our email response into quintiles and the results are in the screenshot. 

2. 70-90 words was optimal for email length

3. 2 Steps in an email sequence is ideal. 3 is ok. Anything over 3, HUGE reply drop off

4. For subject lines, including first name correlated with higher reply rates. I think this goes against 💜 🔮 Will Allred's data so I publish this at my peril. 

5. Monday - Thursday BEST reply days. Claude was saying we shouldn't even send on Fridays. Not sure we will make that leap but might be a good tip for those of you with a small market.

6. Heavy Spintax actually hurt some of our campaigns. It found lighter spintax did better. I think this has something to do with keeping control of the messaging with less variation

7. Industries that performed best for us - SaaS, Schools, Restaurants, E-commerce. This is for sure skewed by our data. We just have a lot of people targeting SaaS and then the people targeting Schools and Restaurants have crazy offers. 

8. Naming a case study actually hurt performance vs. just talking about outcomes. Definitely something I'm going to be keeping in mind. 

9. Generic AI personalization killed reply rates. 

I wanted to dig deeper into this one to see what it meant. We have naming conventions for our custom variables that match some templates we have in Clay so after manually reviewing, I could eye ball it and know what it meant. 

The generic AI that killed our reply rates was this trite, "Hey Eric, I saw you help people send cold email and I had a question." type stuff. 

Half way through the year, Taylor Haren even told me he thinks those are garbage and we reviewed mid year and I agreed

This was the AI that it said was garbage too. Any custom variable that was not in our template library and some custom template ones all correlated with higher response rates. 

I still have all the data. If you could ask a question about the success or failure of our campaigns, what would you ask it? 

DISCLAIMER: this is based on our internal data and might be skewed because of the customers we work with one way or another. If you have a question of your own campaigns, I always recommend not listening to people like me and just doing your own testing.

This account spent $3.2M on Google 

With ‘bad’ ads: 

Explainer: 
- The last column is ‘Search Lost IS (rank)’
- Search Lost IS (rank) tells you %age of auctions lost due to low ad rank. 
- Ad rank = bid, ad quality and landing page experience.
- So a low ad rank = a bad ad right? 
- And Google is saying “we don’t like your ad”

Search online for this situation. 

The most common advice will be to ‘improve your ad quality’ 

But that doesn’t make any sense.

When we’re scaling accounts to $1M+ in spend we almost always expect Search Lost IS rank to go down. 
- You get entered into more auctions
- You are exposed to more queries
- These queries / searchers are lower intent
- Your ad wins the auction less because it’s not as relevant for that specific searcher / query

Here’s an example:
- You are running Google Ads for CRM software
- Your account does well for core terms like “crm software” and “sales crm”
- Your unit economics are attractive so you expand your budget
- You now match to queries such as “service crm”, “sales forecasting software”, etc
- While you support these, they aren’t what you’re known for
- These queries have a lower expected CTR and a higher CPC
- Leading to less auctions won due to “rank”
- But overall the account still performs the algo is still finding pockets of users to show up in those auctions

So provided you’re increasing budget, losing auctions due to rank is completely expected. 

Instead, ask: 
- Does funnel math still make sense?
- Is CPA still within tolerance?
- Are total conversions up?
- Is revenue growing?
