This is $100M GTM process
(no attribution model needed)

Step 1: Create Signal

Signal = any communication that reaches your customers

“Buyer ready” signal = impression frequency X channel diversity
- Minimum frequency: 3.5x weekly impressions per unique contact within your target account
- Channel diversity: minimum of 3 channels in the same week
- If enterprise: signal must reach at least 3 distinct personas within the buying committee
If you hit all of these = call the prospect

What to say in your signal:

- If they know something's wrong but not why → explain the root cause. Dont’ say: "Your sales are low." Say: "Your sales are low because the [X] protocol in your CRM was never designed for [Y] data types.”

-If they already understand the problem → show why your solution is different. Don't say "We solve [problem]." Say "Unlike tools that require manual setup, ours runs on [unique mechanism] so you get results in 48 hours, not 6 weeks.”

Step 2: Detect Signal

This is where most teams fail.

“Hot” / ready buyers need:
- 18-22 touchpoints per account tracked in CRM (less per Lead)
- 40% minimum from paid channels
- 3+ active channels simultaneously
- 70% of buying committee identified + receiving signal
- *Sales can find these “Hot” leads in the CRM.

Cold > Warm have:
- 3–5 touchpoints
- 1 "high-value" intent signal (e.g., attending a webinar, downloading a whitepaper, or 3+ ad clicks).
- Automated Marketing and ads that surround the buying committee. Education sequences work well here.

Top 5 tools that find hidden signals:
- ZenABM / Fibbler: LinkedIn ads
- RB2B: identify website visitors + enrich
- Customer.io: preferred for marketing automation
- Outreach.io: traditional email/sms/call sequencing
- Unify: signal based outbound sequencing

Step 3: Convert
Don’t pass sales a “Hot” lead and expect them to have full context.

Send them:
- The one signal that triggered “Hot”
- All recorded signals in the past 14 days
- Which 3 personas are active?
- What problem are the researching? (grab this from ads & emails they engaged with)

Sales protocol:
First sales touch must happen within 30 minutes, ideally sooner.
 -Don't say: "I saw you clicked our ad 4 times."
- Say: "I noticed your team is looking into [X]—most companies at your stage struggle with [Root Cause from Step 1]. Here’s how we handle that differently."

Sales followup shouldn’t feel like bombardment. Use the 3x3x3 rule for booked meetings:
→ 3 touches
→ 3 channels
→ Within first 3 day of Hot trigger

If the first 2 touches get no response, Sales drops the "pitch" and sends value-add asset:

"I saw the team was looking at [X] integration docs; here is a 60-sec video on how that specifically fixes the [Y] issue."

Marketing targets with CTA video ads:
→ Book a demo
→ Strategy/consultation session
→ Custom proposal

I spent over $3M on Meta ads in January.

And I use 3 attribution models: 

Ad platforms are notorious for taking credit for view-through conversions they didn't drive. They do it to bait you into spending more.

The issue is that your top 1-2% of ads should drive ~50% of your spend and revenue. If you're relying on bad attribution, you won’t be able to find them.

This is why 8-9 figure brands (that NEED their tracking to be faultless), use 3 attribution models:

1. Multi-touch attribution (MTA) - for ad and campaign level optimization. This is your Triple Whale. Great for knowing which ads are performing best, which ones to scale, which to cut. Not as good for comparing channel to channel. It also will overcount total revenue, which you need to be careful about. To make sure your account is well optimized, plot CPA vs Spend on a scatter plot. The top ads should be in the low CPA, high spend zone.

2. Post-purchase survey - for channel level allocation. Get a 35%+ response rate, extrapolate to all new customers, and calculate your cost per new customer response per channel. This tells you which channel to push into. Click-based attribution overvalues lower-funnel performance by up to 250%. Post-purchase surveys catch what click attribution misses - top-of-funnel creative can drive 13X more incremental acquisitions than bottom-of-funnel.

3. Marketing Mix Model (MMM) - for validating direction. You can't use this daily, but it confirms your post-purchase survey is sending you the right way. Then you use post-purchase on a daily basis to optimize channel allocation. Some channels drive low-quality customers that look good on ROAS but don't stick around. MMM helps you optimize for 12-month profit as opposed to just immediate return.

The other thing to know is that view-through attribution is poor signal. Make sure your attribution is set up for 7 or 14 day click, depending on your purchase funnel. One day view will overcount.

Here's what this gives you:

When performance drops, you know exactly where to pull budget to create the smallest impact on revenue while keeping the company profitable. When things are going well, you know exactly where to push budget to scale effectively.

Bottom line:

-> Use MTA for ads and campaigns. 
-> Use post-purchase surveys for channel allocation. 
-> Use MMM to validate you're heading the right direction.

This is how 8-9 figure brands figure out where every dollar should go.

The marketing funnel is 'dead'

Google research calls it "the messy middle."

They found that humans loop in circles between two modes:

1. Exploration (expanding options)

→ They see your ad
→ They read a review
→ They watch a TikTok
→ They forget about you
→ They search a competitor
→ They see a retargeting ad
→ They come back

2. Evaluation (narrowing options)

→ They compare
→ They weigh
→ They hesitate
→ They loop back to exploration
→ They finally buy

This loop is where you win or lose.

Click-based attribution overvalues lower-funnel performance by up to 250%.

It only sees the last touch before purchase.

(Not the 17 loops that happened before)

So how do you actually understand what's working?

You can triangulate with three models:

1. Multi-touch attribution (MTA)

→ Tools like Triple Whale 
→ Best for ad-level optimization and creative decisions
→ Shows which ads are driving clicks and conversions
→ Limitation: still biased toward lower-funnel touchpoints

2. Post-purchase surveys (need 35%+ response rate)

→ Ask customers how they actually found you
→ Best for channel allocation decisions
→ Reveals touchpoints that pixel-based tracking can't see
→ Limitation: memory is imperfect, recency bias is real

3. Marketing Mix Models (MMM)

→ Statistical modeling across all channels
→ Best for validating long-term profitability
→ Shows whether your brand spend is building equity or burning cash
→ Limitation: requires months of data, slow to react

No single model tells the truth.

And even all three models don't show you all the loops.

But it helps...

The takeaway:

→ Don't just make sales ads.
→ Make content that helps people explore (lifestyle videos) and evaluate (comparison content)
→ Be present throughout the loop, not just at 'BOFU'
→ Stop trusting single-touch attribution

The brands winning on Meta in 2025 aren't the ones with the best last-click ROAS.

They're the ones who understand the loop and show up everywhere inside it.

Did you know:

‘Bad’ Google ad keywords don’t exist: 

Just bad bids. 

Example: 
- Your target CPA is $50. Google spends $5 per click and it converts at $80
- You think the keyword just has bad intent, so you pause the keyword 

But what if you dropped your max CPC bid by 30-40% (via smart bidding)? 
- Google is forced to find cheaper auctions (that still convert)
- You spend $3 per click, it converts at same rate, but now at $48 CPA

Yes - you’ll get less volume at this bid…

But you’re within your CPA targets. 

This is because every keyword has a value threshold. A CPC where the math works out. 

You can go through all your old keywords and do this exercise:

1. Pull your "paused for performance" keywords
2. Calculate actual CPA vs target CPA
3. For keywords within 2x your target, test reactivating at 40-50% lower bids
4. Give it 2-3 weeks of data before judging

I've seen "bad" keywords become good performers once the bid matched their true value.

Bottom line:

Before you pause a keyword, ask if you've tested it at multiple bid levels. 

Most advertisers haven't.

Because we got rid of the traditional revenue funnel

And started building Growth Loops.

-A funnel would say: how do we push more people through?
- Loops ask: how do we make the next buyer easier to win?

Funnels usually looks like this:
1. Get traffic
2. Turn traffic to leads
3. Nurture them
4. Sales converts

The assumption is that for every visitor you add to the system:
- conversion rates will hold
- more revenue is created

In reality, growth is a series of loops.

Each loop has 6 parts:
1. Trigger – what starts the cycle
2. Action – user or system behavior
3. Value creation – user gets value
4. Output Artifact – something is produced
5. Distribution – it reaches new users
6. Re-entry – new users re-enter the system and repeat the cycle

A few examples of common b2b loops:

Demand Generation:
1. Publish opinionated education
2. Attract buyers who agree with your worldview
3. Those buyers implement → get results → become proof
4. Use that proof in distribution
5. Proof attracts more pre-educated buyers
6. Repeat

Customer Success <> Sales Loop:
1. CS captures how customers actually win
2. They document the playbook/benchmarks/before-after
3. Sales uses real customer mechanisms in demos and pitches
4. Prospects see themselves in the proof
5. Prospects convert to customers
6. New customers follow proven path
7. CS captures their wins
8. Repeat

How to know if you built a funnel or growth loop?

Stop publishing for 60 days, if:
- Demand collapses = you built a funnel
- Demand slows = you built a loop

KPI’s to track in looped growth systems
 -Cycle time - how fast the loop completes
- Loop throughput - artifacts produced per week
- Loop coefficient - new entrants per cycle
- Decay - how long artifacts remain effective
- Downstream multipliers - impact on sales cycle, win rate, retention etc.

Pro tip: organize your team incentives around these KPI’s
→ It will create cross team alignment
→ Teams work together more, on more impactful sprints of work.

“Google ads isn’t working”

Depends on your sales cycle: 

At $10K/mo ad spend with a 6-month sales cycle, you won't see cash back until month 7.

$10K × 6 months = $60K spent before your first dollar returns.

Tons of businesses would stop at month 3 because "ads aren't working." 

The ads are working. 

The cash just hasn't arrived yet

Here's how to budget for long sales cycles:
→ You need 2x your sales cycle in ad budget runway
→ 6-month sales cycle = 12 months of budget saved up
→ If you can't commit to that, you'll quit before the cash hits

Which in quarters means: 
→ Q1 ad spend → Q3 cash return
→ Q2 ad spend → Q4 cash return

What to track (leading vs lagging):
→ Lagging indicator: Revenue (shows up in 6 months)
→ Leading indicators: Meetings booked, SQLs created (show up in weeks)
→ Optimize for Day 14 events (SQL created), not Day 90-180 events (deal closed)

How to deal with the cashflow gap:
→ Structure deals with upfront retainers
→ First month payment covers your ad spend before the client fully onboards
→ This creates a negative CAC scenario where cash arrives before the sales cycle ends

Always factor in your sales cycle length before you adjust your ad strategy.

More often that not it can be solved on the sales side first.

I wish I fixed these things before they broke:

1. GTM repeatability - what worked stops scaling
- Founder-led sales, heroics, and single-channel growth plateau
- Pipeline becomes noisy, forecasts swing, quota attainment stalls
- Investment in the business hasn’t paid off (or won’t ever)

What makes it worse:
- Randomly testing new channels

How to fix:
→ Run win/loss analysis to understand common patterns
→ Redesign gtm strategy around winning patterns
→ Scale based on LTV:CAC winners

2. Growth becomes expensive
- CAC rises as headcount and channels expand
- ARR per employee drops
- Upmarket drift lengthens sales cycles before orgs are ready
- Partners/affiliates max out & stop promoting

What makes it worse:
- Reducing adspend because “marketing isn’t working”

How to fix:
→ Find winning GTM patterns from your data
→ Align marketing > sales > cs > product around new gtm strategy
→ Hire to support the strategy
→ Control labor and ad spend
→ Invest heavily when you have strategic validation

3. Retention becomes a real growth constraint
- Onboarding & activation begin to show cracks at scale
- Expansion is unpredictable.
- CS stops relaying customer wins to sales and marketing

What makes it worse:
- Adding headcount to cover for bandwidth issues

How to fix:
→ Expedite 10 customers to success
→ Record their process/playbook
→ Create video testimonials, case studies > send to marketing/sales
→ Flood the market with positive sentiment and customer wins.
→ This gets the best-future customers into the pipeline, who CS can win with.
→ Remove more time-intensive customers from the pipeline

For founders/execs: net revenue retention is a weekly reported metric. 100% NRR is standard - and for some high ACV businesses - 120% is required.

4. Product roadmap becomes less about growth
- CEO hands off product vision
- Prod/eng delivers “me too” features, innovation slows
- Teams need different tools to help support efficiency, not growth

What makes it worse:
- CEO setting product strategy

How to fix:
→ Founders need to align Product team around vision
→ Let them run strategy (with approval) & execution (without approval)
→ Run a well managed customer advisory board

5. 1 team turns into 7 silos
- Marketing advertises stale messaging
- Sales close rates decline due to poor lead quality
- CS stops communicating customer wins & case studies
- Product & engineering build features not tied to company strategy
- C-suite feels completely out of the loop; lack of clarity & poor decision making

What makes it worse:
- More cross functional meetings (stop immediately)

The only way to fix is with Growth Loops
→ CS finds successful customers
→ Create case studies & playbooks on “how they did it”
→ Marketing advertises the successes & playbooks
→ Leads come to sales armed better educated on the Unique Mechanism
→ Sales closes faster
→ CS has more success w/ clients. Repeat.

There are only 3 ways to scale Healthcare Google Ads

Increasing budget is the worst one. 

You find some winning keywords and start cranking spend

But eventually it loses effectiveness because:
→ You hit impression share ceilings
→ Cost per click starts climbing
→ You're paying more for the same searches
→ The algorithm runs out of high-intent queries to show you on

You can combat against this. 

There are 3 ways to scale:

(1) Vertical - increase auctions on what's already working. You can increase budgets (if on Max Conv), and you can also increase target CPA. When costs climb too high, pull target CPA back down to control efficiency. Keep an eye on IS (budget). If it’s a high percentage (10%+) you’ve got more room to scale. But after you’ve maxed out auctions - what’s next?

(2) Horizontal - expand keywords to reach new searches. This happens naturally if you're running broad match or phrase match and vertically scale. But you can also do this deliberately: research new customer pain points, expand your TAM, test different angles. If you're only bidding on "CRM software," you're invisible to someone searching "how to organize customer data." Map out the full buying journey and go after each stage.

(3) Diagonal - launch new campaign types to tap new inventory. Performance Max and Demand Gen unlock YouTube, Display, Discover, Gmail. But be careful - these campaigns love to spend on irrelevant placements. You need heavy negatives and placement exclusions from day one and be optimizing for deeper funnel conversion events. Do not optimize for form fills and data leads. Start at 10% of your Search budget and slowly increase as you validate quality. The traffic looks different, but there is incremental revenue in these campaigns.

Quick scaling checklist:

→ Vertical: Can you increase budget AND control CPA with your target levers?
→ Horizontal: What search terms are your customers using that you're not bidding on?
→ Diagonal: Have you tested PMax or Demand Gen with proper conversions and exclusions in place?

I’ve spoken on 200+ stages. One of my favorite tactics to engage an audience comes from something I learned watching The Office, Ferris Bueller's Day Off, and Deadpool. 

It’s breaking the 4th wall.

In TV/movies, it’s when a character shatters the imaginary barrier that normally separates performers from viewers.

Think, Jim's eye rolls in The Office. 
Ferris Bueller's Day Off ending ("It's over...go home")
Or, "There are 206 bones in the human body...207 if I'm watching Gossip Girl", from Deadpool.

It builds an unexpected direct connection with the audience. Like an inside joke. 

Here's an example of one I use. 

One of my SKO slides pokes fun at how the "Sell Me This Pen" pitch would sound at a SaaS company. 

Seller: "We offer a revolutionary solution for scalable handwriting workflows.”

To which the prospect replies, "My pen is good enough."

The point of the slide is to show why "better" rarely wins when a buyer has decided their current solution is good enough. 

But, if you're in the back of the room, the spaces between the words in that text bubble look much smaller.

So, I break the 4th wall with, "Completely unrelated to the point I'm making here - if any of you ever choose to do a job that puts you on stages like this - may I recommend not using the phrase, 'My pen is' on a slide?"

It doesn't have to be a joke. It should be true to your personality. This one is true to mine. And, consider your audience. Mine is Sales. But - even with Sales - there are audiences where I don't use it. I know it's simply not a match for their culture/vibe.

Point is - audiences expect speakers to be "on", polished, and perfectly rehearsed.

Breaking the 4th wall is an easy way to break the monotony of a presentation + create a bond with your audience. 

Public speaking is as much about entertainment as it is about education.

Some surprising things your buyers want from you 🤷‍♀️ (we have 1000s of data points supporting this based on feedback buyers give on why they didn't buy) 

Explain how it works > explain the value
- Buyers cite 4x more that they didn't understand how the product works vs. "I wish I understood the value" 
- A lot of orgs push value first (value is obvi key!!) but if the buyer doesn't know how it works..... they won't sign 

Pricing is not the biggest blocker (shocker!!!) 
- Understanding why pricing is the way it is... is a blocker
- Usage models are confusing b/c they don't know how to forecast costs -> help them through this 
- Long contract lengths are a reason for loss b/c they don't understand what really happens after they sign -> explain the benefits/why

Reps who exceed expectations lose better + have higher win-back rates
- If you are rated 'above expectations'- ~60% of your buyers are willing to re-engage with you 
- If you are rated 'met expectations'- that number drops to 30%.......

BE MORE SPECIFIC!!!!!! How can THEY succeed 
- This is obvious............... but is a reason for loss in 25% of deals sooooo 
- They want: how it fits in their workflow, what their team needs to do differently, examples from similarly sized companies, what does this replace, use cases based on their unique needs

Friendly reminder to: tailor to them, show up the best you can (you have a 2x better chance of winning them back down the line if you do), explain how it fits into their workflow, and explain why pricing/contracting is the way it is 

Happy selling ✌

I spent $150M on Meta.

This is the max any DTC should spend: 

You need two numbers:
- Maximum spend
- Target spend 

1. Maximum spend

Take your gross margins, subtract your operating expenses (OPEX), and what's left is your absolute ceiling for marketing spend as a percentage of revenue.

Example:
- 50% gross margins
- 10% OPEX
= 40% maximum marketing spend

You're breaking even at the company level but maximizing growth velocity.

If you've raised capital, you can go above this, but only while the cash is there. 

People aren't buying unprofitable DTC companies, so if you are living at/above your max you must know your strategy for improving efficiency while keeping scale. 

2. Target Spend: 

Project your 6-month customer profitability, then decide your acceptable payback period:
- Profit even on first purchase? (Durables like mattresses)
- Break even on first purchase? (Some returning customers)
- Profitable by month 3? (Regular consumables like supplements)
- Profitable by month 6? (Reliable sticky consumables like toothpaste)

This becomes your target spend. 

Its defined as a CPA / ROAS target based on those LTV assumptions. 

Example for hair care product with good repurchase rates:
- Initial AOV: $55
- First Purchase Gross Profit: $30 (Before marketing)
- 3 Month Profit: $39
- 6 Month Profit: $46
- 12 Month Profit: $56

Your target spend here should be around $39 per customer 

See the image for an example, you may choose first purchase profitability or 6-month profitability targets, depending on your goals (how aggressive you value growth vs profit today) but 3 months is a good target. 

When you are starting, your max spend might limit this, but when you scale and margins expand and OPEX becomes more efficient, this becomes your target. 

This is your after-marketing profit for the average customer:
- First Purchase: $-9
- 3 Months: $0
- 6 Months: $7
- 12 months: $17

$17 of profit in a year ($26 returned) for $9 invested today is a great return as long as your P&L can handle this (thus the max). 

You won't get this return in the stock market if you took the money out of the business. (which is exactly why people will want to invest in or buy your business)

That cohort will continue to buy in years 2 and 3 and so on as well. 

As long as you're hitting this efficiency, you should spend as aggressively as possible. 

These customers WILL be profitable. 

This isn't burning cash.

It's buying growth at a known return.

Here's how we're using it:

1. Creator discovery

- Use keywords in your niche to find relevant channels
- Filter by subscriber count, average views, and location
- Start with small to mid-size creators (2.5K-50K avg views). Rates are significantly cheaper, and you can test messaging before scaling to larger channels
- Location targeting matters more than most people realize. If your ICP is in the US, you don't want a channel getting most of its views from a different country
- Even if the subscriber count looks great, the audience demo won't match. Discount those heavily when evaluating rates


2. Creator evaluation

- Average views relative to subscriber count (signals real engagement vs inflated follower counts)
- Content alignment with your brand (are they already talking about your space?)
- Past brand mentions (have they worked with competitors or adjacent brands?)
- Audience demographics (does their viewer base match your ICP?)
- 10 extra minutes on evaluation is high ROI


3. Simple outreach

- Don't overcomplicate initial outreach, the goal = conversation
- "Hey [Creator], I'm [Name] from [Company]. We're looking for creators in the [your niche] space to partner with on content. Your video on [specific video] caught our attention because [genuine reason]. Would you be open to a quick call to explore potential collaboration?"


4. Pricing structure

- Start with a flat fee - we use a tiered model based on average views per video
- Small (5K-15K views): $1K-1.5K
- Mid (15K-50K views): $1K-2.5K
- Upper-Mid (50K-250K views): $1.25K-6K
- Large (250K-750K views): $2.5K-11K
- Top-Tier (750K+ views): $50K+ (negotiated)
- Add performance bonuses for creators. This drives better content quality and rewards them if the campaign works
- Make sure usage rights are clear upfront. You'll want to run these as paid ads, not just rely on organic reach
- If you find creators that consistently perform, explore affiliate or commission models for longer-term partnerships


5. Partnership ads

- Once you have creator content, link the videos to your Google Ads account
- Run them as partnership ads across Performance Max and Demand Generation
- Track both organic and paid performance in one dashboard
- Build retargeting audiences from engaged viewers. Someone who watches 75% of a creator video is worth pushing more ads to down the funnel with direct response

80%+ of acquisition is from 1 place

Their growth came from relentless focus on 1 Meta funnel: 

1. Creative

→ 70% video, 30% static
→ Top 1-2% of ads should drive ~50% of spend and revenue
→ 70-80% of creative continues month-over-month
→ Replace 20-30% just to stay flat, add 20% more to grow 20%

2. Media buying 
→ Scaling winners, cutting losers, testing effectively
→ Top 2% of ads should take ~50% of spend
→Testing budget: under 20% of total spend
→ 8-figure brands can cut CPAs 50% with media buying alone

3. Website 
→ Maximizing for revenue per user
→ CVR: 3%+ (top 10% hit 4.7%+)
→ Add-to-cart: 7-10%
→ Checkout completion: 60%+
→ Page load: under 1 second

4. Retention 
→ Email, SMS, subscriptions, or all three
→ LTV:CAC ratio of 3:1 minimum
→ Repeat purchase rate of 30%+
→ Monthly subscription churn under 7%

I use these 4 charts to predict 

1. Cohort Reorder Percentage

- Segment customers by the month they first ordered.
- Track how many total orders that cohort places over time.
- Each line in the chart is a different cohort.

- > Removes AOV from the equation
- > Shows if your retention is actually improving month over month
- > Tells you which acquisition channels bring back buyers vs one-and-dones


2. Monthly Returning Revenue

- In what month do customers come back?
- Month 1? Month 3? Month 6?
- Plot the returning revenue by month after first purchase.

This tells you:
- > Your natural repurchase cadence
- > When to time email and SMS
- > Where your lifecycle gaps are


3. Monthly Returning %

This is the simplest view.
- Stack new vs returning revenue each month.
- Watch the blue (returning) grow.
- It's cumulative. Non-cohort.
- Easy to track and catch big changes/trends

To think about:
- You want to see returning revenue becoming a larger share of total revenue every month.
- If it's flat or shrinking while you scale? Your acquisition quality is slipping.

- Shows how much total revenue each cohort generates over time.

- This is the chart your CFO normally wants to see.

→ Cohort reorder % = are we getting better?
→ Monthly returning revenue = when do they come back?

The fastest way to increase opportunity creation:

Get rid of lead scoring

Replace with Account Scoring - the best measure of probability of revenue

Hand this to your GTM engineer:

Each stage has entry criteria, committee coverage requirements, signal weighting, and time windows. 

1. Signal Categories & Weights

a. Classify every trackable action into tiers:
- Tier 1 (1 pt): Email open, ad impression, social follow, blog visit
- Tier 2 (3 pts): + email reply, content download, webinar registration, multi-page site session (3+ pages)
- Tier 3 (5 pts): Pricing/demo page visit, webinar attended, replied to outbound, engaged with case study
- Tier 4 (10 pts): Inbound demo request, replied with interest, attended event booth, direct LinkedIn DM response

b. Layer on a role multiplier:
- Decision Maker (e.g., VP/C-suite): 3x
- Champion (e.g., Director/Sr. Manager): 2.5x
- Influencer (e.g., Manager/IC who evaluates tools): 1.5x
- End User: 1x
- Blocker (e.g., CFO, Procurement): 2x - only when positive

2. Stage Movement

Unaware → Aware
- Minimum 2 unique committee members have accumulated 5+ weighted points each
- At least 1 must be Champion or Decision Maker
- Signals must have occurred within a rolling 30-day window (creates internal speed & urgency)
- No single signal type can account for more than 60% of total points (prevents gaming from email opens alone)

Aware → Interested
- Min. 3 unique committee members have accumulated 15+ points each
- At least 2 must hold different roles 
- At least 1 Tier 3 or Tier 4 action
- Combined account score crosses 75 points
- All qualifying signals within a rolling 21-day window
- At least 2 different signal channels represented (e.g., email + website, not just email activity)

Interested → Considering
- Minimum 3 unique committee members at 30+ weighted points each
- Decision Maker must have at least 1 Tier 3+ action
- Champion must have at least 2 Tier 3+ actions
- Combined account score crosses 150 pts
- At least 1 direct response signal (reply, DM, inbound request)
- Rolling 14-day window for qualifying signals
- At least 3 different channels
- No active "blocker" negative signals

Considering → Opportunity
- Sales-confirmed: SDR has validated interest via live conversation with at least 1 Champion or Decision Maker
- At least 2 committee members have had direct 1:1 engagement
- Combined account score crosses 250 pts
- No decay events triggered in the prior 14 days
- Account has maintained Considering status for minimum 5 business days

Override Rules
- Any inbound demo request from a Decision Maker immediately advances the account to Considering regardless of other criteria
- If a known Blocker submits a negative signal, account flagged in Slack
- If 4+ committee members engage within a 48-hour window (cluster event), account advances one stage automatically and gets flagged as "surge account" for same-day SDR followup

5. Post campaign
2-3 weeks after the campaign ends, we'll run another incrementality check. If competitor bidding dies down and organic recaptures share, we scale back to normal.

→ Protect brand terms during influencer campaigns
→ Switch to impression share bidding for the duration
→ Promote influencer content as paid ads

Every DTC brand needs a 1st customer P&L:

1. Gross Revenue 

→ First-time orders only
→ This is your raw new customer orders
→ This is before any deductions
→ Compare this to your total revenue, it'll show you what % is not returning.

2. Net Revenue
→ Deduct discounts, returns, and refunds.
→ This normalizes for brands forcing gross revenue by discounting
→ E.g. $400k gross minus 30% off sitewide & 12% refund rate = $232k net

3. Gross Margin
→ Deduct COGS from Net Revenue
→ This tells you if the product itself is profitable before any operating costs
→ If this is thin, no amount of marketing efficiency saves you

4. Contribution Margin
→ Deduct shipping, transaction fees, and fulfillment costs
→ This is your per-order profitability before acquisition costs
→ Reminder, this is without any email, SMS, or retention activities

5. Acquisition Contribution Margin
→ Now deduct your Meta ad spend
→ This is the money you're actually making (or losing) acquiring new customers
→ If you're negative here, you're relying on future purchases to break even
→ Don't confuse this with blended contribution margin, this is new customers only

6. Acquisition MER (aMER)
→ Net Revenue divided by ad spend
→ This is the ratio view of step 5
→ No blended MER which hides returning customer revenue inflating the number

Story time:
- We scaled a brand from mid-eight figures to well into the nine figures. 
- One of the key levers outside of media buying and creative was better understanding their first time profitability. 
- Previously, the marketing spend was generic and broad-targeted. So new customer acquisition was incredibly expensive. 
- Facebook knew it was the easiest to just find returning customers to purchase again, and so they were focused on that. 
- When we forced Meta to prioritize new customers, the cost per acquisition was higher, but the cost per new customer acquisition started to decrease. 
- We got recurring customers instead with email, SMS, and subscriptions (effecient & reliable). 
- 6 months later nCAC was lower than previous CAC since Meta was now dialed in and targeting the right (new) people. 

How can you pull this data?
1. Download customer data by new and returning from Shopify
2. Subtract discounts, returns, and shipping costs. 
3. Subtract your COGS from new customers specifically based on the costs of the products, and the fulfillment, and the transaction fees. 
4. Subtract all of your marketing expenses related to acquisition. 
5. Now you know the profitability of your new customer acquisition and how much retention has to regain to break even. 
6. You know how your profitability would change next month if you did or didn't have your marketing spend turned on. 
7. Now you can calculate your churn and your burn rate and project into the future easily

Should you spend on brand keywords?

We ran a $40k test: 

We wanted to figure out
- What is the optimal amount to spend on ads?
- Is Google Ads taking more credit than it should?
- Could we spend more on Google Ads and drive incremental revenue?

So we ran a 6 week, 3-stage test: 

BASELINE:
→ Week 1: $2.2k ad spend 
→ Week 2: $1.5k ad spend 

TEST 1: (~3x BASELINE)
→ Week 3: $6.6k ad spend 
→ Week 4: $6.5k ad spend 
→ Week 5: $7.5k ad spend 

TEST 2: (~11x BASELINE)
→ Week 6: $16k ad spend 

Then we measured the results: 

1. Layered all data
- Exported Google Search Console data for branded clicks on a weekly basis
- Exported Google Ads data for branded spend, clicks and conversions on a weekly basis 
- Created a table for every week so we could easily see all the data 

2. Compared time buckets 
- Created average weekly stats for Baseline, Test 1 and Test 2 periods 
- Generally, we saw as paid spend increased organic clicks decreased. 
- But we wanted to see exactly how many incremental clicks were driven (after organic decreased) by spending more on ads.

When we spent 3x Baseline (Test 1 vs Baseline)
- Spent ~$5.5k more every week 
- Drove +2,500 more ad clicks
- Lost -5000 organic clicks 
- Net lost -2,500 clicks 
- That means we paid $5.5k more and got less traffic.
- In other words, incredibly loss making

We then ran Test 2 (which was a ~2x increase on Test 1) 
- Spent ~$9.1k more every week 
- Drove +1000 more ad clicks
- Lost -850 organic clicks 
- Net gain 150 clicks 
- That means we paid 9k for a ~62x worse incremental CPA

All in all, it means every time we increased ad spend we ate into our organic traffic.
- Most of the “extra” conversions would’ve happened anyway
- We were paying to intercept traffic we already owned

Dropping spend back down from $11k/week to $1k/week seems drastic.
- Will competitors steal our traffic if we don’t bid?
- Will our brand keeps lose surface area?
- Does losing brand mean losing customers?

But it’s clear from the data that the spend wasn’t incremental.

And now we have it and black and white.

So now we can add that extra $10k into generating net new demand.

Every brand running Google Ads should be running this test every 4 months to make sure they’re not wasting spend. We’ve run this across multiple accounts and the results always vary (spend more or spend less).

I've spent $30M since Andromeda dropped:

Using the creative multiplication strategy:

3x Angles:

1. Pain Point
→ Frustration: "still dealing with X after trying everything?"
→ Fear: "your competitors figured this out 6 months ago"
→ Regret: "how much did that last agency cost you?"
→ Triggers: embarrassment, loss aversion, status anxiety

2. Desire
→ Aspiration: "imagine checking your dashboard and seeing this"
→ Freedom: "what would you do with an extra $40K/month?"
→ Status: "this is what 3x ROAS looks like at scale"
→ Triggers: ambition, envy, possibility

3. Social Proof
→ Testimony: "we switched from X and cut CPA by 34% in 2 weeks"
→ Authority: "10,000 DTC brands use this. here's why"
→ Relatability: "I was skeptical too. then I saw our Q4 numbers"
→ Triggers: trust, FOMO, validation


3x Formats:

1. Static
→ 60-70% of conversions for most brands I manage
→ Smartphone-quality beats studio 84% of the time in Stories
→ Fastest to produce, easiest to iterate. Test 10 statics in the time it takes to shoot 1 video
→ Use when the value is immediately visible (fashion, jewelry, food)

2. Video
→ First 3 seconds decide everything. I track hook rate (3-sec views / impressions) religiously
→ Below 25% hook rate? Kill it. 30-40% is good. Above 40%? Scale it
→ Partnership Ads (running from creator's handle) = 53% lower CAC
→ Use when the customer needs to believe it before they buy (skincare, supplements, transformations)
→ Quick rule: if they need to SEE IT, run statics. If they need to BELIEVE IT, run video.

3. Carousel
→ Best for education-heavy products and comparison selling
→ Card 1 hooks with a problem or question, not your product
→ Average swipe-through on a good carousel is 1.4x higher engagement than single image
→ Use when the buyer needs to understand WHY before they buy

(If Carousels don’t apply to your brand, insert animated statics, GIFs, or another format)


3x Funnel Levels

1. Top of Funnel (they don't know you)
→ Lead with a problem, bold claim, or pattern interrupt
→ 80% of your creative volume should live here

2. Mid Funnel (they've seen you, they're comparing)
→ Education, competitor comparisons, "why us" content
→ Carousels and founder stories work hardest here

3. Bottom Funnel (they're warm, they need a push)
→ Offers, urgency, risk removal, testimonials with CTA overlays
→ Bundles + Free gifts work really well here

And then you multiply them

TOF x Static x Pain Point = text graphic about a problem they have
MOF x Video x Social Proof = UGC testimonial walkthrough
BOF x Carousel x Desire = transformation story with offer on last card

That's 3 combinations there.

There are a total of 27.
- 3 angles x 3 formats x 3 funnels stages

Hope this helps you break out of creative fatigue and scale your account.

John Hefter bought Angry Orange (hear the whole story on Episode 134 of the Operators Podcast)

He saw 100% organic reviews saying "This saved my marriage."

He then put a framework and structure into place to tap into EXACTLY what made the product powerful.

1. Export 
→ Export Your 3-Star and 4-Star Reviews
→ Not 5-stars (too positive). Not 1-stars (complainers).
→ 3-4 stars tell you what's good AND what's missing.
→ Pull last 500 reviews. Use Helium 10 or any scraper.


2. Score Each Review

Review Score = (Emotional Language × 2) + (Repeat Purchase × 5) + (Competitive Comparison × 3) + (Use Case Expansion × 2)

Look for:
→ Emotional: "I can't believe this worked" (score 1-10)
→ Repeat Purchase: "Buying my 3rd bottle" (Yes = 5 points)
→ Competitive: "Tried 6 products before this" (Yes = 3 points)
→ Use Case: "Bought for X, now use for Y and Z" (Yes = 2 points)

Sort by highest score. 
→ Top 20% = your creative goldmine.


3. Turn Reviews Into Ad Hooks
→ "I was about to spend $3,000 replacing carpet. Then I found this orange bottle."
→ "I bought this for one room. Now I use it in 6 places."
→ "This product saved my marriage. (And my dog.)"
→ "I don't believe in miracle products. But this proved me wrong."

Use exact customer language. (Not your voice. Their voice)

Step 4: Test
→ Week 1-2: Create 20-30 ads from top reviews
→ Week 3-4: Test at $20/day each
→ Week 5-6: Scale top 5 to $100/day

Target metrics:
→ Hook Rate: >40%
→ CTR: >2%
→ CPA: 20% better than current

Simple playbook: 
1. Export 500 reviews
2. Score top 20%
3. Extract 5 hooks
4. Create 10-15 ads

I've launched over 20k ads on Meta

And I NEVER analyze losing ads: 

Two reasons:

1. The math doesn't work
- I can take an ad doing a 0.5 ROAS and maybe get it to a 1. 
- Or I can turn it off and take an ad doing a 2 and push it to a 3.

2. You'll learn the wrong lessons
- There are so many reasons an ad can fail. Persona. Camera quality. Audio. Loading speed. Music in the background. The way someone delivers a line.
- We had an ad we thought bombed because of the filming location. Analyzed it, made that call, recorded the ad. Guess what? Still was bad performance. 

So what do I do instead?

Spend 100% of creative energy branching the winners and testing new ideas from the ground up. 

If Ad A works, build off that root:

→ Same angle, new format (UGC to static)
→ Same angle, new visual (talking head to challenge)
→ Same angle, new persona
→ Same angle, new hook

The only exception (nuance is important) 
- If you've tested an angle multiple times / angles / and formats and it bombs consistently then that is the time to cut it. 

Learn from individual wins / learn from aggregate losses

It will help reduce noise in your decision making.

We spend $5.5M/mo on Google Ads.

Here's our Demand Gen checklist:

1. Consolidate for Data Density, Segment by Audience. Do not split Ad Groups by placement (YouTube vs. Discover). Demand Gen is designed to be cross-channel; forcing a placement "chokes" the AI’s ability to find the cheapest conversion across the ecosystem. Instead, use Ad Groups to segment by Audience Theme (e.g., Top 25 Search Terms vs. 2% Lookalikes). This keeps your data signals concentrated in one place while allowing you to see which buyer persona is actually biting.

2. Check image AND video asset quantity. Ads & assets > Assets. You need variety in both formats. We've seen 20% more conversions running image and video together vs video only. 

3. Check headline and description variety. Campaigns > Demand Gen > Ads > Headlines and descriptions. Demand Gen serves across YouTube, Gmail, and Discover. Each placement renders differently. You need variety.

4. Check view-through conversion tracking. Demand Gen drives view-throughs that Search doesn't. We value them at ~30% of click-through. If you're not tracking them, you're undervaluing the entire campaign.

5. Segment device performance. Campaigns > Demand Gen > Segment > Device. Demand Gen skews mobile because of Gmail and Discover. I've seen mobile CPA run 3x worse than desktop. And other times where mobile significantly outperforms.

6. Review your bid strategy. Settings > Campaign settings > Columns > Bid strategy. For Demand Gen, start target CPA at 2x your Search CPA. CPCs are cheap ($0.09 vs $7+ on Search) but conversion rates are lower. Give the algorithm room to learn.

7. If running product ads, check feed health. Google Merchant Center > Products > Diagnostics. Disapproved products mean your ads don't serve for those items.

8. Set your budget for a "Conversion Floor." While the "15x tCPA" rule is great for rapid scaling, it’s often unrealistic for high-CPA accounts. At a minimum, aim for a daily budget that supports 1–2 conversions per day. If your Target CPA is $200, a $300–$400 daily budget is your "efficiency floor." It will take longer to exit the "Learning Phase" than a $3,000/day budget, but it prevents the algorithm from overspending on low-quality placements while it searches for a baseline.

9. Build custom segments from your top 25 converting Search terms. Audiences > Audience manager > Segments. You're reaching people before they search. That's the whole point of Demand Gen.

10. Confirm auto-tagging is on. Settings > Account settings > Auto-tagging. Without it you lose conversion and view-through data between Ads and Analytics.

11. Retract bad leads within 24 hours. This matters more on Demand Gen because the audience pool is broader.

This is 11 out of 31 items we check on every Demand Gen launch.

One wrong setting can burn thousands before you catch it.

Demand Gen:

Plus Demand Gen drove 180 view-through conversions. Column is called "Conversions (Platform Comparable)”
→ We typically value view through at ~30% of click through (the data above does not include any view-through conversions)
→ We don't throw it out completely (it's still contributing)
→ To find exact contribution, run on-off holdout tests

For us, that's a sign to push into it more:

How to run Demand Gen:

1. Launch timing
→ Wait until you have 50+ quality conversions/month
→ Search and PMax should already be running

2. Budget and bidding
→ Daily budget = 15x your target CPA
→ Set target CPA at ~2x your standard campaign performance
→ Optimize for down-funnel events (not just form fills)

3. Assets
→ Use both video AND image (20% more conversions vs video only)
→ Repurpose top-performing assets from other channels
→ More assets = better performance

4. Campaign structure
→ One consolidated campaign (helps Google learn faster)
→ Separate ad groups by placement for granular insights
→ In our structure statics converted better than video so we opted to split for better budget control.

5. Audiences
→ Custom intent audiences
→ In-market segments
→ Lookalikes from customer match
→ Be careful with Optimized Targeting (can dilute results)

Hook types for YouTube ads

Used by Lovable, Claude, Rippling & Google backed:

1. Random Fact
→ Lovable do this one really well.
→ Open with something random and interesting. No product for 15-20 seconds.
→ "Americans eat 3 billion slices of pizza every year" (Lovable spent $3.4M on this one ad)
→ "Humans eat more than 15 billion pounds of chocolate every year" ($2.5M spend)
→ "A hundred years ago, a man invented a glass factory making 240 bottles per minute"

2. Tutorial / Education-First
→ Claude lean on this given they're in a new category
→ Position the ad as content, not advertising.
→ "Let me introduce you to my creative assistant, Claude" ($3M YouTube spend)
→ "Practical tips for getting more out of Claude"
→ "How to quickly learn with Claude"

3. Problem-First
→ Name the viewer's exact pain in the first line.
→ "If your YouTube ads keep getting skipped, you're making this one mistake"
→ "Tired of your CRM losing leads every time a rep quits?"
→ "Stop wasting money on agencies that don't understand your business"

If they think "that's me," they can't skip.

4. Demo & Solution
→ Rippling almost do this exclusively across $4.9M in spend.
→ Skip the narrative. Show the value prop on screen immediately.
→ E.g. hook: "How does Rippling transform onboarding?"
→ Direct product demo, no buildup
→ Feature headline with the product already in action

Or lead with the result. Specific enough that viewers stay to validate.
→ "This ad structure cut our CPL by 42% in 30 days"
→ "We onboard new hires in 4 minutes, not 4 weeks"
→ "This strategy generated $47M in revenue last year"

Most of this matches Google's ABCD framework:

→ Attract in first 5 seconds
→ Brand early but naturally
→ Connect emotionally
→ Direct them to act

We day trade $100k/day on Meta ads:

(this ad spent $1M)

→ Each candle = 1 day
→ Y axis = daily spend. X axis = days
→ Green = CPA in target, so increased spend
→ Red = CPA too high, so decreased spend

This is what's happening

1. Scale into green candles
- When a new ad is working, you'll see green after green.
- Meta is finding the audience and you can push spend aggressively.
- We took this one from launch to $25k/day in the first couple weeks.

2. Find the ceiling
- Every ad caps out somewhere.
- The candles start leveling off and upward momentum slows.
- This one peaked around $25k/day.
- Hard part is knowing if it's a temporary plateau or the real ceiling.
- Only way to find out is keep pushing and watching.

3. Use 3 CPA windows for triangulation
- 1-day CPA for real-time pulse
- 3-7 day CPA for trend direction
- 30-day CPA for overall trajectory
- Don't overindex on 1-day CPA - it's noisy.
- Three bad days across all windows is a big red flag.

4. Pull back when consecutive red candles
- A few red days are normal.
- But when they get bigger and start piling up you need to act fast.
- We dropped from $25k to $3k/day.
- Don't try to spend through it.

5. Scale back in after recovery
- Once CPAs settle and improve, push back up gradually.
- We got back to $10-12k/day and held that range for weeks before the next fatigue wave.

6. Know when the ad is done
- Consistent downtrend with no recovery after pullback = the ad has run its course.
- Don't force it. Move to the next creative.

Do this right and one ad can spend $1M+ profitably.

Should your DTC run YouTube ads?

Answer 2 easy questions:

1. Will you spend enough?
→ On Meta, you can test a creative with 500 views and get a reliable signal.
→ On YouTube, you need 2,500-5,000 views before you reach significance.

→ That means you need $25-50K/month just to cycle through enough creatives and let the algorithm figure out what scales.
→ And if your Google rep is pushing you to diversify into YouTube - ask them the minimum spend to reach statistical significance...

2. Will your creatives work?
→ On Meta, you're fighting for attention from 1st second. Hook rate is everything.
→ On YouTube, viewers get 5 seconds before they can skip. So your peak moment needs to land at the 3-4 second mark.
→ YouTube = giving the watcher a reason to not hit skip... then a reason to stay
→ Same creative doesn't transfer between Meta & YouTube

My take on YouTube for DTC:
→ More spend-intensive to test than Meta
→ Not as scalable for most brands under $500K/month in ad spend
→ Favors bigger brands where 5% of their budget still equals $50K+
→ Smaller brands are almost always better off making Meta more efficient first

I've watched brands burn $50K on YouTube tests that would've generated 3x the learnings on Meta.

Are you scaling Google ads right? 

Here's our PMax checklist:

1. Deploy Search Themes to steer the AI. Campaigns > PMax > Asset Groups > Search Themes. Add up to 50 phrases that define your highest-intent traffic. Unlike Audience Signals (which are "suggestions"), Search Themes act like Broad Match keywords. They tell Google, "I don't care who the person is; if they type this, show my ad when they are likely to convert." This prevents PMax from wandering into "cheap but useless" traffic.

2. Audit Final URL & Asset Expansion. Campaigns > PMax > Settings > Automatically created assets. URL expansion acts as a "wide-net" discovery tool, finding $0.15 clicks on deep pages that would cost $5+ on Search. However, without URL Exclusions, you’re paying for traffic to your "Privacy Policy," "Careers," or "Thank You" pages. The Pro Move: Toggle on the expansion to find new intent, but immediately exclude all non-commercial URLs. Also, watch the Automatically Created Text Assets toggle. If your brand is legally sensitive, turn this off so Google doesn't "hallucinate" new headlines based on your site content.

3. Verify video assets. Campaigns > PMAX > Asset groups > Videos. Minimum 1, ideal 3+. If you don't provide a video, Google creates a "Ken Burns" style montage from your images that looks like a 2005 local car dealer ad. If you don't have a high-quality video, do not leave it blank. Use the "Video Creation Tools" inside Google Ads to at least build a templated version that matches your brand fonts and colors.

4. Set up brand exclusions. Campaigns > PMAX > Campaign settings > Brand exclusions. Without this, PMax bids on your own brand and takes credit for conversions that would've happened organically. Add brand negatives at the negative keyword level too.

5. Review Search term insights. Campaigns > PMAX > Insights > Search term categories. Only way to see what PMax is actually bidding on. Irrelevant categories eating budget? Add negative keywords.

6. Check product listing group structure. Campaigns > PMAX > Asset groups > Listing groups. Don't run all products in one group. Segment by margin, bestsellers, or category.

7. Set up audience exclusions. Campaigns > PMAX > Asset groups > Audience signals > Exclusions. Exclude existing customers if focused on acquisition. Exclude job seekers, competitors, irrelevant segments.

8. Check asset performance ratings. Campaigns > PMAX > Insights > Asset performance. Google rates each asset Best, Good, or Low. Replace Low performers. One bad asset drags down the whole group.

9. Review placement reports. Campaigns > PMAX > Insights > Placement reports. PMax spends across Search, Display, YouTube, Gmail, Maps, Discover. Check where money is going and whether those placements convert.

This is 9 out of 36 items we check on every PMax audit.

One wrong setting and PMax will spend your budget on wrong traffic without telling you.

Some are lvl 5 Charmanders

The mistake I see constantly:

→ You put a Charizard in the same ad set as a Charmander.
→ The Charizard eats all the spend.
→ The Charmander never gets a chance to grow.

Or a Charizard starts losing HP
→ So you pause it and swap in a Charmander.
→ That poor Charmander can't handle $1,500/day overnight
→ He's knocked out fast

Here's how we manage our pokemon

Oops I mean ads:

1. Diagnose with hit rate
Look at how many placements and ad sets a single ad has won in. If it's hitting 2x+ return across 4+ placements, that's your Charizard. If it only works in one specific pocket, it's fragile. Don't trust it with big budgets.

2. Keep weight classes separate
Your dominant winners get their own scaling lanes (CBO/ASC). Testing ads fight for spend in separate campaigns. The moment you mix them, the big ad starves the small one. Even if the small one is profitable.

3. Never swap 1 for 1
If your top spender is fatiguing, don't pause it and replace it with something that's only proven at $300/day. Trim the budget 20%. Let the new ads earn their way up. Respect the weight class.

The whole game is structuring your account so your best ads don't eat your second-best ads alive.

→ If you find winners, you need a more rigorous testing system

How to predict when your Meta ads stop working: 

1. Get every active ad
2. Look at how many days it's been running. 
3. Weight each ad's age by its share of total spend.

The result is a single number:

The spend-weighted average age of your creative portfolio.

E.g. 3 active ads:

→ Ad A: 5 days old, $30,000 spend (60% of total)
→ Ad B: 30 days old, $15,000 spend (30%)
→ Ad C: 45 days old, $5,000 spend (10%)

(5 x 0.60) + (30 x 0.30) + (45 x 0.10) = 16.5 days

In this case, $50k is being spent on 16.5 day old creative. 

Is spend-weighted average age = 15: 
→ Account is looking healthy 

Is spend-weighted average age = 60
→ Most budget is being spent on 'old ads'

And if you launched new ads recently but your number is still high, it means those new ads aren't getting spend.

So they're either not promising or they're not getting testing budget. 

This number should be relatively stable in a well-managed account. 

Check the image: 
- The blue line below shows creative age across the account.
- If it's trending upward month over month you're falling behind
- Increase creative production because fatigue is building.

(One caveat: if you have poor media buying this metric won't work right - you might just be spending on new bad ads or missing new good ads).

I've spent $260M on Google

9 ad metrics to run higher ROAS ads:

1. Attributed Branded Searches
Tracks how many people searched your brand after seeing your ad. View-through attribution, 1-30 day window. Works on YouTube, PMax, Demand Gen.

2. Conversion Lag Report
Shows the delay between click and conversion. If your lag is 21 days and you're judging performance on a 7-day window, you're cutting campaigns that were about to work. I've seen CPAs drop by 70-80%+ once the full window closes. This ties into cohort bake analysis. If you're not adjusting for lag, your forecasts are wrong too.

3. New Customer Acquisition Reporting
Separates new vs returning customers in your conversion columns. We turned this on for a PMax account spending $400K/mo. 62% of "conversions" were existing customers buying again. Real new-customer CPA was 3.1x what the dashboard showed.

4. Invalid Click Rate
Shows what % of clicks Google flagged as fraud and refunded you for. Industry average sits around 5-7%, some verticals hit 15-20%. If yours looks suspiciously low, Google might not be catching everything.

5. Search Exact Match Impression Share
Not the same as regular Impression Share. This one only counts searches that exactly matched your keyword. If regular IS is 40% but Exact Match IS is 90%, your keywords are solid. You're losing share on broad match queries you probably don't even want. I've seen accounts panic-shift to exact match because regular IS looked low, when their Exact Match IS was already 90%+.

6. Overlap Rate
Inside Auction Insights. Tells you how often a specific competitor appeared alongside you. 80% overlap means they're bidding on nearly everything you are. Track it monthly. When it spikes, someone new entered your auctions. That's how we caught a competitor scaling into one of our client's categories before anyone noticed.

7. View-Through Conversions
People who saw your ad, didn't click, then converted later. Shows up as Conversions (Platform Comparable) One YouTube campaign got flagged for having 3 conversions. Nobody checked the 41 view-throughs sitting in Conversions (Platform Comparable).

8. Search Lost IS (Rank) vs Search Lost IS (Budget)
Two separate columns. Both tell you WHY you're losing impression share. Lost to rank happens when you're scaling and is normal. Lost to budget = your daily budget runs out. For brand campaigns, minimize Lost IS (budget) to stop competitors. Use incrementality tests to spend the right amount. For nonbrand campaigns, either make your smart bidding more restrictive or increase your daily budget.

9. Hidden Search Terms
Not a native column. Export the Search Terms Report, sum visible spend, compare to total campaign spend. The gap is what Google won't show you. In some accounts, 40%+ of spend goes to terms you can't even see. This one still frustrates me. You're paying for traffic Google won't even let you audit.

Add all 9 to your column set. Takes 5 minutes.

How to write LinkedIn posts that attract total strangers to follow you

1. ask yourself: "can anyone else write this?" before you post anything. if the answer is yes, rewrite the hook. a stranger scrolling your feed needs a reason to stop. generic advice gives them nothing. only you writing from only your experience gives them something.

2. write your hook like you're telling a friend what happened. not "here are 5 tips for LinkedIn growth." more like "last week my client went from zero engagement to their best post ever. here's exactly why." one is preaching. the other is a story you want to hear.

(free training on hook writing here btw: https://lnkd.in/dE-_BMT7)

3. introduce yourself inside the post. don't assume strangers know who you are. drop one line early that signals what you do and who you do it for. "I've spent 4 years helping founders write on LinkedIn" tells me everything I need to trust what comes next.

4. educate with step-by-step actions, examples, or a framework. these are the posts that get saved. saves correlate with follower spikes. people save things they're scared of losing because they'll want to use them later.

5. when you find a post that attracts new followers, post it again the following week. and the week after. the impressions will vary. but the follower-to-impression ratio stays almost identical. winners compound.

6. mix posts for strangers with posts for your existing audience. strangers need context. existing followers need depth. you need both. roughly 2 stranger-facing posts per week is a good place to start.

7. stop writing to your followers. write to the person who has never heard of you. they're the ones you're trying to attract.

TL;DR:

- document your life
- write to strangers
- repeat and repurpose winners

Are you running Google Ads right?

Use this chart to find out:

Ask yourself two questions.
1. What's your budget?
2. What's the search demand?

Top Left: (HARD)
→ High budget, low search demand
→ Not enough search intent to narrow even if you wanted to
→ Go broad. Layer in YouTube and Demand Gen to generate awareness
→ You're building a category so cast a wide net.

Top Right: (BEST)
→ High budget, high search demand
→ Google has plenty of data to find your customers
→ Don't restrict audiences. Go broad.
→ Use observation mode. Collect audience data instead of constraining with it.
→ The algorithm knows who converts better than you do.

Bottom Left: (HARDEST)
→ Low budget, low search demand
→ The hardest quadrant to be in
→ Not enough data to go wide and not enough demand to filter.
→ Do deep keyword research and find pockets of intent competitors missed.

Bottom Right: (MEDIUM)
→ Low budget, high search demand
→ The only quadrant where narrow targeting makes sense
→ You can't afford every auction so pick the right ones
→ E.g. layer in household income, in-market segments, geography

Some examples of clients:
→ Treatment center, $3M/mo budget with massive search volume = high budget, high demand
→ Local dentist, $5K/mo budget in a city with 10K+ "dentist near me" searches = low budget, high demand
→ VC-backed AI tool, $150K/mo budget for a category that barely exists = high budget, low demand
→ Niche B2B manufacturer, $8K/mo budget with 200 monthly searches = low budget, low demand

Cheatsheet:
→ High budget + high demand = Go broad, observation mode
→ High budget + low demand = Go broad, create demand
→ Low budget + high demand = Go narrow, be selective
→ Low budget + low demand = Go deep, research everything

Is creative or media buying your problem?

Find out with 12 charts:

Creative and media buying are tightly connected - they both drive your CPA and ROAS.

But if you ONLY use grouped metrics, you lose a TON of visibility.

Think about how you run your business:

You don't evaluate every department purely on business profit
→ Customer service: Response time, satisfaction scores
→ Operations: Fulfillment speed, error rates
→ Finance: Cash flow, margins

Each has its own metrics. Each solves a different problem.

Same with ads.

Your media buyer manages distribution and efficiency.

Your creative team manages attention and conversion.

📊 Media Buying Metrics
→ Change Consistency (Daily): Are changes being made regularly or in random bursts? (Good buyers make consistent, data-driven adjustments)
→ Account Control: Are winning creatives scaled and losers cut or are there a lot of "lost" ads on either end? (easier said than done)
→ Change Distribution: Are changes thoughtful and well-balanced across campaigns?
(Not just turning everything on/off reactively)
→ Change Balance: Are changes skewing too positive or negative?
→ Churn/Retesting Control: Are winning creatives being retested properly?
(Launch → Perform → Fatigue → Retest)
→ Prediction Accuracy: Can they forecast performance when scaling?

📊 Creative Production Metrics
→ Creative Churn: How quickly are creatives fatiguing?
→ Sentiment Analysis: Which selling points/hooks are performing best?
(What messages are actually resonating with your audience)
→ Production & Slugging Rate: How much are you producing vs. how much hits?
→ Gender/Demo Analysis: Are you reaching the right audience?
→ Spend by Format: Is budget allocation matching what converts?
(Video vs. Static vs. Carousel - track what formats drive efficiency)
→ Creative Spend Ratio: Are you investing enough in production?

The diagnosis:
If creative metrics are declining → You need more/better creative
If media metrics are declining → You need a better buying strategy

Most common mistake?
Blowing up a working system because your metrics don't show you where the problem is. It's disheartening for employees and unproductive

Bottom line:

Creative and media buying both drive CPA/ROAS.

Even if they are managed by the same person (they should be) that doesn't give an excuse to blend the metrics.

Measure them separately or you'll fix the wrong thing.

I just read a post from a CEO who was in disbelief that a customer churned b/c they're going to try DIYing the vendor's AI solution.  It included the quote - "Good luck, see you in 6 months when you realize how hard it is."

I think we're going to see a lot more of this from tech companies in 2026. This isn't me picking on anyone. DIY is a really tough competitor. And, it hurts to lose to it. 

But, wishing for a customer's failure has never served me well in Sales. 

It's understandable that our knee-jerk response is to name all of the reasons why DIY is a bad idea. 

Often, our points are valid. 

But, the delivery is defensive. We erode trust because we fail to be collaborative or helpful. 

Instead, here's something that worked for me when I was up against DIY:

#1 - I asked questions about how they were thinking about rolling it out. Not "gotcha" questions. Qs that were genuinely curious in nature that helped me understand their beliefs/assumptions. I sought to understand (vs. seeking to correct them). Often, this exposed a flawed assumption. 

#2 - I shared ideas/tactics from other execs that were taking a DIY approach, so they could learn from them. I stopped fighting against DIY. This built trust.

#3 - Lastly, I offered at least one idea for how I could partner with the team as they thought through their DIY approach. I prescribed suggestions on areas where I knew DIY typically fell down. It gave me the chance to get in with the teams and illuminate the roadblocks that made DIY harder than they assumed.

More of those DIY deals started to convert. Not all of them. Just more of them.

TLDR - there's a great Brent Adamson quote - "Before you tell someone why they're wrong, first tell them why they're right". 

When competing against DIY, I stopped trying to be "right". I started trying to be useful.

I ran GTM at $23m SaaS

For 4 years, I sent the CEO (3) RevOps report every Monday 9am:
- GTM efficiency
- Pipeline Health
- Forecast

Report 1: GTM Efficiency
Tells you if your S&M spend is working/scalable

A. The Magic Number
$1 of ARR for every $1 of S&M spend:
>0.75 = generally considered efficient, worth investing more
<0.5 = broken GTM, fix before scaling
>1.5 = step on the gas, you're leaving money on the table

B. Rule of 40 = Revenue Growth % + FCF Margin %

You can hit 40 two ways:
- 60% growth + (-20%) margin → hypergrowth mode
- 20% growth + 20% margin → efficient mature business

The composition tells a different story depending on your stage:
 - $2M–$5M ARR: growth % dominates. A 80/(-40) score is fine
- $10M–$20M ARR: balance matters. Pure growth story gets harder to sustain
- PE target ($20M+ ARR): margin is weighted heavily (they're buying cash flow potential)

C. NNR: is your existing base growing or leaking?
↳ World class: 130%+
↳ Strong: 110-130% (healthy upsell, low churn)
↳ Growing: 101%-110% (basically flat, expansion offsets losses)
↳ Warning: 90-100% (churn eating into base)
↳ Broken: <90% (fix leaky bucket, then scale)

D. LTV:CAC: do your unit economics actually work?
↳ 4:1 - scale, channel is profitable
↳ 3:1 - channel is viable and worth investing into
↳ 2:1 - channel is break even considering all costs (incl. employee time)
↳ 1:1 - channel not profitable. If not in testing phase, kill

E. CAC Payback: how many months until you recover acquisition cost?
↳ SMB: good = 12mo | acceptable = 12-18mo | warning = 18mo+
↳ Mid market: good = 18mo | acceptable = 18-24mo | warning = 24mo+
↳ Enterprise: good = 24mo | acceptable = 24-36mo | warning = 36mo+

Report 2: Pipeline Health
Tells you which deals to kill and which to accelerate before the quarter slips

→ Coverage ratio vs quota (healthy = 3–4x) 
→ Stage distribution: is your funnel top-heavy or bottom-heavy? 
→ Aging deals flagged the moment they exceed 2x average cycle time 
→ Concentration risk: alerts when 1 deal represents >40% of pipeline 
→ Where your qtr is at risk: coverage gap by quarter
→ Sales velocity: pipeline needed to hit next quarter goal

Report 3: Forecast Accuracy
Tells where your forecast is optimistic vs realistic

→ MAPE: your forecast error score 
→ Bias detection: are you systematically over or under-forecasting? 
→ Rep-level accuracy breakdown: who's sandbagging, who's wishful thinking
→ Forecast trend: is your forecasting getting better or worse quarter over quarter? 
→ Segment-level breakdown: Enterprise vs Mid-Market vs SMB

This report system means leadership wakes up Monday knowing:
- Which deal to call, which rep to coach, and which spend to cut 
- Pipeline coverage vs target (are we on track or not?) 
- The 2-3 deals that need attention asap 
- GTM efficiency score

→ $1,000 spend at a $39 CPA, start scaling in

- If it's below the green line, scale it hard

How to bid on brand keywords

Without overspending:

1. Set brand keywords to broad match

Broad gives Google the full universe of brand queries - e.g. misspellings, brand + product, brand + location. These convert at 5-6x non-brand rates. Restricting to exact or phrase match cuts them off.


2. Set bid strategy to target ROAS

I typically start brand at 500%. This is the guardrail. If a non-brand query sneaks in through broad match, Google will only bid on it if it can hit 5.0x ROAS. Brand queries hit that easily and will dominate the spend. The algorithm filters out non-brand terms on its own.


3. Monitor "Search lost IS (budget)" daily

If it's above 0%, your target ROAS might be too low (you're overbidding). Raise target ROAS until lost-to-budget hits zero. That means your CPCs are efficient enough that your budget lasts the full day. Or increase your budget to capture search demand.


4. Check the search term report weekly

Broad match + target ROAS should keep search terms clean. If non-brand terms are still showing up at 5.0x ROAS, they might be worth keeping. If not, add them as negatives.


Two levers:
→ Match type controls reach
→ Bid strategy controls efficiency 

Go wide on match type. Go tight on bid strategy.

How we spend $5.5M/mo on Google Ads:

Treat Google's AI like an employee.

1. Set the right KPI
→ If you told a sales rep to make 100 calls and you'll pay them $1k, they call the easiest numbers.
→ Same with Google. Tell it to optimize for 'all leads' and it'll find the cheapest person who submits info. Instead ask Google for 'booked appointments' - or the furthest down funnel event you can reliably send back - and it'll find those.

2. Give fast feedback
→ When a new hire doesn't do a good job, you correct it ASAP.
→ Same with Google. Bad lead comes in? Retract it within 24 hours. Don't allow for the algorithm to learn that bad leads are acceptable. It'll help the algo find higher quality leads

3. Give clear SOPs
→ You wouldn't drop a new hire at their desk with zero onboarding and expect results.
→ Same with Google. Give really clear instructions: search themes, negative keywords, audience signals etc. Provide as much clear information as possible on what constitutes as good traffic.

4. Use probation period
→ You don't fire someone after their first week because they haven't closed a deal yet.
→ Same with Google. It needs at least 30+ conversions a month before the algorithm learns anything useful. Killing a campaign on day 3 because CPA looks high is judging someone before they've finished training.

5. Do performance reviews
→ A manager who never does check-ins gets blindsided when Q4 numbers tank.
→ Same with Google. Pull search term reports, placement reports, and 90 day CPA trends. There are lots of leading indicators that can help you catch spend before it's wasted.

I’ve helped 5 eCom brands exit for ~$500m. 

5 things that meant a bigger exit:

1. Retail-ready positioning
- PE loves when growth is primarily on Meta only because it gives them channel expansion opportunities. They want to open retail, Pinterest, TikTok, and more.
- When PE did small tests in retail, there was already strong awareness from paid digital. Customers recognized the product and picked it up off shelf.
- Meta ads focused on unique selling points that made the product feel superior. This meant PE was willing to pay a much higher multiple despite retail not being launched yet, on the assumption that retail would be a big expansion lever.

2. Cost-cutting opportunities
- I'll be honest, agencies like us normally get cut during PE acquisitions. We're not cheap, and though we provide a lot of value, companies often undersell our impact to PE. 
- Whenever PE sees an easy cost-cutting opportunity, they’re probably going to take it. This increases the projected profit of the business and thereby the multiple they pay.
- We tell our clients this when they’re near exit window to help them make themselves look more attractive. 

3. Product expansion potential
- They had successfully launched 2-3 products and had more ideas to expand.
- By showing you can expand from one product to two or three successfully, you give PE buyers hope they can expand to 10-15 key products and grow the overall TAM.
- Be careful though. You want to prove a few small tests work really well. Then stop… PE will pay you a multiple based on projected expansion from things you haven't tested, even if those things wouldn't have gone well for you based on lack of experience or would have added opex.

4. Profitable customer acquisition with high retention
- Their 24-month LTV to CAC ratio was above 3x. Customers were profitable in less than six months.
- They also had reliable new customer growth for 3+ years. PE needs to see that your acquisition engine isn't a fluke.

5. Premium product with real margins
- They had 70%+ margins after shipping.
- They sold premium products that delivered a strong experience to the customer.
- They had competitors, but because their marketing focused on building the brand (not just driving immediate conversions), they kept their perceived value high and were able to keep margins high.

Exiting a DTC brand to PE is not an easy task.

And you should start at least 3 years before your exit, putting the pieces of the puzzle in place, to look as attractive as possible 
- Focus on growing core channels 
- Tease expansion opportunities 
- Focus on a building a defensible brand 
- Get laser focused on LTV and customer acquisition 

I’ve gone through this process 5 times now at different levels - if you are looking to sell in the next 3 years reach out! 

And if this is your goal - good luck! 

It’s an amazing ride.

I've reviewed 1000s of target account cold emails for my workshops this year. Biggest issue I see? We pitch solutions before we've articulated a relevant business problem worth solving. Want to tee up business problems that don't reek of vendor-speak? Here's how I just did it, using call transcripts + Claude Cowork:

1. Create a Slack channel called "call-summaries". 

2. I use Zapier to send my discovery call transcripts to that Slack channel. 

3. Create a Slack channel called "discovery call analysis". 

4. Create a new task in Claude Cowork. Prompt it with this:

"Every Friday at 7 am, please review the last 7 days of call transcripts in the Slack channel, "call-summaries". Help me understand how these prospects articulated their business problems + why those problems are important to solve right now for their business objectives (in their words). My goal is to sound less like a seller, and more like a business partner. To achieve that goal, I need to tee up problem statements that will resonate with executives (instead of pitching solutions that sound like a shiny Marketing brochure). What business problem patterns can you recognize across these calls? Post the results to the "discovery call analysis" Slack channel".

I just ran it. It returned 3 business problem patterns that occurred in multiple calls this past week (along with direct quotes). 

Pattern 1: Reactive sellers in a world that demands proactive ones.
Every prospect described sellers who wait for business to come to them - through partner leads, inbound, or existing account management. None of them have a muscle for creating demand from cold. 

Pattern 2: The status quo is the real competitor.

Good news + bad news if you're targeting accounts with an AI mandate. 

Good news: They're 2.1x more likely to switch from their current vendor to buy your AI solution.

Bad news: They're 5x more likely to choose the vendor with the lowest price. 

"We have an AI solution" isn't enough to drive competitive differentiation anymore. If your biggest competitor doesn't already have AI in their product, they will soon. 

So, if we're NOT the cheapest date, we aren't going to win on the basis of "we have a better AI solution". In times of uncertainty - better rarely defeats "good enough".  

We win when we reset the buyer's buying criteria. 

Not by being deceitful or self-interested. 

But, by first seeking to understand HOW they arrived at their belief system re: the business problem + ideal solution. 

So, if it's an inbound request - try asking:

- How did the group decide that this was a problem worth solving now?
- How did the group decide that SOLUTION CATEGORY was the ideal way to solve it?

This applies regardless of whether you're selling AI or not. 

Example. 

I sell Sales training workshops for companies losing to buyer status quo. 

I'm not going to win vs. a cheaper competitor if they haven't sized how much buyer status quo is impacting their pipeline. My unique differentiator is that my training is specifically for companies losing to status quo. If a prospect believes "all Sales training is the same" - they're going to pick the cheapest training provider. 

So, if the answer to question 1 is something like, "It's been a while since we refreshed our sales training", I know I'm likely to lose to a cheaper competitor, unless I help them size how much pipeline is being lost to status quo currently. So, I give them a formula to do the math. It also helps me understand if they should even be looking at me as an option. If status quo isn't a big loss reason, I provide a referral. 

If the answer to question 2 is "We met as a team and thought it would make sense to look at some training options" - it tells me they're not 100% sold on training as the solution category. So, it's my job to get them thinking about pros and cons of other solution categories, beyond training. Because, at a certain point, they'll be asked this question internally by leadership. And, rather than hope it doesn't happen and have to objection handle it when it does - I want to be someone who's helping them think through it, early.

→ You're churning creative faster than the algorithm can optimize
→ Good ads getting no spend / not tested

→ You're riding legacy winners that are slowly dying
→ About 30% of ads churn naturally every month
→ If you're not producing enough new concepts, there's nothing behind your top performers when they fall off

→ Launch enough to offset standard ~30% monthly creative churn
→ But don't launch too much to dilute spend across unproven concepts
→ Exact number depends on your spend level & category competition
→ As a rule of thumb I suggest $3,000 for every ad / $10,000 for every concept (3 variations per ad / but not slight variations, make them big enough to tell at a glance).
→ But if you've never calculated this ratio, start there and incrementally move up or down
