There are 3 types of ad fatigue

Only 1 needs a new ad:

1. Algorithmic Cannibalization

Problem: too many similar ads running at once. Meta's algo found a winner and started suppressing the others because they hit the exact same audience segment. Diagnose by objectively looking at the ads and asking a) do they speak to a different audience and b) do they look visually different?

Generally, this is similarity within your own account, but similarity with competitors' ads can also cause fatigue. 

Fix: Pause the losers to consolidate spend. Or differentiate the angle so the algo treats the ads as separate audiences.


2. Contextual Irrelevance

Problem: ad suddenly stopped working. The ad was fine, but the angle 'expired'. For example trying to run a "New Year, New You" ad in March. This is the easiest to diagnose.

Fix: Keep the visual, swap the copy. Very cost efficient to do a hook refresh and keep the rest of the asset. You can also find other ways to make your ad relevant today.


3. Natural Decay

Problem: The ad has hit its peak audience and started sliding down the efficiency curve. You'll know this is happening in advance as you'll see frequency climbing, CTR dropping and CPA creeping up.

Fix: New creative. But "new" doesn't mean start from scratch. 60% of what we launch are iterations on proven winners (new hook, different opening scene, updated offer). The other 40% are swings on totally new concepts. With 10% being big swings and the other 30% being more grounded in research and experience. This ratio keeps your hit rate stable while you replace what's decayed.

I'm supporting an e-comm brand spending $570k/mo

When we first looked at the account, this is what we saw. 
→ $60k was on ads launched in January
→ $510k was on ads launched before Jan

They were heavily reliant on previous ads that were performing well due to seasonality, which was hiding the fact that their new creative production system was underperforming. 

We broke out the new ads, understood why they weren't working, and reverted back to a previous system with some improvements. 

New ads are now taking over at the same time those previous ads are fatiguing, so scale continues to go up despite those historical ads starting to decay because we have clear replacements for them. 

Once we diagnosed each ad individually:
→ Cannibalized ads got paused to let winners breathe
→ Irrelevant hooks got refreshed (same visuals, new copy)
→ Decayed ads got replaced

Can your Meta ads scale?

Use these 4 charts to predict: 

Chart 1: Account Control

- This shows how much spend your best ads received 
- Were your winner ads scaled to their maximum?
- Or were your best ads ignored and you lost out on gains 

This is what you are looking for:
1. No high-spend/high-CPA ads (top right - Red)
2. Few low-spend/low-CPA ads (bottom left, mostly new creates- Green) 
3. Handful of well-scaled winners (far right, good performance - Purple)


Chart 2: Creative Churn

- Are you launching enough ads for your ad spend?
- Each color is a new month of ad launches.
- Every ad cohort shows how much of your creatives churn over time.
- Use this to estimate how many ads you need to scale based on projected churn and growth rates.


Chart 3: Churn/Retesting Control

- This shows the age of your creatives getting spend.
- Dark colors = newer ads (last 7-30 days)
- Light colors = older ads (90-180+ days)

If your chart is dominated by light colors, you're relying on old ads. They will fatigue.
If dark colors are consistently taking spend, your creative machine is working.
You can bring back old ads, but you shouldn't see an overall trend of older ads building up.


Chart 4: Change Balance

When are you actually making changes? 

A lot of accounts only get attention Monday through Friday. Some only get it twice a week.

What that looks like: 
- Mon-Thu performance climbs
- Saturday and Sunday your account fatigues
- Monday you're rebuilding
- Wednesday you're back
- Thursday and Friday you scale
- Then it starts over

Look for consistent changes across all seven days. The total number of increases and decreases should be similar.

Bring all these graphs together to make conclusions: 
- Poor account control + irregular changes = spend more time in account
- Poor account control + wrong changes = evaluate changes and improve strategy
- Not enough creative to combat churn = production problem
- Enough creative but reliant on old = quality problem

There is actually a limit to cold email reply rates.

Knowing this can hopefully free you from testing things that won't matter.

Let me explain.

I have worked with customers in the past that are obsessed with getting the reply rate as high as possible. They think if they send a good enough email, every single person who could possibly see it is going to respond.

We've run tests that show this just isn't the case.

We had the opportunity to work on behalf of Forbes at Web Summit. We had the list of speakers. We had all their emails. We cold emailed them from infrastructure that had warmed up for four months. The pitch was simple: "This is our booth. We want to interview you for Forbes. Book a meeting." And we sent them a link to Forbes.com.

That only got a 30% reply rate. Basically all positive.

When I say "only" 30% — if I were a speaker at an event and Forbes wanted to interview me, I would think the reply rate would be even higher than that.

We also helped a customer email their own customers. We found data that showed they needed a new product, and we could fix the problem for free.

Still only a 10% reply rate.

I say all this because these two examples are pretty undeniably good offers. And they still did not get 40, 50, 60% reply rates.

When you're sending emails, there are so many reasons why somebody doesn't respond. They didn't even see it. It got mixed up with everything else in their inbox. It's just not the right time for them.

When you've run a couple of experiments and the reply rate is staying pretty steady, I would think more about experiments around lists and experiments around offers versus trying to change the copy to see if an AI personalization or a fancier way of saying something is going to move the needle.

List segmentation and changing your offer matter way more.

What experiments have you run that changed your thinking on reply rates?

Are you missing winning ads? 

Use this chart to find out: 

1. Plot all ads from last 90 days
2. Filter for just prospecting ads
3. Put CPA on Y axis, spend on X axis (log scale)
4. Combine performance across ad sets
5. Draw line on your CPA target 
6. Draw a line on your spend threshold 

You’ve now created 4 quadrants. 

Top Left: Grey
- High CPA, low spend
- Choose to either test these ads more = let them spend and move right on the graph - or kill them 

This is going to be the majority of your ads, probably 65% plus. 

Top Right: Red 
- High CPA, high spend 
- These ads have enough spend for us to be confident they should be turned off 

Ideally, you have zero, ass in this quadrant, and you've cut them before they got this far. 

Bottom Left: Blue 
- Low CPA, low spend 
- These are your future winners. They are profitable. We need to spend more on them to see where they land. 

Normally, there are 5 to 15% of ads in this quadrant at any given time that you should be scaling or at least testing further. 

Bottom Right:
- Low CPA, high spend 
- These are our scalable ads. We need to push into these ads more. Expect 1% of all ads to sit here and drive 50% of revenue. 

This is your top 20% of ads that are driving 80% of your performance

This chart also shows how good your media buyer is: 
- Too many red ads = overspending on losers. 
- Too many blue ads = not scaling the right ads fast enough
- Too few red ads = haven’t tested enough creative

If you're thinking about using cold email because you think it's another touch that will increase the ROI on other channels, you're looking at it the wrong way.

I've seen this play out dozens of times.

Early on in my career, companies would work with us and say, "Hey, even if we don't get replies, at least we're getting our name in front of them."

I used to say, "OK sure, we can do that." Send them the invoice. They'd pay and then cancel the next month because they weren't seeing any real attribution.

Here's the thing: cold email doesn't damage your brand (probably a whole post can be made about this) but it also doesn't build your brand.

I always ask people this: what was the most recent cold email that you received an hour ago?

Nobody can remember. At all.

Cold email doesn't have as many risks as people might believe to damage your brand as long as you follow the rules and follow best practices. 

Don't ignore unsubscribe requests. Don't follow up 12 times. Don't email people about products they literally built.

But on the flip side, I'm also very confident that it doesn't positively increase your brand either.

It's one of the only marketing styles that is really direct response and doesn't leave lasting impressions on people. For better or worse.

That's just my experience with it after 5 years and 8 million emails a month.

If you want brand awareness, invest in content and community. If you want pipeline, use cold email. They're different tools for different jobs.

In every outbound messaging workshop I run with sellers, ~8% of the team's cold emails fall into the "ugly baby" category. 

Ugly baby = showing up to a baby shower, uninvited, to let someone know how busted their baby is. 

And, it's especially common for people who use AI to automate their cold emails. 

Here's an example of one I received this AM + why it falls flat + how to change the tonality: 

1 - The opener confidently tells me what my business does. But, it's incorrect. Automation is the opposite of what I teach. This is why talking AT the reader often falls flat. The first line is the most important real estate of a cold email. This is the risk of using AI/automation to do "personalization-at-scale". Inaccurate personalization is worse than no personalization at all. You'd be surprised how often I see this. 

2 - Then, it tells me how ineffective I am at running my business. Even if they're correct, no one likes to be told their baby is ugly. Instead, root the problem in empathy + unsure tonality. "Not sure if it feels tougher to..." is a great way to tee up a problem statement, without insulting them. Point to a problem in the environment - not the reader themselves. 

3 - Then, it assumes its assumption is correct and pivots to a pitch. "We help founders like you". Like me? What am I like? Ah, yes...per above...incompetent! 

4 - The CTA is great. It's an offer to help size the pain of my current state. Offers that do this make fabulous CTAs. Problem is - the rest of the message makes me feel that if I showed up to this call, I'd be speaking to an arrogant know-it-all. 

Our cold email message is our prospect's movie trailer to what our sales experience will feel like. 

How we open is how we win (or lose). Cold outbound shouldn't be an afterthought.

2. Y-axis: CPA
3. X-axis: Total spend (LOG SCALE)
4. Each dot = one ad

What we found:

BEFORE
- Scattered mess. General ASC structure dumping everything in.
- Facebook prioritized ads with high engagement that weren't converting.
- Average CPA sitting at $253. Couldn't scale.

AFTER:
- Tight clustering at low CPA with 10 ads driving half the spend and revenue.

WHAT CHANGED: 
1. Ads above target CPA got paused or spend-capped. The bulk of ads can't spend much but can still perform efficiently at low spend levels.
2. Retest old winners. Retested with new ad copy, headlines, and landing pages. Found winning variations that had been cut for unclear reasons.
3. Scale the top 1-2%. They should take up ~50% of spend and revenue. 

I'm not saying don't test new ads.

Absolutely test. Creative teams are ESSENTIAL to growth.

But separate creative testing from media optimization. 

If your account looks like that scattered "before" chart, more ads won't fix it.

After this we started testing new creatives. But now the structure was dialed in, so the creative team had better data to learn from.

No more “was that actually a good ad or did meta just spend a lot?”

Testing became more effective. Win-win.

In platform performance improved dramatically

But importantly total MER and nCPA also improved dramatically. 

I’m not against the Meta Sequencing argument but prove it with data, and make sure its not an excuse to do nothing. 

In this case, control resulted in the company scaling well into 9 figures.

Here's something nobody talks about in cold email deliverability.

Your offer quality directly affects whether you land in the inbox.

Not indirectly. Directly.

Here's the cycle:

Bad offer → nobody replies → email providers see zero engagement → they assume you're spam → more emails go to junk → even fewer replies → inboxes burn faster → you buy more domains → those burn too.

Now flip it:

Good offer → people reply → email providers see real engagement → you stay in the inbox → more people see your emails → more replies → inboxes last longer → you need fewer domains → your costs drop.

This is why two agencies can run the exact same infrastructure 

Same warmup tool, same sending volume, same ESP, same domain setup

One has offers people respond to. One doesn't.

They're the ones with the best offers.

Every time someone asks me "how do I fix my deliverability" my first question is "what's your reply rate?"

If it's under 1%, your deliverability problem might be an offer problem.

Fix the offer and watch the technical metrics fix themselves.

It's a virtuous cycle when it's working. And a death spiral when it's not.

I've been selling for 22 years. We're living in a new era of exec-level uncertainty. The closest I've experienced was the 2008 financial crisis. Here's the best advice I can share re: what I got wrong when selling in an uncertain market + what ended up working. 

I was working at CEB at the time. We sold an annual best practice research subscription to CXOs and their teams. An annual subscription cost ~$40k-70k. 

Exactly the type of line item a CFO was eager to cut when the economy was falling apart. 

"Ahhh what's this one? Access to an online portal of best practices, webinars & meetings?". 

I'd try to defend the value of the product. They'd tell me, "It's this or letting go of an employee." These were Enterprise CXOs. Yet, you could hear the desperation in their voice. They were worried about losing their jobs, too. 

I'd love to write a LinkedIn post saying how I miraculously turned them around. I didn't. I lost a lot of clients that year. 

Because I was talking ABOUT the value of our product. I wasn't delivering value in the conversation. 

"Access to our best practice research will help you understand how others are navigating this crisis! There's never been a time when this type of research matters more!". 

The following year, CEB conducted the Challenger Sales research. 

The research studied the question, "What type of sellers are winning in this environment?". 

Instead of pitching the value of the membership, we started booking convos on the back of that question. 

Execs came to those calls curious about what others were doing. 

"What are you seeing from other Manufacturing companies? Are they hiring for a different profile? Are they reorganizing? Where are they making cuts?"

My Sales calls became "here's what we're seeing" convos. I barely talked about the product.  

So, I stopped pitching our product in my outbound. I started teeing up convos to share what we were seeing/hearing from other CXOs navigating this mess. 

We ended up winning a ton of those clients back (and new ones, too). 

Eras of uncertainty (like the one we're in right now) can make or break us. 

Pitch a product ("Our AI Agent helps companies....") and you'll often be met with "Let's hold off for a few months". 

Pitch a relevant POV ("Saw your CEO talking about X. ACME tested a few different tactics to achieve that. Open to hearing what they tried, what worked, and what didn't?") and you'll often be met with curiosity. 

Execs are hungry to know what others in their position are doing. What worked? What failed? What bets are other CXOs testing? It's why execs go to dinners and events. 

Remove your product, your pitch, and your value prop from your outbound + discovery.

Right now, POV that helps execs gain decision confidence is a better door opener than what you sell.

Should you lower your MER?

Not always: 

A worse efficiency might be better: 

I just walked a client through a model where their ad performance improved by 44%, yet their MER dropped. They thought they were burning cash. 

Year 1: 
- $20M revenue
- Revenue Mix: 50% organic / 50% paid
- Half of traffic is free. You’re relying on organic. High value but low scalability
- MER: 20% (Looks fantastic - very efficient!)

Then imagine you start spending more on ads

Year 2:
- $50M revenue
- Revenue Mix: 22% organic / 78% paid
- More traffic is paid. You’re using paid ads to grow
- MER: 21.1% (Oh no… it increased)

Here’s what happened: 

1. You worked twice as hard, improved your creative, optimized your funnel, and your efficiency ratio went down.
2. Why? Because you bought a bigger chunk of revenue, your "blended" margin drops.
3. But, because your ROAS improved (from 2.5x to 3.7x, your Net Contribution Dollars (Revenue - COGS - Ad Spend) doubled.
4. So even though MER dropped… you are making more cash. 

Key here is to not optimize for MER.

Instead, optimize for net contribution dollars.

Else you will make the mistake of lowering ad spend to keep MER high.

→ 2,000 clicks (up from 1,000)

→ 50% = lower by 40-50%
→ 75%+ = you're massively overpaying per click

In the last 12 months, I've reviewed 473 LinkedIn posts.

The difference between an 8 impression post and an 80k post?

It's all decided in that first line. 

Not the body or the structure. Not even the topic.

The hook.

Here's one lesson I've learned from writing + editing 1,000s of hooks:

Most beginners write hooks that describe the post.

But the hooks that work create a need to read it.

Example:

Describes the post → "5 tips for LinkedIn writing:".

Creates a need → "I spent 3 hours rewriting the same hook last Tuesday. Here's what I finally realised:".

The former is descriptive. The latter is enticing.

Your hook has one job:

Make reading the next line feel utterly unavoidable.

That's the skill. 

Master it and everything else on LinkedIn gets easier.

For 3 years people scared me away from using images in cold emails.

"Images hurt deliverability."
"Images trigger spam filters."
"Images increase email size."

All true.

But here's the math nobody does.

Let's say plain text gets you 80% inbox placement and 1% reply rate on 10,000 emails.

80% x 10,000 x 1% = 80 replies.

Now let's say adding an image drops inbox placement to 70%. But the image — a screenshot, a chart, a personalized mockup — increases reply rate to 1.8% among people who see it.

70% x 10,000 x 1.8% = 126 replies.

That's 57% more replies with WORSE deliverability.

The deliverability crowd will tell you the first scenario is better because your domain health stays cleaner long-term. And they're right. Probably. Maybe.

But the revenue crowd will tell you 126 replies beats 80 replies every day of the week. And they're also right.

Here's where I've seen images work:

1. Screenshots of the prospect's website with a specific callout
2. A before/after chart relevant to their industry
3. A Loom thumbnail (not embedded video, just the preview image with a play button)
4. A simple product screenshot that answers "what does this actually look like"

Here's where images don't work:

1. Stock photos
2. Marketing banners
3. Your company logo
4. Anything that looks like a newsletter

The real answer, like everything in cold email: test it.

Run 5,000 with the image. Run 5,000 without. Measure replies, not inbox placement.

Worse deliverability x higher conversion can absolutely beat perfect deliverability x mediocre conversion.

I spent $150M on Meta. 8 ads spent $1M+ each.

They had 2 things in common:

1. Ad looked nothing like old ads
2. Ad looking nothing like competitor ads

Average DTC ad:
→ Creator talking to camera:
→ Generic script: "I've been using this for three weeks and here's what happened."
→ Before/after. Green screen. Problem, discovery, result, CTA.

Which by the way is completely fine. It works.

BUT - that's also the problem.

The auction is saturated at the format level.

So your CPA feels like it can never get below $50 at scale (or whatever your CPA is)

The $1M ads looked nothing like other ads

Example 1: 
→ A single static image. $2M+ in lifetime spend. A client found this ad. 
→ They reviewed all their concepts and realized that one USP mattered more than anyone else.
→ They found a visually striking way to illustrate that USP. (Tried a few formats until one stuck)
→ The ad accidentally became a magnet for comments. Full of people talking about how much they love the brand. 

Example 2:
→ A doctor who partnered with a brand. He had a musical, genuinely funny way of explaining why he worked with them.
→ They knew music performed well as a way to communicate their key USP
→ They knew actors with a white coat performed well to build credibility. 
→ They found a doctor who they could build a relationship with and get to know over time. 

Online playbooks to teach us "better creative" = best practices + top formats. We've been encouraged to scroll ad library… sort by longest running (or now high impressions) and just rip that. 
But sometimes the most scalable creative is the one that looks nothing like what everyone else is running.

Ask these three questions: 

1. What is one USP my brand has that no competitor is claiming and clearly matters?
2. What format would feel unique compared to competitors?
3. What unique asset, relationship, or story do I have? 

This is really hard. 
Your hit rate will be low on these ideas. 
But when you find one that hits. It’ll be a huge winner.

Most people use LinkedIn outbound wrong.

Where people are getting it wrong is they think: email somebody, then connect with them on LinkedIn the next day, then follow-up email, then LinkedIn message. 

That sounds great in theory. But the math just doesn't work out. 

The volume you can send on email versus connection requests you can send on LinkedIn is completely different.

Instead, we want to create an order of operations where we're reaching out to the most engaged, highest likelihood to reply leads first.

1. Engaged leads from your other channels. Automate connecting and reaching out to any person who is an engaged lead, inbound forms, cold email replies, ad responders, whatever. 

These people already showed interest somewhere. LinkedIn is your follow-up.

2. De-anonymized website visitors. Anybody visiting your website who was identified with your favorite de-anonymization platform like Snitcher or Visual Visitor. 

They were looking at you. Now go find them.

3. People in your ICP engaging with your current customers. As long as you have marketing rights, reach out and mention that you work with that company. 

When you name-drop the case study, they know exactly who you're talking about.

4. Your competitors' LinkedIn engagement. Connect with and message people commenting on and reacting to your competitors' posts. These people care about the category. They're already educated.

5. Your golden ICP. After all of the above, then go cold to your best-fit prospects.

By the time you go through these five tiers, it's going to be another month gone by, and you have more engagers to reach out to, more website visitors, more competitor activity to scrape. The cycle repeats.

This is a much better strategy than blasting your connection requests at a cold list.

Here's three things I see beginners worry about in cold email that I don't worry about anymore.

5 years and 8 million emails a month later. Here's what I've learned.

1. CTA changes.

"Would you be interested in speaking about this 15 minutes next week?" versus "Any interest in this?" 

I don't think changing your CTA so slightly from one of these to the other has any meaningful change on success anymore. 

People either want what you're offering or they don't. The call to action is not the variable that moves the needle. 

2. Gaming email deliverability.

Trying to come up with some kind of warmup schedule or email deliverability hack that other people aren't doing. 

Obsessing over rotation patterns and trying to find the magic configuration. That's really more of the thing that wastes people's time. 

3. Finding free hacks instead of paying for tools.

I used to spend a lot of time trying to scrape data for free. The amount of time it would take me to do that was never worth it. 

Just pay for the thing that works. The hours you spend building a workaround cost more than the tool subscription.

IM8 Health is launching 1,000 ads a month.

But with a risky offer... 

A small batch of their ads offer a "free starter kit"

I'm all for strong offers. And it seems to be working well for them here, but for any new brands trying to learn from them, you need to be very careful. 

Heres where I've seen it backfire: 
→ Free kits pull in discount-first buyers. 
→ High likelihood to get kit then cancel.
→ Discount buyers churn as much as 50% faster.
→ Lower LTV across the board. 
→ Trained customer to not buy at full-price

In the end to retain that discounted customer you need:
→ More post-purchase education
→ More proof they made a good choice
→ More content building brand affinity

The better play:
→ Invest in education-first creative up front. 
→ Build understanding of why the product matters. 
→ Replace deep discounts with value-adds (free shipping, samples, bonus gifts)
→ Test bundles ("build your own kit") instead of free kit 
→ Protect margins while still giving people a reason to buy

Either way do this to maximize LTV
→ Ensure at least some ads are education-heavy (Can retarget purchasers too)
→ Build the site around educating for values (not just the discount)
→ Set up post-purchase emails to explain how to use it to get the best results (and how often)
→ Include usage support in the packaging. 
→ Do everything you can to ensure the user has a great and consistent experience (no matter what ad they came through). Education is an important part of that. 

 it looks like IM8 is pushing mostly top-of-funnel creatives and using this to convert people who are at the bottom of the funnel. If you're a new brand trying to learn from this, focus on their top-of-funnel creatives and having a good structure for onboarding more than the specific ads

Your lead lists have more garbage in them than you think. And here's how you can work on fixing it.

The problem comes down to three things:

1. The data is scraped from self-reported data that people mislabel.

Companies are notoriously bad at putting the correct industries on LinkedIn. Someone marks themselves as "Information Technology" when they're really a logistics company with a website. You need to look at their actual websites and company descriptions and use AI to verify fit — not just trust the label.

2. The data is possibly outdated.

You need to figure out when the data was last updated from your provider. If it's stale, you need to either scrape Google for current information or get a more expensive data provider that will pull the data live. That "150-person startup" might have gone through layoffs and now has 12 people. Or got acquired.

3. Data providers can't predict every use case.

What counts as a "B2B SaaS company" versus an "e-commerce company"? Some people say e-commerce is any company with a Shopify store. But Biden for America was built on Shopify. Your definition of ICP doesn't match the category labels that data providers use.

You have to build a layer on top of their data to work with this.

Here's how we fix it:

For the self-reported data problem, use AI to look at websites and company descriptions to make a real fit determination. Show AI what 30 good companies look like, then keep editing your prompt until it gets all 30 correct. Then run it on everything.

For outdated data, check when it was last updated. If it falls outside your range, scrape or pay for live data.

For the use case problem - use Claude Code or Codex with the batch API to throw as much AI inference at it as possible. Rent GPUs if you have to. This is a problem that AI has made solvable for the first time.

The data will never be perfect. But you can get a lot closer than most people think.

What's the best Meta bidding strategy:

Cost cap or highest volume?

I use them both:

1. Testing
→ New ads need room to find their audience (especially highly novel ones)
→ Cost cap here typically kills good ads too early
→ Best play here is normally to use highest volume

2. Scaling
→ If I see a proven winner, I want to push it hard
→ Only 1% of ads will drive 50% of ad spend
→ Let Meta find every possible conversion
→ We sometimes run the same winner in both highest volume and cost cap campaigns to see which delivers better at scale

3. Stragglers
→ I see an ad starting to underperform
→ It's starting to come outside of target CPA
→ There's still a bid/budget range where it's profitable
→ Use cost cap (set target cost per result or bid) to keep the ad efficient and still drive profit
→ Got to be careful with cost cap. Sometimes it underspends even though performing well. Sometimes it overspends without hitting target.

Be careful about using Meta ads manager to make these decisions...
→ Fine for relative comparisons between ads
→ In-platform (ads manager) typically over inflates BOFU
→ Likely your real CPA > in-platform CPA
→ Easy to set the cost cap too high, only to realize multi attribution shows the CPA is higher and you've overbid.
→ Use MTA (Triple Whale, Northbeam, etc.), post purchase surveys and MMM (marketing mix modeling) to make better decisions.

My big takeaway:

Don't only use one bidding strategy.

Every company and product is different, your account structure should reflect that.

What's your setup look like?

PMax is beating Google Search.

Turn on ASAP only if:

1. Conversion volume. Don't touch PMax until you're over 50 conversions per month on Search. Stay with Search-only (and maybe Manual CPC) until you build that volume. Between 50-100? Test PMax at 10-20% of budget. Over 100? PMax can scale.

2. Tracking. Is GCLID captured on every form submit? Are UTMs applied to all Google campaigns? Does your CRM data reconcile with Google Ads within tolerance? If any of these are missing, PMax will train on incomplete data. We've seen cost per customer rise from $800 to $1,900 in three months because tracking wasn't set up correctly.

3. Conversion actions. Are you optimizing to form submits or to SQLs and opportunities? Go as bottom funnel as possible. If you optimize to form fills, PMax finds the cheapest clicks. YouTube pre-roll, Gmail promos, Display. And if your conversion action is higher up the funnel (like MQLs), negative keywords and negative placements become even more important.

4. Search. Do you have stable performance from Search campaigns first? Are your keywords, match types, and negatives dialed in? PMax works best as a scaling layer on top of working Search. If Search isn't performing yet, fix that first. We've spent $800K+ on nonbrand Search since March 2025 on this account alone.

5. Negative signal process. Do you retract spam leads from Google? Unqualified leads? Test or duplicate submissions? Removing bad conversions teaches PMax what not to look for. If you get bad leads, it's probably because you're not retracting. Our PMax leads convert to customers at around the same rate as our nonbrand Search campaigns.

6. Brand exclusions. Always exclude brand traffic in PMax using brand exclusion lists and negative keywords. This stops PMax cannibalizing brand search.

Failed any of the above?
→ Run Search-only with Manual CPC (if very low conv volume) for 30-60 days
→ Use Exact Match and Phrase Match only
→ Bid on high-intent terms specific to your product

Passed all six?
→ Introduce PMax at 10-20% of total Google spend
→ Compare cost per qualified lead against Search weekly
→ Scale when PMax matches or beats Search on down-funnel metrics

We did this on the account in the image.
→ Non Brand Search: $262 CPA
→ PMax: $87 CPA

Same spend, but PMax is 3x cheaper.

AI is not going to fix your cold email campaign.

I know that's weird coming from a guy who uses Clay and Claude Code for basically everything. We run AI personalization, AI list building, AI copy generation, AI analytics.

But here's the thing.

AI makes good campaigns better. It does not make bad campaigns good.

If your offer doesn't work, AI-personalized first lines just mean people read a more relevant email about something they still don't want.

If your targeting is wrong, AI enrichment just gives you more detailed data about the wrong people.

Cold email works when you have a large enough TAM to make it work, a clear problem with a clear solution, a buyer who can say yes without feeling like they have to rip and replace huge systems, and a deal size that justifies the cost per meeting.

Cold email struggles when your target market is too small, your deal size is too low, or you are in a commoditized industry with no specialization in your offer.

AI amplifies whatever you feed it. Feed it a strong offer and good targeting, and it works well. Feed it a weak offer and bad targeting, and it just burns through your domains faster.

Fix the fundamentals first.

I've helped 5 eCom brands exit for ~$500m.

The acquirer always wanted lower CPAs:

This is how:

1. Creative

- Target ~1 new concept per $10k in monthly spend.
- Good split = 70% video (builds awareness), 30% static (closes sales)
- Complicated product / new brand = more videos
- High SKU count = more statics
- At $500k/mo that's 35 video concepts, 15 static. 2-3 hook variations per video, 5-8 per static. Roughly 70 videos and 90 statics.
- Cut 70%+ of creatives before they hit two weeks.


2. Media buying

- Scale the top 1-2% to take ~50% of total spend. Scale 15-20% every 3-5 days.
- Pause or spend-cap everything above target CPA once its tested.
- Retest old winners with new copy, headlines, landing pages
- Limit budget changes to 10-15% max, but make changes twice as often. We saw 28% ROAS improvement from this alone on a DTC brand.
- Keep testing budget at 15-20% of total spend. Per ad minimum = Target CPA x 30-50.


3. Website optimization

- CVR benchmark: 3%+ (top 10% hit 4.7%+)
- Add-to-cart benchmark: 7-10%
- Checkout completion benchmark: 60%+
- Sometimes a landing page with 10% higher CPA leads to faster repurchases and higher LTV.
- Optimize for PSV and LTV not just CPA


4. Subscription optimization

- Monthly subscription churn: under 7%
- 12-month retention: 40%+
- Repeat purchase rate (non sub): 30%+
- Segment by subscription vs one-time, 4/8/12 week frequencies, product categories, acquisition channels
- The gap between 2x and 4x purchase frequency is a 2x LTV multiplier.


5. CRO

- Target email opt-in: 2-5%.
- Run distinct landing pages for each avatar.
- Example avatars for a supplement brand: general nutrition, gut health, weight loss


6. Tracking optimization

- Click-based attribution overvalues lower-funnel performance by up to 250%.
- TOF creative can drive 13X more incremental acquisitions than BOF. Click attribution tells you the opposite.
- Post-purchase surveys catch what clicks miss. Track nCAC on every ad.


7. Ad copy and headlines

- Ad copy can boost performance by 30% from our internal testing.
- Give creators selling points, not scripts. Let them share real experience in their own words.
- Target 40%+ hook rate, 2%+ CTR, 2-3 hook variations per video concept minimum


8. Data reporting and analysis

- Max spend: Gross margin - OpEx = max marketing %. Example: 50% margin - 10% OpEx = 40% max
- Target CPA: Project 3-month customer profitability. Example: $55 AOV, $39 profit at month 3 = $39 target CPA


Acquirers want:

- Profitable customer acquisition
- Reliable new customer growth for 3+ years
- LTV and margins optimized

Pull each lever and they'll happily acquire you

Are you running Google Ads right?

Use this chart to find out:

Ask yourself two questions.
1. How many conversions do you get per month?
2. How much do your conversion values differ from each other?

Top Left:
- High volume of conversions and low value variance
- Every conversion is worth roughly the same
- Google has enough data to hit a target and every lead looks the same
- Go for tCPA

Top Right:
- High volume of conversions and high value variance
- Some conversions are worth 5x or 10x others (and you're tracking that value)
- Google has enough data AND meaningful value signals to chase your best customers
- Go for tROAS

Bottom Left:
- Low volume of conversions and low value variance
- You don't have enough data for Google to reliably hit a target yet
- Let the algorithm learn. Don't constrain it with targets it can't achieve.
- Go for Max Conversions

Bottom Right:
- Low volume of conversions and high value variance
- Still not enough data for targets, but your conversions have different values
- Let Google learn while at least prioritizing higher-value outcomes
- Go for Max Conversion Value.
- 

Examples: 
- PLG SaaS, $300k/mo ad budget with 2-3 pricing plans = high conversions, low value variance
- Rehab clinic, $3M/mo budget with wildly variant insurance payouts= high conversions, high value variance
- Startup SMB SaaS, $25k/mo ad budget with one subscription = low conversions, low value variance
- Enterprise SaaS, $30k/mo ad budget with F500 ICP = low conversions, high value variance

Cheatsheet:
→ High volume + low value variance = tCPA
→ High volume + high value variance = tROAS
→ Low volume + low value variance = Max Conversions
→ Low volume + high value variance = Max Conversion Value

I've changed my mind on a lot of things when it comes to cold email best practices. But these 3 principles have never changed. Not once.

Everything else people sell courses about? Noise on top of these.

1. Deliverability

If your emails don't land in the primary tab, nothing else matters. Not your copy. Not your list. Not your offer.

We always keep the amount of inboxes we need to send for a customer plus anywhere from 50 to 100% extra capacity warming up. That way we can switch out anything that's not working immediately. We monitor this daily for customers having issues and weekly across all customers automatically with Claude skills.

Most people skip this because it's boring. That's why most people's campaigns don't work.

2. The list

Accurate data on the right people. What doesn't work is a mediocre list with 30% bad contacts in it. You should spend as much time on list building as copywriting.

3. Copy with a clear offer that is easy to say yes to

There's a huge difference between copy that sounds clever and copy that converts cold traffic.

I think Alex Hormozi's framework — "We help customers accomplish their goal in this time without this risk" — is the perfect offer framework for cold email. But you also need to think about what's easy to say yes to. If you pitch "We help B2B companies speed up their sales process with a new CRM in 30 days without losing sales momentum," that's still a very tough ask. Changing out somebody's entire CRM is a big commitment. You want to go in with something easier to say yes to.

Shout out David Ogilvy — "your first line gets them to read the second line, and the second line gets them to read the third line" — one of my guiding frameworks. And Josh Braun is one of the best in the game at cold email copywriting if you want to study someone.

People ask me about send times, follow-up cadences, A/B test frameworks, personalization tokens. Those are all optimizations on top of these 3 things.

If your deliverability is broken, your list is wrong, or your copy doesn't resonate. no optimization saves you.

Get these 3 right and you're about 80% of the way to what most agencies charge $10K+/month to do.

There's 1 reason why AI won't replace marketers.

Eugene Schwartz wrote why in 1960’s “Breakthrough Advertising”

Markets don't respond to messages.

They respond to messages they haven't been numbed to yet.

He called it market sophistication.

The claim that launches a category - "lose weight fast" - works once.

The 1st brand that says it owns the market.

The 2nd brand gets ignored.

The 5th brand gets mocked.

The market evolves. The message has to evolve faster.

But here's the problem:

AI is only trained on what the market has already seen.

Every prompt you run is pulling from a dataset of things that have already been said, already been published, already been processed by the very audience you're trying to reach.

AI can’t tell you what stage your market is at.

Or which claims are already dead.

It definitely can’t tell you what the market needs to hear next -
because that hasn't been written yet.

---

Todd Brown takes this further with what he calls the unique mechanism.

The insight is this:

It's not enough to have a better product.

You need a better explanation for why your product works.

One that the market hasn't heard before.

One that makes their previous understanding feel incomplete.

That's not a copywriting skill.

It’s a thinking skill.

It requires you to look at your market, your product, and your competitors - and find an angle that doesn't exist in the conversation yet.

AI can’t do that.

Not because it lacks information.

It is, by design, a summarizer of what already exists.

---

This is what I call second-order thinking in marketing.

First-order thinking asks: what should I say?

Second-order thinking asks: what has my market already heard so many times that saying it again will actively hurt me?

First-order thinking asks: what makes my product good?

Second-order thinking asks: what explanation of why it works has never been named before?

First-order thinking asks: what's the best way to write this?

Second-order thinking asks: what does this market need to believe before any of my words will land?

AI is exceptional at first-order.

It will never touch second-order.

---

This is why output 6x'd and results didn't.

Most are using AI to move faster.

And think less.

If one person can now produce what 6 people produced, but revenue didn't move - the output was never the constraint.

The insight was.

The marketers who win in an AI-saturated world won't be the ones who produce the most.

They'll be the ones who understand their market so precisely that every message feels like it was written for one person, at exactly the right moment, saying the thing no one had thought to say yet.

That skill has no shortcut.

And it never will.

A complicated 10 LTV differentiated niche with a dedicated buyer product may perform best with only ABOs

Most people need a mix.

Before you write a single email, there's one question that determines everything — your copy, your CTA, your follow-up sequence, your entire funnel.

Most people skip it and wonder why their campaigns underperform.

The question: Can I ask for the meeting directly, or do I need to earn the right to ask?

That's the difference between generating meeting-ready leads and generating hand raisers.

A meeting-ready lead is someone who responds to your cold email and says "yes, let's talk next week." They're ready to book.

A hand raiser is someone who says "yes" to a lead magnet or a Loom video. They're interested, but they are not ready to meet with you right now. They require much more follow-up and warming before you book the meeting.

I see too many people going wrong here. They start using lead magnets, get excited about the response rates, and then try to immediately book meetings,  forgetting that not everyone is ready after one touchpoint. 

Everyone should try to start with getting meeting-ready leads. But if you can't, maybe your offer is very cyclical and prospects are locked into contracts, or it's a commoditized offering and you need to differentiate, you're going to run into problems. That's when you pivot to hand raisers.

Here's what we do at GEX. We offer a free campaign launch before people become customers. That generates meeting-ready leads. But when we paired that with a follow-up email offering to share a list of every new hire on LinkedIn or all the people engaging with their competitors' content — notified monthly — we 5x'd our response rates.

Sometimes it's not even one or the other. Email one goes for the meeting-ready lead. Email two follows up with a hand-raiser offer. Layer them together.

Which approach are you running right now?

Create a bar chart of media buying changes by day. 

We often see:

🔴 Chart 2: How big changes are they making? 

Take data from Chart 1 and map the count of positive and negative changes. Categorize into 3% buckets

Three red flags you may see
1. Always the same change, "10%", no matter what the data shows
2. Rarely making changes (you want consistent small optimizations)
3. Often making big changes 50%+/- (destabiizes algorithm)

Example image is gold standard. 
→ Shows an even number of budget decreases and increases

→ Very rare to see a big budget change of 50% +/-

→ When they make bigger changes, does CPA go down?

How I max out Target ROAS campaigns:

1. Check minimum requirements
To run tROAS you should hit these minimums every 30 days:
→ Display = 15.
→ Shopping = 15.
→ App = 300
→ Demand Gen = ~30
→ Search = 15
→ Performance Max = ~30

If you don't have those numbers (across your account, ideally not all centralized in Branded keywords), stay on Max Conversion Value.

2. Set tROAS
→ Pull your "Conv. value/cost" column (ROAS) over last 4 weeks & exclude last 3-7 days to account for conversion delay (if you experience that).
→ Set your target at or below that number.
→ Don't try to set tROAS above historical just yet. I've seen accounts lose 40%+ traffic overnight from doing that. It kills your volume and lets your competitors come in.

3. Train with real value
→ Upload offline conversions with conversion values
→ E.g. MQL: $50, SQL: $250, Closed Deal: $10,000
→ Encourages Google to shift budget to higher value clicks (probably more expensive but it's worth it)

 4. Check Search Lost IS (Budget)
→ This tells you if tROAS is in-line
→ If Search Lost IS (budget) is >0%, your tROAS might be too low. Raise tROAS until lost-to-budget hits zero. Or increase your budgets if you are hitting your desired ROAS
→ This keeps CPCs efficient throughout the day

5. Adjustments
→ Want more volume? Lower tROAS in 5-10% increments
→ Want more efficiency? Raise tROAS in 5-10% increments
→ Wait 1-2 conversion cycles after any change before judging.

Cheatsheet:
→ Turn on tROAS at the right time
→ Set tROAS around historical performance
→ Watch Search Lost IS (Budget) to adjust tROAS
→ Make gradual changes & wait 1-2 conversion cycles

Here's a strategy to turn your lead list into five or more experiments with Claude Code and Clay.

One thing we think about a lot with our customers is how the list is the message. I don't know who said that first, but it definitely wasn't me, so credit to whoever coined it.

What we mean is this: if you know you can sell to any founder with less than 20 employees, that's a pretty big list. 

But if you know the best founder for you is someone who has founded a company before, has been in business less than two years, has 10 to 20 employees, and has no accounting or finance job titles on their LinkedIn company page...

That person should be receiving a completely different message than someone who has one or two of those traits but not all of them.

We use Claude Code or Clay to enrich our lists for any criteria that might change how we'd message somebody.

For example, if somebody has been in business for two years, they're just getting systems ramped up. That's a way different message than somebody who's been in business for 10 years and has figured all this out already. 

If somebody is a CEO versus a founder, and there's no reason to change your message, then there's no reason to separate them in the list.

We separate the list by what data points change our messaging.

This way we can slice and dice our data and have different email campaigns for multiple layers of ICP fit. Sometimes your golden ICP (where everything is true about that person) might only have a thousand leads in the entire campaign. 

But I guarantee you'll get a higher response rate on those leads than on your broader ones, because you can niche your messaging down more and more.

The list is the message. Use that when creating your campaigns.

Don't let Meta pick your winning ads

Instead do this:

What Meta does well
- Meta optimizes toward ads that drive conversions.
- If they make you more money, you spend more money.

What Meta doesn't do well:
- Their reporting has cookie loss.
- They struggle to attribute top funnel ads that convert days or weeks later
- Optimize for business outcomes, e.g. Retail lift. Amazon spillover. LTV.

Which means Meta can make bad decisions:
- Kill an ad driving retail purchases they can't measure.
- Scale an ad with great engagement but terrible downstream economics.

And I've seen the bigger and complex your brand is beyond Meta and a single conversion. E.g. retail, Amazon, subscription, varying gross margins across products

The bigger the gap between what Meta optimizes for, and what outcome you actually want.

This is exactly how we pick our winning ads:

1. Set up one ABO for testing and top of funnel scaling
2. Set up one ASC per product for additional scale
3. Use a multi-touch attribution tool focused on new customer CPA (not Meta's reported CPA)
4. Watch the difference between total clicks, first touch and last touch attribution to know which ads drive top of funnel vs bottom of funnel
5. Check the predicted LTV and AOV by ad. An ad with a higher CPA but 2x the AOV or stronger rebill rate might be your most profitable ad.
6. Plot all ads with spend on X axis and CPA on Y axis (adjusted for these assumptions)
7. Draw a Poisson confidence curve at 90% confidence against your target CPA
8. Any ad past that curve with enough spend? Cut it.
9. Any ad below target CPA but barely spending? Underscaled. See if forcing spend drives performance.
10. Budget changes: 20% at a time. Big swings push ads into relearning.
11. Check twice a day at $150k+/month spend. More smaller moves always wins.
12. Scale winners into new placements first, then increase budget
13. If one ad monopolizes spend in a campaign, duplicate the campaign, pause that ad in the duplicate, lower budget on the original

Meta's goals are not your goals. 

Meta does not have as much data about your business as you do.

And fixing GTM Efficiency:

A. Magic Number & NRR decision tree

Magic Number = Net New ARR × 4 ÷ prior quarter marketing & sales spend

↳ >1.5 = step on the gas, you're leaving money on the table 
↳ >0.75 = efficient, worth investing more
↳ <0.5 = broken GTM, fix before scaling

NRR: is your base growing or leaking?
→ 130%+ = world class (expansion is doing the heavy lifting) 
→ 110–130% = strong (healthy upsell, low churn) 
→ 101–110% = flat (expansion barely offsetting losses) 
→ 90–100% = warning (churn eating into base) 
→ <90% = broken (fix the leaky bucket before scaling anything)

Diagnose & fix:
→ Low Magic Number + high NRR = good product, broken acquisition 
→ Low Magic Number + low NRR = PMF problem. Don't touch GTM yet 
→ High Magic Number + rising CAC = channel saturation. Wall is coming 
→ NRR + Magic Number are declining = you're scaling a leaky bucket 
→ NRR flat + GTM headcount growing = efficiency eroding quarter over quarter

B. Rule of 40 = Revenue Growth % + FCF Margin %
↳ 60% growth + (−20%) margin = hypergrowth, acceptable if CAC payback is trending down 
→ 20% growth + 20% margin = efficient, but are you leaving expansion revenue on the table?
→ <30 combined = board conversation is coming

Benchmarks by stage:
- $20M ARR: growth % still dominates. Burn is acceptable if NRR is strong
- $35M ARR: investors start stress-testing margin trajectory
- $50M+ ARR: PE is watching & buying cash flow potential

C. LTV:CAC by channel 

= (ACV × Gross Margin % × Avg Customer Life) ÷ CAC

→ 4:1 = scale the channel
→ 3:1 = viable, invest more
→ 2:1 = break even
→ 1:1 = kill if more longer than 3mo

Common mistakes:
1. Not including employee time in CAC
2. Blending LTV:CAC across channels

3:1 blended ratio can hide a 1:1 channel dragging down a 5:1 channel. 

D. CAC Payback: months to recover acquisition cost 

Formula: CAC ÷ (ACV × Gross Margin % ÷ 12)
→ SMB: <12mo = good | 12–18mo = acceptable | 18mo+ = warning 
→ Mid-market: <18mo = good | 18–24mo = acceptable | 24mo+ = warning 
→ Enterprise: <24mo = good | 24–36mo = acceptable | 36mo+ = warning

Diagnose & fix:
- CAC payback lengthening + sales cycle lengthening = ICP drift (you're selling to the wrong accounts)
- CAC payback lengthening + win rate stable = pricing problem
- CAC payback fine but Magic Number declining = cost structure problem

E. GTM Headcount Efficiency 

= Net New ARR ÷ Total GTM Headcount

Benchmarks:

At $2M–$10M ARR: 
→ >$200K net new ARR per GTM head = highly efficient 
→ $100–200K = market rate 
→ <$100K = headcount outpacing rev

At $10M–$20M ARR 
→ >$300K new ARR per GTM head = highly efficient 
→ $150–300K = market rate 
→ <$150K = headcount outpacing rev

At $20M–$50M ARR benchmarks: 
→ >$400K net new ARR per GTM head = highly efficient 
→ $200–400K = market rate 
→ <$200K = headcount is outpacing rev growth

I've seen clients with a 0.8% positive reply rate printing money.

I've seen clients with a 4% positive reply rate struggling to stay afloat.

The difference? One was selling $80K contracts. The other was selling a $500 product.

Reply rate is a vanity metric if you don't connect it to revenue.

Here's what to calculate instead:

1. Size your TAM. How many companies actually fit your ICP? If it's 3,000, you'll burn through them in 2 months at scale. Plan accordingly.

2. Find your positive reply rate. Not total reply rate — positive replies divided by emails sent. That's your real conversion.

3. Multiply by deal value and close rate. One positive reply on an $80K deal with a 25% close rate is worth $20K. One positive reply on a $500 deal with a 20% close rate is worth $100.

Those are fundamentally different businesses that require fundamentally different outbound strategies.

The $80K business needs precision targeting and can afford to send fewer, better emails. The $500 business needs massive volume and tight unit economics to make cold email work at all.

Before your next campaign: how much is one positive reply actually worth to your business?

That number changes everything about how you run outbound.

The most common thing I hear from founders: "Cold email doesn't work for my business."

5 years of doing this, I've never found a business where some version of cold email doesn't work. The problem is what you're trying to accomplish with cold email, not the channel.

When people say "cold email doesn't work for my business," what I hear is: "cold email isn't helping me grow revenue." I think they're picking the wrong kind of outbound.

There are 3 types:

Type 1: Meeting-ready leads

Direct ask. "Want to save 40 hours/month on bookkeeping?" → "Yes, let's talk."

Works when the prospect already knows they have the problem. Accountants, agencies, SaaS with obvious pain points. You just need to show up at the right time.

Type 2: Hand raisers

Give value first. "I built a list of 200 companies engaging with your competitors on LinkedIn. Want it?"

Works when the prospect doesn't know they have a problem yet. Complex sales, high-trust products. You're not asking for a meeting. You're starting a conversation by providing something useful upfront.

Type 3: Partners, recruiting, and affiliates

Not selling. Connecting. "We send 8 million emails a month and need deliverability partners" or "We're hiring SDRs who want to learn at scale."

This is the most underused cold email funnel. Nobody thinks of recruiting or partnerships as cold email use cases, but the mechanics are identical.

I think every business should be using cold email. It just matters: can it work to get you meeting-ready leads? Can it work to get you hand raisers? Or does it work to help you build partnerships, affiliates, and recruit new employees?

And how much energy can you spend converting a meeting-ready lead to a deal closed versus a hand raiser to a deal closed versus a partner or affiliate?

BREAKING: Allbirds sold for ~1% of their $4Bn valuation. 

I analyzed their P&L. This killed them:

→ I love AllBirds. Their shoes are amazing.
→ I bought 2 pairs a year for 3 years straight
→ They raised $200M from VCs. $348M in an IPO. 
→ Hit peak valuation of $4 billion. 

But I just checked AllBirds 2025 P&L.
→ 90% SG&A, up from 64% in 2021 (benchmark = ~30%)
→ 41% gross margin, down from 53% in 2021 (benchmark = ~55%)
→ -52% operating margin (for every $1 in, $1.52 out)

But marketing spend was fine (around 19-25%)

So what went wrong?
→ Opened 60 retail stores in expensive locations.
→ Revenue per store dropped 41% when they went from 22 locations to 40.
→ SG&A exploded because they built infrastructure for a $4 billion valuation brand on $190M in revenue.

All because they went too WIDE
→ Launched merino wool workout clothes that made people sweat through their shirts.
→ Sold wool leggings that functioned very poorly.
→ Sold running shoes that couldn't compete with On and HOKA.

They were a product brand that rushed products.

AllBirds had a winning opportunity
→ Huge TAM (everyone needs casual, comfortable footwear)
→ Great margins (selling $100+ products)
→ High LTV (E.g. I bought multiple times, shoes are a huge market)

But they treated it as if their TAM was small, so they expanded quickly and diluted themselves too thin.

Instead, they should have gone DEEP:
→ More colorways, fits & sizes
→ International expansion of the core product
→ Fix the things that cause churn (e.g. for me the soles wore unevenly, durability needed improving)

Takeaway:
→ If you have a great brand, but TAM is small, go WIDE.
→ If you have a great brand, TAM is big, go DEEP

And if people love your product? Make it better.

If there are first-time founders out there that need to start cold email for zero dollars, this is how I would do it.

There are four problems you need to solve: deliverability, list building, copywriting, and sending. Let's take each as a checklist.

**1. Deliverability.**
It's not best practice, and I wouldn't even say it comes across as professional, but if you want to do cold email for zero dollars, sending from your personal email address will do the trick until you close enough deals to invest. Your personal email likely has years of reputation on it, and it will work fine for the low-volume use case we're going to do here.

**2. List building.**
You need a way to build lists and store them. You could save files locally and use the free tiers of Codex or Claude Code to do research and find 50 contacts to reach out to. If you need their emails, most email platforms have great free trials you could work between. Start a Prospeo free trial, for instance.

3. Copywriting.
Any ChatGPT or Claude instance can help you get started for free. I would suggest creating cold emails in the style of Josh Braun if you really don't know what to do here. His frameworks are simple and they work.

4. Sending.
A new repo was just dropped that controls your browser, and you could use the "send later" function inside of Gmail to do the sending. It cuts a couple corners here and there, but if you have absolutely no money to get started, this is how you'd be able to do it.

Now here's the progression when you're ready to invest:

$50/month: Smartlead or Instantly for sending + scheduling. They have built-in lead databases.

$200/month: Add 3-5 domains and inboxes. Buy a list from Prospeo or Clay. Use Million Verifier to clean it.

$500/month: I'd just invest in more domains and inboxes at this level. A/B testing across segments.

$2,000+/month: Waterfall enrichment. Intent signals. 50+ domains. Multiple campaigns. This is where agencies like us operate.

Start sending. Upgrade later.

LOTS of marketers are moving ad spend to YouTube.

We spend ~$1M/mo. Here's how YT ads work: 

1. Audience-first targeting
- YouTube = targets who someone is.
- Search = targets what someone searches.
- Google uses browsing history, purchase signals, and in-market data to decide who sees your ad.
- So if someone searches "workout clothes" on YouTube and gets served a B2B software ad, it's because they've shown intent / fit someplace else.
- Note: YouTube still has some search targeting, but its superpower is audience.

2. Platform
- YouTube ads live inside existing Google Ads campaigns.
- You're probably already running YouTube ads and don't realize it.
- Performance Max, Demand Gen, and Video campaigns all serve on YouTube. Even Search text ads can show up in YouTube search results. 

3. Attribution
- YouTube typically creates intent that shows up in your Search campaigns later.
- This means it can be harder to see direct conversions - but there are ways to measure: 

- E.g. we ran a YouTube lift study on a client account.
→ Track branded search volume week over week
→ Monitor Search CAC before and after YouTube launches
→ Found it pulled down Search CAC by 6%.
- E.g. Google just rolled out a new metric called Attributed Branded Searches (still in beta). It tracks how many people searched for your brand after seeing your YouTube ad, even if they never clicked. 

4. Creative
- Test YouTube ads with repurposed assets: 
→ Grab Meta statics and videos
→ Record a quick Loom-style walkthrough or talking head
→ Turn a slide deck into a simple video ad
→ Upload these into the campaign manager 
- Then once you see ROI you can invest in higher production assets. 

5. Conversion tracking
- YouTube has an advantage most video platforms can't match.
- Because it lives inside Google Ads, YouTube campaigns pull conversion data from your Search campaigns to train the algorithm.
- So if Search already knows who converts, YouTube sees that signal. 
- It doesn't start from scratch.

→ A paused subscriber is way more likely to come back than someone who fully cancels

4. Build winback sequence

→ Don't email about resubscribing for 14 days. They literally just told you they want to leave
→ Day 14-30: make your move. The offer needs to be better than what they had when they left

I've run 20,000 ads and spent $150M on Meta.

Benchmarks I've found over 6 years:

1. 1 new creative concept per $10k in monthly spend. At $500k/month that's 50 concepts (~3 ads per concept, more for static-heavy). 

2. At $100k/mo, aim for 70% new concepts and 30% variations. As you scale past $1m/mo, max out at 50/50. But never drop below 50% new. 

3. 70% of your creatives should be cut before week 2. Only 10-20% will ever hit your performance threshold. If you're keeping most of your ads alive, you're probably losing money. 

4. Your top 1-2% of ads should drive 50% of total spend. If they don't, you haven't found real winners yet or you haven't utilized them well enough.

5. Big swings have lower hit rates (5-10%) but higher total potential. These are the ads that can scale to $1m+ in spend.

6. 70% video, 30% static for most ecom brands. New brands need more video (more education, less BOF audience). Clothing should lean heavier static (lots of SKUs to show).

7. 15-20% of budget goes to testing. Under 10% and your creative pipeline dries up. Over 25% and you're burning cash without enough scale behind winners.

8. When you 2x spend, expect 20-30% ROAS decline. A $30 CPA at $50k/month might become $40 at $200k. Scale requires better ads, better optimization, better structure, or lower targets.

9. Limit bid and budget changes to 25% max. For 90% of changes, smaller and more frequent changes outperform bigger ones. 

10. Meta always targets returning customers. Aim to keep returning conversions under 15-20%. Accept it and plan around it.

11. Ad copy can improve performance up to 50%. But a great ad outperforms by 500%. Copy matters, but the creative itself is where the real leverage is.

12. A great media buyer improves ROAS 100%+ vs a bad one. Creative strategists make better decisions when they're working off clean data and with better media buyers, because the scaled ads are actual winners.

There are 8 ways to attribute Meta ads

1. MER / nCAC
→ MER (Marketing Efficiency Ratio) or nCAC (New Customer Acquisition Cost).
→ It tells you how many new customers did you get? How much revenue? How much did you spend on marketing.
→ MER and nCAC are the only metrics that can't lie to you. Every platform will inflate its own numbers

2. Post-Purchase Surveys
→ "Where did you first hear about us?" on checkout
→ Measures what people remember. I've seen click attribution overvalue lower-funnel across dozens of accounts.
→ I use this for channel-level budget decisions

3. Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM)
→ Uses your historical spend and revenue data to estimate channel contribution. Doesn't need any user-level tracking to work.
→ It tells you where you are on the diminishing returns curve for each channel. Way more useful than just knowing if something's working.
→ I run this monthly or quarterly to gut-check what surveys are telling me

4. Incrementality / Geo-Lift Testing
→ Turn spend on or off by region and measure the impact on sales.
→ Useful if you're in retail
→ Answers "What happens in Dallas when we kill retargeting for 4 weeks?"
→ Quarterly, for the big strategic questions

5. Multi-Touch Attribution (MTA)
→ Triple Whale, Northbeam, Rockerbox. I can see who bought, where they came from, and validate the attribution myself instead of trusting Meta's dashboard.
→ This powers my Account Control Charts (CPA vs Spend). Shows me which ads are efficient but under-scaled and which ones are burning cash.
→ I use this daily for ad-level decisions

6. Platform-Reported Attribution
→ What Meta, Google, TikTok report in their own dashboards
→ I use these for purchase velocity. Compare 1-day vs 7-day vs 28-day windows to understand how fast people convert after seeing an ad.
→ Always compare click-based vs view-through. If most conversions are view-through, your numbers are inflated.

7. GA4 + Server-Side Tracking
→ GA4 defaults to last-click and it's a Google product. I don't use it for attribution decisions.
→ But CAPI and server-side tracking (Elevar, etc.) is non-negotiable. After iOS 14.5 your pixel is missing half the picture. This feeds better data to every other tool on this list.

8. Cohort-Based LTV
→ Meta at $40 CPA with $180 twelve-month LTV beats TikTok at $30 CPA with $95 LTV.
→ Return rate % and purchase frequency are the two I watch closest. They explain most of the LTV gap between channels.
→ Review monthly. Your CPA targets should come from this.

And of the 8, these are the best 3 to start with:
1. MTA (Triple Whale) for which ads to scale or cut
2. Post-purchase surveys for which channels get budget
3. MMM for quarterly validation

When all three point the same direction, I push budget.

The interesting part is when they disagree.

That's where I start digging into the other attribution methods to identify the nuance.

We spend $5.5M/mo on Google Ads.

Here's our Demand Gen checklist:

1. Consolidate for Data Density, Segment by Audience. Do not split Ad Groups by placement (YouTube vs. Discover). Demand Gen is designed to be cross-channel; forcing a placement "chokes" the AI’s ability to find the cheapest conversion across the ecosystem. Instead, use Ad Groups to segment by Audience Theme (e.g., Top 25 Search Terms vs. 2% Lookalikes). This keeps your data signals concentrated in one place while allowing you to see which buyer persona is actually biting.

2. Check image AND video asset quantity. Ads & assets > Assets. You need variety in both formats. We've seen 20% more conversions running image and video together vs video only. 

3. Check headline and description variety. Campaigns > Demand Gen > Ads > Headlines and descriptions. Demand Gen serves across YouTube, Gmail, and Discover. Each placement renders differently. You need variety.

4. Check view-through conversion tracking. Demand Gen drives view-throughs that Search doesn't. We value them at ~30% of click-through. If you're not tracking them, you're undervaluing the entire campaign.

5. Segment device performance. Campaigns > Demand Gen > Segment > Device. Demand Gen skews mobile because of Gmail and Discover. I've seen mobile CPA run 3x worse than desktop. And other times where mobile significantly outperforms.

6. Review your bid strategy. Settings > Campaign settings > Columns > Bid strategy. For Demand Gen, start target CPA at 2x your Search CPA. CPCs are cheap ($0.09 vs $7+ on Search) but conversion rates are lower. Give the algorithm room to learn.

7. If running product ads, check feed health. Google Merchant Center > Products > Diagnostics. Disapproved products mean your ads don't serve for those items.

8. Set your budget for a "Conversion Floor." While the "15x tCPA" rule is great for rapid scaling, it’s often unrealistic for high-CPA accounts. At a minimum, aim for a daily budget that supports 1–2 conversions per day. If your Target CPA is $200, a $300–$400 daily budget is your "efficiency floor." It will take longer to exit the "Learning Phase" than a $3,000/day budget, but it prevents the algorithm from overspending on low-quality placements while it searches for a baseline.

9. Build custom segments from your top 25 converting Search terms. Audiences > Audience manager > Segments. You're reaching people before they search. That's the whole point of Demand Gen.

10. Confirm auto-tagging is on. Settings > Account settings > Auto-tagging. Without it you lose conversion and view-through data between Ads and Analytics.

11. Retract bad leads within 24 hours. This matters more on Demand Gen because the audience pool is broader.

This is 11 out of 31 items we check on every Demand Gen launch.

One wrong setting can burn thousands before you catch it.

Years ago, I heard someone describe ineffective Account Managers in a way that's always stuck with me. "Nice people, talking to nice people, gettin' nothing done". AM team not hitting expansion targets? Here are 2 problems to watch out for (+ what to do instead):

1. Confusing a "point of contact" with a "champion". 

A stakeholder can become the POC for a vendor simply because they drew the shortest straw. It doesn't mean they have the will or skill to act as our change agent inside the business. The Challenger Customer taught me how to spot the difference between a Mobilizer vs. a Talker. Talkers = friendly people who return our calls, take meetings, and make it FEEL like we're making progress, because they "love us"! But, they're the same people who have every excuse for why they didn't have time to get to it in this week's team meeting. Mobilizers often ask us harder questions and push back, which we can misread as resistance. But, it's because they're thinking 4 steps ahead about where the group is likely to have differing opinions. They're testing how we'll hold up if they bring us in front of the leadership team. It's their political capital at stake. 

How to fix it? Teach the team the difference between the two. Create a common language around it. I hate the term "champion" in Sales. It's too easy to confuse interest w/ influence.   

2. An anti-shrinkage mindset 

Most AMs operate with a mindset of preventing churn, not creating growth. So, they cycle through delivering service, exceeding expectations, driving value -waiting to earn permission to sell. But, there's no upper boundary to that cycle, so it never ends. CEB/Gartner did a great study on this and named it the  Account Manager's"permission threshold". Learning that opened my eyes to my own flawed beliefs as an expansion AM. My own permission threshold was a big part of why I'd hesitate to initiate x-sell/upsell convos. 

How to fix it? Growing an account requires a new sale to an existing customer. It's is a prospecting motion, not a service motion. Stop leaving AMs out of prospecting/outbound training. Almost all of my outbound workshops now include AM/CSM teams. Call it whatever you want - but expansion AMs need to learn the same influence skills as AEs.

Last quarter a client asked me which intent signal they should use. Hiring data? Funding? Website visits?

I told them to use all of them, but not how they expected.

Most people pick one signal, build a campaign around it, and pray. That's backwards. You don't know which signal predicts a response until you let the data tell you.

Here's the framework we use across 50+ clients.

Run 3 campaigns at once:

1. Entire TAM. No signals. Just firmographics. This is your baseline — and sometimes it wins.

2. Focused segments. One signal per campaign. Hiring SDRs. Recently funded. Using a competitor tool.

3. Trigger-based. Real-time events. Job posting today. Funding this week. Website visit yesterday.

Now here's the move nobody talks about.

Every positive response across all 3, take that company and run it through every signal source you have. Pull hiring data, tech stack, funding history, news, social activity. Everything.

Look for patterns.

Maybe the companies that respond all hired a VP of Sales in the last 90 days. Maybe they all use HubSpot. Maybe they all posted about a specific pain point on LinkedIn.

You wouldn't have found that by guessing upfront.

We also run a catchall workflow in Clay with  Clayagent, every signal we can think of, just "what's notable about this company right now?" Sometimes the signal that predicts responses is something you'd never think to look for.

Sometimes you genuinely don't know WHY someone responded. That's fine. Not every response has a readable signal. But the ones that do give you your next 10 campaigns.

Stop picking signals from a menu. Let the data tell you what works.

I rebuilt a $5M Google Ads campaign

Assisted by AI.

Here's exactly what I did:

1. Export the existing account

→ Pulled keywords, ad copy, and 3 months of performance data from Google Ads
→ Saved as Excel so the AI can see structure, match types, what's paused vs active
→ Included conversion data so it knows what's actually working

2. Voice-briefed Claude Code

→ Used Wispr Flow to dictate my brief instead of typing it out
→ Uploaded the existing campaign structure as an Excel. Keywords, match types, paused vs active, 3 months of performance data. Second tab had all existing ad copy.
→ Walked it through the file. Which columns matter, what the tabs are.

3. Uploaded internal SOPs + IP

→ We uploaded two core docs as md files. They have years of accumulated IP.
→ Our Meticulous Google Ads Management SOP & our Copywriting SOP.
→ Think of it as giving the AI a senior media buyer's playbook.

4. Plan before building

→ Told it to work in phases.
→ Phase 1: build out all keywords and categorize them into campaigns and ad groups.
→ Phase 2: I review the keyword build, make corrections, upload revisions.
→ Phase 3: build two RSAs per ad group using our ad copy SOP.

NOTE: I haven't sent the prompt to the AI (yet)

5. It planned the account structure

→ Built three campaigns: Brand, Competitor, Non-Brand
→ Caught the first error here. It wanted to break competitors into multiple campaigns. I kept it as one.
→ The main competitor eats most of the spend anyway. I can manage bids at ad group level.

6. It built the keyword structure

→ Categorized every keyword, filled gaps, organized ad groups
→ Errors started showing up. Consumer-intent terms mixed with B2B keywords. Navigation queries in brand. A major competitor lumped in with much smaller players.
→ Exported into a spreadsheet and went line by line
→ Removed login and dot-co terms from brand (navigation, not purchase intent)
→ Separated a product into its own ad group (completely different buyer)
→ Moved a major competitor into its own ad group (too much volume to share with smaller ones)
→ Cut keywords that attract the wrong type of user
→ Around 15-20 corrections before uploading revisions back in

7. It built the ad copy

→ Fed the corrected keywords back in
→ Because it already had our Copywriting SOP loaded, it knew how we structure headlines, CTAs, and descriptions
→ Built 2 responsive search ads per ad group following our framework
→ Still had to review every ad.
→ Caught a couple headlines that were too generic and rewrote them.


Quick summary:
→ The AI got the structure maybe 70% right on the first pass.
→ I caught errors at every phase. In the plan, in the keyword build, in the ad copy.

Overall, pretty promising.

But a human review catches errors that would have leaked huge amounts of spend.

First time running a full build this way.

Going to keep refining it.

Everyone tells you to write like this:

Short lines.

Like this.

Full stop after each one.

It's "mobile optimised" and "easy to read".

It's also annoying to read if your audience is smart and perfectly capable of processing a full paragraph.

That formatting style exists for a reason:

It works for broad audiences who typically read at a lower level. But if you're writing for founders, executives, people with higher reading abilities and the desire to actually read things, you're optimising for the wrong reader. And you might be actively putting off the right one.

Same goes for walls of text, long hooks, emojis. 

None of it is universally good or bad. The question is never "does this trick work?", it's "does this trick work for my audience?"

Think about what a formatting rule is actually designed to do before you blindly apply it.

Different playbooks for different people.

Pulling ad performance from Meta's API?

Do this or you'll get bad data:

Facebook's data is changing daily.
- They reconcile ad data for 3-4 days after reporting
- They retroactively remove bot traffic
- They shift attribution spend around

So instead you need to do a Rolling 7-Day Fetch.

Here's how it works:

1. Set your script to run every morning
2. Instead of pulling just yesterday, pull the last 7 days
3. Wipe those 7 days from your database
4. Replace them with the fresh API pull
5. Repeat daily

Every morning you're overwriting old data with reconciled numbers.

With the rolling window you get:

→ Accurate CPAs
→ Better attribution
→ Cleaner data for decision making

I built this into our GitHub runner and the corrections were important.

Even a 2-3% CPA shift changes how you optimize a campaign.

Anyone else running reconciliation windows? Curious what setup you're using.
