We offer tested a brand from $400k/mo to $2M/mo

Implement these 4 things we learned: 

1. Bundles over percentage discounts

→ Percentage discounts train people to wait for the next sale
→ They compress margins and attract buyers who never pay full price
→ Bundles protect margin because you control the COGS of what's included
→ They increase AOV instead of shrinking it
→ And they give you something to actually test. E.g. different products, combos, pricing, themes etc. 


2. Free product improved take rate

→ Found when we added a free item to the bundle, it increased take rate.
→ But the free item had to be recognizable
→ If they can't confirm the value of the freebie, they don't trust it
→ The free product also filtered the audience for us
→ The person who wanted that specific item needed to be the ideal customer for the rest of the catalog
→ Wrong freebie = wrong customer
→ We were qualifying buyers through the offer before they even hit the site


3. Subscriptions need compounding value

→ Free gift on the first order gets the click
→ Additional gifts at future shipments keep retention
→ We showed what they'd get at month 2, month 4, month 6
→ Then let them prepay for a full year and lock in every gift upfront
→ This worked incredibly well for cashflow, LTV, and AOV.


4. Don't rely on CVR alone

→ A bigger discount can lift conversion rate but kill margin
→ Measure the full stack: CVR, AOV, margin per order, 60-day LTV
→ The winner is the offer that produces the most profit per customer over 60 days

The brands scaling hardest right now aren't necessarily running the best ads.

More likely they figured out the best offer.

Want to get paid to speak? Here are 5 things that helped me get started (without a book, a PhD, an exit, or an Olympic medal):

1) Host a Series 

Hosting the "Winning the Challenger Sale" series was a difference-maker for me. It reduced the risk, because prospects already knew my POV + presentation style. You don't need a big show. You can build rabid fans with small audiences. 

Tip: Prompt Claude with "I want to start a video series/podcast. What are the steps I need to know to do so?". 

2) Say Yes to Unpaid Podcasts/Lives/Shows/Events

I've guested on 300+ podcasts/shows. I said yes almost every time I was asked, no matter how big or small the show. But, it helped me practice and refine my talk tracks + get exposure to new audiences. It pays to not be a snob here. 

Example: I was Alex Bruschi's first guest on his podcast, Sales Stories IRL. A year later, he invited me to be in a video with Corporate Bro. I would've never had that opportunity without Alex. 

3) Be Generous & Loud About Your POV on LinkedIn

I didn't do any outbound. I gave away all of my best how-tos in posts, comments, and DMs. I was diligent about sharing what I learned from my failures (vs. only sharing the wins). LI is a way for someone to get to know your POV, before they know you. 

Tip: My "how-to" posts often follow the same choreography. Here's the problem I was up against, here's what I used to believe, here's what changed that belief, here's what I do now. The "after" means more when someone understands the "before" state. 

4) Seek Out Speaking Opps With Your Current Employer 

Before I ever charged for speaking engagements, I did a LOT of them for free. This helped me build a list of client logos and references.

Tip: Offer to run a 30 min session for the team on the topic you want to speak about. Then, offer to run those for customers. Don't do this if you're underperforming in your current role. Fix that first. Brian LaManna did 5 SKOs this year, while being a full-time AE. He's a great example of someone doing this well. 

5) Be Known for Something Specific

Find a lot of unique, interesting ways to talk about the same problem. When I started posting, I wrote about being a Relationship Builder who had to learn to be a Challenger. Sellers inside of companies doing Challenger related to that. 

Tip: Get crystal clear on what makes you unique. Every great brand has a memorable slogan. What's yours?

I generate 8,900 qualified calls every month.

With a 3-step funnel:

Google Ads → High Friction Questionnaire → Call

1. Qualifying questionnaire

→ 5-7 questions minimum. Mirror what the call center actually asks on the first call. E.g. Budget, authority, need, timeline.
→ Make questions progressive. Easy first (name, zip), then harder (budget, timeline).
→ If they don't qualify, kick them out the quiz and don't let them progress further.


2. Track past the lead

→ Form submits don't always correlate with end outcomes.
→ Track if the lead: picked, call length, call quality, call conversion
→ Feed that back to Google via GCLID. Move your primary conversion action as far down funnel as possible while keeping 30-50 conversions per month.
→ Get Google to optimize for "qualified call" instead of "form submit."


3. Match page friction to the sales cycle

→ Your landing page should handle about 30% of the work your reps do on the first call.
→ Low-friction pages = high-volume, low-intent calls, agents burning out
→ High-friction pages = lower volume, pre-qualified calls, higher close rates


4. Align media and call center on one scorecard

→ Make sure media + call center are optimizing for same metrics.
→ Put all data on one shared dashboard. CPL, contact rate, qualification rate, cost per qualified lead.
→ This will help one send LESS leads that convert higher. Example:
→ 100 leads at $20, 2% close = 2 customers for $2,000
→ 40 leads at $50, 12% close = ~5 customers for $2,000

Note, healthcare is where I run the heaviest qualified call volume.

So all the above is adapted to ask for:
→ Insurance verification upfront (commercial vs Medicare vs Medicaid)
→ Geographic qualification (in-network, licensure)
→ Level of care screening (outpatient vs inpatient vs residential)
→ Timeline (seeking treatment now vs researching for someone else)

These alone cut unqualified call volume by 30-40%.

→ More friction upfront
→ Track conversions past the lead
→ Media and call center need one scorecard

Here’s how to choose Meta ad account structure:

Answer 3 questions:

1. Who's the media buyer?

Check your Meta campaigns change log (clock icon top right)

If less than 4 changes per week:
→ Your media buyer is hands off
→ Choose CBO or cost cap campaigns that don't require daily operations 

If daily changes:
→ Your media buyer is hands on
→ You can run ABO campaigns
→ These require constant attention

Tim is my partner. He's an ex hedge fund trader who runs all our client accounts. He's inside the accounts every single day (weekends + holidays included). Hence we run a very heavy ABO structure. 


2. What's the product?

If single hero SKU & clear audience: 
→ Use ASC 
→ I've seen 9-figure supplement brands run purely on ASCs.

If multi product catalog & overlapping audiences
→ ASC will concentrate spend on 2-3 ads
→ Here you need manual control.
→ ABO is best


3. What's performance like? 

Big mistake is picking a structure, and trying to make the ads fit it.

Instead, double down on whatever structure is working. 
→ Are high spend / high CPA ads getting cut?
→ Are low spend / low CPA ads getting room to scale?
→ Is 10-15% of new creative hitting?

Cheatsheet on how we run accounts ($3M/mo ad spend)
→ ABO for creative testing and scaling
→ ASC for scaling (one per product)
→ Same ad IDs across campaigns to maintain social proof
→ When ASC concentrates spend on one ad, we duplicate the campaign, pause the monopolizer, or break the starved ad into its own ad set
→ Exclusions on scaling: 180-day purchase pixel + active subscribers synced from Klaviyo

That said, if you are testing and scaling and doing these three things well, focus on optimizations and creative over structure:
1. Ads are being tested well (Low CPA ads get scaled)
2. Ads are being cut before they waste money (No super high CPA / High Spend ads)
3. Ads are being scaled well (Top 1% of ads drive 50% of account with different angles)

→ Anthropic's skill pulls impression share lost to budget per day on mobile
→ Again, this is a really cool workflow
→ For context: "impression share lost to budget" tells you what % of searches your ads didn't show up for because your daily budget ran out
→ If this is happening, you can increase budget and get more conversions
→ In the Anthropic skill you can then ask for a budget increase and it'll action it.
→ We do something similar but layer in geo-level pacing on top (where needed)

↳ Multi-touch for optimization decisions: which campaigns are influencing deals through the cycle

Our goal was pipeline generation, so first touch was prioritized. 
Later, when conversion became the constraint, we used multi-touch to understand what’s helping deals close.

1. Every campaign tagged with UTMs before it launched
2. Pipeline sourced vs. pipeline influenced reported separately

2 // We stopped funding slow payback channels

We looked at CAC payback period by channel:
- We prioritized channels that have a 75% payback period relative to sales cycle length.
- We had a 12mo sales cycle. Any channel with a 9mo payback made the cut.
- All other channels were divested 90%

3 //  We selected 1 industry

Our data showed that 1 industry was responsible for 68% of closed-won revenue. 

But it’s not how we chose our focused industry:
↳We wanted the industry that returned the most revenue, the fastest. 
↳ Based on industry close rate, LTV, and sales cycle.
↳Formula: (Close Rate × LTV) ÷ Sales Cycle Length

We divested all other industries and pointed all campaigns towards one vertical.

4 // Campaign Strategy 

Strategy: ABM targeting logic + demand gen creative diversity

We found which accounts were in active demand.
So the only variable was creative & messaging.

That made testing clean:
↳ Same audience & timing. Different message
↳ Zero noise from audience variance
= we solved for creative performance faster

We always had 3 message angles running:
- Pain-led: "here's what's breaking without us"
- Outcome-led: "here's what good looks like"

Your ad copy is a filter.

Use it like one.

Comfrt is a $1B+ TikTok native brand.

But 68% of revenue was from Shopify. How?

→ Comfrt sells weighted hoodies.
→ They're no.1 apparel brand on TikTok Shop
→ Over 5,000 affiliates live / 1M total sign ups lifetime (according to hudson)

They ran a geo-lift study with WorkMagic
→ 14.7% incremental lift from TikTok Shop ads
→ 68% of that lift was showing up as Shopify revenue, not TikTok revenue

Which means the customer journey is NOT:
- See TikTok ad
- Click through
- Buy on TikTok Shop

And instead is:
- See TikTok ad
- Google the brand later
- Buy on Shopify (or Amazon)

So even though TikTok has:
- Low performance in MTA
- Weak click through
- Average ROAS

A proper incrementality test shows that it's driving the sale.

Comfrt isn't alone.

→ Liquid I.V.: 62% of TikTok-driven orders happened on Amazon. Last-touch credited TikTok with 12 conversions. Real number was 9,500+
→ True Classic: 5.51x more orders than last-click showed
→ WorkMagic 94% tests showed TikTok underreported

Before you think a channel is dead, run these checks:

1. Compare DTC revenue vs channel ad spend
→ Look for correlation with a 1-3 day lag
→ When TikTok spend goes up, does Shopify direct/organic follow?
→ Also check Google Trends for your brand name vs TikTok spend timing

2. Compare post-purchase surveys to platform data
→ Look for channels that get mentioned a lot but have poor ROAS
→ You need at least 100+ responses for it to be statistically valid

3. Run a geo-lift test
→ Turn off TikTok in specific regions for 3-4 weeks
→ Measure total revenue vs control regions

4. Adjust your CPA targets
→ If 68% of the value shows up elsewhere like Comfrt, your true TikTok CPA is roughly 1/3 of what the dashboard says
→ Apply the same logic to YouTube, podcasts, influencer, OOH

Are you overspending on new customers?

How you can check:

1. Start with one month of acquisition
→ How many customers did you acquire?
→ What was your total spend and CPA?
→ What's your AOV and gross margin on that first order?
→ E.g. 5,263 customers at $38 CPA, $200K spend, 65% gross margin.

2. Model retention month by month

→ Group every customer purchase by month from first acquisition
→ What % of those customers come back in month 2? Month 3? Month 6?
→ What's the AOV on returning orders?

3. Track cumulative revenue vs. cost for that cohort

→ Month 1 you might be down $36K after acquisition
→ Month 2 retention brings in $41K. You break even.
→ By month 3 you're $40K positive and climbing

Once you have a baseline, run these:

4. Sensitivity tests

→ What happens if gross margin falls from 70% to 60%?
→ What happens if you 2-5x spend and CPA goes up?
→ What if you add 30% subscriptions? Retention jumps from 25% to 37%, but AOV drops because you're giving a discount to get them on. Deficit shrinks short term, but ending cash position goes up because those returning customers all pay out.
→ Does your break even month stay the same or get pushed out?

And then answer three final questions:
→ Am I making or losing money this month?
→ Is this cohort profitable over its lifetime?
→ What happens to cash when all 12 months of cohorts stack up?

Our Google PMax campaign is generating spam leads

How we're fixing it

Context:
- New account we just took over
- 8 call booking in the first week
- 6 of them were spam

Small dataset but enough to warrant diagnostics: 

DIAGNOSTICS: 

1. Conversion tracking

→ Is the booking event firing cleanly on the confirmation page?
→ Are duplicate conversions being counted from the same user?
→ Is the offline import healthy and matching back to the right clicks?
→ Are we retracting spam from our conversions?

2. Negative keywords and search themes

→ Are any competitor, job-seeker, or freelancer terms leaking in?
→ Are the search themes narrow enough to actually match the ICP?
→ Has brand been separated out cleanly?

3. Audience signals

→ Has the customer match list been uploaded and refreshed recently?
→ Is first-party CRM data feeding in (closed-wons, not just leads)?
→ Are similar audiences being built off revenue, not form fills?

4. Asset groups and placement

→ Are site links pointing to the right pages, not the FAQ or blog?
→ Are creative variants slipping into low-intent Display or Gmail placements?
→ Has Google's auto-generated AI asset been turned off?

5. Landing page friction

→ Are there qualifying questions in the form?
→ Is anything in place to filter low-intent or bot traffic?
→ Does the page speak to the ICP, or is it generic enough that anyone books?

Everything above was fine. But we found the fix.

FIX: 

- We were optimizing for "book a call." So the algorithm did exactly that. It found the cheapest people willing to book. 
- We switched the objective to "showed up to the call."
- This is a custom event we're firing into Google Ads once the sales rep updates the CRM
- The algorithm now has to find humans who actually attend.
- Book rate has dropped but the bookings coming through are showing up


A few takeaways:
- PMax rewards whatever signal you feed it. And it does a really good job at it
- "Book a call" is a weak signal
- "Showed up" is a strong signal

If your PMax is producing volume but quality feels off, the fix usually is choosing a further bottom funnel conversion event.

Turn marketing from a cost center to a growth engine

In 3 simple steps:

I’ve worked with 15+ b2b marketing teams and they all had the same problem -

↳ finance sees marketing as a line item
↳ sales thinks it’s a support function
↳ execs know it's a black box

Here's how to flip it:

1 // Run marketing on a P&L

Simple math:
↳ Marketing spends $100K
↳ Sources $120K in new logo ARR
↳ That's a 1.2 contribution margin

Below 0.7 = cost center
0.7–1.0 = breakeven
Above 1.0 = growth engine

When marketing reports this number, the conversation changes. You're not defending spend. You're reporting return.

2 // Measure every dollar against pipeline

Three numbers matter:
↳ Pipeline sourced (marketing created the opportunity)
↳ Pipeline influenced (marketing touched the deal)
↳ Deal velocity (how fast deals move)

If a budget line can't tie to one of those three, it's overhead. Cut it or justify it as brand investment with a separate P&L line.

MQLs, impressions, campaigns launched - become supporting KPIs moving forward.

3 // Own a leading indicator the CEO asks about

Most marketing teams report lagging metrics like Pipeline and Revenue. The same numbers sales already reports.

Pick one leading indicator marketing uniquely controls:
↳ Qualified account engagement
↳ Hand-raiser volume from ICP accounts
↳ Intent signal density in your TAM

Put it on the weekly exec dashboard.

When the CEO starts asking about your number before the sales number, the classification has already changed.

- - -

Marketing becomes a growth engine the moment it adopts sales vocabulary - pipeline, margin, velocity - and stops reporting vanity metrics that don’t tie to revenue.

The reclassification is about changing the unit of account.

Here's the subject line framework we've been using for the past year or so. 

Our guiding principle: the job of the subject line is to get our prospects to open. That's the only goal.

There are two main frameworks to think through:

Framework 1: The subject line looks like something a colleague or customer would send.

"pizza order" — we used this for a restaurant platform client. Looks like an internal email. Open rates were insane.

"sales reports" — looks like something from your team.

"quick question" — classic for a reason. I know people love to hate it and I hate it too, but it still works. Did I mention that I hate it?

These work because they bypass the "this is a cold email" filter in the prospect's brain.

Framework 2: Put your offer in the subject line to entice them.

Subject: "[Company]'s competitors"
Preview text: "I have a list of people engaging with {{competitor}}..."

The subject creates a gap. The preview text hints at something valuable. Together they create enough curiosity to earn the click.

The worst subject lines try to sell. "50% Off Our Platform" — deleted without opening.

The best subject lines look like they came from someone you know. The best subject lines look like something they should already be keeping their eyes on. Or they can be punchy enough to earn the click from a very short offer.

How to find winning ads

Using calculus:

→ Each hill is a creative concept that works
→ Climbing uphill = iterating toward the local maximum
→ Jumping across = testing new concepts to find taller hills

When I ran marketing at Carpe, this is exactly how I thought about creative testing.

Your ad account sits on an invisible landscape. 

Your job is finding the tallest peaks.
→ Find a concept that works? 
→ Iterate to climb the hill (different hooks, creators, offers, etc)
→ Each test helps you map the landscape 
→ Hopefully, your iterations bring you closer to the best version of that concept.

But what if the hill you're on is capped at a low ROAS? 
→ Take a big swing 
→ Try a totally new concept, format and angle
→ Jump from the hill you're on to a completely different point
→ Sometimes you land in a valley - that's a dead creative
→ Sometimes you find a winning ad. This is your 10-25% hit rate. 

Then I heard Connor Rolain (Head of Growth, HexClad Cookware) describe creative testing almost identically on the Operators podcast. 

He called it "finding a local max on some imaginary gradient."
→ Concept testing = exploring different areas of the map.
→ Iteration testing = climbing toward the peak.

Couple important points
→ Creative fatigue shifts the whole landscape underneath you
→ Andromeda rewards you for sitting on multiple hills. More winners = more surface area

How do you think about creative testing?

This Google ads account hit $325k/mo in 60 days

Full playbook:

Context:
→ Was at $70k/mo in spend.
→ Customer volume tripled.
→ CPA held under $10k (the client's KPI).

This is how:

1. Down-funnel conversion actions

→ Google optimizes for whatever conversion event you ask, which means if you try to optimize for form fills, you'll get form fills (but unlikely to get down funnel conversions).
→ The deeper the event you optimize for, the better the lead quality Google goes after.
→ Integrated Google Ads with Salesforce so we could track deeper funnel admission events and optimize toward them directly.

2. Three qualified conversion types

→ We had leads coming from Phone Calls, Form Submits, and Live Chat.
→ Different customers engage through different channels, so capturing all three stops us from losing intent based on preference.
→ All three feed the same qualification layer so the algorithm compares intent across channels on equal footing.

3. Qualified Call actions

→ Created a 'qualified call' event to send back to Google from call tracking platform.
→ This only fired on what sales reps were happy with.
→ Think of this as another down funnel conversion action.

4. A well-structured account

3 separate targetings:
→ High intent keywords (more budget, higher Target CPA) 
→ Low intent keywords (lower budget, lower Target CPA)
→ Competitors 

5. Dynamic headline insertions on the landing pages

Raised conversion rates by 7%.
→ Dynamic headlines personalize the landing page to match the incoming search.
→ Message match lowers bounce and raises relevance across ad, click, and page.
→ Higher relevance also improves Quality Score, which compounds into lower CPCs.

Summary:

→ Push conversion tracking as deep as your CRM allows
→ Only qualified contacts should count as conversions
→ Segment campaigns by intent to better control budget and bids
→ Dynamic headline insertion lifts CVR and Quality Score

How to convert more buyers

By creating less content:

There are two layers every content system needs:

Layer 1 is your top of funnel. This is your testing ground. Post at volume, hooks, messages, concepts. Goal: pull your target audience into your ecosystem.

Layer 2 is your Core Content. This is a single, definitive, evergreen document that leadership writes once and updates annually - or when predicting market shifts. It covers everything your buyer needs to understand about the problem you solve. It is the source of truth for your entire content operation.

Goals:
1. TOFU content creates awareness
2. Core content converts to leads, deals and revenue

Once someone consumes 1-3 pieces of your top of funnel content, you know something about them:
↳ Which problem resonated
​​↳ Which angle/message made them engage

These signals tell you which slice of your core content to serve them next.

Not the whole guide. A chunk of it - the piece that matches what they already showed interest in.

Now you have a dynamic buyer journey - one the buyer designs based on what they consume.

Same logic applies from MOFU to BOFU. The system reads what they've consumed and decides what to serve next.

This type of orchestration wasn’t possible 9mo ago.

AI can take your prospects on a buyer journey they actually want (vs just guessing).

Here's how I open a discovery call with an outbound-originated opp.

"Mind If I share what I learned about your business, before we start talking about {solution}? I don’t want to assume I've got everything right, simply because I researched COMPANY beforehand.

It looks like COMPANY sells a PRODUCT/SERVICE to STAKEHOLDER ROLES at CUSTOMER VERTICALS/TYPES. It seems like the problem you're solving for those customers is X and the company makes money by XYZ. What did I get wrong?”

Here's why I do it this way:

1. 82% of B2B decision-makers think sellers are unprepared during the 1st meeting (source: Gartner). 82%!!!!! 

Watch their face/tone change when they realize you took the time to prep. Most common reaction? "Thanks for taking the time to learn about our business. Most sellers don't". Anyone can do this. It takes 2 mins to prompt AI for these answers. The bar is on the floor. 

2. Most disco calls are 30 mins. I hate wasting my time. I hate wasting prospects' time. There's no reason for them to spend 7 mins educating me on something I could've easily researched beforehand. More time for the good stuff.  

3. The "what did I get wrong" question invites correction. Correction = discovery. It also sets the tone that we're not a know-it-all. Overly assumptive, know-it-all reps sound naive. The discovery motto I teach is "be specific - but seek to be corrected, not correct". 

From here, it's an easy transition into "It looks like your CEO is asking the business to...." to ground the conversation in an exec-level objective, before digging in to associated business problems. 

Great outbound discovery builds trust by helping prospects think differently about their business, before we ask them to think differently about ours. 

How we prep and how we bring that prep to life = two skills that make or break whether we earn that trust in the first few mins of the call.

Should you use target CPA or ROAS on Google Ads?

Answer these 3 questions:

a) Do your purchase sizes vary?

→ All purchases within ~20% of each other (single product, flat fee)? Use tCPA. There's no value signal to optimize around.
→ Purchases vary 3x+? tROAS. Let Google find the higher-value pockets.

b) Are you uploading conversion values?

→ Not yet? Start with tCPA. tROAS without $ values is just tCPA with worse reporting.
→ Already passing offline values (e.g. MQL: $50, SQL: $250, Closed: $10,000)? Use tROAS as it shifts budget toward the higher-value clicks.

c) Do you hit the minimum 30-day conversions?

→ Search, Shopping, Display: 15
→ Demand Gen: ~50
→ App: 300

If yes, continue with previous answers. Else, stay on Max Conversions or Max Conversion Value.

If you switch to tROAS, set the target right:

→ Pull your "Conv. value/cost" column (ROAS) for the last 4 weeks, excluding the last 3-7 days for conversion delay
→ Set target at or below that number
→ Don't set above historical. I've seen accounts lose 40%+ traffic overnight.

A few rules I use once tROAS is live:

- Watch Search Lost IS (Budget). Above 0% = target too tight. Raise it.
- Adjust in 5-10% increments. Wait 1-2 conversion cycles before the next change.
- On launches (influencer, PR, brand campaigns), override all of this. Use seasonality bid adjustments due to a higher expected CVR.

There are 12 ways to scale winners:

→ 10-20% bumps, as often as twice daily

2. Dupe into a winning ad set
→ Ad set already has momentum and learnings
→ Ad set has proven it's inside a good audience pocket

3. Dupe into a new ad set
→ Fresh learning phase, almost resetting the audience

→ CBO version of horizontal scaling
→ This forces budget where you want it to go

→ Take proven Meta winners to TikTok, YouTube Shorts etc
→ More of a business-level scale play

6. Run in cost cap campaign
→ Works really well when you have volatile performance 
→ Don't set and forget this, you need to actively manage
→ Spending under budget + good performance? Raise the cap
→ Spending at budget and performing? Raise the budget

7. Creative iterations
→ Take your winning ad, change the hook
→ Take your winning ad, change the creator
→ Take your winning video, make it a static 

8. Expand placements
→ Open Reels, Stories, Audience Network
→ More inventory = more room to spend
→ Double check dimensions aren't limiting delivery

9. Run winners in ASC
→ Set up an ASC campaign

→ Better CVR = lower CPA = more room to spend profitably

→ Launch in CA, UK, AU 
→ This is incremental spend & typically gets lower CPMs
→ You'll need to sort out fulfillment + logistics

How to convince your CEO that marketing is working

With the right attribution model:

The key is to focus on the primary constraint, instead of using a model to evaluate the entire funnel.

When your constraint is lead generation, first-touch is your primary model:

Marketing Sourced Pipeline = First-Touch Attribution

Why: First-touch identifies the channels and campaigns filling the top of the funnel, revealing what initially brought a person into your world. This is critical for lead gen.

If you're running paid, content, events, or even outbound - first-touch tells you where to double down on efforts and spend.

The mistake: using multi-touch here dilutes the signal. You can't optimize lead gen if you're spreading credit across 7 touchpoints.

When your constraint is conversion, multi-touch is your primary model:

Marketing Influenced Pipeline = Multi-Touch Attribution

Why: Multi-touch identifies the touches accelerating deals, showing what moved a person from lead to closed-won. This is essential for conversion.

If you're running nurture sequences, retargeting, ABM — multi-touch shows you what's actually working in the middle and bottom of funnel.

The mistake: Using first-touch here ignores the work marketing does after the lead is created. You look like a cost center when you're actually driving velocity.

How to apply each model:

Step 1: Identify your constraint
↳ Not enough leads? Lead gen is your constraint.
↳ Leads aren't converting? Conversion is your constraint.

Step 2: Pick your primary model
↳ Lead gen constraint = first-touch
↳ Conversion constraint = multi-touch

Step 3: Report accordingly
↳ Marketing sourced pipeline → first-touch attribution
↳ Marketing influenced pipeline → multi-touch attribution

Most teams pick an attribution model based on what their tool defaults to. Or what sounds sophisticated.

The right model depends on what you're trying to solve.

Match your attribution to your constraint, and you'll finally be able to prove marketing impact to your CEO.

How I max out Search campaigns:

1. Split your ad structure out:
→ Brand: under 20% of spend
→ Competitor: ~10%
→ Non-Brand: ~70%

2. Layer match types in order
→ Exact first for each theme
→ Phrase once Exact hits 15+ conversions/month
→ Broad only with Smart Bidding and a strong negative list

3. Max out your RSAs
→ 2-3 RSAs per ad group

4. Train the algorithm with downfunnel signals
→ Upload offline conversions via GCLID(MQL, SQL, Closed Deal)

→ Move your primary conversion as far downfunnel as you can hold 30-50 conversions/month

5. Review & scale weekly
→ Conduct search term reports 2-3x per week / use an AI workflow (we do and flag keywords automatically)
→ Promote high-scoring terms with volume to their own ad groups.
→ Minimize Search Lost IS (Budget) as long as it's profitable / incremental.
→ Then expand into new themes and service lines.

6. Know your max efficient ceiling
→ Search Volume = Impressions ÷ Search Impression Share
→ Max Revenue = Search Volume × CTR × CVR × Revenue per Conversion
→ Max Efficient Spend = Max Revenue ÷ Target ROAS
→ Example: 100k monthly searches × 3% CTR × 10% CVR × $12k per conversion = $3.6M potential revenue. At 4x target ROAS, your ceiling is $900k/month. Once you're around 80% of that number, the next dollar is better spent in PMax / Demand Gen.

Cheatsheet:
→ Split brand / competitor / non-brand first
→ Exact → Phrase → Broad in order
→ Max out RSAs
→ Feed downfunnel signals
→ Minimize Lost IS (Budget) before expanding
→ Know your ceiling before you scale past it

If your campaign is getting decent out of office / negative reply rates, people are clearly reading, and nobody's responding positively, there's a good chance you're raising an objection you're not addressing. 

And you'll never know it because the prospect won't tell you.

They just delete. 

Every cold email creates an implicit pushback in the reader's mind.

"We help companies scale outbound" — they think "I already have an agency."

"We reduce your cloud costs by 40%" — they think "Switching sounds like a nightmare."

They read. They think the objection. They're gone.

Read your own email like a skeptical buyer. What's the first pushback? Now address it in one sentence. Not defensively. Casually.

"We help companies scale outbound (most of our clients already had an agency, we work alongside them, not replace them)"

"We reduce cloud costs by 40% (no migration required, we optimize your existing setup)"

One sentence. Inserted naturally. Kills the objection before it fully forms.

But don't start here.

If your targeting is wrong, objection preemption won't save you. If your offer is weak, addressing objections just highlights the weakness. And critically — don't bring up objections the prospect wasn't thinking about. If you're selling accounting services and you write "even though we're a small firm," you just planted doubt that didn't exist.

This is an advanced move. Use it when you've validated the campaign is reaching the right people, they're reading, and something in the copy is creating friction.

Do you know the b2b buyer journey?

There are 5 stages. Most marketers only think about the last two.

I. "I want to learn"

Individual buyers are heads down exploring topics, sharpening their skills, picking up on trends and best practices. They're studying, not shopping.
At this stage, a buyer might: 
↳ Start following a brand after reading something that actually taught them something 
↳ Forward a piece of content to a colleague 
↳ Work their way through podcasts, webinars, long-form articles
↳ Quietly build a mental shortlist of approaches and vendors worth tracking

They might even try to solve the problem on their own - and the key is to give them the tools they need to do it.

This is the foundation. It's where you get noticed, earn trust, and land in their head before a specific business problem shows up.

II. "We want a solution"

Now the buying group has aligned on the top-priority problem and what happens if they don't fix it. They start scanning for solutions.

The vendor that clearly articulated their solution (not their product) as the right fit for this class of problem earns a seat at the table for round two.

Example: Enterprise pipeline dropped 27% in 2025. Marketing and sales have both taken shots at it and neither has the answer. Something has to change.
The Champion might be weighing: 
↳ Sales training investments 
↳ Hiring SDRs and AEs with proven enterprise chops 
↳ Standing up an ABM program 
↳ Rebuilding outreach scripts from scratch 
↳ …and a dozen more

III. "We want a solution like yours"

After stacking options against fit, resources, and budget, the group lands on a direction. Now they start evaluating vendors and booking discovery calls.

Example: "We're going to launch ABM."

Their options: 
↳ License an ABM platform and run the vendor's playbooks 
↳ Hire an ABM agency 
↳ Buy a course or workshop 
↳ Bring in an experienced consulting firm

Your job as the vendor is to be on the shortlist.

IV. "We want your solution"

The buying committee has picked their preferred solution and is now selling it internally. They need stakeholder consensus and support to move into vendor evaluation.

This is where high-intent signals show up and real opportunities get created.

Example: "We want to hire you to run a pilot ABM program. What's the scope, budget, and resources?"

This is the moment to invest in fully personalized buyer enablement. 

V. "We're ready to buy from you"

Budget approved. Resources allocated. Procurement and POC are next.

These 5 stages are what an actual buyer journey looks like. The first three often take the longest, and they're what determines whether you even make the consideration set.

Most B2B companies skip them entirely and try to harvest demand from in-market accounts.

Then wonder why the pipeline dried up.

There's a copywriting framework called PAS.

(PAS = Problem Agitate Solution)

The reason it works in that order is simple:

When the reader sees a problem first - one they currently experience themselves - they resonate with that emotionally a lot quicker and easier than if they read a solution first, then worked backwards.

Once the writer resonates with the reader's emotions, the reader is putty in their hands.

I've learned this after writing 1,214 LinkedIn posts:

It's not about the word choice. It can be.

But 9 times out of 10, it's about word order.

Should your DTC expand to retail & Amazon

Answer 5 easy questions:

1. Is your CAC sustainable at scale?

→ Sustainable means you've tested scaling budget 20-30% and CPA held
→ You should be able to roughly predict next month's CPA
→ You're probably spending at least $250k/mo on ads

2. Can your margins absorb the channel fees?

→ Amazon takes 30-35% all-in
→ Retail wholesale is 40-50% off MSRP
→ You need to be profitable + have the cashflow with above margin losses in mind

3. Can DTC run without your full attention?

→ Channel one needs to run without you before you add channel two
→ The second channel will likely split your attention 80:20 in favor of new
→ You must not be a bottleneck in Meta performance (creative / LP approval etc)

4. Are people searching for your brand?

→ Amazon and retail only convert if people already know your brand
→ Otherwise you're starting from zero on every new channel
→ Retail and Amazon work best as MOFU/BOFU engines early on

5. Do you have a working retention engine?

→ Email flows, SMS, subscriptions
→ Repeat purchase rate above 30%
→ DTC has to keep generating revenue while you're focused elsewhere

Answered no to any of these?

Don't expand.

Expansion cheatsheet:
→ Stable CAC for 60-90 days that holds when you scale
→ Margins stay profitable after Amazon's 30-35% or retail's 40-50% cut
→ DTC runs without you in the day-to-day
→ People are searching for your brand organically
→ Retention engine keeps DTC revenue steady while you ramp channel two

Every DTC brand needs to see this.

Columbia, Yale and MyCustomAI ran 6 models (e.g. Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro etc) through thousands of controlled shopping experiments with position, price, rating, reviews and sponsored tags.

1. Position bias

→ Picture a product page with 8 products in 2 rows of 4.
→ Move a product from the bottom-right slot to top-row middle = 5x more purchases (Claude Sonnet 4)
→ GPT-4.1's favorite slot on the grid is GPT-5.1's LEAST favorite
→ Gemini 3 Pro's top-row preference drops selection from 27% to 2% with one row shift

2. Model resets

→ Every big AI release is a potential demand hit to your brand
→ Fitness watch: Claude Sonnet 4 picks Fitbit Inspire 45%, GPT-4.1 picks it 25%
→ iPhone cases: GPT-4.1 picks Mikeke 62%. GPT-5.1 picks Mikeke 5% and defaults to ESR 95%.
→ When Anthropic launched Opus 4.5 → Fitbit Inspire jumped to 77%. OpenAI shipped GPT-5.1 → it dropped to 6%.

3. Sponsored tags vs editorial picks

→ A product picked 10% of the time drops to ~8% when the 'ad sponsored' tag is added on the listing
→ Same direction across all 6 AI models, in both browser and API-only setups
→ An "Overall Pick" editorial badge takes that same 10% baseline to 20-42%
→ Paid placement inside AI buying flows is a negative signal

4. Winner-take-all brands

→ In commoditized categories, AI agents pile picks onto 1-2 brands they already recognize and ignore the rest
→ Staplers: Amazon Basics gets 80-94% of picks across every AI model tested. Bostitch picks up ~15%.
→ The other 6 brands in the test (Arrow, Swingline, Rapid, Deli, M&G, Marspark) got ~0% picks. Even when their prices and ratings were competitive.
→ Humans browse and compare, so smaller brands still capture some share. AI agents default to the most familiar name and don't look further.
→ If the AI doesn't already know your brand, you don't lose share. You disappear from the consideration set entirely.

5. Title edit optimization

→ An AI seller agent rewrote one product's title using competitor sales data
→ "Floor Lamps for Living Room..." was rewritten to start with "Office Floor Lamp..."
→ GPT-5.1 picks went from 9% to 89% on that single change
→ AI agents weight the first words of a title heavily. Front-load the search term.

6. Reviews vs price

→ +0.1 rating on a 5-star scale = you can charge 25-67% more without losing share
→ Doubling your review count = 17-43% more price headroom
→ Agents care more about ratings and reviews than pricing

What this means for DTC:

→ Optimize the first few words of your product title
→ Expect demand shocks every time GPT, Claude or Gemini updates
→ Fight for editorial badges more than before
→ Track how often each major AI picks your brand
→ Optimize for high review velocity and ratings

Instead of ROAS, they track CM ROAS

Standard ROAS = Revenue / Ad Spend.
CM ROAS = (Revenue - Variable Costs) / Ad Spend.

Variable costs = COGS, shipping, payment fees, expected return rate, return processing.

Example on a $100k Meta spend:

Revenue: $300k
Ad spend: $100k

Payment fees (3%): $9k
Returns + processing (15% rate): $51k

Contribution margin: $120k

ROAS = 3x
CM ROAS = 1.2x

Make decisions on ads based on the CM ROAS not the ROAS.

Here is the template we use to do a full GTM audit before launching any ABM program…

It includes:

GOALS & GAPS
↳ Revenue target and historical/expected marketing contribution
↳ Current pipeline: volume, velocity, and where deals are stalling
↳ Average sales cycle length - and where time is actually being lost
↳ ACV and whether your current motion is built for it
↳ What's been tried before and why it didn't work

ICP & ACCOUNT SELECTION
↳ What percentage of your revenue comes from net new vs. expansion? (If renewals and upsells are outpacing new business, your ICP for new acquisition may be undefined)
↳ Are you prioritizing accounts where you have the highest median deal value or the highest volume of activity?
↳ What does your win/loss data say about which accounts you actually close vs. which ones waste pipeline?

CLOSED WON/LOST ANALYSIS (180d)
↳ Won: finding the right combo of industry, revenue band, sales cycle length, & median acv that produce the best deals.
↳ Lost: which combos produce a negative ICP (deals we don’t want)
↳ Remove any expansion/renewal deals
↳ Won account tiers using low end of Will scores to determine firmographic priority 
↳ This produces an initial account list of best and worst combos. We pull the closed won account that match is profile - and enrich for static signals (i.e. tech stack) for a full ICP view

BUYING COMMITTEE
↳ How many stakeholders are involved in a right fit ICP deal, and are they all mapped before outreach begins?
↳ What roles are on the committee: economic buyer, champion, technical evaluator, security/compliance, procurement?
↳ Are there third parties involved in the decision: system integrators, consultants, managed service partners, and are they in your outreach motion?
↳ Who owns relationship-building with each persona: marketing, sales, or nobody?

STACK
↳ CRM: Is account and contact data clean enough to run programs from?
↳ Are you tracking account-level engagement or just contact-level activity?
↳ Intent data: do you have it, is it connected to your account list?
↳ Where is data falling through the cracks between tools?

SALES MOTION
↳ Is the sales process built for a multi-stakeholder, long-cycle deal?
↳ Does sales have account research before the first touchpoint?
↳ How many active touches does sales make per account per quarter?
↳ Is there a defined multi-threading strategy per account?
↳ Where do deals stall - and is there a play to unstick them?

ALIGNMENT
↳ How often do marketing and sales review target accounts together?
↳ Does sales have visibility into marketing touchpoints before they reach out?
↳ Is there a shared definition of a sales-ready account - or does marketing throw leads over the wall?
↳ Most ABM programs with deal complexity fail not because the strategy was wrong - but because nobody ran a proper closed won/lost and ICP analysis before building

Are you running Google Ads right?

Use this chart to find out:

Ask yourself two questions.
1. What's your budget?
2. What's the search demand?

Top Left: (HARD)
→ High budget, low search demand
→ Not enough search intent to narrow even if you wanted to
→ Go broad. Layer in YouTube and Demand Gen to generate awareness
→ You're building a category so cast a wide net.

Top Right: (BEST)
→ High budget, high search demand
→ Google has plenty of data to find your customers
→ Don't restrict audiences. Go broad.
→ Use observation mode. Collect audience data instead of constraining with it.
→ The algorithm knows who converts better than you do.

Bottom Left: (HARDEST)
→ Low budget, low search demand
→ The hardest quadrant to be in
→ Not enough data to go wide and not enough demand to filter.
→ Do deep keyword research and find pockets of intent competitors missed.

Bottom Right: (MEDIUM)
→ Low budget, high search demand
→ The only quadrant where narrow targeting makes sense
→ You can't afford every auction so pick the right ones
→ E.g. layer in household income, in-market segments, geography

Some examples of clients:
→ Treatment center, $3M/mo budget with massive search volume = high budget, high demand
→ Local dentist, $5K/mo budget in a city with 10K+ "dentist near me" searches = low budget, high demand
→ VC-backed AI tool, $150K/mo budget for a category that barely exists = high budget, low demand
→ Niche B2B manufacturer, $8K/mo budget with 200 monthly searches = low budget, low demand

Cheatsheet:
→ High budget + high demand = Go broad, observation mode
→ High budget + low demand = Go broad, create demand
→ Low budget + high demand = Go narrow, be selective
→ Low budget + low demand = Go deep, research everything

Are your Meta ads going to new people?

How to check:

It's called Rolling Reach
- Track unique reach inside a rolling time window
- Anyone not seen in the prior window counts as "new" again

STEP 1: Pick a refresh window.
- The window is how long before a customer counts as "new" again.
- Meta will pull this for you starting from x date but I like using a rolling window (12 months rolling)
- My default assumption is that most people have forgotten you after 12 months.

STEP 2: Pull two reach numbers from Ads Manager.
At the account level, not per-campaign (you need deduped reach across everything):
→ Pull A: Reach for the last 12 months ending THIS month
→ Pull B: Reach for the last 12 months ending LAST month (same window, shifted back one)

STEP 3: Do the math to get your two bars.
→ Blue bar (total reach in the window) = A
→ Orange bar (new reach this month) = A − B

STEP 4: Repeat STEP 2 and 3 for 1, 3, 6, and 12 month windows.

Each chart answers a different question:

1 month chart:
- Unseen for 30 days = new
- Use it for short-term acquisition pace and creative testing

3 month chart: Is the quarter pulling in fresh audiences?
- Unseen for 90 days = new
- Use it for quarterly funnel health and seasonal brands

6 month chart: Are you reaching forgotten-but-warm people?
- Unseen for 6 months = new
- Use it for mid-cycle re-engagement

12 month chart: Is the business actually growing reach?
- Unseen for 12 months = new
- Use it for true net-new growth

Conclusions you can draw:
- If new reach is flat but spend is up → you're hitting the same audience
- If 6-month and 12-month new reach both climb → you're hitting new audiences
- If all new reach jumps right after a creative drop → that creative is unlocking new audience pockets

Two metrics to track alongside:
- Net new reach (how many fresh customers you're adding each period)
- Cost per incremental reach (what you're paying for them)

I've spent $200M+ on Google ads

I can predict how far Search will scale:

1. Use existing ad data
→ Search Volume = Impressions ÷ Search Impression Share
→ Grab Search Impression Share from current Search ads
→ Example: 50,000 impressions at 40% IS = 125,000 total searches
→ Works best when you're already at scale with tight keyword targeting

2. Use Google Ads forecasting tool
→ Build a campaign (don't launch it)
→ Add all target keywords
→ Set max CPC high enough to capture all available impressions
→ The "Impressions" forecast approximates total search volume

3. Use keyword planning tools
→ Pull volume from Google Keyword Planner, SEMrush, Ahrefs
→ Cross-reference against your actual data

E.g:
→ Ahrefs: 80,000
→ SEMrush: 70,000
→ Ads Data: 125,000
→ Google Keyword Planner: 90,000

Rough estimate: 100,000

Now you can calculate Max Potential Revenue.

→ Search Volume: 100,000
→ CTR: 3%
→ CVR: 10%
→ Revenue Per Conversion: $12,000

Max Potential Revenue = Search Volume × Stretch CTR × Stretch CVR × Revenue
Max Potential Revenue = 100,000 × 0.03 × 0.10 × $12,000
Max Potential Revenue = $3.6M/mo

Then calculate Max Efficient Spend.

→ Max Potential Revenue: $3.6M/mo
→ Target ROAS: 4x

Max Efficient Spend = Max Revenue ÷ Target ROAS
Max Efficient Spend = $3.6M ÷ 4 = $900K/month

What this means in practice:

Situation 1:
→ Spending $600K
→ Hitting $2.4M revenue (4x ROAS)
→ You still have room to grow

Situation 2:
→ Spending $900K
→ Hitting $2.4M revenue (2.67x ROAS)
→ You've hit the ceiling

Once you know your max, stop pushing past it.

Deploy the next dollar into the next channel.

Next time you hear an objection, take a pause and isolate whether it's a current state or future state objection, before you respond. Here's how. 

Current state objections = cost of inaction isn't big enough to warrant action. There may be pain, but the pain of same is tolerable. Ex: "Let's revisit this in 2027."

Future state objections = concerns with perceived risk of buying/implementing the solution. Prospect agrees the pain of same is intolerable, but has concerns re: whether this is the right solution, right implementation plan, or right partner. Ex: "We're going to need more time to evaluate the options internally before we schedule the next call."

Current state objections and future state objections are very different problems to solve in the mind of the buyer.

Current state objections = is this problem is worth solving, and worth solving now? 

Future state objections = is this solution, from this vendor, the right way to solve the problem, right now?

Pitching ROI/case studies to a current state objection doesn't work. I can agree you have a "better" solution to a problem, yet still be fine tolerating "good enough". 

Pitching COI to a future state objection doesn't work. I can agree we have a problem worth solving, yet drag my feet b/c of concerns with whether it's the right solution or implementation plan to address it. 

Bonus:

Once I started doing this as an AE, I counted how many of my prospect objections were rooted in current state vs. future state.  I realized I was heavy on current state objections. It helped me see that I was jumping to solution WAY too quickly. I wasn't framing the cost of inaction. I was playing solution show and tell. 

Give this a try.

Not only will it help you address the right problem with your buyer, but it teaches us a lot about where we may be rushing our Sales convos!

How to temporarily ramp ad spend for DTC promos

Without messing up your ad account:

- We were at $10k/day in spend
- Brand had a promo and needed to spend $50k over 72 hours
- That's ~$16k/day = 60% temporary budget increase
- We then needed to ramp down immediately 

How to ramp spend fast: 

1\. Forced spend to promo assets intra-day
- Don't wait for Meta's pacing to figure it out. 
- Manually push capital into the ad sets that were ripping during the sale window. 
- Kept non-promo assets live at their normal baselines.

2\. Used Meta's Budget Scheduling
- Schedule aggressive budget increases for the exact promo window (say Tuesday through Thursday). 
- Meta pushes heavy spend into that window, then automatically reverts when the schedule ends.
- No permanent changes to your daily baseline. 

3\. Dedicated ASC for promo creative
- Spun up a separate Advantage Shopping Campaign just for promo assets.
- This let us pour budget into promo-specific creative without disrupting the evergreen campaigns that were still running.

4\. Monitored intra-day, not daily
- Watch hourly to make sure the budget was actually delivering and the CPAs weren't blowing out.
- Adjust bids and budget throughout the day

Summary: 
- Budget scheduling to spike temporarily
- Dedicated ASC keeps promo and evergreen separate + protects account structure

Barry Hott said manually controlling ad-level budget allocation is a waste of time. I respectfully disagree. This is why.

Here's what we agree on:
→ Meta will optimize toward ads that drive conversions.
→ If they make you more money, you spend more money

We may be talking about sightly different things:
→ I'm not advocating for micromanaging which add gets $50 vs $80 within an ad set.
→ But "let the machine work" has become a blanket argument for hands-off media buying.

And that's where it falls apart.

There are 3 caveats:
→ Meta can only see what Meta can see.
→ Their in-platform reporting has cookie loss. Especially top-of-funnel ads where the conversion happens days or weeks later.
→ The better they can prove to you they drove those conversions, the more likely you are to spend with them. They know this.

And on your side, you're optimizing for business outcomes:
→ Total revenue.
→ Retail lift.
→ Amazon spillover.
→ Rebills.
→ LTV.

So even if Meta was perfect at picking the right ads (they normally aren't), they're still missing data that's crucial to good optimization.

This creates a gap.

Meta might kill an ad that's driving retail purchases they can't measure.

Or scale an ad with great engagement but terrible downstream economics.

And this gap gets bigger:
→ The more retail or Amazon presence you have
→ The longer the purchase funnel
→ The bigger the brand and stronger the awareness

If you rely on Meta's attribution, they're going to drive returning and bottom-of-funnel customers to you. That's what they can prove.

You can adjust this with exclusions and creative strategy but no reason to stop there.

You need more control over your account. More control over your adjustments on a daily basis.

That doesn't mean day-trading your account. I've seen that destroy accounts too. The media buyer making 50% budget swings every Friday, resetting learning phases, killing ads after 48 hours. That's worse than doing nothing.

The answer lives in the middle. But where in the middle depends on your business.

A single SKU supplement at $30k/mo? Meta is a B+ buyer. Let ASC do its thing and put your energy into creative production.

A complex subscription brand at $500k/mo with different LTVs, big gaps between MTA and in-platform, and retail spillover? You need hands on the wheel.

That's why manual budget control still matters. Not at the ad level, but at the strategy level.

I’ve ran 100+ ABM programs

Here’s how I’m using CTV in my campaigns:

PHASE 1 // BUILD YOUR ACCOUNT CLUSTER

A. Define the cluster around behavior signal

Your segment needs a set of unifying triggers

75–300 accounts is the sweet spot for ABM-CTV economics

Example: 

PE-backed in the last 18 months, recently changed CRO, specific tech stack, and/or headcount growing 20%+. The tighter the shared pain point, the more your creative can speak directly to it

B. Export a clean account list with domains + HQ addresses 

CTV platforms match accounts via IP address, which maps to physical office locations. You need HQ address (street, city, zip) for best match rates. Remote-first companies will have lower match rates - flag these before upload or exclude from your ICP

C. Verify the list size will hit minimum viable frequency 

↳ You need 8+ impressions per account per week to drive awareness lift. 
↳ Budget $150-300 per target account per month. A 100-account list needs $15K–$30K/month to get real signal. Fewer accounts + smaller budget = diluted frequency = no measurable lift

PHASE 2 // CREATIVE PRODUCTION

A. Script a 30-second spot that names the pain, not your product 

B2B CTV viewers are in lean-back mode. First 5 seconds must earn attention by naming a problem they recognize instantly

↳ Structure: Problem → Stakes → CTA. Product name comes last. 
↳ One CTA only - drive to a landing page, not a demo form

B. Build a cluster-specific landing page

Your CTA drives to a dedicated URL that mirrors the ad's message. If the spot speaks to PE-backed RevOps leaders, the landing page opens with that framing

PHASE 3 // LAUNCH & SEQUENCE

A. Run CTV as the first touch in a multi-channel sequence 

CTV's job is warming, not converting

Sequence: 
CTV impressions (weeks 1–3) → LinkedIn retargeting to same account list → personalized SDR outbound. Wait 10–14 days after campaign start before SDR touches begin

B. Layer LinkedIn retargeting using the same account list 

Upload the same account list to LinkedIn Campaign Manager as a Company List audience. Run sponsored content or conversation ads to title-matched personas at those accounts. This reinforces the CTV impression across a different device and context. StackAdapt handles this natively if you want unified reporting

PHASE 4 // MEASURE WHAT MATTERS

A. Set a 14–30 day view-through attribution window in CRM 

CTV drives view-through conversions, not click-through. Configure the attribution window and create a custom field for CTV-exposed accounts. Track pipeline velocity and deal stage movement for exposed vs. unexposed accounts

B. Measure lift, not last-touch attribution 

Split your cluster into exposed and holdout groups

↳ Compare site visit rate, email reply rate, meeting book rate, and pipeline stage velocity between groups over 60 days. 

Most teams skip CTV because they can't measure it cleanly. Set up the holdout group, run for 60 days, & let the pipeline velocity data make the case to ELT.

Rand Fishkin said the best way to sell something is to not sell anything. I respectfully disagree. Here's why.

Here's exactly what he said:

→ Don't sell anything
→ Earn the awareness, respect, & trust of those who might buy

Here's what we agree on:

→ Buyers who trust you close faster
→ Content that earns attention compounds over time
→ Nobody wants to be sold to before they're ready

We may be talking about slightly different things:
→ Rand is building brand gravity at scale - pulling buyers toward a category over years.
→ I'm talking about B2B companies at $2-10M ARR that need pipeline in the next 30 days, not the next 18 months.

And that's where it falls apart.

"Earn awareness" assumes buyers need to discover you first.

But signals tell you they're already in motion:
→ They've engaged with three of your LinkedIn ads and never converted. 
→ A new CRO just joined their org.
→ They're hiring for a role your product replaces.
→ They've visited your pricing page twice this week.
→ A past champion just moved to a new company.

These aren't cold audiences. They're accounts that crossed into awareness without your content touching them.

And on your side, you're not optimizing for trust over time.

You're optimizing for:
→ The right message at the right moment.
→ Campaign spend that hits accounts already in motion
→ Revenue that compounds the content flywheel Rand is describing.

This creates a gap.

A team that reads Rand's quote goes all-in on content and ignores the 12 accounts in their CRM showing Level 4 signals right now. 

Or worse: they serve a tofu ad to someone who visited pricing 2x this week. They're spending budget to earn trust that's already been earned.

And this gap gets bigger:
→ The more channels you're running simultaneously
→ The more signal-rich your category is
→ The higher the competition, 

The brand that shows up with the right message at the right stage wins the consideration set

Signals don't replace trust. But they tell you which stage of awareness the buyer is already in - so you can match the message instead of defaulting to the top of the funnel.

That doesn't mean abandoning brand-building for pure demand capture. I've seen teams over-correct into pure intent targeting and watch their pipeline dry up six months later. 

The answer is sequencing, not substitution.

Early-stage brand with low awareness and a category you're still defining? Rand is right. Earn the awareness first. Content is your highest-leverage asset.

Established brand with a defined ICP, signal infrastructure, and accounts actively moving through the buying journey? You have people at Level 3, 4, and 5 right now. The content earns long-term gravity. The signals tell you who to activate this month.

That's why awareness isn't just something you earn - it's something you can detect. Not instead of great marketing. But so you stop wasting it on the wrong message at the wrong stage.

How to grade multiple creative agencies

And squeeze the highest ROAS:

- You're at $500k/mo on Meta.
- Internal creative team + external agencies shipping creative
- They're all sending you reports claiming wins.

Who do you double down on?

1. Measure algorithm adoption

Calculate spend per creative
- Take your total Meta spend for the month.
- Divide it by the number of creatives each agency launched.

Check the results:
- Agency A delivers 50 creatives. Meta allocates $50k across them. That's $1k per creative
- Agency B delivers 15 creatives. Meta pushes $200k through them. That's $13k per creative
- Agency B is winning the algorithm

2. Make adjustments

Reframe how you think about agencies
- Think of agencies the same as Media Buying
- You have bids (volume) and budget (ad spend)
- If they're not getting enough ad spend, lower the volume

Adjust volumes
- Tell Agency A to cut volume. Go from 50 to 25 and focus on quality
- They may get better at lower volumes
- They may get better over more feedback + direction

NOTE:
- It’s sometimes hard to change volumes on agencies because you’re in contracts with minimum volumes etc. 
- Either negotiate this upfront or use platforms where you can adjust your spends.
- Example I use Billo for all my clients - ads are great and cost between ~$150 per ad. 

3. Build in house but keep agencies on

- Agencies are great for injecting volume and fresh angles in year one
- But building an in-house creator team is the long-term moat
- Takes 6-12 months of pain. Hiring, training, testing, failing
- You still want agencies to provide creative for fresh angles (even when you have an inhouse team)

Summary:
- Grade agencies on algorithm adoption
- Adjust volume before cutting an agency
- Keep agencies on even after you build in-house

→ Cut keywords that attract the wrong type of user

2. Target CPA bid strategy (1%)

→ Account was on Maximize Conversions.
→ The algo was chasing conversion volume regardless of CPA
→ Switched to Target CPA, set below current actuals to force cheaper conversions (5%)
→ Incremental tCPA adjustments every few days as performance stabilized (5%)

3. Negative keywords (5%)

→ Almost nothing in the account. Spend was leaking to terms that never convert
→ Built a proper negative list from the search term report
→ Usually the fastest single CPA win in any takeover

4. Ad copy (3%)

→ Generic headlines with no keyword-to-ad match
→ Rewrote 2 RSAs per ad group following our copywriting SOP (6 keyword-focused headlines, 7 features/benefits, 3 CTAs)
→ Caught a couple headlines that were too generic and rewrote them before pushing live

5. Account structure (1%)

→ Brand, competitor, and non-brand were jammed in together
→ Split into three campaigns: Brand, Competitor, Non-Brand
→ Kept competitors as one campaign (the main competitor eats most of the spend, manageable at ad group level) instead of breaking out into multiples

Cheatsheet:
- Fix keyword intent first (5%)
- Move from Maximize Conversions to Target CPA (1%)
- Pull the search term report and build a negative list (5%)
- Rewrite ad copy to match the keywords (3%)
- Split campaigns by intent: Brand, Competitor, Non-Brand (1%)

How to spend more acquiring new customers

Without losing money:

Plot this chart:

- Pull your order history.
- Group customers by the year they first bought.
- Track what each cohort spends over time.

1\. Cumulative LTV by cohort year
→ Your 2022 cohort might average $89 on day one
→ By year 2, they've spent $180+
→ If that number climbs year over year, your CPA ceiling is higher than what you're paying

2\. LTV as a percent of initial purchase
→ Strips out initial AOV so you isolate retention vs base
→ 2023 cohorts at 208% by year 2 vs 2022 at 195%? Something improved
→ This is the chart your email/SMS team needs

3\. Repurchase timing
→ Map when customers actually come back
→ Days 20-40 is usually the biggest window. If thats you:
→ 0-13: educate, make sure they use the product
→ 14-90: push the repurchase (running out, time to reorder)
→ 90+: win-back (you bought around this time last year)

4\. Retention rate by cohort
→ What percent of each cohort returns each year?
→ Improving? LTV projections get more aggressive
→ Dipped? A bad launch or stock issue will show up here

5\. Back-test the projections
→ Project historical cohorts forward, compare to actuals
→ Model says $254k but actual was $335k? It's conservative
→ That gap is your real CPA headroom

The data tells you exactly how much more you can spend per customer and still be profitable at month 3, 6, 12.

There are only 3 ways to scale Google Ads

Search is the worst one.

You find some winning keywords and start cranking spend

But eventually it loses effectiveness because:
→ Impression share for "inner circle" keywords hits a ceiling at ~80%.
→ Cost per click (CPC) climbs 15-25% month over month.
→ You’re paying more to show ads for the same, limited high-intent queries.
→ The algorithm runs out of new queries with real intent to target.

You can combat against this.

There are 3 ways to scale:

(1) Search -   Use exact and phrase match to capture your core audience. Remember it is capped in volume. Scale search by expanding match types cautiously or by geographic layering. Expect 10-30% monthly volume growth before hitting diminishing returns. Increase auctions on what's already working. You can increase budgets (if on Max Conv), and you can also increase target CPA. Keep an eye on IS (budget). If it’s a high percentage (10%+) you’ve got more room to scale. But after you’ve maxed out auctions - what’s next?

(2) PMax - Uses Search, Discovery, YouTube, Gmail. Launch after non-brand search gets 30 quality conversions per month. Ensure all optimization is for down funnel events (do not optimize for form fills, ends up bringing junk leads. Use YouTube inventory within PMax(typically 30% of total conversions come from YouTube within PMax campaigns).

(3) Demand Gen - Use when you want to fill the top of your funnel and avoid bid inflation on Search. Launch when PMax gets to 50 quality conversions per month. Target custom intent audiences, affinity segments, and in-market users on YouTube with a goal of +10-30% funnel volume increase in 3-6 months. Scale  by testing different video ad lengths and creative angles: e.g. longer form for brand stories. Lets you focus on deeper engagement metrics like view-through rate and watch time, which grows branded search.

We added $2.3m in pipeline in 90 days 

Using signal-based ABM

But getting there meant tearing down a broken system:

1 // Firmographics are tablestakes, not signal

"B2B SaaS companies with $10M–$50M ARR." 

↳ ARR range + headcount + industry = qualified account was built for a world where that was the only data you had. 
↳ It tells you who could buy, and nothing about who’s about to buy.
↳ Every competitor is doing this

2 // Pain-based segmentation without a pressure trigger

Companies with “marketing and sales misalignment" are your entire TAM.

The vintage ICP model assumes pain = readiness

Pain is static. 
Pressure is an event

3 // Strictly targeting titles 

2 VPs of Marketing, identical ICP accounts, same ARR & headcount 

↳ One just got burned by a failed ABM rollout.
↳ One just signed a 12-month agency retainer.

Opposite buying windows, and not trigger to segment them.

So we tore it down. 

And we built the signal based ABM model:

1. The LTV-Weighted ICP We reverse-engineered our closed-won data, but we weighted the score: 

(Close % × Avg Deal Size × Expansion % × Retention) / Avg Sales Cycle. 

↳ We realized a segment with a 40% close rate but 18-month churn is significantly worse than a 25% close rate with 36-month expansion.

2. "Negative" ICP & Committee Mapping 

We analyzed closed-lost and churned accounts to find which signal combinations and specific buyer titles actively stall deals. 

We built a strict exclusion model to protect SDR bandwidth and ad spend.

3. Propensity-to-Buy Validation 

Before rolling it out, we tested our hypothesis against historical data. We scored old accounts using our new model to verify that our "top decile" actually yielded the highest historical win percentage.

Outcome: we built an ABM model that isolates the 2% of our TAM in "active demand"

And split the TAM into 3 tiers:
1. Perfect Fit + Active Signals = White-Glove Outbound w/ air cover ads
2. Firmo Fit + No Signals = ABM & SDR Nurture 
3. Partial Fit = Auto-DQ

How I use AI to spend $3M/mo on Meta

1. Creative tagging
→ Every static + video ad gets run through an AI model and tagged.
→ Every frame is analyzed and audio is transcribed
→ 40+ dimensions inc: format, selling point, who's in it, the setting etc
→ Then I pull performance against those tags.
→ Can draw conclusions like: "UGC about pain point in kitchen outperforms founder ads in office about features by 40%."

2. Creative gap analysis
→ I build a creative heatmap. Selling point on one axis, format on the other.
→ We look for gaps in heatmap to indicate we've missed testing
→ Also use it to find winning selling points that can be scaled across formats (or vice versa)
→ Without this you either repeat what worked until it fatigues or throw random stuff at the wall.

3. Data routing
→ Before asking AI anything, I run it through a routing layer. Its job isn't to answer the question.
→ It looks at the context and decides: which client? Which data source? Do I need call transcripts, Slack threads, Facebook performance data, or internal numbers?
→ We manage multiple brands and cannot have the wrong client's data leaking into analysis.

4. SQL over raw analysis
→ We spent weeks rebuilding our whole backend data architecture - now running off databases.
→ I give our AI access to write SQL and query the database directly.
→ SQL also forces the data to stay segmented. The AI pulls exactly what it needs.
→ And I never let it analyze ad copy, CTAs, and landing pages as one aggregate. Break it by persona. E.g. this ad copy works for this person, this landing page works for that one.

5. Verifying every output
→ I treat AI output the same way I treat a manual spreadsheet.
→ Check the sums, verify the tables, make sure the data actually says what the summary claims.
→ Even one extra loop of "is this accurate?" catches most hallucinations

Across all of this, AI makes me faster at finding insights.

It doesn't replace knowing which ones actually matter.

I've audited 200+ ABM programs

The biggest predictor of ABM success isn't your ICP, messaging, or your team. 

It’s a financial issue

The first question I always ask:

“Walk me through the math. What are we actually buying here?”

Maybe 5 had a defensible answer.

The ABM programs that get renewed are decided before launch, not after.

Here’s how to set it up correctly:

STEP 1 // BUILD YOUR COST MODEL

Total ABM investment breaks into 3 buckets:

A. Media spend
↳ LinkedIn, CTV, programmatic, direct mail
↳ Budget $150-300 per target account per month for air cover
↳ 100 accounts = $15K-$30K/month minimum

B. Tech stack
↳ Intent data, ABM platform, enrichment tools
↳ Annualize and divide by # of programs

C. People cost
↳ % of SDR, marketing, ops time dedicated to ABM
↳ Burdened salary × time allocation

Add all three = Total Program Cost

STEP 2 // MODEL YOUR EXPECTED PIPELINE

Formula:
Target Accounts × Expected Engagement Rate × Meeting Conversion × Opp Conversion × Avg Deal Size = Expected Pipeline

Example with real math:
↳ 100 accounts
↳ 25% engagement rate (25 engaged accounts)
↳ 40% meeting conversion (10 meetings)
↳ 70% opp conversion (7 opportunities)
↳ $75K avg deal size
= $525K in pipeline

STEP 3 // CALCULATE PROGRAM ROI

Pipeline ROI = Expected Pipeline / Total Program Cost

If your program costs $50K and generates $525K in pipeline:
↳ Pipeline ROI = 10.5x

But leadership cares about closed revenue, not pipeline.

Revenue ROI = (Expected Pipeline × Historical Close Rate) / Total Program Cost

↳ $525K × 30% close rate = $157.5K expected revenue
↳ $157.5K / $50K = 3.15x revenue ROI

STEP 4 // BUILD THE SENSITIVITY TABLE

This is what separates amateurs from operators.

Show leadership 3 scenarios:
↳ Conservative: 20% engagement, 25% close rate
↳ Base case: 25% engagement, 30% close rate
↳ Aggressive: 35% engagement, 35% close rate

Map each scenario to pipeline and revenue ROI.

When leadership asks "what if it doesn't work?" you already have the answer.

STEP 5 // TIE TO EXISTING BENCHMARKS

Pull your historical data:
↳ What's your current cost-per-opportunity from other channels?
↳ What's your average CAC payback?
↳ What's your LTV:CAC ratio by segment?

Show how ABM compares. If your current CPO is $8K and ABM delivers at $7.1K, that's the story.

The pitch isn't "ABM is cool." The pitch is "ABM delivers pipeline at a lower CPO than our current mix."

Programs that launch with this model don't get cut at month 9.
They get expanded.

CEOs keep telling me they want AI-native teams

What they really want is $1M ARR per employee. It’s not realistic:

It's aspirational. 

One client wants a 3-year roadmap to get there.

The problem: the metric is fun to talk about. But hitting $1M/employee looks completely different depending on your GTM motion.

I've seen 4 GTM models actually get there. Each one has a different org shape, a different leverage point, and a different way to break.

1 // ABM-Enterprise

The motion: manufacturing pipeline from a fixed list of named accounts. AEs run 12–18 month campaigns against 5–10 accounts each. Marketing operates in 1:1 and 1:few modes including executive surround, custom content, committee mapping. 

The setup: enterprise deals are sticky because the switching cost is organizational. Low logo churn means the revenue base compounds quietly in the background while AEs hunt net new logos.

The risk: concentration. At $250K ACV, losing 5 customers means losing $1.25M ARR and you can't backfill fast.

The insight: ABM requires relationship alignment across marketing, sales, and CS

2 // Expansion-Led Land & Expand

The motion: land smaller, expand fast. The real revenue is built post-sale.

The setup: CS/AM is the engine. You need significantly more CS/AMs than AEs, and they carry real expansion quota. Expansion deals close faster than new logo deals, which is where the NRR leverage comes from.

The risk: this model only works if the product has genuine expansion vectors.

The insight: You're not landing customers, you're landing beachheads. Expansion ceiling matters most.

3 // Inbound-Heavy Marketing Engine

The motion: marketing generates demand, AEs close it, CS expands it.

The setup: you need roughly 1.5x as many CS/AMs as AEs, and they need to carry expansion quota. Most companies underinvest here and wonder why nrr is flat.

The risk: this model runs on MQL volume. If demand gen consistency slips, AEs starve within a quarter. 
The insight: You're not building a sales team. You're building a pipeline manufacturing operation with a sales team attached to it.

4 // Partner-Led Growth Engine

The motion: the partnerships team is the engine: they recruit, enable, and activate the channel so AEs don't have to generate their own pipeline.

The setup: partner-sourced deals cost less to acquire and partners who implement also expand, which is where the NRR lift comes from. The AE team stays lean because 50-60% of pipeline arrives pre-qualified

The risk: activation rate. A partner who can't sell your product confidently won't sell it at all

The insight: you’re building a revenue network where every partner is a distributed pipeline source - but only if you treat enablement like a product

The "$1M revenue per employee" benchmark is real (especially with AI), but the shape of the org is the lynchpin
