AM teams - if a lot of your renewals fall in Nov/Dec, here's an easy play to run this month to avoid getting a surprise no on your renewals. It'll cost you $0.

It's the 180 Day Call. 

I didn't come up with it. This was taught to me when I worked at CEB. 

6 months prior to the renewal, we asked the client 3 direct questions (in a call):

"If you had to make a decision on renewal today, would you say yes or no?"

"If you had to predict one internal objection, hurdle, or competing priority that unexpectedly creates an obstacle at renewal time - what would that be?"

"What would your CXO say if you asked for budget to renew today?"

Then, we shut up and let them talk. Sought to understand. We didn't show up with a 50 pg slide deck of utilization. We didn't pitch. We left the call with a clear understanding of where we were falling short + where/how company priorities had shifted + a plan to course-correct.

It's simple, but it was one of my favorite tactics I learned as an AM.

Here's why: 

- If I heard bad news, it gave me 6 more months to work on the fixable stuff. I wasn't scrambling and draining my company's resources to save it in Dec.

- It created trust with the buyer because I wasn't trying to convince them to renew. I made it clear I was comfortable hearing the truth (which, in some cases, meant bad news). 

- It elicited potential renewal red flags, concerns, competing priorities, and internal blockers I was not expecting. 

- It exposed my flawed assumptions (ex:, thinking "they have 100 regular users, with high utilization, so they must be seeing value", when the sponsor was quantifying'value differently)

But, like a lot of stuff in Sales, the easiest thing for us to do is to skip these. We tell ourselves, "that customer has been with us forever - they always renew". Or, "I don't want to ask...what if they say no".

So, the real trick to making it work was that the company tracked 180 day completion rates in CRM on the opportunity. With as much accountability as they tracked new logo sales meetings booked. 

As a result, 180 day call completion rate was positively correlated to a higher renewal rate. 

So often, WE are the ones who don't make it safe for customers to tell us the truth. Because hearing bad news is never enjoyable. 

180 calls forced me to have uncomfortable conversations with enough time to do something about it. Win for the client, win for us.

We spend $72M/year on Google Ads

How to run advanced competitor brand campaigns: 

1. Cherry pick easiest target
List every competitor in a Google sheet and create a matrix of every dimension you compete on. E.g. pricing, features, support, use cases. Cherry pick the competitors where you have an obvious and clear advantage and you look different. There’s no point trying to compete against a big incumbent who is likely to outprice and/or out-product you. The more selective you are here, the better.  We found a huge range in CPAs depending on the competitor we go after.

2. Build dedicated landing pages
Build dedicated pages that directly address "why us vs. them" for each major competitor.  List their pain points. Show your advantages. Make the comparison obvious. Conversion rates go up because you're meeting the searcher exactly where they are.  It’s important to be as factually correct on this page as possible. There’s no point lying or bending the truth to convert a lead that ultimately doesn’t have the right expectations, and then ultimately churns and has a low LTV. We found a 30% reduction in CPL just with dedicated landing pages.

3. Segment LTV by competitor  
This is where most competitor campaigns fall apart. You need GCLID and UTM parameters flowing all the way through to your CRM, tied to the specific competitor keyword that brought them in. And then from there, you track win rates by competitor, not just leads. You track LTV by competitor. Some competitor traffic converts at lower rates but higher deal sizes. Some converts faster but churns. 

4. Improve Keyword Intent
Not everyone searching a competitor name is in-market. Some are job seekers looking to work there. Some are existing customers searching for support or login pages. We aggressively remove terms from the start, things like "careers," "jobs," "login," "support," "help desk." (You should already have these in your NKL anyways!) Otherwise you're paying for clicks that were never going to convert. It seems obvious, but we see this mistake in almost every competitor campaign audit we run. When budgets get large enough we use Negative Nancy. It’s our AI agent that runs every week on client accounts and ingests every keyword that drove clicks. If the intent of the keyword is poor, we add it to negative keywords inside Google ads (this by itself can lower CPLs by 30% in 24-48 hours).

SUMMARY: 

→ Cherry pick weakest competitors 
→ Build dedicated landers 
→ Full funnel tracking from ad click to closed deal 
→ Negative keywords 

If you're running competitor campaigns and not seeing pipeline like this, the issue is usually one of these four things.

Win-back rate is something every sales leader should measure and here's why: it's an indicator of how efficiently your team is recovering lost pipeline 

Inbound + outbound are measured: 
- leads, MQLs, SQLs, closed-won
- prospects, meetings, opps, closed-won

You can apply the same principle to lost: 
- lost leads, winnable leads, in pipeline, recovered

We measure "rebound rate" and "win-back rate" 
- rebound rate = # leads who are interested in re-engaging with us 
- win-back rate = when a lost deal comes back in the pipeline, what's our win rate? 

These two metrics allow us to forecast lost as it's own funnel, and give us insight into: 
- how much pipeline is winnable? how much isn't? why?
- Sales process- do people want to speak to us again? 
- Are we re-engaging at the right time? should we adjust?
- How much of lost can we forecast back to won?

As an example, one client sees their win-back rate is ~3x their win rate at 57%. Meaning, when a lost opp goes back in the pipeline- they have a 57% chance of it being closed-won.

Alternative Meta campaign structure

Use to maximize profit control:

- Meta has a BIG blind spot.
- It doesn't know your LTV or contribution margin.
- It only knows what converts cheapest right now.

Hedge against this by grouping campaigns by unit economics.

Example: Men's gym brand launching new SKUs.

Campaign 1: Flagship product

→ Three flavor variants of the standard whey (chocolate, vanilla, peanut butter)
→ $45 AOV, ~40% contribution margin, $18 gross profit per unit
→ Repeat rate, payback window, and LTV are the same across all three flavors
→ One campaign, one CPA target (~$20). Let Meta pick the winner across flavors.

Campaign 2: Bundle offer (2x the price but 3x profit and better LTV)

→ 1 tub of the flagship protein + free shaker + free creatine tub
→ $90 AOV. The "free" extras cost you ~$5 in COGS but add ~$40 of perceived value
→ ~64% contribution margin, $58 gross profit per order
→ Let's say it's the same customer as Campaign 1.
→ Separate ABO and ASC, CPA ceiling pushed to ~$40 because the margin can absorb it

If you lump both into the same ASC, Meta optimizes for the cheaper purchase if ROAS is the same despite POAS being better on campaign 2. Your bundle looks like a loser, but only because the CPA ceiling it's being measured against is wrong for it.

Media buyer view:
- Meta has clean signal inside each campaign.
- Now, you can scale the bundle without cannibalizing flagship spend, and you can kill a losing flavor without killing the whole launch.

CFO view:
- Margin per campaign is visible and controllable.
- The bundle with 3x the gross profit per order isn't getting starved while Meta chases a $20 CPA on the flagship.
- Each campaign gets measured against its own payback window. A blended window overpays on the cheap product and underpays on the profitable one.

Point is consider business outcomes in your Meta ad account structure too.

I've thought on many walks with my dog about how to build a great company list from multiple sources. This video goes over the best way I can think of today. 

I think there's a spectrum of how to create lists. 

Standard filters -> Lists fully made with AI

The standard filters you can get from LinkedIn data via BlitzAPI and Google Maps data

Lists fully made with AI filters need to be found with tools like Exa/Parallel Web Systems or DiscoLike/Ocean.io

Each method has it's tradeoffs. 

So I put them into 4 buckets

1. List where standard filters are more than enough. Like when you want to email any CEO/Founder with 10-20 employees for some reason. Blitz API can handle this alone. Say you want everyone with google my business profiles. Go to google maps first and then find contacts via Blitz/prospeo or your other favorite tools. 

2. When standard filters are good but won't get everything. Companies that provide marketing agency services won't ALWAYS say that they are in marketing services/advertising services. 

So you want to use standard linkedin filters via a tool like Blitz, then move to a tool like Discolike/Ocean for AI targeting. Then you have a database to work off of. Use that database as exclusion and run Exa to find more until it runs 10 times in a row and only adds one company because of non fit or dedupe against your current list

3. Standard list filtering just won't cut it. Targeting SaaS companies. There's too many industries to account for. You need Disco/Ocean/ or prospeo with their new company filtering release. Exa to follow to clean up anything you didn't find. 

4. No fitlers will work. must start with Ocean/Disco and clean up with Exa

All the way, using an ICP prompt loop strategy that creates task sub agents to ensure the companies fit your ICP for every company that it pulls.

How FIGS 12x'd profit on a scrubs brand.

I analyzed their P&L to find out:

→ FY25 revenue: $631M (+14% YoY)
→ Net income: $2.7M → $34.3M (12.7x)
→ Adj EBITDA margin: 9.3% → 11.8%
→ Active customers: 2.65M → 2.9M
→ AOV: $114 → $120 (Q4 hit $126)

Where did the extra profit come from?

1. Non-scrubs grew AOV

→ Scrubwear is still 77% of revenue
→ But non-scrubs (outerwear, loungewear, underscrubs, a New Balance footwear collab) grew 26% YoY in Q4 and hit 23% of total revenue
→ TEAMS, their B2B platform for hospital group orders with custom embroidery is growing

2. Product marketing

→ 250+ healthcare ambassadors drive ~35% of website traffic through organic content
→ They deliberately cut back on promotions in 2025 to protect brand health
→ 5 Community Hub stores in medical districts (LA, NYC, Philly, Houston, Chicago) that drive local awareness without paid spend
→ Result = marketing dropped from ~16% to ~14% of revenue and growth accelerated

3. Tariff cost absorption

→ Contract manufacturing across Vietnam, China, Jordan, Pakistan
→ Vietnam alone has 20% import duties
→ Absorbed it and did not raise prices, while still expanding Adj EBITDA margin 250bps
→ One-time $5.6M Q4 inventory write-off dragged the print. Without it, profit was closer to $38-40M.

Bottom line:
→ 14% revenue growth at 67% gross margin generated ~$50M in new gross profit. Marketing only ate $4.5M of it.
→ Non-scrubs growing 26% YoY and pulling AOV up without extra ad spend
→ 250+ ambassadors doing the acquisition work that paid media used to do
→ Absorbed 120bps of tariffs instead of passing them through. Risky, but it protected the brand.

How to layer $500k/mo ad spend across:

Google → Meta → CTV→ Direct Mail:

1. Google Search (first $250K/mo)
→ Search: brand, competitors, non-brand. Start here.
→ PMax: add at 30+ qualified conversions/month. If you skip Search, PMax wastes money. If you skip PMax, Search caps growth.
→ Demand Gen: add at 50+ qualified conversions/month. Opens YouTube, Gmail, and Discover inventory.
→ Max the Google stack before you go anywhere else.

2. Meta (layer on top of Search, within the same $250K)
→ Build warm audiences, e.g. website visitors, email lists, lookalikes from your Search converters.
→ Meta CPMs for warm audiences are relatively cheap
→ Google + Meta outperforms either one alone.
→ Creative: video testimonials from clients, before/after CPA comparisons, case study stats (e.g. scaled a client from $8M to $67M in 18 months).

3. Programmatic + CTV via Trade Desk (next $200K)
→ Run both through Trade Desk instead of buying direct.
→ Start with retargeting your full funnel across desktop, mobile, and connected TV
→ Then flip to prospecting on cold audiences as budgets scale.
→ CTV ads are non-skippable for the first 15-30 seconds. You have guaranteed attention. You want to make sure the watcher has a reason to not click skip.

This is where it gets really fun...

4. Direct Mail (final $50K, layered on top of CTV)
→ CTV targeting is IP-based.
→ Every household IP maps to a physical address.
→ You now can send mail to anyone who watched your CTV ads.
→ e.g., a handwritten-style letter to leads with an offer and a QR code

Summary
- Max the Google stack (Search → PMax → Demand Gen)
- Meta layers on top of Search intent
- Programmatic + CTV via Trade Desk which captures IP address.
- CTV captures the IP. That IP maps to a home address. 
- Send a direct mail piece with a bottom-funnel offer to everyone who watched.

I’m working with a head of partnerships at a $42m SaaS

“It’s a 1:1 relationship channel… ai can’t help”. But what she missed cost the company upwards of $9m in annual pipeline.

She wasn't wrong about everything.

Some things in channel partnerships will always be human:

1 // Partner recruiting. You can automate the introduction, but the relationship needs ongoing nurture. Dinners, gifts, and constant 1:1 personal touchpoints are what keep these relationships alive - and what keep them activated.

2 // Consistent rep training. Especially with complex b2b, sellers won’t sell unless they feel confident about the product and sales process. Part of the weekly touchpoint with your partners is giving them the training on new products/features, value positioning, discovery, all of it.

But her reluctance to see the broader strategy was costing her deals, and had the ELT looking directly at her for results.

What I discovered:

Problem 1: Internal sellers had no prioritization. They each owned a partner territory, but woke up every morning not knowing which accounts to attack. 

Solution: 
→ We organized all reps around a single target account list
→ Segmented by territory
→ Ran signal research to find the 10% of accounts in active demand in each territory

Now reps knew who to call and who to set in person meetings with.

Problem 2: Partners had no idea who the reps were when they showed up. The relationship had already been established, but out of sight / out of mind. 

Solution:
→ We ran ABM-style air cover ads targeting partner accounts, always providing value.
→ Followed up with weekly updates - new case studies, new incentives, seller tactics.
→ Sports tickets, dinners and perks ran in sync with ABM
Reps stopped walking into cold rooms.
Problem 3: Partners had no idea which accounts to prioritize either

It was one big guess.

This is where a two-layer account research model came in:

→ Layer 1 (Internal): Which accounts should YOUR sellers be targeting in each partner territory? (Signal-based prioritization, same playbook as above)
→ Layer 2 (Partner-facing): Once we knew the right accounts, we packaged that intel for the partner's sellers; territory by territory, account by account, rank ordered by buying signal strength.

We ran the exact same signal research playbook at the opportunity level and handed partners a prioritized hit list they could actually use.

Partners stopped guessing. Deal velocity picked up immediately.

What she didn't realize: partner channels aren't a sales motion. They're an ABM motion.

The best partner programs run like account-based plays with air cover, signal research, coordinated touchpoints, intel shared across every layer of the funnel.

The 1:1 relationship is the activation layer. The infrastructure underneath is what scales it.

CEO: LinkedIn said we NEED to launch AppLovin

CMO: No. 

CEO: What do you mean… No. 

CMO: We’re not ready yet… 

CEO: We’re at $5m/y. We've been on Meta for 3 years.

CMO: Exactly. And we're still not crushing it there.

CEO: Our ROAS is fine. We're profitable.

CMO: Fine isn't scaling. What's our top 2% of ads driving in terms of spend?

CEO: I don't know off the top of my head.

CMO: It should be 50% of spend and revenue. If it's not, we haven't figured out our creative engine yet.

CEO: But diversification is how real brands grow. Look at any 8-9 figure company - they're everywhere.

CMO: That's what founders tell the press. It's not what I see in the data.

CEO: What do you mean?

CMO: 8-9 figure DTC brands aren't diversified. 80% of their acquisition comes from one place. They got there by focusing on one funnel and optimizing it relentlessly.

CEO: So you're saying AppLovin and Amazon are bad ideas?

CMO: I'm saying they're premature ideas. We're spending what, $160k a month on Meta?

CEO: Around there.

CMO: We need to spend more. I’ve seen brands in our niche spend $500k a month on Meta alone. The limitation on Meta isn't scale. It never was.

CEO: Then what's the limitation?

CMO: Getting creative, optimization, and unit economics right. Once you have that, Meta is hyperscalable.

CEO: So what should we be focused on instead of new channels?

CMO: Four things. Creative - are we launching one new concept per $10k in monthly spend? Media buying - is our testing budget under 20% of total? Website - is our CVR above 3%? Retention - is our LTV:CAC at 3:1?

CEO: I... don't know all of those numbers.

CMO: That's the problem. We're trying to add new channels when we haven't mastered the fundamentals on the one we have.

CEO: But what if Meta stops working? Eggs in one basket and all that.

CMO: The 7-figure brands I see want to diversify too fast. They start testing Snapchat, TikTok, Pinterest. Now they have a bunch of channels they're doing an okay job at instead of one funnel they're crushing.

CEO: Okay, but at what point do we actually expand?

CMO: When we are producing the right number of creative, with a consistent 10% hit rate, and 1% are huge winners (driving 50% of rev). 

CEO: That’s it? 

CMO: And when media buying creates reliable results, and we are first order breakeven by month 3, LTV:CAC of 3:1+ and we are regularly optimizing and testing our conversion funnels.

CEO: And then?

CMO: Then you can think about diversification. I'd expect we could hit mid-8 figures before we actually need to.

CEO: So the path to $10M is... doing Meta better?

CMO: The path to $10M is is through better media buying and creative. We've seen 8-figure brands do it with optimization alone. No new channels required.

CEO: So what do I tell the investors 

CMO: What do you mean?

CEO: I told them we’re diversifying in the last investor update

CMO: Show them our revenue next quarter. They'll forget what you said.

I just launched a $500k ABM program

I structured it like a VC fund deploying capital:

↳ VC’s make cheap, wide bets at the bottom. 
↳ Concentrate capital on what shows traction. 
↳ Goes all-in on the highest-conviction plays.

I expect an 80% failure rate - and that’s by design. 

TIER STRUCTURE // THE PORTFOLIO
Tier 1 → 1:1 → 20–50 "Must-Win" accounts → $5K–$15K spend per account 
Tier 2 → 1:Few → 100–300 high-fit accounts → $1K–$5K spend per account 
Tier 3 → 1:Many → 500+ programmatic → $100–$500 spend per account

CAPITAL ALLOCATION // $1M SPLIT
↳ Tier 1 (Whales): 40% → bespoke content, exec time, direct mail 
↳ Tier 2 (High-Fit): 40% → clustered ads, field events, research 
↳ Tier 3 (Coverage): 20% → programmatic, intent tracking, nurture

Good VCs don't set their portfolio on January 1st and ignore it.

They watch for signals. When something shows life, they double down.
Same mechanic here.

A Tier 3 account starts spiking intent data - leadership researching competitors, reading your docs, they get upgraded to Tier 2. More SDR focus and more capital. 

Capital is gated. It only flows to accounts that earn it.

VCs also expect most bets to fail.

$500K invested → 100 accounts targeted 
↳ 80 don't close in year one 
↳ 20 close at $150K ACV = $3M in new revenue

That's not a failure rate. That's the model working.

The J-Curve is real: 
↳ Months 1–9: capital flows out, pipeline builds 
↳ Month 9–12: closed revenue starts showing 
↳ Programs that survive month 9 don't get cut. They get expanded.

WHERE THE ANALOGY BREAKS DOWN

VC funds don't have a sales team context-switching between deal sizes.
ABM does.
↳ AEs can't toggle between a $500K Tier 1 motion and a transactional Tier 3 deal 
↳ If sales isn't segmented by tier, leads get mishandled and marketing capital burns

The other kill switch: content.
↳ You can't write a custom whitepaper per Tier 2 vertical from scratch 
↳ Build modular base assets that can be skinned per industry 
↳ Otherwise content costs destroy ROI before pipeline matures

The pitch isn't "ABM is cool."

It's that you're not running a marketing campaign. You're running a risk-adjusted acquisition fund.

And like any fund - the math has to work before you deploy a dollar

How to scale Google Ads

Using this 3x3 matrix: 

There are only 3 problems stopping your scale:
1. Visibility → Your ads aren't showing
2. Engagement → Your ads show but don't get clicked
3. Conversion → You get clicks but no conversions

And there are only 3 ways to solve this:
1. Budget/Bid 
2. Quality 
3. Targeting

You can fix every problem with the 3 solutions:

Box 1: Low Visibility
Symptom: High IS Lost (Budget)
Fix: Increase budget OR reduce targeting to focus spend on highest-value segments

Box 2: Low Visibility, Low Quality
Symptom: Quality Score and CTR below average
Fix: Probably the toughest one. Improve your expected CTR, ad relevance, and landing page experience. Make sure your offer is competitive. See what competitors are driving traffic to. Quality Score isn't always reliable but if multiple components show "Below Average" that's a clear signal.

Box 3: Low Visibility, Wrong Targeting
Symptom: Low impressions despite budget, keywords too narrow
Fix: Expand keyword universe, add phrase/broad match with Smart Bidding

Box 4: Low Engagement
Symptom: Good IS, low CTR, competitors have better ad positions
Fix: Increase bids to get higher positions where CTR improves

Box 5: Low Engagement, Low Quality
Symptom: Good IS, low CTR, ad relevance below average
Fix: Rewrite ad copy, tighten the match between keyword and ad and landing page, add in Assets

Box 6: Low Engagement, Wrong Targeting
Symptom: Good IS, low CTR, ads showing to wrong audience
Fix: Tighten match types, add negatives, refine audience signals, rework ad copy

Box 7: Low Conversion
Symptom: Good CTR, low conversions, Smart Bidding limited by budget
Fix: Increase budget OR eliminate Search Lost IS (Budget) so CPCs stay efficient. If you're on tCPA or tROAS, any lost-to-budget inflates your CPCs.

Box 8: Low Conversion, Low Quality
Symptom: Good CTR, low conversions, poor landing page experience
Fix: Improve page speed, relevance, form experience, mobile optimization

Box 9: Low Conversion, Wrong Targeting
Symptom: Good CTR, low conversions, wrong traffic
Fix: Add negative keywords, review search terms, tighten audience targeting. Check what conversion action you're optimizing for. If you're optimizing for form fills instead of qualified leads, the algorithm finds cheap clicks that don't convert downstream.

How to use this in practice:

Pull these metrics for any struggling campaign:

→ Impression Share
→ IS Lost (Budget)
→ IS Lost (Rank)
→ CTR
→ Conversion Rate

1. Walk through the diagnosis tree. 
2. Identify which box you're in. 
3. Apply the fix for that specific box.

Hope this helps.

How marketing angles correlate with customer quality:

1. Urgency
- Pros: You get more sales
- Cons: The sales are typically from people who would of bought anyway. You've bought forward sales, not generated new sales

2. Mechanism 
- Pros: You hit the early adopters 
- Cons: Easy to undersold by people using the same mechanism

3. Proof 
- Pros: Get people exactly like the proof you showed 
- Cons: You can have the best proof, but people just don't believe it 

4. Pain 
- Pros: Huge TAM
- Cons: Tends to only get struggling people. Struggling people are annoying as hell. You need to really hold their hand 

5. Identity 
- Pros: People do what it takes to maintain their identity. 
- Cons: Looks scammy "Millionaires take action, you should take action". Super hard to change someones identity

A client needed a highly targeted list of regulated financial-advice firms in the UK. Not "financial services companies". Regulated advice firms, split by whether they were independent or sat inside a larger network.

The thing that cracked it was a sentence in a website footer.

Here's the build. 

Three sources to find every firm that could possibly fit: every financial services and investment management company on LinkedIn, the Companies House database (scraped with Browser Use), and the FCA registry (they have a downloadable API). 

Then the hard part was finding which of these are in-network vs independent, how are they regulated, how many advisors do they have. 

Advisor count came from LinkedIn. Regulation and network status had to come from the websites themselves.

In-network firms are required to put compliance language in their footer. So we used Exa to find what that language actually looks like. 

Once we had the pattern, it was over. Compliance text gets copy-pasted verbatim across an entire network, so footer-matching told us instantly who was in-network and who wasn't.

Claude Code built the orchestration and ran it in goal mode overnight — clear outcome, "check every page of every site for these keywords, don't stop until it's done." About three hours.

I’ve spent $150M+ on Meta ads.

My DTC tactic tier list:

F Tier
→ Engagement objectives. There is no point paying Meta to optimize for engagement. Only optimize for purchases.
→ Frequency capping. You're better off putting more energy into making better ads that can scale.

D Tier
→ Lookalike audiences. Meta's algorithm finds your buyers better than any seed list you'll ever build.
→ Retargeting campaigns. Most of this is showing ads to people who were going to buy anyway. Incrementality is near zero.

C Tier
→ CBO vs ABO debates. Spend less time on campaign structure and more time making creative. For most brands you shouldn't use an ABO because your media buyer is not in the account enough. However, if they are in the account, ABO can dramatically lower your CPAs given you have more control.
→ Advantage+ Creative enhancements. Letting Meta auto-crop and overlay text is how you end up with off-brand ads everywhere. Just make more ads instead.
→ Heavy Offer/promo-led creative. Works but you're training customers to wait for the next sale. Keep it balanced.

B Tier
→ Interest targeting. Still works well for me on launches but Broad and ASC outperform it at scale. Always keep advantage + audiences on.
→ UGC ads. Table stakes now. Still works but goal is authenticity and scale so it takes finding good creators.
→ Static image ads. Underrated. Fast to produce, easy to iterate, still convert.
→ Cost caps / bid caps. Good for controlling CAC but they throttle spend when you want to scale.
→ Whitelisting / partnership ads. Decent format but the lift over standard UGC is overhyped for a lot of brands.
→ Long-form video (60s+). 15-30s normally outperform for DTC but occasionally long form ads rip if they are compelling.

A Tier
→ Advantage+ Shopping Campaigns. ASC is Meta's campaign that almost everyone should run. Feed it creative and get out of the way. Better for low SKU count brands that have the same customer base.
→ Creative diversification. More concepts = more shots on goal. The brands scaling fastest ship 100+ new ads a month.
→ Big creative swings. The ads that 10x your account are never the safe ones. Ugly, weird, unexpected stuff wins.
→ Landing page testing. There's a LOT to gain from landing page testing (overlooked vs creative testing)
→ A strong UGC productiong Platform like Billo. Every month I spend $1M on the ads I get from their platform. It’s the easiest way for me to ramp UGC ads in 7 days and ads only cost ~$150. 

S Tier
→ Creative testing frameworks. A system for testing hooks, formats, and concepts at volume. After 8 years, this is the only thing that consistently compounds.
→ Founder story ads. Especially when your founder is also your ICP. Nothing I've tested outperforms a founder who can sell on camera.

8 years in and I keep landing on the same conclusion.

- Build a system that tests creative at volume.
- Make sure your media buyer can squeeze those creative best

There is no such thing as a "B2B SaaS" filter. There's no clean "e-commerce brand" one either. And if you pull "financial services," you will miss every bank.

This is why client vertical lists come back full of junk.

A few real examples from a TAM we built this week, US companies, 50–5,000 employees, six verticals:

Bacardi is an e-commerce/retail brand. It lists itself under beverage manufacturing. Hit just "retail" and you'll never see it.

Manufacturing and logistics companies notoriously aren't all on LinkedIn, and the ones that are file themselves under wild industries.

Healthcare is the worst. Pull "healthcare" and you've blended medical device makers, healthcare SaaS, hospitals, and health insurers into one pile that means nothing to the client.

Don't filter your way to a vertical, define it, then qualify into it. 

We pull broad from our internal database and Prospeo's v2 type/business-model filters, merge and dedupe, then run every company through a written definition of what that vertical actually means to this specific client. 

"Banks count as financial services here. Fintech does not."

How I max out Target ROAS campaigns:

1. Check minimum requirements
To run tROAS you should hit these minimums every 30 days:
→ Display = 15.
→ Shopping = 15.
→ App = 300
→ Demand Gen = ~30
→ Search = 15
→ Performance Max = ~30

If you don't have those numbers (across your account, ideally not all centralized in Branded keywords), stay on Max Conversion Value.

2. Set tROAS
→ Pull your "Conv. value/cost" column (ROAS) over last 4 weeks & exclude last 3-7 days to account for conversion delay (if you experience that).
→ Set your target at or below that number.
→ Don't try to set tROAS above historical just yet. I've seen accounts lose 40%+ traffic overnight from doing that. It kills your volume and lets your competitors come in.

3. Train with real value
→ Upload offline conversions with conversion values
→ E.g. MQL: $50, SQL: $250, Closed Deal: $10,000
→ Encourages Google to shift budget to higher value clicks (probably more expensive but it's worth it)

 4. Check Search Lost IS (Budget)
→ This tells you if tROAS is in-line
→ If Search Lost IS (budget) is >0%, your tROAS might be too low. Raise tROAS until lost-to-budget hits zero. Or increase your budgets if you are hitting your desired ROAS
→ This keeps CPCs efficient throughout the day

5. Adjustments
→ Want more volume? Lower tROAS in 5-10% increments
→ Want more efficiency? Raise tROAS in 5-10% increments
→ Wait 1-2 conversion cycles after any change before judging.

Cheatsheet:
→ Turn on tROAS at the right time
→ Set tROAS around historical performance
→ Watch Search Lost IS (Budget) to adjust tROAS
→ Make gradual changes & wait 1-2 conversion cycles

Google can only attribute data for 90 days.

What to do if you have LONG sales cycles:

E.g. A 180-day sales cycle means your closed-won signal arrives 90 days after Google stops attributing.

1. Go up the funnel

The closed deal can't be your primary conversion. The signal arrives too late for Smart Bidding to learn from it. Switch primary to something that fires within 30 days of the click, like a booked discovery call or an SQL stage in your CRM. You need 30+ of those per month at the bid strategy level (not the campaign level), otherwise there's not enough volume to train on. Keep the closed deal in as secondary so the reporting still lives in Google Ads, but don't ask the algorithm to optimize around it.

2. Upload values 

A booked demo and a closed $50k deal shouldn't look identical in Google. Pipe your CRM values back in through offline conversion imports or Enhanced Conversions for Leads. An MQL might be worth $50 to you, an SQL $250, a closed deal $10,000. Once those values land in the platform, Smart Bidding starts shifting budget toward the clicks that become pipeline instead of the clicks that become spam form fills. Extra credit if you build a predictive LTV model.

3. Model bake-time

You still need a way to judge CPA while the cycle is running. Pull 6+ months of historical lead data, group by month cohort, and chart cumulative close rate at day 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90. That gives you a baseline curve. When a 30-day-old cohort should be sitting at X% closed based on history, you can tell if you're ahead or behind schedule months before the deals close.

4. Switch attribution model 

Data-Driven is default so shouldn’t be an issue. But last-click strips credit from the YouTube or Search touch that happened 90 days before the close. If you care about the top-of-funnel work that gets the cycle started, DDA spreads credit across the full path. It's also the only setting that plays nicely with Smart Bidding now that the old position-based models have been retired.

5. Campaign testing duration

If your cycle is 90 days, you need at least 120 days of data before you can fairly judge CPA. I've seen accounts kill winning campaigns in week 4 because the dashboard looked bad. The CPA was fine, the leads just hadn't closed yet.

Cheatsheet:
→ Smart Bidding only learns inside your conversion window
→ Give it a proxy that fires well before that window closes
→ Pipe CRM values back in so it optimizes on pipeline quality
→ Use cohorted close rates to judge true CPA while the cycle is still running

Does ketchup belong on hot dogs? Is candy corn delicious? Is Nicholas Cage a good actor? Is NYC pizza > Chicago deep dish? Is Bravo good TV?

Try walking into a room of 17 people and asking any one of these Qs. 

Some will ride or die for Summer House (SH reunion next week, anyone?). Some will be indifferent. 

Some will defend Nicholas Cage's acting skills. Others will say his movies are trash. 

The room will fight a battle of opinions. On topics that are completely inconsequential. 

This is exactly what's happening when sellers try to go from interested champion --> buying group consensus. Except, they aren't insignificant decisions. Because the buyer's political capital is tied to it. 

Bob wants to protect status quo. 
Jane wants to solve the problem with a different category of solution. 
Carl doesn't think this is even the right problem to prioritize right now.
Tina is quietly quitting and totally indifferent to the entire convo. 
Barry just wants to have their voice heard and is talking just to talk. 

Sellers spend a lot of time learning how to sell to a champion. 

But, going from "I agree this is a business problem worth solving" --> "We agree this is a business problem worth solving" is often where big deals go to die. 

The single biggest mistake I made in my career is jumping quickly into solution preso when I got in front of the buying group. 

My belief system was, "If they all see how great our solution is, they'll all agree it's better than what they're doing today to solve the problem". 

Problem is, a "better way" rarely wins when the competitor is "good is good enough". It's why status quo has a better win rate than any seller. 

Buyers would look me in the face, agree we had a better solution, and STILL say,  "but let's revisit this in 6 months". 

Because I was skipping right past the most important job to be done. Getting the group to reach consensus on whether the problem our solution solves was worth solving, and worth solving right now. 

There are 2 major jobs to be done when building buying group consensus:

Job #1 - "WE agree this is a problem worth solving, and worth solving now."
Job #2 - "WE agree you're the right partner and solution to solve it."

If your team's deals are getting stuck here, here's a workshop I ran for 30 Minutes to President's Club: https://lnkd.in/gvHh2RWD

It's the 7 tactical steps I take to reach buying group problem consensus. 

(PS - I also offer this in a workshop format for Sales teams. Sellers bring in stuck accounts and we work through exercises to unstick them.)

Here is my 5-step "Do I Actually Have a Deal?" checklist:

1) Can I quantify the cost of inaction (COI)?

This is not ROI. This is not, "Every day you wait, you're missing out on the opportunity to improve/increase X by 40%". ROI = by doing something, you might see this return. COI = by changing nothing, you ARE seeing this cost/risk/consequence. Every vendor pitches ROI. Few arm their champions to make the case for change with COI. 

2) Do I know what other priorities and categories of spend I'm competing with?

This is not "which of our competitors am I up against?". This is, "What other investments/priorities might take precedence over this one?". Ask buyers this question directly. Make it easy for them to be honest with us. Don't rush to convince them to prioritize ours, before we deeply understand the others.

3) Do I know the 10 other stakeholders involved in deciding whether the problem our solution solves is worth solving, and solving now?

Sometimes it's more. Sometimes it's less. But it's rarely just 1 person. Do we know who they are? More importantly, does our BUYER know who they are? Have this candid convo with our buyers. "In other companies i've worked with, here is how and where CXO tends to get involved, and here are the places where they typically push back and why. How might that look different with your CXO?". Do that for all of the roles that tend to get involved.

4) Does my buyer have the skill and will to be a change agent?

We could have the perfect solution to a large problem. But, our success/failure often lies in the hands of the messenger. Do the heavy lifting to help your buyer craft a change narrative. The key here is effort reduction. Make it easy for them to advocate effectively. Dumping solution collateral on them has the opposite effect.

5) Do I know the steps to signature?

We know we're supposed to do this. But, sometimes we get happy ears and don't. I've made this mistake a million times. If you don't know, don't feel stupid asking. It feels worse to lose a deal we should've won. "I was reflecting on our conversation on Monday and realized I made a rookie mistake. I can't say with confidence that I know the exact steps to get to a signature. Mind if we break that down together?".

A big part of being great at Sales is being willing to put our egos aside.

If we don't know the answers to those 5 Qs, make it a priority to get them.

And, if you're managing sellers, be consistent about asking your reps these 5 questions in pipeline reviews.

If we do it repeatedly, they'll learn to come prepared to deal reviews with the answers. It helps them build habits (not just for quarter-end, but all year-long).

There are only 3 ways to scale Google Ads

Increasing budget is the worst one. 

You find some winning keywords and start cranking spend

But eventually it loses effectiveness because:
→ You hit impression share ceilings
→ Cost per click starts climbing
→ You're paying more for the same searches
→ The algorithm runs out of high-intent queries to show you on

You can combat against this. 

There are 3 ways to scale:

(1) Vertical - increase auctions on what's already working. You can increase budgets (if on Max Conv), and you can also increase target CPA. When costs climb too high, pull target CPA back down to control efficiency. Keep an eye on IS (budget). If it’s a high percentage (0%+) you’ve got more room to scale. But after you’ve maxed out auctions - what’s next?

(2) Horizontal - expand keywords to reach new searches. This happens naturally if you're running broad match or phrase match and vertically scale. But you can also do this deliberately: research new customer pain points, expand your TAM, test different angles. If you're only bidding on "CRM software," you're invisible to someone searching "how to organize customer data." Map out the full buying journey and go after each stage.

(3) Diagonal - launch new campaign types to tap new inventory. Performance Max and Demand Gen unlock YouTube, Display, Discover, Gmail. But be careful - these campaigns love to spend on irrelevant placements. You need heavy negatives and placement exclusions from day one and be optimizing for deeper funnel conversion events. Do not optimize for form fills and data leads. Start at 10% of your Search budget and slowly increase as you validate quality. The traffic looks different, but there is incremental revenue in these campaigns.

Quick scaling checklist:

→ Vertical: Can you increase budget AND control CPA with your target levers?
→ Horizontal: What search terms are your customers using that you're not bidding on?
→ Diagonal: Have you tested PMax or Demand Gen with proper conversions and exclusions in place?

ASC might be killing your growth

Here's what to do:

- Meta keeps pushing you to consolidate everything into one ASC.
- I've seen two ways that breaks an account.

PROBLEMS:

1. ASC latches onto one or two ads and starves new viable creatives before they can scale. These are 'false losers'. Essentially Ads that look bad inside ASC but would win in any other structure.

2, Legacy top performers hog budget. If you drop a validated new ad into the same ASC it'll often get ignored and not get spend

FIXES:

1. Pull out false losers:

- Filter your ASC for ads with under $500 in total spend
- Inside that bucket, find ads that drove a few conversions at or below your target CPA
- Pull 5-6 of those out of ASC and drop them into a manual ABO campaign to force spend
- If they scale in ABO and hit target CPA, you have a structural testing problem in your ASC

2, Use a graduation flow:

- Validate new concepts in ABO, graduate proven winners to ASC
- Graduate winners into ASCs separated by unit economics (ideally gross profits but you can also go for AOV)
- Rule of thumb: if AOV gap is 2x or more, split the ASC

Don't assume Meta knows best.

Sometimes you have to manually pull winning creatives out of a structure that's ignoring them.

How are you structuring your ASCs right now?

Every DTC brand needs a 1st customer P&L:

1. Gross Revenue 

→ First-time orders only
→ This is your raw new customer orders
→ This is before any deductions
→ Compare this to your total revenue, it'll show you what % is not returning.

2. Net Revenue
→ Deduct discounts, returns, and refunds.
→ This normalizes for brands forcing gross revenue by discounting
→ E.g. $400k gross minus 30% off sitewide & 12% refund rate = $232k net

3. Gross Margin
→ Deduct COGS from Net Revenue
→ This tells you if the product itself is profitable before any operating costs
→ If this is thin, no amount of marketing efficiency saves you

4. Contribution Margin
→ Deduct shipping, transaction fees, and fulfillment costs
→ This is your per-order profitability before acquisition costs
→ Reminder, this is without any email, SMS, or retention activities

5. Acquisition Contribution Margin
→ Now deduct your Meta ad spend
→ This is the money you're actually making (or losing) acquiring new customers
→ If you're negative here, you're relying on future purchases to break even
→ Don't confuse this with blended contribution margin, this is new customers only

6. Acquisition MER (aMER)
→ Net Revenue divided by ad spend
→ This is the ratio view of step 5
→ No blended MER which hides returning customer revenue inflating the number

Story time:

- We scaled a brand from mid-eight figures to well into the nine figures. 
- One of the key levers outside of media buying and creative was better understanding their first time profitability. 
- Previously, the marketing spend was generic and broad-targeted. So new customer acquisition was incredibly expensive. 
- Facebook knew it was the easiest to just find returning customers to purchase again, and so they were focused on that. 
- When we forced Meta to prioritize new customers, the cost per acquisition was higher, but the cost per new customer acquisition started to decrease. 
- We got recurring customers instead with email, SMS, and subscriptions (effecient & reliable). 
- 6 months later nCAC was lower than previous CAC since Meta was now dialed in and targeting the right (new) people. 

How can you pull this data?

1. Download customer data by new and returning from Shopify
2. Subtract discounts, returns, and shipping costs. 
3. Subtract your COGS from new customers specifically based on the costs of the products, and the fulfillment, and the transaction fees. 
4. Subtract all of your marketing expenses related to acquisition. 
5. Now you know the profitability of your new customer acquisition and how much retention has to regain to break even. 
6. You know how your profitability would change next month if you did or didn't have your marketing spend turned on. 
7. Now you can calculate your churn and your burn rate and project into the future easily

Do your Google ads leads take months to convert?

Do this to predict performance:

1. Pull 6+ months of lead data.

→ Export every lead with two fields: date generated and date closed
→ If a lead hasn't closed yet, record days since generated
→ Only keep leads with 90+ days of history

1. Calculate days-to-close for every closed lead.

→ Closed date minus generated date
→ Group leads by month cohort (January leads, February leads, etc.)

2. Plot the bake curve for each cohort.

→ X axis: days since lead generated (0, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90)
→ Y axis: cumulative close rate at that day
→ You'll see the curve climb and then flatten (the flat point is full bake time)

3. Average the cohorts into one baseline.

→ Take the last 6 months
→ For each day on the X axis, average the cumulative close rate
→ That gives you your baseline conversion curve

4. Apply the curve to current leads.

→ A 30-day-old lead should be at X% closed based on history
→ If this cohort is tracking below the curve, quality is dropping
→ If above, you're ahead of forecast

How to read the chart:

→ Curve flattens before day 60 = short cycle, safe to judge campaigns fast
→ Curve still climbing at day 90 = long cycle, don't cut campaigns early
→ Gap between cohorts = something changed (creative, targeting, seasonality)

On a recent account, the projected bake % flagged a PMax campaign degrading at day 45. Lead volume still looked identical to the good months. Waiting for CPA to confirm would have cost another 45 days of bad spend.

A few things to keep in mind:

- You need at least 6 months of closed-won data before the curve is usable
- Longer cycles need more cohorts (12+ if median close is 60+ days)
- Always segment by campaign type, Search bakes differently than PMax
- The curve shifts when the sales team changes process, so re-baseline quarterly

The list is the message. I don't know who first said it, but it's one of the truest things in outbound.

When the list is segmented precisely enough, the email almost writes itself. 

When it isn't, you end up writing clever copy to paper over the fact that you don't actually know who you're talking to.

Most platforms only let you segment by what a company is. Industry, size, tech stack. 

Useful, but it rarely changes your message on its own. CEO vs founder doesn't change what you say. Industry often doesn't either.

What changes the message is who they sell to. A company selling into legal teams has a completely different world than one selling to restaurant owners — different buyers, different pain, different proof. That difference is the message.

Prospeo's v2 now lets you filter on exactly that. Who a company sells to, the size of their customers, the department they sell into. That's not a nice-to-have filter. 

That's a segmentation axis that actually splits a list into groups that need different emails.

If a data point would change what you say, it's a reason to split into a separate campaign. 

If it wouldn't, don't split. "Who do they sell to" almost always changes what you say.

Want faster Google Ads PMax results?

How to use audience signals:

1. What they do:

→ Guide Google's ML on who to prioritize early in the learning phase
→ Don't restrict targeting (PMax still expands outside your signals)
→ Shorten time to first conversions
→ Reduce variance in the first 2-3 weeks of a fresh campaign

2. Inputs & exclusions

Inputs:
→ Customer Match built from closed-deal emails (strongest seed)
→ Website visitor list filtered to 90-day converters
→ Top 3-5 search terms from Search as a custom segment
→ One tight in-market segment that matches your buyer

Exclude:
→ Broad affinity segments (too wide, dilutes the signal)
→ All-visitor remarketing lists (trains on tire-kickers)
→ Demographics set too narrow (PMax ignores them, you've wasted the slot)
→ Life events for products where life-stage isn't the trigger

3. Launch order

→ Day 1: Customer Match plus converter list (strongest prior)
→ Day 1: search-term based custom segment (Google's docs explicitly flag this to boost ML)
→ Week 1: add in-market and one affinity, only if pacing is behind
→ Week 2: remove the weakest signal instead of adding more

4. When to use:

→ Fresh launches with no account conversion history
→ Accounts under 30 conversions/mo (algorithm is starved)
→ New products or new geos where past signals don't apply
→ Big budget changes that reset learning (50%+ up or down)

Cheatsheet:

→ Audience signals speed up learning without narrowing reach
→ Use Customer Match plus search-term custom segments
→ List size matters more than list variety (1,000+ minimum)
→ After week 3, let the conversions do the training

What audience setup is everyone running on fresh PMax launches? Curious what's working.

DON’T only track new ads launched

Also measure: 

1. Total spend on last batch of ads
2. Number of ads in that batch
3. Calculate spend per ad launch, month on month

Example scenario: 
- December: $400 per ad launch
- January: $600 per ad launch
- February: $1,200 per ad launch

In this case, spend per ad launch is increasing.

This implies ad quality is increasing. (Woo!)

But if it's falling (and you're turning ads off promptly) - it implies your ads are poor and cannot justify spend.

Benchmarks to aim for:
→ $1k minimum for smaller accounts
→ $5k for accounts spending $500k+/month
→ $3k is a good average

And if you're finding you're below benchmark and have already been testing extensively and can't work out what's going on... you can use the 3x3x3 framework to find untested pockets.

3 Angles:
1. Pain Point (frustration, fear, regret)
2. Desire (aspiration, freedom, status)
3. Social Proof (testimony, authority, relatability)

3 Formats:
1. Static (60-70% of conversions for most brands I manage)
2. Video (first 3 seconds decide everything)
3. Carousel (best for education-heavy products)

3 Funnel Stages:
1. TOF (80% of creative volume lives here)
2. MOF (education, comparisons, "why us")
3. BOF (offers, urgency, risk removal)

3x Angles * 3x Formats * 3x Funnel Stages = 27 combinations

Check which of your ads fit into each combination + create ads that fill in the gaps.

E.g. have you done lots of pain point x static x BOF, but ignored desire x video x MOF?

Bottom line:
- Measure ad spend per launch
- Aim for ~$3k per launch
- If you're under benchmark, use 3x3x3 framework

Hope this helps!

Here's something I do before every Sales call with a prospect:

1. Go to their LinkedIn page. 
2. Scroll down to "Activity". 
3. Click "Show All". 
4. Click the "Comments" button. Scroll through. 
5. Click the "Reactions" button. Scroll through. 

Obviously, it's great if a prospect posts original content. But, many execs don't (wish more did). 

Instead, I'm looking for 2 patterns in their comments and likes. 

What subject matter are they engaging with? 
Who are they learning from? 

Those patterns give me clues to their beliefs and assumptions. Beliefs and assumptions dictate behavior. And, prospect objections are usually rooted in differing beliefs/assumptions (re: the problem, the root cause, the urgency/size of the problem, or the category of solution to solve it).

This prep wasn't always as fruitful as it is right now. 

In periods of uncertainty (like we're in right now, thanks to AI), execs tend to look up, left and right.

I’ve analyzed dozens of ABM programs that run for years and 'produce nothing'

Every time, issues traced back to the same broken principles. Here’s the 10 that matter:

1. ABM is a resource-allocation discipline, not a campaign type

The entire bet is concentrating finite GTM resources on a defined account set. If you aren't deliberately under-serving the rest of the market, you aren't doing ABM. That’s just demand gen with an account list bolted on.

2. The account is the unit (by way of the committee)

B2B is bought by groups of 6-10+. The job in ABM is to orchestrate the buying committee, never a single lead. An account is “covered” when the committee is mapped and multi-threaded.

3. Let signals pick the account and the moment

Intent is a time-bound state. Static lists rot; the modern unit of work is the signal + the account. A signal sitting in a dashboard is a missed opportunity and speed-to-signal is the edge.

4. Fit is a gate; intent and engagement are the timing

Fit tells you who could buy (static). Intent and engagement tell you who's buying now (dynamic). Keep them in separate fields so you always know which lever you're pulling - and so low-fit/high-intent noise never masquerades as opportunity.

5. Match intensity to tier, or forfeit the return

The economics live in the gradient. Tier 1 converts ~6× better than Tier 3. Run the same playbook across every tier (we call this "tier collapse") and you get mediocre middle-tier economics everywhere. Concentration is the point.

6. Alignment is engineered

Shared list, shared definitions, shared signals, shared comp, shared cadence - built into org design and the CRM, not promised in a kickoff. If marketing is paid on MQLs and sales on revenue, no meeting will align them.

7. Build the motion before the machine

Design account selection + alignment + one play, prove it by hand, then automate. Most failed programs buy a platform first. Tools execute the proven strategy.

8. Coverage and clean data are upstream of everything

Identity resolution, lead-to-account matching, committee coverage: get these wrong and every score, campaign, and report downstream is silently wrong. Most "ABM isn't working" is actually a coverage or data problem.

9. Measure the Three Rs, and prove lift

Reputation and relationships move first; revenue lags two quarters. Report all three to survive the lag, and prove impact with treated-vs-control cohorts instead of fighting attribution theology.

10. ABM fails operationally (not creatively)

The wins and losses are in the boring systems layer - coverage, matching, tiering, hygiene, cadence - not in the campaign creative. Elite teams obsess over the plumbing precisely because that's where programs live or die.

Every ABM program I’ve worked on has been fixed using these 10 principles. Notice creative and messaging aren’t on the list?

I've tested 20,000+ ads on Meta.

How to decide how many to produce each month:

1. Budget
- If your ads fatigue fast or you're growing rapidly, push higher.
- My target is one concept per $10k in monthly spend.
- Drop that to $5k if you're under $50k/mo.
- A concept is the core creative idea (not an ad).
- You produce multiple ads off each concept.
- So a brand spending $500k/mo on Meta = 50 concepts.

2. Video / static split
- Set spend goals by format first.
- For ecom, start at 70-80% video.
- Products that need explaining or have an important mechanism: more video
- Products where the look is the key USP: more static
- As a benchmark, at $500k/mo spend: 35 video, 15 static concepts.

3. Ads per concept
- For video, test 2-3 hooks per concept
- Only test one hook if it's unproven and you want to keep test spend low.
- For statics, aim for 5-8 variations per concept.
- Most of your video variation testing should be hooks.
- For our $500k brand: 70 videos and 90 statics to test.

4. New vs iterations
- For established brands, I aim for roughly 50/50.
- The split swings depending on how you define an iteration, so just track performance for both.

5. Now decide styles
- Style decisions come last.
- For new ads: call customers, study competitors, watch organic in your niche, and imitate what's working.
- For iterations: take top performers and find new creators for the same concept, re-edit winners with new hooks/music/captions, and ask the top creators to make their own variations.

A reasonable split for the 35 video concepts:
→ 5 manufacturing or installation
→ 5 founder stories
→ 5 promo concepts for your current sale
→ 2 on-the-street interviews
→ 3 customer interviews
→ 5 UGC concepts
→ Spread the rest across iterations of past winners

I've used this exact approach to take brands from $20m to $85m and $50m to $150m/yr in revenue, with better profit.

If you're stuck on production:
→ Billo for fast, low-cost video to start
→ Simon Robert at Statiq for reliable statics

I've audited 200+ ABM programs

Winning ones use the right incentive plans:

And 99% failure rate when marketing and sales misalign:

↳ Marketing cherry-picks high-volume, low-fit accounts to hit lead targets
↳ SDRs book low-quality meetings to hit meeting count
↳ Reps deprioritize ABM accounts because pipeline attribution goes to marketing
↳ Everyone hits their number and pipeline decay over time

Incentive plans create alignment between marketing, sales, and executives. It's the fastest way to get teams on the same page to promote the right behavior. 

Three comp changes that actually move the needle:

1 // Pod-level shared metrics & comp plan

a. Define the pod: ABM marketer, SDR, AE all assigned to the same tier 1 accounts.
b. Set the pipeline target & run the conversion math from # of accounts + acv to pipeline. Lock it into a CRM object.
c. Accelerator logic:

100% attainment: 1.0x multiplier
100-109%: 1.15x 
110-124%: 1.25x
>125%: 1.50x (AE) / 1.40x (SDR) / 1.35x (Mkt)

d. Run the weekly pipeline council meeting. Agenda:

Pod pipeline vs target
- AE disposition rate - current vs 80% gate
- SDR conversion rate - current vs 25% gate
- Marketer coverage - current vs 70% gate
- Which accounts are stuck and why

If SDR's conversion rate is 18% in week 6, everyone in the pod knows. The AE starts caring about meeting quality. The marketer starts warming accounts better.

2 // Marketing comped on target-account pipeline

a. MQLs naturally optimize for quantity
b. They are not scored as high as in a demand gen system. In ABM the are just: a strong signal.

The switch: measure marketing on pipeline created from accounts on the list.

They only win when the accounts they work become real pipeline. Which means they start caring about fit, coverage, and if the SDR is converting.

3 // SDR comp tied to meeting quality

Meeting count only optimizes for volume

The switch: comp on opp conversion rate - the # of meetings reaching Stage 2 divided by meetings held, rolling 90 days.

A garbage meeting now hurts. It sits in the denominator without contributing to the numerator. Book enough of them and the multiplier drops.

Implementation note::

Create governance structure in your CRM (not the comp plan). This idiot-proofs any ambiguity between revops and sales when deciding 'what is a qualified meeting?' because definitions written in 2 places drift apart.

The Executive ask:

If you're not willing to touch the comp plan, you're managing an ABM slide deck, not an ABM program.

Alignment is a compensation problem.

Fix the operating system and build the UI around it.

I don't write prompts for list qualification anymore. Instead, I use a skill I call it the ICP prompt loop.

I tell Codex (or Claude Code): "This is the input I'll give you. This is the output I want. Write the prompt that makes that happen." 

Then I feed it what we actually mean by giving it human verified data. 

"This is what we count as a B2B SaaS company, this is what we count as manufacturing, this is what financial services means to this client, and so on"

Then it runs on 10 real companies and shows me its work: "This one is B2B SaaS. This one we thought was, but isn't, and here's why. This one is manufacturing and I agree."

I correct it. It revises the prompt.

The rule that makes it work: it does not get to run across the full dataset until it shows me 10 companies with zero edits from me, three times in a row. 

One edit anywhere and the counter resets. It keeps feeding me 10 at a time until we get three clean rounds.

This week we used it on a 6-vertical TAM. Sonnet 4.6 on the batch API did the actual qualification for about $50 because there were too many companies for task sub-agents.

This way, you stop guessing whether your prompt is good and start proving it on the only thing that matters, real rows from your actual list.

Harsh Google Ads truth:

There is no such thing as “bad keywords”:

Just bad bids. 

Example: 
- Your target CPA is $50. Google spends $5 per click and it converts at $80
- You think the keyword just has bad intent, so you pause the keyword 

But what if you dropped your max CPC bid by 30-40% (via smart bidding)? 
- Google is forced to find cheaper auctions (that still convert)
- You spend $3 per click, it converts at same rate, but now at $48 CPA

Yes - you’ll get less volume at this bid…

But you’re within your CPA targets. 

This is because every keyword has a value threshold. A CPC where the math works out. 

You can go through all your old keywords and do this exercise:

1. Pull your "paused for performance" keywords
2. Calculate actual CPA vs target CPA
3. For keywords within 2x your target, test reactivating at 40-50% lower bids
4. Give it 2-3 weeks of data before judging

I've seen "bad" keywords become good performers once the bid matched their true value.

Bottom line:

Before you pause a keyword, ask if you've tested it at multiple bid levels. 

Most advertisers haven't.

We day traded this Meta ads account from $5M to $40M/yr

By making 40-50 changes per day:

- Account scaled from $400k to $3.5M/mo in 18 months
- ROAS is up 2x

BEFORE we came in, I checked their Meta Change Log.
- Open ads manager
- Click the little clock icon
- Export to CSV

I ran some basic analysis.

1. No weekend management

- Every day your account is either improving or decaying.
- Every day is an opportunity to adjust your bids, and buy into or out of inventory
- The same way day traders are buying in and out of stocks / currencies
- If you're spending $200k/mo+ and missing weekends, you'll suffer on weekdays. E.g:
- You spend Monday and Tuesday recovering.
- Maybe by Wednesday you're back to baseline.
- Thursday and Friday you actually build.
- Then it resets again on the weekend

People always say “but it takes time for ads to get into learnings” what im NOT saying is that you should touch EVERY ad every day. What im saying that is that learnings don’t magically stop happening on the weekends. 

2. Big irregular swings

- The Meta algo seems to prefer when you buy and out of inventory with small changes
- E.g. make 5-20% bid and budget changes
- The account previously was making 5-10 budget changes, typically 50%-100% in size
- This tends to throw accounts back into learning

We day trade in a Meta friendly way:

- 40-50 small changes per day
- 5-25% adjustments based on performance
- Morning and evening for large accounts
- Monday through Sunday

The above can add up to 100% extra ROAS.

How to scale Google Ads qualified leads 

There's only two ways:

1. Conversion Signal

Examples
→ All Calls = top of funnel (anyone who picks up the phone)
→ Form starts = top of funnel
→ 3-minute calls = mid funnel
→ Qualified leads / SQLs = bottom of funnel
→ Sales or revenue = deepest signal

Setup
→ Move the signal as deep down the funnel as your conversion volume allows
→ Minimum 30 conversions per month before the signal is trustworthy at scale
→ New conversion actions get treated as top-of-funnel until they stabilize
→ Primary vs Secondary action matters (Secondary doesn't optimize the algo)
→ Use "One" not "Every" for call counting unless you specifically want repeats

2. Match Type

Only 3 match types:
→ Exact = tightest, only the searched term
→ Phrase = tighter, must contain the phrase
→ Broad = loosest, the algo decides relevance

Setup:
→ Tighten when efficiency drops or the signal is noisy
→ Broaden when scaling and the signal is clean and deep
→ Search term report 2 to 3 times a week is non-negotiable above $1M per month
→ Bad terms go straight into negative lists (we run 30,000+ negatives at MCC level on high-spend accounts)
→ Above $2M per month you can't stay narrow forever, but you compensate with conversion-side rigor

3. Use together:

- The further up the funnel your conversion signal sits, the tighter your match types need to be.
- So if your conversion action is All Calls, your match types should be exact and phrase.
- If your conversion action is qualified leads or revenue, you can go to broad match

Hope this helps

I tested Meta's engaged view vs 7dc over 5000+ orders

Here's the correlations I saw:

→ Analyzed for a single brand
→ Laid out post-purchase survey responses on daily, weekly & monthly basis
→ Compared to attribution model which correlated most closely with post-purchase response (Strong indicator of top of funnel impact which I prioritize)

RESULTS:

One scenario (weekly):
→ 7-day click: ~82% correlation with post-purchase response
→1 day engaged view alone: ~26% correlation
→ 7-day click + 1-day view: 86% correlation
→ 7-day click + 1-day engaged view: ~91.5% correlation

I’ve run this analysis for multiple brands now. 

Some land at 7dc being a better indicator
Some land at 7dc1dev being a better indicator

TAKEAWAYS:

If your product is impulsive and short-cycle:
→ Example: apparel, beauty, accessories
→ Adding in engaged view catches people who stop, watch, and then google you later (engaged view)
→ You credit view-through conversions that are actually impactful.

If your product is slow-converting:
→ Example: high ticket, considered, multi-touch
→ You want to be a bit more careful with engaged views as the purchase may be impacted by many things and they may get served a lot of ads. Meta still likes to over credit and so not every engaged view is truly impactful.
→ On the flip side, making the click window too short, e.g. a 1-day click is a mistake here, ensure you are using long click windows.

A client wanted six verticals of US companies, 50–5,000 employees, properly qualified: B2B SaaS, retail/e-comm/CPG, manufacturing/logistics, insurance, healthcare, financial services.

Here's the stack.

We keep every company we've ever gathered for any client in a Supabase of ~15M Clay-enriched companies, wired to a TypeSense search engine (~$200/mo) so we can query it in milliseconds instead of waiting on Supabase. 

We pulled everything matching from there first, free, because we already enriched it.

Whatever we couldn't cover, we uploaded as an exclude list and searched the gaps in Prospeo v2, one custom company search per vertical (their type + business-model filters are genuinely good now). Merge, dedupe.

1. CRM active list filtering: Tier = Tier 1 & Last Activity Date > 30 days

Can your ad scale to $10k/day

Depends on your LPV rate:

Link clicks = clicked your ad
Landing page views = user hit your landing page
LPV rate = landing page views ÷ link clicks.

Our data shows a positive correlation between ad scalability and LPV rate

Which is a proxy for site speed.

Some notes:

1. Mobile vs desktop

→ Mobile LPV runs 5-10 points lower than desktop.
→ Slower connections, plus the Meta in-app browser is janky.
→ If your overall is 90%+, your desktop is probably 95%+ and mobile is sitting at 85-88%.

2. Placement bias

→ Reels and Stories run lower LPV than Feed.
→ People are in fast-scroll mode and bail before the page loads.
→ Reels at 80-85% on a healthy account is normal, not a leak.

3. Site speed

→ Shopify stores with heavy apps, big hero videos, or unoptimized images sit in the 75-85% range.
→ A site that loads in under 2.5 seconds reliably hits 90%+.

I’ve been in B2B marketing for 16+ years

My biggest failures in ABM, demand gen, brand/experiential all boil down to 1 thing

Before I thought that campaigns failed because:
- Copy and creative was poor
- Wasn’t moving accounts through ‘awareness stages’
- Strategy was incorrect & too tactical

Looking back after 16 years: my foundations were broken

The first failure point is ICP. 

Yeah, we know the wrong ICP determines everything downstream. Get it wrong and you're building a house of cards.

Claude can help us get an ICP decision faster, but you have to feed it with proper context about the company.

Here’s the data and prompting I include in ICP analysis: 

1 // Revenue stage mapping

Your ICP can’t focus only on new logo efficiency. You have to look at the whole pipeline - it’s a balancing act of “new revenue now” vs “the best revenue”

Feed Claude that data at each stage:

→ New logo acquisition 
→ Onboarding and time-to-value 
→ Retention (NRR) 
→ Expansion (upsell, cross-sell) 
→ Even advocacy revenue

2 //  Decide how heavily you weight NRR

This is the leadership debate that comes out of #1. 

→ If you weight NRR heavily, you build toward logos that expand
→ If you weight new logo volume, you build toward acquisition efficiency

Neither is wrong. But they produce different results - is your org thinking short term or long term revenue?

Your GTM strategy is the 20% of your accounts that are driving 70% of net revenue retention

3 // Know what your ICP can't tell you

You need to define the motion:

→ Acquisition ICP ≠ Expansion ICP 
→ Enterprise logo ICP ≠ high-NRR ICP 
→ Fast-close ICP ≠ high-LTV ICP

Win rate on ICP-fit opportunities runs 2–3x higher when you avoid 90-110% NRR ranges. 

ICP customers: 110–130% <<< focus here
Off-ICP customers: 70–90% NRR

The second failure point: thinking the ICP is static (it's actually a Product)

I’ve realized that ICP’s change as industries and technology shifts. In the ai era -that means your ICP is shifting weekly. Here’s what to do:

→ Feed Claude sales transcripts and 2nd party data (reviews, forums) weekly. It will tell you how your ICP is changing the way they think. If their thinking changes, your messaging needs to change with it.
→ This means your messaging doc is the living, breathing element that needs to get shared across all revenue stages (see #1).
→ The companies that move quickly WITH their ICP, build trust and authority with them faster. 

My last point: treat your ICP doc like it’s a Product. It needs constant work, attention and testing. That’s why I put product marketers on the Product team (especially in this ai transition period that we’re in).

Leaders: how do you weigh NRR when building your ICP? Do you build toward expansion potential or optimize for acquisition efficiency first?

How to bid on brand keywords

Without overspending:

1. Set brand keywords to broad match

Broad gives Google the full universe of brand queries - e.g. misspellings, brand + product, brand + location. These convert at 5-6x non-brand rates. Restricting to exact or phrase match cuts them off.

2. Set bid strategy to target ROAS

I typically start brand at 500%. This is the guardrail. If a non-brand query sneaks in through broad match, Google will only bid on it if it can hit 5.0x ROAS. Brand queries hit that easily and will dominate the spend. The algorithm filters out non-brand terms on its own.

3. Monitor "Search lost IS (budget)" daily

If it's above 0%, your target ROAS might be too low (you're overbidding). Raise target ROAS until lost-to-budget hits zero. That means your CPCs are efficient enough that your budget lasts the full day. Or increase your budget to capture search demand.

4. Check the search term report weekly

Broad match + target ROAS should keep search terms clean. If non-brand terms are still showing up at 5.0x ROAS, they might be worth keeping. If not, add them as negatives.

Two levers:
→ Match type controls reach
→ Bid strategy controls efficiency 

Go wide on match type. Go tight on bid strategy.

We launched a fully AI managed campaign for a customer using "Autoresearch" as the foundation and it doubled their positive lead rate. Here's what we did. 

 If you haven't seen me talk about this before, "autoresearch" is a GitHub repo that Andre Kapathi put out that basically helps people run local machine learning easily on their computers. 

I had the idea that instead of running a loop every 5 minutes to try to improve an outcome, we can run it every week on the data from cold email campaigns in order to increase positive response rates.

The first thing we needed to do was get the context together for all of the different messaging and audience targets that it could use and lock in a CTA for the campaigns that we wanted to optimize for. I didn't want it to just invent that. 

It could give away this software for free and then call that experiment a win. We needed the CTA to be locked in.

After we gathered all the context from the sales team and their calls and the audience targets that we wanted to go after, we made the underlying dataset using Clay Prospeo and stored it all in Supabase. 

The main learning that we got here was that you never want to have what I call a "game-time decision." For it to say, "Hey I want to run an experiment with this data point," you need to give it all the data points it might use so that it's not inventing ways to pull that data that you don't approve. 

We fed it the campaigns that we are already running and just let it rip, trying to optimize for more replies.

We're running over 150 campaigns in their Smartlead account right now and had two weeks in a row where we've increased the reply rate and the positive response rate. 

Keep in mind the CTA is locked in so it's always going towards what we want, which is a product sign up.

→ Are you cutting losers before they burn cash?
→ Are your top 10% of ads generating 50%+ of revenue?

Chart 2: Creative Churn
→ Tracks how fast your creative inventory turns over relative to performance.
→ Each color = a different month's creative cohort.
→ High churn without performance gains = production issue.
→ Low churn with declining performance = you're riding old winners too long.

Chart 3: Production & Slugging Rate
→ How many ads you're launching vs your targets.
→ More importantly: What % are "hits" (spending $5k+)?
→ If only 3/100 ads spend meaningfully, you have a creative quality problem

Chart 4: Performance Trends Basic CPA vs spend over time.
→ Can you scale spend while holding or improving CPA?
→ If your line trends up and right (more spend, worse CPA), you need better creative or better structure.

Chart 5: Creative Allocation
→ Are you spending the most on your lowest CPA ads?
→ Your top 1% of ads should drive ~50% of total spend.
→ If your budget is scattered across mediocre performers, your account structure is broken.

Chart 6: Gender/Demo Analysis
→ Shows who's actually buying vs who you think is buying.
→ Most brands guess at their audience.
→ This chart tells you where to focus production.

Chart 7: Churn/Retesting Control
→ Darker colors = more new creative testing.
→ Are you dependent on old ads or consistently launching fresh creative.
→ If you see long stretches of light green, you're not testing enough.
→ If it's all dark with declining performance, you're churning too fast without learning.

Chart 8: Creative Utilization
→ Y-axis: How many placements/audiences per ad
→ X-axis: Total spend per ad
→ Are you taking your winners and testing them across different audiences, placements & campaign structures
→ Your best ads should have 5+ variations running.

Chart 9: Spend by Format
→ Are you producing video/static/UGC in proportion to what actually performs?
→ If 70% of your spend goes to video but you're producing 80% static, you have a production allocation problem.
→ This chart shows the gap between what you make and what works.

The goal is to find data that shows you WHICH problem you actually have:

Is it creative production?
→ Low hit rate
→ Poor creative allocation
→ Format mismatch

Or is it media buying?
→ Bad account control
→ Poor utilization of winners
→ Scaling issues

Creative and media buying both drive CPA/ROAS.

Even if they are managed by the same person (they should be) that doesn't give an excuse to blend the metrics.

Google ad account scaled 4.6x from $70k to 325k:

CPA held under target. Here’s how: 

Context:
→ Was at $70k/mo in spend.
→ Customer volume tripled.
→ CPA held under $10k (the client's KPI).

1. Down-funnel conversion actions

→ Google optimizes for whatever conversion event you ask, which means if you try to optimize for form fills, you'll get form fills (but unlikely to get down funnel conversions).
→ The deeper the event you optimize for, the better the lead quality Google goes after.
→ Integrated Google Ads with Salesforce so we could track deeper funnel admission events and optimize toward them directly.

2. Three qualified conversion types

→ We had leads coming from Phone Calls, Form Submits, and Live Chat.
→ Different customers engage through different channels, so capturing all three stops us from losing intent based on preference.
→ All three feed the same qualification layer so the algorithm compares intent across channels on equal footing.

3. Qualified Call actions

→ Created a 'qualified call' event to send back to Google from call tracking platform.
→ This only fired on what sales reps were happy with.
→ Think of this as another down funnel conversion action.

4. A well-structured account

3 separate targetings:
→ High intent keywords (more budget, higher Target CPA) 
→ Low intent keywords (lower budget, lower Target CPA)
→ Competitors 

5. Dynamic headline insertions on the landing pages

Raised conversion rates by 7%.
→ Dynamic headlines personalize the landing page to match the incoming search.
→ Message match lowers bounce and raises relevance across ad, click, and page.
→ Higher relevance also improves Quality Score, which compounds into lower CPCs.

Summary:

→ Push conversion tracking as deep as your CRM allows
→ Only qualified contacts should count as conversions
→ Segment campaigns by intent to better control budget and bids
→ Dynamic headline insertion lifts CVR and Quality Score
