Is your Healthcare Google Ads under-optimized?

This 37 point checklist will tell you: 

1. Check device CPA separately. Go to Campaigns > Segment > Device. I've seen Desktop CPA at $1,375 and Mobile at $7,355. Same exact leads. Adjust bid modifiers accordingly.

2. Verify conversion actions are set to Secondary, not Primary. When you reactivate old conversions, they default to Primary. Google will optimize toward them immediately. Set all but one to Secondary.

3. Click every site link and make sure it loads. I often see site links accidently pointing to dead pages. Even big accounts ($500k+ /mo spend sometimes make this mistake) 

4. Search your negative keyword list for "free," "trial," "demo." Broad match negatives can block high-intent queries like "free trial." 

5. Confirm conversion count is set to "One" not "Every." If a lead gets uploaded twice, Google counts two conversions. The algorithm thinks performance is 2x better than reality.

6. Segment Search Partners separately. Go to Campaigns > Segment > Network. Search Partners are usually 2x worse than Google Search. If CPA is bad, turn them off.

7. Verify your negative keyword list is still applied. Shared lists can disappear during account transitions. Check it's attached to all campaigns.

8. Switch from Max Conversions to Target CPA if efficiency is bad. Max Conversions spends your entire budget no matter what. Set Target CPA 30-40% below current to stabilize.

9. Check when negative keywords were last added. Go to Change History > last 90 days. If none added in 60+ days - you're likely burning budget. 

10. Check if RSA headlines are over-pinned. If every headline is pinned, Google can't test combinations. Only pin Headline 1 if you need brand name first.

11. Make sure RSAs have all 15 headlines and 4 descriptions filled. Fewer headlines = fewer combinations = less chance of finding winners.

12. Add dynamic keyword insertion to headlines. Use {KeyWord:Fallback Text} to match the search query. 

13. Check match type distribution. If Broad match is 80% of spend and CPA is bad, move keywords to Phrase or Exact. 

14. Set audiences to Observation, not Targeting. Targeting limits reach. Observation lets you get data. Adjust bids on winners later.

How to max out your AOV:

It all starts with the initial price of your product.

Example: $5 Toothpaste

1. Premium pricing

→ In a commodity category you can charge a premium
→ The realistic ceiling is about 4-5x the category average
→ So your $5 toothpaste becomes a $20 product.

2. The multi-pack limit

→ You can sell more than one unit
→ In practice that's 3 to 5 units per order
→ 5 units x $20 = $100. Push past that and conversion rate will likely drop off

3. The upsell

→ Bolt on one complementary product or a discounted gift
→ Expect roughly half your buyers to take it, for another $10-30
→ Call it +$20 blended across the whole order

So for a $5 product, your max AOV is likely:
→ ($20 x 5 units) + $20 upsell = $120

Once you're near that number, squeezing AOV harder is wasted effort.

The better lever is retention.

Cheatsheet:
→ Note your category's average price
→ Calculate / find your category's premium price
→ Determine your total multi-pack limit
→ Add an upsell amount
→ Calculate your max AOV
→ Get as close as possible
→ Then move all of your focus to keeping the customer

Just gave a talk about how to turn Codex/OpenClaw/Hermes (whatever you'd like) into a real employee for your business in 3 steps. Here it is for those that couldn't be at the event. 

I fully believe that these models are incredibly intelligent now and their tool calling has gotten so good. If you aren't using AI as an employee in your business, you just haven't put the energy in to get it done. 

Everyone can get started in 3 steps. The first 2 you should drop what you're doing this Friday afternoon and get them done right away. The last step takes more time. 

The agents need context, connections, and practice creating in order to be useful. 

1. Tips to gather context

For most of us, our world is recorded digitally and written down in Slack and CRM systems. 

Give these tools access to whatever you're comfortable with and have it start building a company brain for yourself from the transcripts of your calls, the conversations in your Slack, and your email. 

Whatever you can give it go for it. 

Someone asked me yesterday how I keep the context organized. The truth is beyond just asking Claude to organize itself I don't think about this at all. 

With a million-token context window, that's as much text as the Bible. My business for sure isn't that complicated. 

Have it create a local brain in markdown files. Use Obsidian (which is free) if you want to get fancy.

2. Give the agents connection to tools

This is going to sound like the dumbest suggestion but it was really a blocker for my team to get the API keys that were necessary in order to make the most use of these agents. 

It felt like "we have too many tools, I wish I just had a list of everythign so I could get it done in 10 minutes."

Your search history on your browser has everything.

Grab the last 30 days of the sites you visit and dedupe them in a google sheet. 

Pick out the ones you want to give access to your agents and you're done. 

3. Build a loop so it can actually work for you. 

After we built this, it feels so obvious but I think this is the number one tip to get people to start using AI. 

Tell your agent to run a scheduled task any time new work is created 

A client call
An internal call
check slack every 30 minutes

Wherever a record of work is created. 

 Use the schedule task for it to read the task. Based on the context that you gave it in your company brain and what it has done for you in the past, try to suggest the plan for how the agent would execute this for you. 

Edit and accept as necessary so the agent can start doing real work. 

 This proactive loop, where a suggestion for work that the agent can take on so that you can get a message every day in Slack after a meeting or something, is the thing that really increased the rate of learning for our agent. 

Instead of us coming up with ideas of how the agent could help us, the agent was doing the work for us. It has been absolutely pivotal in making this work.

Brand ads can be your best performers

If you follow this ad storyboard:

→ Make sure it's a video
→ Use compelling + high quality imagery (story quality > production quality)
→ Make it scream quality (Product quality, not production quality… notice the theme)

1. Hook
→ Call out the exact buyer and the problem they're trying to solve.
→ You start with the customer, never the product.
→ On screen: open on the buyer or their problem, and get the product in frame inside the first 3 seconds.

2. Brand bridge
→ Introduce the one feature that makes you different.
→ This is the one thing you want your brand to be known for in this ad.
→ Example: "This is why we source our chia seed chili sauce locally..."
→ On screen: Show the unique feature, e.g., the location you source from, hand crafting, the ingredient going into the product. Anything to give proof to the brand bridge

3. Tieback
→ Tie that feature straight back to the benefit
→ "...and here's how that specific magnesium helps you fall asleep faster."
→ Bonus points if the unique brand feature solves the problem in a unique / better way.
→ On screen: show the payoff. Someone actually using it, the result, the calm version of the problem you opened on.

4. Action
→ End on a soft, confident CTA.
→ Don't push any offers on this ad.
→ On screen: keep it clean. Product in frame, one clear next step.

Then judge it like any other ad.
→ 35%+ hook rate, CTR in range, CPA where it needs to be.
→ If CPA is too high, drop it
→ It must perform well

These are ads your competitors can't copy:
→ Anyone can clone your offer
→ But they can't clone your brand story and videographic proof of it

I've built over a dozen 1:1 ABM programs

Here's how I structure teams to maximize win rates:

The atomic ABM unit is a self-contained pod. Each one owns a named territory and has every function represented inside it.

The pod model:

ABM Practitioner → owns account research, signal activation, content and campaign orchestration for the territory.

SDR → converts warm signals and creates relationships with buyer committee. Turns them into qualified meetings through 1:1 and in-person experiences.

AE → provides deal context, runs discovery, and owns the close.

Hired Guns:
↳ RevOps owns the system, data, and scoring
↳ GTM Engineer builds the pipelines and automations
↳ SE handles technical evaluation when deals require it

Customer Success → gets pulled into pods when there's an expansion or renewal opp, or when the account is a known logo you're trying to deepen.

Territory assignment:

If your AE team is geo-based, they're likely high ACV and need to be in-market. If reps don't need physical presence, assign by vertical.

The economics:

Run the conversion math backwards from your revenue target. At $100K ACV with a 25% win rate, you need 4 qualified opps per closed deal. If the pod costs $400K/year fully loaded, you need 4 closed deals to break even. That's 16 qualified meetings per year minimum. A high performing pod will 3x that number.

The goal:

The pod is responsible for one thing: setting qualified meetings. The AE/CSM are there to gain context and ensure a clean handoff.

Accountability & reporting structure:

The ABM pod reports qualified booked meetings. 
The AE reports win rates. 

The connective tissue: the marketing leader and sales leader report on the same revenue number but own different parts of it.

↳ Marketing owns the front: qualified meetings booked and ROI of the pod
↳ Sales owns the back: pipeline progression and close rates

Shared revenue number with divided accountability.

This is the structure that keeps marketing and sales aligned without stepping on each other.

How to fix Meta when your CAC spikes 

Without panicking:

Don't touch anything...yet. 
- I've spent over $150M on Meta
- Single-day CAC swings can feel really painful
- Run this diagnostic before you click a button:

1. Start with blended revenue

Zoom out to the P&L. Are new customers actually down for the business today, or is it attribution lag that catches up tomorrow? If blended new customer revenue is flat, you don't have a problem (yet)

2. Isolate the channels

If blended revenue really is down, find out where. Half the time Meta didn't fail at all. You skipped a scheduled SMS or email, organic lift dropped, and the shortfall traces back to that.

3. Check your site CVR

Before you blame the ads, check the site. It's the cheapest thing to fix and the easiest to miss. Example: is it a checkout that broke overnight, or a page that crept over 3 seconds to load, or a discount code that expired?

4. Check both attribution models

If Meta is genuinely the culprit, look at where the spend moved. An ad can look terrible on last-click and still be your best buyer-driver in the post-purchase survey.

5. Diagnose at the ad level

Now read three numbers together instead of one:
→ CPM up, CTR and CVR normal = more competition in the auction 
→ CPM normal, CTR down = creative fatigue (the most common cause)
→ CPM normal, CTR up, CVR down = landing page problem
→ Frequency climbing while performance drops = you've saturated the audience

6. Rule out the season

Compare year over year. Q4 CPMs run 30-50% higher than Q3, so month-over-month comparisons overstate the problem. Is there any seasonality at play that you have forgotten to account for? 

7. Change appropriately 

When you do make a change, make it small but more often. Example: Cut budget changes in half, 10-15% max. I took an account from 2.3x to 2.84x ROAS in 30 days by only tweaking bids and budgets with zero new creative.

How to run multi-geography Meta ads

Advanced Meta ads feature:

→ You consolidate a geo campaign
→ Running CA/US/UK all at the same time
→ But see CA/UK is not getting spend BUT good ROAS (Maybe its not directly tracked or maybe Meta is being dumb, either way).
→ So you want to give it budget
→ Typical advice = split off into own campaign

But this fragments data

So instead:

1. Open up the ad set
2. Click through to Meta's locational level bid modifiers (value rules)
3. Apply a positive modifier on the underspent geo (start at +20%, push to +50% if needed)
4. Track CA/UK CPA and spend share via breakdown view
5. Once spend share lifts and ROAS holds, walk the modifier back down in 10% increments
6. If after 14 days at +50% nothing changes, this tactic won't work. Instead, break it out into a new ad set / campaign

This is what's happening:
→ Meta concentrates spend where bids are cheapest, even when your ROAS is higher elsewhere, the algorithm isn’t perfect at splitting spend. 
→ A bid modifier overrides that bias and tells the algorithm you'll pay more for conversions in CA/UK
→ Spend share inside the geo usually lifts within 3-5 days

How I max out Google Search campaigns

I've spent $400M on adsSplit your ad structure out:
→ Brand: under 20% of spend
→ Competitor: ~10%
→ Non-Brand: ~70%

2. Layer match types in order
→ Exact first for each theme
→ Phrase once Exact hits 15+ conversions/month
→ Broad only with Smart Bidding and a strong negative list

3. Max out your RSAs
→ 2-3 RSAs per ad group
→ 15 headlines (6 keyword-focused, 7 features/benefits, 2 CTAs)
→ 4 descriptions

4. Train the algorithm with downfunnel signals
→ Upload offline conversions via GCLID(MQL, SQL, Closed Deal)
→ Retract bad leads so the algorithm stops finding lookalikes of junk
→ Move your primary conversion as far downfunnel as you can hold 30-50 conversions/month

5. Review & scale weekly
→ Conduct search term reports 2-3x per week / use an AI workflow (we do and flag keywords automatically)
→ Promote high-scoring terms with volume to their own ad groups.
→ Minimize Search Lost IS (Budget) as long as it's profitable / incremental.
→ Then expand into new themes and service lines.

6. Know your max efficient ceiling
→ Search Volume = Impressions ÷ Search Impression Share
→ Max Revenue = Search Volume × CTR × CVR × Revenue per Conversion
→ Max Efficient Spend = Max Revenue ÷ Target ROAS
→ Example: 100k monthly searches × 3% CTR × 10% CVR × $12k per conversion = $3.6M potential revenue. At 4x target ROAS, your ceiling is $900k/month. Once you're around 80% of that number, the next dollar is better spent in PMax / Demand Gen.

Cheatsheet:
→ Split brand / competitor / non-brand first
→ Exact → Phrase → Broad in order
→ Max out RSAs
→ Feed downfunnel signals
→ Minimize Lost IS (Budget) before expanding
→ Know your ceiling before you scale past it

How to audit it:

Note - did this for an 8-figure brand recently. 

Found 65% of spend going to the wrong audience. 

1. Age and gender

Breakdown > By Delivery > Age, then Gender.
→ Running a demographic-specific angle? The delivery split should roughly match the product.

2. Country and region

Breakdown > By Delivery > Country, then Region.
→ Selling US-only? Confirm spend isn't leaking to cheap international impressions.

3. Placement

Breakdown > By Delivery > Placement.
→ This is where Audience Network and Right Column eat 20-30% of spend with junk engagement and crash CVR rate.
→ Reels, Feed and Stories all convert differently. Watch for CPA by placement and consider breaking out. 

4. Platform and device

Breakdown > By Delivery > Platform & Device.
→ Facebook vs Instagram. iOS vs Android. Mobile vs desktop.
→ I've seen accounts where Android looked 4x cheaper to acquire but the LTV was a third of iOS. 

5. Time of day

Breakdown > By Time > Time of Day (Viewer's).
→ Useful for higher-AOV or considered purchases. If conversions cluster at 7-10pm, dayparting cuts the wasted morning spend.

Cheatsheet: 
→ Trust the algorithm to optimize. Don't trust it to follow your intent.
→ Every setting you choose, pull the matching breakdown and confirm it.
→ Run it monthly. This kind of leak only shows up when you open the breakdown

Clever hack to increase contribution margin.

You need a weighing scale:

1. Histogram your AOVs and plot them against your shipping provider's weight cutoffs.

2. Find where the cost spikes (e.g. shipping jumps from $3 to $5.50 once you cross 0.99 lbs).

3. Engineer the lower-tier bundle to land just under that limit. 

4. For the tier above, skip the weight that sits just over the line and design the bundle heavy enough that the added revenue absorbs the higher shipping cost, dropping shipping as a percentage of total revenue.

5. Set your free shipping threshold just above your average AOV, so it naturally pulls people into the optimized bundle.

Shipping is one of the few lines in a DTC P&L you can engineer down without touching CAC or COGS. Customers get no extra value from a 1.02 lb order vs a .99 order in most cases but it costs drastically more. 

Takeaway is to engineer bundles around offer psychology AND weight tiers.

How to think about conversion lag reporting:

Example:
→ This account spends ~$100k/week and looked like it was bleeding money at day 7
→ Day 7 CAC: ~$1,300
→ Day 21 CAC: ~$900
→ Day 40-45 (full maturity): ~$715

Here's how to run conversion lag reporting so you don't kill a winner by accident:

1. Set up measurement first
→ Open Goals → Measurement → Attribution in the account
→ Measure from first interaction
→ Set the conversion window to cover full maturity (45 days here)
→ Pick the conversion action that maps to revenue

2. Map your conversion delay
→ Pull the share of conversions that land each day after the click
→ If half land day 1 and the rest trail for weeks, you have lag to model
→ Take your early CPA and double it to estimate where it settles
→ Or optimize toward an upper-funnel action like leads (90% fire day 1, so the signal comes in clean)

3. Forecast from your CRM
→ Pull your historical lead→customer rate (this account runs 6%, currently dipped to 3%)
→ Multiply current leads by that rate to project customers and true CAC
→ Run a lookback every month comparing your forecast to actuals
→ Tighten the rate each month as the real conversions mature

Summary
→ A short measurement window makes a healthy account look broken
→ 51% of conversions land day 1, the rest take up to 45 days
→ Double early CPA or move to a leads action to read the real number sooner
→ Forecast off your historical lead→customer rate, then tune monthly

Can broad match beat exact match?

Yes. If you do it right:

When narrow wins vs broad
- Exact match usually wins on lowest cost per conversion
- It only bids on the obvious, highest-intent terms
- That's where "broad burns budget" comes from

BUT - narrow caps out fast
- Broad adds conversion volume while holding close to efficiency
- The game is how much more volume you can get at close to the same CPA

This is an example account:
→ Exact: ~$3.3K spend, 194 conversions, $16.93 cost/conv
→ Broad: ~$104K spend, 6,100 conversions, $17.10 cost/conv

About 31x the conversions, within ~1% of exact's cost per conversion.

How to run broad properly:

1. When to run broad
Don't open with broad. Layer exact first on each theme. Move to phrase once it clears 15+ conversions a month. Add broad only after Smart Bidding is mature and tracking is clean. Broad learns from conversion history, so turn it on before you have that and you pay for the algorithm to learn.

2. Negatives
Negatives are the fastest CPA win in any account, and broad depends on them. Run an aggressive list from day one. Pull the search term report weekly. Keep the terms hitting your target, negative the rest. One tell: regular Impression Share at 40% but Exact Match IS at 90% means the gap is broad-match junk. Cut it.

3. Bid guardrail
Go wide on match type, tight on bid strategy. Put broad under tROAS or tCPA so a loose query gets a bid only when it clears the target. Set the target at or above your trailing CPA. Set it below at the start and you can lose 40% of traffic overnight. Watch Search Lost IS (Budget): above 0% means the target is too tight. Move it 5-10% at a time and wait a conversion cycle or two.

4. Feed clean signals
Broad hands term selection to Google, so your conversion data steers it. Fire conversion actions at every stage and weight the down-funnel ones heavier. Retract bad leads within 24 hours so Google stops building lookalikes of your junk (this matters more on broad than anywhere else). 

Hope this helps

TAM mapping is GTM intel every B2B SaaS needs

How to set it up:

1 // ICP modeling

I'm looking firmographics and technographics that change on 12+ month cadences. Anything under a year is a buying trigger or signal.
- Industry & subindustry
- Geo's
- Headcount bands (100-999, 1000-4999, 5000-9999, 10k+)
- Revenue bands (VSMB, SMB, Mid Market, Enterprise)

For TAM mapping to be cost effective - stay under 10,000 accounts.

2// Account map the universe

We aim for 90%+ accounts mapped in the ICP. Regardless of what software everyone thinks is the best - they're all relatively the same. 

That's why you triangulate 3+ different softwares and dedupe them. I use:
- AI Ark
- DiscoLike
- 1 Industry specific database

No one database will achieve 90% mapping. 

Two tips before enrichment
1. backtest the entire account list against your ICP definitions. Quick Claude prompt can tell you % accuracy.
2. The remaining 10% is your alpha - create a Clay workbook that signal sweeps for any missing accounts. These will accumulate over time - and be the accounts that give you an advantage over anyone doing standard waterfall account mapping.

3 // Account-level enrichment

One time enrichment fields:
- Account name
- Industry & Subindustry
- Domain
- Parent/Subsidiary relationship
- HQ address

**the field almost no one tracks: Account Awareness Stages (read the last section)

Dynamic enrichment:
- Employee headcount (quarterly)
- Headcount growth (quarterly)
- Revenue band (annually)
- Funding stage/announcement
- Tech stack (multi-field, biannually)

Dynamic stakeholder enrichment (Quarterly refresh)
- First/last name
- Title 
- Months in current role
- Buyer committee tag: Champion, Decision Maker, Blocker, Influencer, End User

4 // Stakeholder-level enrichment

Stakeholder enrichment above, plus:
- Work email (verified)
- LinkedIn URL
- Mobile / direct dial
- Department
- Seniority level (IC, Manager, Director, VP, C-Suite)
- Reports-to name/title (helps you map the org chart)
- Last contacted date
- Last engagement date
- Last replied date
- Custom person-level signal fields - these signal fields are mapped up to the account for unified scoring.

This ad funnel books 8,900 qualified calls/month

Full explainer

1. Google Ads
→ Start with Search on high-intent commercial keywords ("near me," "best," "top," "service + city"). Informational queries can wait.
→ Layer PMax only after Search is profitable. Feed it your closed-won customer list as audience signals, never run it cold at the beginning.
→ Build aggressive negative lists day one. Free, jobs, salary, DIY, reviews, "how to." Audit search terms weekly.
→ Tight geo targeting. Radius around service area or licensure footprint. Set location to "Presence" only.
→ Run competitor brand both ways. Bid on top 3-5 competitors' brand terms, defend your own with branded Search.

2. Qualifying questionnaire
→ 5-7 questions minimum. Mirror what the call center actually asks on the first call. E.g., Budget, authority, need, timeline.
→ Make questions progressive. Easy first (name, zip), then harder (budget, timeline).
→ If they don't qualify, kick them out the quiz and don't let them progress further.

3. Track past the lead
→ Form submits don't always correlate with end outcomes.
→ Track if the lead: picked, call length, call quality, call conversion
→ Feed that back to Google via GCLID. Move your primary conversion action as far downfunnel as possible while keeping 30-50 conversions per month.
→ Get Google to optimize for "qualified call" instead of "form submit."

4. Match page friction to the sales cycle
→ Your landing page should handle about 30% of the work your reps do on the first call.
→ Low-friction pages = high-volume, low-intent calls, agents burning out
→ High-friction pages = lower volume, pre-qualified calls, higher close rates

5. Align media and call center on one scorecard
→ Make sure media + call center are optimizing for same metrics.
→ Put all data on one shared dashboard. CPL, contact rate, qualification rate, cost per qualified lead.
→ This will help one send LESS leads that convert higher. Example:
→ 100 leads at $20, 2% close = 2 customers for $2,000
→ 40 leads at $50, 12% close = ~5 customers for $2,000

Note, healthcare is where I run the heaviest qualified call volume.

So all the above is adapted to ask for:
→ Insurance verification upfront (commercial vs Medicare vs Medicaid)
→ Geographic qualification (in-network, licensure)
→ Level of care screening (outpatient vs inpatient vs residential)
→ Timeline (seeking treatment now vs researching for someone else)

These alone cut unqualified call volume by 30-40%.
→ More friction upfront
→ Track conversions past the lead
→ Media and call center need one scorecard

What's the best Meta bidding strategy:

Cost cap or highest volume?

I use them both:

1. Testing
→ New ads need room to find their audience (especially highly novel ones)
→ Cost cap here typically kills good ads too early
→ Best play here is normally to use highest volume

2. Scaling
→ If I see a proven winner, I want to push it hard
→ Only 1% of ads will drive 50% of ad spend
→ Let Meta find every possible conversion
→ We sometimes run the same winner in both highest volume and cost cap campaigns to see which delivers better at scale

3. Stragglers
→ I see an ad starting to underperform
→ It's starting to come outside of target CPA
→ There's still a bid/budget range where it's profitable
→ Use cost cap (set target cost per result or bid) to keep the ad efficient and still drive profit
→ Got to be careful with cost cap. Sometimes it underspends even though performing well. Sometimes it overspends without hitting target.

Be careful about using Meta ads manager to make these decisions...
→ Fine for relative comparisons between ads
→ In-platform (ads manager) typically over inflates BOFU
→ Likely your real CPA > in-platform CPA
→ Easy to set the cost cap too high, only to realize multi attribution shows the CPA is higher and you've overbid.
→ Use MTA (Triple Whale, Northbeam, etc.), post purchase surveys and MMM (marketing mix modeling) to make better decisions.

My big takeaway:

Don't only use one bidding strategy.

Every company and product is different, your account structure should reflect that.

If I were starting ABM from zero today, I’d run all of it from Claude Code: TAM mapping, signal capture, awareness scoring, routing

Here’s the system architecture I’d use:

1 // TAM Mapping

Hookup Claude Code and Deepline with DiscoLike, Ocean.io, PandaMatch 🐼 + 1 other industry database. Each sees a different slice of the market, making coverage a competitive advantage

The workflow is fan-out → union → dedup → validate. Call every source in parallel, pool it all, resolve to one clean master

The pipeline I'd run:

1. Define a testable ICP using geo, headcount, revenue, tech stack, funding stage
2. Seed from closed-won only. Cluster wins into segments, run lookalikes per cluster
3. Call all lookalike sources at once and collect everything they return. When the data comes back, save it in a holding area exactly as each source sent it
4. Normalize identifiers. Domain is your join key. Map to one industry taxonomy and strip legal suffixes
5. Deterministic dedup first, fuzzy for edge cases
6. Enrich after dedup so you don’t pay for duplicates
7. Claude scores ICP fit + tiers*
8. Refresh quarterly

*Lookalike similarity is not ICP fit. A company can look statistically identical to your customers and have zero budget, wrong buying motion, or a competitor. Claude Code is the validation layer for lookalike databases

2 // Signal Capture

Every signal about a target account webhooks directly into Supabase. Every tool you bolt between the source and your database is a place signals die silently

6 categories of signal, each seeing a different kind of intent:
1. Ad engagement: account-level interaction with paid campaigns
2. Job changes: champion joints new target accounts
3. 3rd party intent: accounts researching your category
4. Web de-anon: matching accounts to anonymous site traffic
5. 1st party engagement: email opens, page visits, form fills on owned channels
6. Product signals: sign-ups, usage, activation

The pipeline:

1. Source fires a webhook at a Supabase endpoint
2. Every source sends a different payload shape. Normalize into one signals schema on arrival - type, account, timestamp, raw payload
3. Write the normalized signal to Snowflake as the permanent record. Supabase isn't storage - it's the real-time event bus

Keep this layer dumb. Only job is receive → normalize → store. The moment you put intelligence in your capture layer, every tweak to your scoring model means touching ingestion code

3 // Awareness Scoring
Your CRM moves accounts up levels in real time on point thresholds. Claude runs nightly: reasoning → confidence → next action. 

4 // Routing

3 inputs decide each account's fate: ICP fit, awareness level, and signal recency. 

Fit + engagement + fresh signal → work it now. Right company, too quiet → monitor. 

Wrong fit, or already a customer → suppress. 

Reps work accounts where fit and intent converge - not whatever got loaded into the CRM.

Every signal webhooks directly into your database. 6 categories:
- Ad engagement
- Job changes
- 3rd party intent
- Web de-anon
- 1st party engagement
- Product signals

Keep this layer dumb. Only job: receive → normalize → store. The moment you put intelligence in capture, every scoring tweak means touching ingestion code.

3 // Awareness Scoring

Set custom gates for each stage (Identified → Aware → Interested → Considering → Decision).

Examples:
- Identified > Aware: 3+ stakeholders engaged in ads
- Aware > Interested: decision maker downloaded lead magnet
- Interested > Considering: multiple pricing page visits within 7 days

Your CRM moves accounts up in real time on point thresholds.

4 // Routing

3 inputs decide each account's fate: ICP fit, awareness level, signal recency.

Fit + engagement + fresh signal → work it now
Right company, too quiet → monitor
Wrong fit → suppress

Reps work accounts where fit and intent converge. Not whatever got loaded into the CRM.

That's ABM strategy. Everything else is just lead gen with better targeting.

→ Sold it in a 9-figure acquisition
→ Took it through a 10-figure IPO

Big takeaways:

1. The 95/5 rule
Only 5% of your market is shopping right now. Performance ads make you fight every competitor for that 5%, at 3x the cost of an organic buyer. Brand wins the other 95% before they start shopping.

2. The 60/40 split
Preston says fastest-growing brands spend 60% on brand, 40% on conversion. Binet and Field show the data across 500+ brands over 50 years.

3. Two things predict growth
Byron Sharp boiled it down to: a) Be remembered when someone's ready to buy and b) Be easy to buy when they are. Everything brand does serves one of those.

4. The commodity test
The second a customer asks "this cup or that cup," you've lost. You want "is it a YETI or isn't it." If a cheaper lookalike beats you on a spec sheet, you don't have a brand yet.

5. Lasers and chandeliers
Chesky's line on Airbnb: performance is a laser, it lights one corner. Brand is the chandelier that lights the whole room. You can't light a room with a hundred lasers. 

6. Brand is a relationship
You can't sprint it. A brand is trust earned over years. The DTC playbook that kills it: chase revenue, raise money to fund the growth, build for a quick exit.

7. The sea of sameness
Copy the Ads Library and you win for a quarter. Then every brand running that playbook dies together. Preston builds from his own story instead. Different makes more money than optimized.

8. Branded search is the scoreboard
When someone searches your name instead of clicking an ad, revenue per session is higher and at a higher margin. It's the cleanest proof brand works, and the number a CFO respects. Grow it faster than revenue and your brand is getting stronger.

None of this means turn off your conversion ads.

But there's more to building a DTC than what last click shows.

When I scale I plot this chart:

→ For every ad, plot traffic against funnel stage
→ Funnel stages: impressions, click, landing, add to cart, checkout, purchase
→ Now you see the drop-off through every stage of your funnel

There are three main scenarios.

1. Early drop off

→ Impressions are high, but clicks look low
→ The ad gets attention but doesn't resonate enough to earn the tap
→ Check hook rate, hold rate, CPM, drop off, audience and demographics.
→ This is a creative problem. Fix the ad.

2. Middle drop off

→ Clicks are strong, but add to carts fall away
→ The ad was compelling enough to click, then the landing page doesn't land
→ Usually the selling points on the page are different from what the ad promised
→ This is a page problem. Match the page to the ad

3. Late drop off

→ Add to carts are healthy, but checkout and purchase drop
→ They wanted it enough to grab it, then the price surprised them
→ The product isn't compelling against the number
→ This is an offer problem. Look at price, bundle, shipping

I love getting called out on LinkedIn

So I wrote a Substack.

Barry Hott pushed back on my changelog analysis.
Taylor Holiday pushed back on quality vs quantity.
Nick Bauer pushed back on cutting ads by ad-level ROAS.

I can debate them because I have data that supports my view.

And that's the whole reason I post.
- I write to share what I'm seeing
- I write to get it argued with
- I write to come out the other side with a sharper version.

But all three were pointing at the same underlying mistake. That I think is really important and I want people to know.

Each one is my post about a sub-KPI getting treated as the overarching goal.

Changelog cadence, quality vs quantity, ad-level ROAS. They're all proxies. Useful readings of how the account is doing. The moment you make a proxy the thing you optimize against, you stop improving the business and start gaming the number. And fair enough, a single post about one proxy can read like I'm telling you to chase it.

But that's the trap Goodhart warned about: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

What that looks like inside an ad account:

→ Chase hook rate and you buy attention from people who'll never convert. Hook rate climbs, conversion tanks.
→ Pause every ad past a 30-day age cap and you kill creatives that were still printing money.
→ Cut every ad with weak ad-level ROAS and you strip out the losing tests the algorithm needs to find the winners.
→ Benchmark creative volume and you flood the account with junk variations to hit a number.

Each one is a sensor. It tells you how the account is doing. It was never meant to be the thing you optimize for.

The goal of a company isn't a number on the dashboard. It's making more value for the customer at a lower cost to produce it. Watch the sub-KPIs. Steer with the headline metrics: blended ROAS, CAC, contribution margin.

Unicorn DTC brands have a 1st time customer P&L

Steal this one: 

1. Gross Revenue
→ First-time orders only, before any deductions
→ Compare to total revenue to see what % isn't returning
→ E.g. $200k of $500k total = 40% from new customers

2. Net Revenue
→ Deduct discounts, returns, and refunds
→ Normalizes for brands forcing gross with sitewide discounts
→ $200k gross minus 30% off and a 12% return rate = $116k net

3. Gross Margin
→ Deduct COGS from net revenue
→ Tells you if the product is profitable before any operating cost
→ If this is thin, no amount of marketing efficiency saves you

4. Contribution Margin
→ Deduct shipping, transaction fees, and fulfillment
→ Per-order profit before you spend a dollar acquiring anyone
→ Still no email, SMS, or retention in here

5. Fully-Loaded Acquisition Costs
→ Don't stop at ad spend. Stack UGC, whitelisting and creator licensing, agency fees, affiliate commissions, software
→ $50k in ad spend becomes $67k all-in
→ True cost multiplier: 1.34x your ad spend

6. Acquisition Contribution Margin
→ Subtract the fully-loaded cost from contribution margin
→ Ad-spend-only reads +$2,420. Fully loaded reads -$14,580
→ Negative means you're relying on future purchases to break even

7. Acquisition Efficiency
→ Two metrics: fully-loaded aMER and nCAC
→ CPA reads $25. Fully-loaded nCAC is $33.50
→ The platform number understates your real cost by 34%

8. The Two-Cap Operating System
→ Cap 1: a minimum MER ceiling that protects cash flow
→ Cap 2: a max nCAC target that protects unit economics
→ Breach Cap 2 and you're CPA constrained, out of room to scale

9. Retention Breakeven & Cash Position
→ Shows the exact dollars retention has to recover to break even
→ Tracks your running cash position as you acquire
→ At this spend, every new customer costs you $7.29 before retention kicks in

10. What If You Turned Ads Off
→ Models next month with zero new customer spend
→ Applies your churn rate to returning revenue
→ Revenue drops ~45%. That gap is your burn rate

How to pull it:
1. Export customer data by new vs returning from Shopify
2. Drop your inputs into the yellow cells, the rest auto-calculates
3. Work down: net revenue, gross margin, contribution margin
4. Stack every acquisition cost in section 5: media, UGC, agency, affiliates, tools
5. Read fully-loaded aMER and nCAC, then run both caps
6. If acquisition CM is negative, section 9 shows what retention owes you

3 ABM signals everyone tracks that have zero correlation with closed-won deals:

I see the same vanity signals show up in every underperforming pipeline.

1 // Anonymous website traffic

"Account visited your pricing page 7 times this week"

Intent data vendors sell this hard. The problem: unless you can tie the visit to a known buyer with authority, you're chasing ghosts.

Forrester and practitioners like Chris Walker have consistently shown that anonymous web visits — even high-intent pages — don't predict pipeline when isolated.

That same account "visiting pricing 7 times" is often doing competitive research, not buying.

2 // Content downloads

Gated content downloads remain one of the most tracked "intent signals" in ABM platforms.

The people downloading whitepapers are often researchers, students, competitors, or early-career folks with zero buying authority.

HockeyStack and similar attribution tools have shown download-to-close rates that round to zero in most B2B segments.

3 // High "account engagement score" driven by email opens

Most MAP-derived account scores are heavily weighted on email opens — which since Apple MPP (2021) are largely fabricated.

Accounts can show "high engagement" entirely from bot opens. This inflates account scores and sends SDRs chasing accounts that have never had a human interact with anything.

What actually predicts closed-won:

→ Known buyer with authority engaging multiple times
→ Champion + decision maker both active on the account
→ Multi-threaded engagement across channels (not just one signal type)
→ Recency + frequency + role seniority combined

Stop optimizing for signals that look good in dashboards but don't convert.

Build your scoring model on what actually closes.

I've spent $400M on ads & made $1.5Bn

Do this to max out Google ads:

1. Cut CPA to scale

→ If your Search Lost IS (budget) is at 50%, your budget is gone by 2pm and you're missing out on auctions
→ Drop your target CPA and Google moves to cheaper clicks (that still convert).
→ At a similar conversion rate, twice the clicks halves your CPA.

2. Send bad leads back

→ Google accepts negative conversions.
→ When your CRM marks a lead spam or disqualified, upload it back within 24 hours with a retract tag.
→ Google stops building lookalikes of your worst leads. Lead quality improves without changing a keyword.

3. Check who's new

→ Turn on New Customer Acquisition reporting.
→ On one $400k/mo PMax account, 62% of the "conversions" were existing customers. Real cost to win a new one was 3.1x the dashboard figure.
→ If you're paying to re-buy people who'd have returned anyway, the account isn't what you think.

4. Adjust bids

→ There's no such thing as a bad keyword. Just a bad bid.
→ Pull your "paused for performance" keywords. Anything within 2x your target CPA, switch back on at a 40-50% lower bid.
→ Google moves to cheaper auctions that convert. I've seen "dead" keywords come back at $48 CPA on a $50 target.

5. Let PMax scout Search

→ Run PMax at the same daily budget next to your Search campaign, then open its search term insights.
→ If that spend converts on real queries, your Search had room.
→ Move them into Search at a higher budget and repeat until PMax stops spending there.

6. Stop narrowing audiences

→ Narrow targeting only works when budget is small and demand is high.
→ Everywhere else, go broad and add audiences as observation layers.
→ Let Google find the buyers, then read who converted.

7. Plug Search Partners leak

→ PMax sends spend to Search Partners with no campaign-level toggle to stop it. I've seen it eat 30% of budget on junk leads.
→ Account settings, content, excluded placements. Block syndicatedsearch . goog, searchpartners . google and searchpartner . google.
→ Turn on Limited inventory.

8. Use Broad match with guardrail

→ On brand campaigns, go broad match to catch every misspelling and brand-plus-product search (they convert at 3-4x non-brand).
→ Put a Target ROAS of >50% above target, so Google only bids on a junk query if it can hit that return.

9. Send multiple conversion events

→ Fire a conversion event at every stage (MQL, SQL, closed customer).
→ A buyer fires three conversions. A dead-end form-fill fires one. Google optimizes toward buyers.
→ Google tells you to pick one conversion action. I run multiple at $2M/mo on this strategy.

How to scale a winning ad

Answer: inject absurdity.

Take the winning ad and make it weird in any way that:

Strange and accurate is the key.

I ran GTM at $23m SaaS

For 4 years, I sent the CEO (3) RevOps report every Monday 9am:
- GTM efficiency
- Pipeline Health
- Forecast

Report 1: GTM Efficiency
Tells you if your S&M spend is working/scalable

A. The Magic Number
$1 of ARR for every $1 of S&M spend:
>0.75 = generally considered efficient, worth investing more
<0.5 = broken GTM, fix before scaling
>1.5 = step on the gas, you're leaving money on the table

B. Rule of 40 = Revenue Growth % + FCF Margin %

You can hit 40 two ways:
- 60% growth + (-20%) margin → hypergrowth mode
- 20% growth + 20% margin → efficient mature business

The composition tells a different story depending on your stage:
 - $2M–$5M ARR: growth % dominates. A 80/(-40) score is fine
- $10M–$20M ARR: balance matters. Pure growth story gets harder to sustain
- PE target ($20M+ ARR): margin is weighted heavily (they're buying cash flow potential)

C. NNR: is your existing base growing or leaking?
↳ World class: 130%+
↳ Strong: 110-130% (healthy upsell, low churn)
↳ Growing: 101%-110% (basically flat, expansion offsets losses)
↳ Warning: 90-100% (churn eating into base)
↳ Broken: <90% (fix leaky bucket, then scale)

D. LTV:CAC: do your unit economics actually work?
↳ 4:1 - scale, channel is profitable
↳ 3:1 - channel is viable and worth investing into
↳ 2:1 - channel is break even considering all costs (incl. employee time)
↳ 1:1 - channel not profitable. If not in testing phase, kill

E. CAC Payback: how many months until you recover acquisition cost?
↳ SMB: good = 12mo | acceptable = 12-18mo | warning = 18mo+
↳ Mid market: good = 18mo | acceptable = 18-24mo | warning = 24mo+
↳ Enterprise: good = 24mo | acceptable = 24-36mo | warning = 36mo+

Report 2: Pipeline Health
Tells you which deals to kill and which to accelerate before the quarter slips

→ Coverage ratio vs quota (healthy = 3–4x) 
→ Stage distribution: is your funnel top-heavy or bottom-heavy? 
→ Aging deals flagged the moment they exceed 2x average cycle time 
→ Concentration risk: alerts when 1 deal represents >40% of pipeline 
→ Where your qtr is at risk: coverage gap by quarter
→ Sales velocity: pipeline needed to hit next quarter goal

Report 3: Forecast Accuracy
Tells where your forecast is optimistic vs realistic

→ MAPE: your forecast error score 
→ Bias detection: are you systematically over or under-forecasting? 
→ Rep-level accuracy breakdown: who's sandbagging, who's wishful thinking
→ Forecast trend: is your forecasting getting better or worse quarter over quarter? 
→ Segment-level breakdown: Enterprise vs Mid-Market vs SMB

This report system means leadership wakes up Monday knowing:
- Which deal to call, which rep to coach, and which spend to cut 
- Pipeline coverage vs target (are we on track or not?) 
- The 2-3 deals that need attention asap 
- GTM efficiency score

BE CAREFUL. If you pay variable whitelisting fees

Make sure you're doing this:

→ More creators and performance partners now charge a % of ad spend instead of a flat fee. Usually 5-15%.
→ It aligns incentives. But it changes how you have to optimize
→ If you scale an ad that has a 10% whitelisting fee, the in-platform CPA is wrong, and you're less profitable than you think

1. Separate fixed fees from variable fees
→ A flat $5k usage fee is sunk. It doesn't change a single day-to-day decision in the account.
→ A % of spend fee is different. Every dollar you scale costs you more, so it has to change how you buy.

2. Raise the hurdle by the fee
→ Treat the % of spend fee like a CPM premium on a programmatic buy.
→ If the ad carries an 8-15% partner fee, raise its ROAS/CPA target by that exact percentage.
→ It costs more to run, so it has to perform proportionately better to earn the scale.

10% fee = 10% higher ROAS target for the same profitability.

3. Measure P&L by creative source & delivery
→ Tag new customers by the creative partner and the delivery
→ You could be paying 10% to the creator and then 10% to a whitelisted publisher page
→ Calculate CAC by creative source and delivery combinations
→ Measure LTV per source & delivery too in case these drive higher or lower value customers
→ Determine if the real contribution margin is worth you scaling into the ad or pulling back on the partners all together

How to know which ads to kill or scale

1. Take every ad you're running
2. Plot it on a graph
3. Y axis = CPA
4. X axis = Spend (log)
5. Choose your target CPA
6. Define your kill CPA (typically 2-3x tCPA)
7. Draw those lines horizontally

Now you have three types of ads:

Scale = Green
→ CPA below your target line, with spend already behind them
→ Expect about 1% of your ads here. They'll drive 50% of revenue
→ Move budget 20% at a time so you don't trigger relearning

Test = Yellow
→ CPA sits between your target and kill line
→ This is most of your account, usually 65%+ of ads
→ Push more budget and watch where it lands. Drops toward target you scale, climbs past kill you cut

Kill = Red
→ CPA above your kill line with enough spend behind it
→ Enough data to be 90% confident it never hits target
→ Ideally you have zero here. If an ad got this far, you cut too slow

How are you deciding what to cut in your accounts?

We saved a client from a 0.41% to a 3.34% reply rate in 15 days.

Only one of the five changes had anything to do with infrastructure. The rest was strategy.

Here's the whole list:

1. Super spintax. 20 variations in the subject line, the unsubscribe language, and the signature block. Not just a little bit of spintax, far more than we thought we would need. 

2. Buy domains early. A parked, aged domain beats a fresh one you warmed for two weeks. 

We keep 50-100% extra inbox capacity warming as insurance with live inboxes. Another 50-100% of the domains we need just sitting in the registrar. 

3. 100% Gmail. We buy Gmails through Zapmail and Hypertide, and we added Zapmail's ZapShield, which puts inboxes on Google Cloud enterprise servers. 

We split-tested it: a 20-50% reply-rate lift depending on the campaign.

4. Find the winners, pile on. We run two inboxes per domain usually. If one domain is proving to be particularly strong by reply rate then stack up to five on the outlier domains getting the best reply rate. (Credit to Felipe Fuhr for this one.)

5. Kill anything under 1%. Every week I pull a report and cut about 10-15% of our infrastructure. Every inbox lives in a database as active, insurance, or cancel with the trailing 7 day reply rate. 

More copywriting variance, more infrastructure, bought ahead of time.

That's the whole game right now.

I ran a test to find local business owners across 5 different providers. The cheapest option won. It was also the best.

Here's the problem with local lead gen: a plumbing company, a dentist, a local shop don't have a LinkedIn profile. 

And almost every big database are built on LinkedIn data. So they just don't have these people.

So we put 5 options against each other: SmartLead Email Finder, Prospeo, Blitz API, OpenWebNinja (which is really just a Google search), and an open-source website scrape.

The winner wasn't a paid API.

It was scraping the business's own website with an open-source library and reading it with a local LLM.

Here's the stack:

1. HTML2Text (open source) converts the homepage, about, team, and contact pages into plain text an LLM can read.

2. Gemma 4  (the 12B version $$$) running locally on Ollama reads it and pulls the owner's name. It's on my laptop, it's free, and it doesn't matter how many sites I process, I can just rip through all of them.

3. If that comes up empty, we Google "who owns [business] in [city]" through OpenWeb Ninja including the AI overview answer and parse that with Gemma 4 too.

The whole website-scrape side costs $0, because the LLM runs locally and the library is open source. OpenWebNinja is the only paid piece, and it's cheap.

It's exactly what I'd do if I were to pass to a teammate. "Here's 100 local businesses, go find the owner." They'd check the website and Google it. We just automated that.

We still check Blitz and Prospeo first. If someone literally put "I own this business, here's my site" on their LinkedIn, that fidelity is worth paying for. But when the LinkedIn scrapers miss, the free website scrape catches what they leave behind.

If you do any local lead gen: download HTML2Text, pull Gemma 4 from Ollama, grab an OpenWebNinja key, and point your AI agent at it.

If I had $1 for every time I've heard, "executives don't open or read cold emails", I'd be retired in Montana.

It's a story we love to tell ourselves because it feels so much harder to reach an executive vs. a non-executive. 

But, I partnered with Gong and 30 Minutes to President's Club on a study of 1M sales opps as part of my "Selling to the C-Suite" course. And, the data tells a different story. 

When you compare an executive vs. non-executive recipient, the difference in open rate is only 1.5%. 

However, when you compare the difference in reply rate, it's a staggering 30.2% difference. 

Execs DO open cold emails. 

But, I agree they rarely read them. They skim them. 

They skim for clues re: If it's relevant to their business and their objectives. They skim to the bottom to see what you want from them. A 'quick 20 min call to learn more about your priorities' is rarely a net positive return for them, when we've spent the entire email talking about our product. 

Their time is expensive. So, they have to be judicious with it. It's likely why we see such a difference in reply rate. 

But, it doesn't mean they don't reply. 

If you've been in a workshop with me, you'll know I teach an outbound messaging framework for execs called Problem Prompting. 

Problem prompting takes advantage of this incredible moment we're in. 

One where AI has completely upended status quo for every single function in a business. I've yet to meet an exec who feels completely and utterly confident navigating it. 

There's no better time to be in Sales than during a period of uncertainty. It's when execs start looking up, left, and to the right. 

They're seeking to understand - What are others doing? Is it working? What would they do differently? How did they do it? What are the pros and cons of A vs B? 

Problem Prompting taps into that. It offers an idea, not a product pitch.

The idea is the entry ticket to the exec conversation.

Google says optimize for one conversion action.

We spend $2M/mo doing the opposite. It works: 

Google's own help docs say:

→ If you have multiple standard conversion goals 
→ Tracking different stages of the same conversion funnel
→ We recommend that you set only one of them as the account-default goal

We do the opposite.

1. Track the whole funnel

→ We fire conversion events throughout the full funnel 
→ E.g., MQL fires, SQL fires, customer fires
→ A buyer trips three conversions on the way through.
→ A MQL would only fire one

2. Weight the down-funnel events

→ The customer event is worth more than the MQL
→ So we tell Google that by sending more conversion events (the deeper funnel ones)

3. Learn from richer signal

→ Instead of 100 conversions a month feeding the model, we're closer to 150
→ And it's learning from people who actually became customers, which is a very different thing than 150 form-fills

Summary
→ One conversion action keeps the signal clean but blind to lead quality
→ Stack MQL, SQL and customer so a buyer counts three times
→ Weight the down-funnel events so the valuable ones don't get drowned out
→ More total conversions, and a model that optimizes toward people who actually buy

My barber has no problems and I had an outbound inspiration talking to him about this while getting a haircut 6 months ago. 

He's got a shop. Four other barbers cutting alongside him. Same setup for years. His income hasn't really moved in five.

One day in the chair I asked what he was working on in the business. What he was trying to fix or build next.

He looked at me like it was a strange question.

"I don't really have problems. I'm just chilling."

He has SOME problems. He's on his feet cutting hair all day at a minimum.

But he's fine doing that forever. He's not adding chairs. Not adding locations. Not trying to grow.

And that's the whole thing.

When a company isn't trying to grow, it stops having problems you can sell it on.

Growth is what creates the problems. You hire people, now you have to manage them. You open a location, now you need a way to run it. You sign more customers, now the old way of doing things breaks.

Those new problems are the openings. They're the reason someone reads a cold email about a solution instead of deleting it.

I'd be willing to bet most positive responses to cold email have something in common. they're trying to grow.

Here's a deal killer in competitive deals + 3 Qs that helped me stop losing to it. 

You get an inbound lead. They tell you they're looking at you + 2 competitors. 

For years, that would trigger my "I need to show why we're a better option" reaction. 

I'd ask disco questions to understand their problem. Then, I'd explain our differentiators and why those made us a better option vs. our competitors. 

Here's where I fell down. 

I never slowed down to see if there were other priorities or categories of spend I was unknowingly competing against. 

As a result, I lost a lot of deals to "We've decided to put this investment on hold. Instead, we're going to invest in {different category of solution} or {different priority}".

After losing enough of them, I learned to add 3 Qs to my inbound discovery:

1) "How did the leadership team arrive on X as the right problem to for the business to solve right now?"

Listen for "I" vs "we" language. If you're hearing "I" language, it might be a signal your prospect doesn't have consensus for change. This is job #1. 

2) "How did the leadership team arrive on X as the right solution lever to address this problem?"

Most problems have multiple categories of solutions they could buy to address it. Just because they're talking to us, doesn't mean OUR category of solution is the one they've chosen. 

3) "What other investments or priorities might take priority over this one?"

Language choice is important here. It's not "Were there other...". This is where we lean into assumptive language. Buying is rarely linear. Buying groups change their mind, back up, and hit restart. Assume this is not the only priority for them right now. 

Most importantly, make it easy for them to be honest with you. 

Don't rush to convince them to prioritize your category of spend, before you deeply understand the others.

I've advised early-stage founders for years.

Most are tracking the wrong GTM metrics.

Rule of 40. Magic Number. NNR.

These are built for $20M+ companies with historical data and predictable revenue. At seed or Series A, you don't have that luxury.

Here's the GTM scorecard I give founders under $10M ARR:

Metric 1: Win Rate by Source

Tells you which channels actually close.

↳ Inbound vs outbound vs referral
↳ Track close % for each, not just volume
↳ If outbound closes at 8% and inbound at 22%, you have a channel allocation problem

Early stage benchmark: 15-25% overall win rate on qualified opps. Below 15%, ICP or sales process needs work.

Metric 2: Time to First Revenue

Tells you if your sales cycle is sustainable.

↳ Days from first touch to closed-won
↳ Segment by deal size and buyer type
↳ Watch for deals that drag past 60 days with no clear next step

Early stage benchmark:
↳ SMB: 14-30 days
↳ Mid-market: 30-60 days
↳ Enterprise: 60-90 days

Anything 2x these ranges = qualification problem or missing champion.

Metric 3: Pipeline Coverage

Tells you if next quarter is at risk.

↳ Total qualified pipeline / quota
↳ At early stage, 4x coverage is the floor
↳ Below 4x with a 20% win rate = you're going to miss

Early stage benchmark: 4-5x coverage. Higher than mature companies because your win rate is still volatile.

Metric 4: CAC Payback (Simplified)

Tells you how fast you recover acquisition cost.

↳ (S&M spend per customer) / (monthly revenue per customer)
↳ Skip the LTV calculation until you have 12+ months of retention data

Early stage benchmark:
↳ Under 12 months = healthy
↳ 12-18 months = acceptable if ACV is growing
↳ 18+ months = burning cash faster than you're building

Why these 4 and not 12?

At early stage, you need signal, not dashboards.

Every metric you add dilutes focus. These 4 tell you:
1. Are we selling to the right people?
2. Are we closing fast enough?
3. Do we have enough pipeline?
4. Are we spending efficiently?

Answer those, and you have a GTM motion worth scaling.

How to FORCE Meta to acquire new customers

I spend $30M/year doing this:

→ Left alone, Meta won't prospect for new customers.
→ It harvests the cheapest conversions it can find
→ The cheapest conversions are people who were going to buy anyway.

1. Exclude existing customers
→ Upload your customer and purchaser lists, then exclude them from every prospecting campaign.
→ This helps push the bid into cold inventory.

2. Cap existing-customer spend
→ In Advantage+ Shopping, define your existing-customer audiences and set the budget cap to 0-10%. Meta is forced to spend the rest finding new buyers.

3. Track NC ROAS through an MTA
→ Calculate nCAC against new customers. Count marginal creative, tools, team, and agency fees on top of ad spend.
→ Expect true CAC to run as much as ~50% above platform CPA. A $40 reported CPA is closer to $60 loaded.
→ Ask "First time hearing about us?" on the thank-you page so you can split new from returning.
→ Track the new-customer column in your MTA instead of blended ROAS. Bad = 4x ROAS ASC that's 70% returning buyer

4. Run prospecting creative
→ Cut offer-led hooks like "Here's 10% off." They convert people already deciding, which is harvesting.
→ Open on the problem, agitate it, then prove the fix.
→ Mine your reviews for the exact words new customers used before they found you, and lead with those.

5. Map cohort LTV
→ Plot cumulative LTV by year/month customers bought
→ Identify how much MORE a customer spends over their life time
→ The full LTV is your CPA ceiling (1/3 for 3x LTV:CAC)
→ Now you know the extent to which you can outbid competitors

In short:

- Exclude existing customers from every prospecting campaign
- Cap existing-customer spend to 0-10% in ASC
- Track new-customer ROAS in your MTA
- Run problem-led prospecting creative
- Map cohort LTV to set your CPA ceiling

We run AI on millions of cold email leads a month. We almost never write the prompts ourselves. Here's the trick.

Writing a good prompt by hand is slow. And most of us aren't actually prompt engineers. But running a frontier model on millions of rows to score ICP fit and write custom variables gets expensive fast.

So we stopped doing both.

Now we build a tiny loop:

1. A frontier model (Claude Code or Codex) drafts the prompt itself.
2. It runs that prompt on a 10-row sample.
3. It grades its own output against the goal, I evaluate manually if I agree. then rewrites the prompt where it missed.

It repeats until two clean rounds in a row. No human writing prompts. The model reviews its own work and tunes itself.

Then the part that saves the money.

We take that polished prompt and run it on the cheapest, fastest model we can find. A small hosted model. Gemma. Ornith. Whatever's cheap.

The frontier model was the prompt engineer. The cheap model is the worker.

The prompt is the asset. You pay the smart model once to build it, then a cheap model runs it across your whole list for a fraction of the cost.

We already do this two ways. One loop tunes ICP-fit scoring. Another tunes the custom variables on every lead. Both stop themselves when the output stops needing edits.

The cost gap is real. Running the cheap model can be up to ~90% cheaper. Frontier quality, cheap-model price.

If you're running AI over a big list and writing every prompt by hand, you're doing the expensive version of both jobs.

Just audited a $5M/yr B2B Google ad account

Found $500k/yr opportunity. Might work for you:

- Deals worth $20k to $300k
- Very good unit economics
- Spending on Google & Meta
- Mostly working fine

Opportunities:

1. Conversion events
→ It was bidding on one down-funnel event that fires under 100 times a month. Not enough signal across that many campaigns and geos.
→ Add a second primary action one step up the funnel. Lead plus qualified lead. More signal for the algorithm, less risk than bidding straight to the bottom.
→ I spend $6M/mo+ on ads and my biggest accounts run on multiple conversion actions.

2. Target CPA over Max Conversions
→ Max Conversions gives you no control at the ad group level.
→ Target CPA lets you bid up the ad groups driving down-funnel conversions without breaking them into separate campaigns.
→ Once that's stable, move to value-based bidding off your lead scores.

3. Kill single ad group campaigns
→ Consolidate thin markets into fewer campaigns so each one gets enough conversion volume to learn.
→ Or push thin markets to PMax for more inventory and signal.

4. Go wide on broad match
→ Broad match ad groups across a wide keyword set, then pull the search term report 1 to 3 times a week and cut everything irrelevant. Early on I'll spend 2-3 hours per report finding negatives.
→ Broad is also where Google is going. It shows in AI Overviews far more than exact or phrase.
→ Don't pin headlines at this volume. Let the algorithm choose the copy.

5. Stress test brand spend
→ Run a holdout. Brand on for a week, off the next, repeat.
→ Compare paid and organic brand clicks in Search Console to find your marginal CPA on brand.
→ Results will vary. I've run this and halved brand budget on one account, doubled it on another.

6. Send traffic to location pages
→ The specific location page beat a near-identical generic landing page by 10x on a similar account.
→ Personalize the page off the ad or UTM clicked.
→ Keep one landing page test running at all times.

Easily stacking all these improvements together which will likely result in a $500k+ jump (Image assumes they all weight roughly equally but in reality can’t predict the exact increases)

Cheatsheet:
- Bid on multiple conversion actions
- Run Target CPA instead of Max Conversions
- Consolidate thin markets or push them to PMax
- Go broad match, then cut junk with weekly negatives
- Holdout test brand to find its marginal CPA
- Send paid traffic to location pages & always keep one test live

You should too. This is why:

-> Meta's learning phase is an arbitrary line drawn on a scale of statistical significance. Meta wants to hand you a binary answer to something that's a gradient.

How I know if I've paused the WRONG ad

Before it's too late:

The WORST mistake you can make on Meta is not squeezing a good ad to it's maximum

Real story:

→ Was working with an 7-figure account
→ They paused ad set because it had a low ROAS (but measurable performance)
→ They wanted to be more efficient and push a limited budget elsewhere
→ Week later their evergreen ads began to see lower performance

I was suspicious about what was going on, so we ran a quick check.

Net New Reach per Dollar

1. Pull A: account reach for the last 12 months, ending this month (deduped, account level)
2. Pull B: account reach for the last 12 months, ending last month
3. Net new reach = A − B (people who hadn't seen you in a year)
4. Divide that by the month's ad spend
5. That's your net new reach per dollar
6. Run it for the month before the pause and the month after. If it drops, the ad you killed was bringing in the new people.

Cost Per ThruPlay

1. It's a native column in Ads Manager. Add "Cost per ThruPlay"
2. A ThruPlay counts when someone watches the video to the end, or 15+ seconds on a longer one. So it measures real attention.
3. A low cost per ThruPlay means the ad cheaply holds people. Low ThruPlay cost = good first touch ad.

Read the two together:

→ High net new reach per dollar + low cost per ThruPlay = a Reach Instigator. It cheaply pulls fresh people in and holds them. Don't pause it without a replacement, even on weak ROAS.
→ Low net new reach per dollar + low cost per ThruPlay = engaging, but only to people who already know you. That's a closer, safe to pause.
→ High net new reach per dollar + high cost per ThruPlay = reaching new people who aren't watching. Cheap impressions, weak attention. Not pulling much into the funnel.
→ Low on both = doing neither job. Pause it.

Hope this helps.

I've spent $400M on Google ads

Dirty secret to making it stupidly profitable:

Absence of mistakes.

1. Auto-apply
→ Google applies its own changes to match types, budgets and assets without telling you
→ You end up debugging a performance drop you didn't cause
→ Settings → Account → switch off every auto-apply recommendation

2. Optimized targeting
→ On by default, it spends past your audience signal into cheaper, lower-intent traffic
→ CPA holds steady while lead quality drops
→ Turn it off on every campaign until the account converts on qualified leads

3. Search Partners
→ No campaign-level opt-out, takes up to 10% of spend on placements no one searched
→ Conversions come back unqualified at a third of budget
→ Exclude it at account level and push that spend to Search and YouTube

4. Display expansion on Search
→ One checkbox turns a high-intent Search campaign into a display campaign
→ Impressions jump, conversions don't follow
→ Uncheck it so Search stays Search

5. Wrong conversion signal
→ Optimizing to form fills trains Google to find more form fillers
→ It has no idea which ones buy, so volume climbs and your sales team fills with junk
→ Move the primary conversion to qualified lead or booked call, and pass it back with the GCLID

6. Primary conversion under 30/mo
→ Under 30 conversions in 30 days, the algorithm never gets enough signal to train
→ It guesses, CPA swings week to week, and the creative takes the blame
→ Move the primary up-funnel until it clears 30, then walk it back down as volume grows

None of these are clever.

But that's exactly why they get missed.

→ Revenue per Conversion means real customer value
→ If you optimize on form fills, use closed-deal revenue here anyway.

3. Max Efficient Spend

→ Max Efficient Spend = Max Revenue ÷ Target ROAS
→ Worked example: 100k searches × 3% CTR × 10% CVR × $12k per conversion = $3.6M revenue ceiling
→ At 4x target ROAS, your max efficient Search spend is $900k/mo
→ Past that you're bidding above your own breakeven

4. The 80% rule

→ At 80% of ceiling, the next dollar belongs in PMax or Demand Gen
→ The last 20% of searchable demand is bid up by everyone else in the auction
→ Your CPCs climb faster than your CVR. Marginal CAC explodes.
→ Example how this would look: $1.1M Search spend at a 4x ROAS ceiling of $900k. CAC inflates 38% in 60 days. This is the marginal CAC exploding

5. Where the budget actually goes after Search saturates

→ PMax. Only if you have 50+ down-funnel conversions/mo and Search is profitable first.
→ Then Demand Gen. Cheaper CPCs, broader inventory.

6. The PMax probe trick

→ Sometimes Search feels capped but isn't
→ Turn PMax on alongside Search at the same daily budget
→ If PMax allocates over half its spend to Search AND those conversions hit, your bid was too low
→ Promote the converting search terms into Search, raise the bid, repeat
→ True ceiling = when PMax's Search allocation drops below 10% of its spend

Failed the 80% check?
→ Stop adding budget to Search
→ Start PMax at 10-20% of total Google spend
→ Move incremental dollars to Demand Gen for warmer traffic

Passed the 80% check?
→ Check match-type mix (Brand under 20%, Competitor ~10%, Non-Brand ~70%)
→ Audit RSAs. Under-filled headlines shrink your auction surface.
→ Then add budget

Summary:
→ Search has a math ceiling. Calculate it before you scale.
→ 80% of ceiling means stop adding Search budget
→ Past 80%, every dollar fights your own dollar in the auction
→ Channel reallocation beats Search inflation

From our experience of sending millions of emails per month, Google has a higher chance of blocking your sending from the inbox than outlook and here's how to fix it. 

We see more of what is categorized as a "sender bounce" from Google inboxes than we do outlook inboxes. 

A sender bounce is when an inbox provider blocks you from sending the email and soft bounces it. We have seen it's not as detrimental as sending to an email that doesn't exist, ( as you can see in the screenshot below). 

And these sender bounces can creep up on you out of nowhere. The screenshot below was from a campaign that was doing fine targeting enterprise accounts. 

Then out of nowhere, we get a huge bounce alert. 50% of emails are bouncing. 

When we looked into it, it was 100% of all emails from Email variation B. 

Thank goodness the fix is pretty easy.

Everything about the email campaign below is the same. The inboxes we are using are both the same. The subject lines are the same  with 5 variations of spintax. 

The signatures and unsubscribe language is all the same. The difference?

The body text of Email A has 20 variations of spintax per line and Email B has just 3 versions of spintax. 

So if you ever see sender bounces spike even though you know you double validated your list with tools like LeadMagic verifier or something, check the variation in your copy.

We've seen it to be the main culprit when it comes to keeping sender bounces low.

And it worked:

→ This business had variable supply that was constantly changing.
→ Sometimes we have supply, and we want to max it out.
→ Sometimes we have no supply, and we need to minimize loss.

Example businesses:

→ Addiction treatment centers. Open beds fill and empty by the hour.
→ Hotels. Rooms get booked up and then can go unsold.
→ HVAC. Today's open job slots go unused.

1. Bid schedule

→ Bids re-paced at midnight, 8am, 10am, noon, 2pm, 4pm, 6pm, 8pm.
→ Every run re-read new orders and current supply, then reset the target.

2. Conversion-lag multiplier

→ A booking today doesn't turn into revenue today. There's a lag between the two.
→ We applied a 1.77x multiplier to new bookings to estimate downstream sales.
→ That gave the bid a forward estimate of sales to optimize against.

3. Supply threshold

→ Supply is how much open capacity you have right now.
→ Plenty of supply, bid aggressive. Empty capacity is lost revenue, so go fill it.
→ Near sold out, pull back to minimize paying for customers we can't fulfill.

4. Holidays

→ Conversion rates fall around holidays as people delay buying.
→ We treated every holiday as a CVR risk and paced bids down into it.

Summary:
→ Tie the bid to the constraint that limits revenue (here, available supply).
→ Build in the lag between the order you see and the revenue you bill.
→ Pace down into low-conversion windows like holidays before they land.
→ Anchor every lever to cost per sale.

Are you testing too many ads for Meta?

How you can check:

1. Count your weekly baseline
→ Pull how many ads you shipped per week over the last 30 days.

2. Tie volume to spend
→ Brief 1 concept per $10k of monthly spend, 3 ads per concept. At $365k/month that's ~37 concepts and ~110 ads.
→ Base it on next month's planned spend. If you're scaling 25%, brief for that higher number.

3. Check your portfolio age
→ Spend-weighted, your active ads should average 45-55 days old.
→ Older than that and you're leaning on past winners you haven't replaced.

4. Check your hit rate
→ Aim for 10-15% of ads clearing your performance bar.
→ At 6%, you're paying for volume and getting almost no winners.

5. Adjust off hit rate
→ If you're under 10%, more ads won't fix it.
→ Improve concepts until the hit rate climbs back.

Quick cheatsheet:
- If your hit rate drops as you ship more, you're testing too many.
- The ceiling is the volume that holds your hit rate above 10%.

Which conversion event should you send to Google Ads?

It depends:

→ Events further in the funnel are higher quality.
→ But they are lower in volume
→ Which means the algo has less to train off on
→ But if you train too low in the funnel, you get spam / junk leads

How to choose the right event:

1. By campaign
→ Search: 15 conversions in 30 days to run Smart Bidding
→ PMax: 30 conversions/month before launch
→ Demand Gen: 50 conversions/month before launch
→ Target ROAS: 15 conversions/month, but only with dollar values uploaded per stage
→ High-ticket B2B: stay on manual CPC until 50 conversions/month

2. Example for high volume account:
Imagine healthcare account
→ 600 form submits/month
→ 200 booked calls/month
→ 90 showed-up calls/month
→ 25 closed deals/month

They're running Search plus PMax
→ PMax needs 30 conversions/month.
→ "Closed deal" is 25, just under.
→ "Showed up" is 90, so clears the requirement
→ We therefore optimize for "showed up" and keep "closed" as a secondary for reporting.
→ Sometimes we’ll also include "closed" as primary for extra signal. 

3. Example for high ticket B2B
Imagine SaaS client closing $100k deals:
→ 40 booked calls/month
→ 12 SQLs/month
→ 3 closed/month

They're only running Search
→ SQL at 12 is under the 15 requirement

Two options.
→ Keep manual CPC and bid on intent yourself.
→ Or fire on "booked call" (clears 30+) and SQL. And let the algo push spend toward the bookings that actually turn into SQLs.

Note:
→ Once you pick the deepest event that clears the conversion volume requirement retract any junk signals within 24 hours.
→ A booked call that no-shows is a bad signal. Send it back so Google stops chasing more leads like it

Plot this chart:
- X-axis: dollar spend on non-promo ads only.
- Y-axis: total new customer revenue
- Window: rolling 90 days.

Make significant changes in spend and wait (i.e. 20k/day and 40k/day) (plan them independently of other changes)

Shout out to Brayden Cruz for the idea here.

Then check for positive correlation
→ As non-promo ad spend rises, does new customer revenue rise with it?
→ Run it as a log correlation, returns flatten as spend scales
→ You're looking for a statistically significant positive slope
→ Then you want to evaluate estimated incrementally vs cost for impact.

How to predict how far they'll scale:
1. Plot every ad in your account on a scatter chart.
2. CPA on the Y-axis.
3. Total spend on the X-axis (log scale).

And then add two lines (using Poisson formula)

The red line (your cut line):

For a brand targeting $50 CPA:
→ At $250 spend, cut if CPA is $121+
→ At $1,000 spend, cut if CPA is $72+
→ At $5,000 spend, cut if CPA is $58+

At each threshold you're 90% confident that ad is never going to hit your CPA. The more data you have, the tighter the range gets.

The green line (your scale line):

→ $250 spend at a $32 CPA, scale aggressively
→ $500 spend at a $36 CPA, scale aggressively
→ $1,000 spend at a $39 CPA, start scaling in

And then you can track this over time 

→ So you can see how ads move and progress from blue into either green or blue 

→ You can visually tell if you’re killing ads early or late 

An easy way to think about it.

- Every ad is a blue dot.
- If it's above the red line, cut it quick
- If it's below the green line, scale it hard
- If it's in the middle, push the spend and see where it lands.

Crazy. Perfect tracking for 2 years

And 1 week of errors dropped conversions 40%.

It came down to a tracking outage:

→ The Salesforce API token expired (it rotates every ~2 years)
→ Offline conversions stopped flowing into Google
→ It failed with no alert in the account
→ Top-of-funnel "all calls" kept firing
→ And offline qualified calls conversions stopped

1. Optimizes toward whatever fires
Google kept optimizing as if nothing changed. The only signal coming in was "all calls," so it treated those as the goal.

2. Pours spend into the wrong action
Since calls were the only conversions it could see, it pushed more and more budget toward getting more of them.

3. Fills the campaign with junk
The traffic turned into competitor searches. On one day, 85% of the clicks were people looking for a competitor.

4. Compounds every day
A week of bad signal was enough to retrain it. Then it kept training on worse data until the account was 40% down.

Call volume stayed the same (which makes sense)
- But 3 minute call length jumped 50%
- And 5 minute call length fell 20%
- Which implies call quality fell

How we pulled it back:

1. Track the duration mix
We saw the ratio of short calls to qualified-length calls changing. This is a leading metric before revenue.

2. Demote the broken signal
Move "all calls" to secondary. Keep qualified call durations and VOBs as the only primary conversions.

3. Exclude the corrupted window
Goals > Bidding Adjustments > Exclusions. This tells Google to ignore the corrupted learning period, so it stops bidding off bad data.

4. Fix it at the source
Reconnect the integration and put a reminder on the token expiry.

Summary:
- When tracking breaks, Google doesn't stop.
- It optimizes toward whatever signal is firing, which is almost never what matters to your business.
- Two years of clean data, and a few days of bad data undid it.
- Check your conversion sources early
