I understand the desire to write LinkedIn posts that exaggerate our work, experience, knowledge, or results to make ourselves sound more impressive.

LinkedIn is largely a platform where everyone brags about their successes. It's easy to play the the comparison game. 

So, you start fudging a detail here and there. Exaggerate some minor details about your experience.  Copy/paste someone else's work, with a few tweaks, so you can call it your own. Make claims about your work you can't really back up, but sound good in content. 

Because you want to sound impressive, too. 

And, frankly, most of us have insecurities, imposter syndrome, and compare ourselves to others. I sure do. 
 
But, the single most meaningful ingredient for success is trust. 

I'd argue it's even MORE important in an AI world, where it takes ~90 secs to spin up a completely delusional, yet pretty, version of reality. 

And, every time we do this, we erode our reader's trust. In between the lines, we imply they're too stupid to tell. 

I had a ton of insecurity about starting a speaking business. I didn't write a published book. I didn't have a badass story of 3 exits. I never climbed Mt Everest. I was just an AE. 

Instead of trying to make myself sound like I was at the same level as those speakers who did, I carved out a different lane. 

I led with what made me "weak". Never a CRO. Never got any of the fancy speaker certifications. 

And I used that to show how I was different. Not better. Not "as good". Different.

I spoke like your Sales team, not a polished speaker. I could relate to your Sales team's flawed beliefs and assumptions, because I held those same beliefs and assumptions, too. I didn't show up with a wagging finger. Because I had made the same mistakes they did. 

Buyers like different. Different registers clearly in the brain. "As good" registers like two apples. "Different" registers like an apple and a hammock. 

I write this with a lot of empathy. I know it's tough to get out of the comparison game our brain loves to play. 

But, trust is built when we tell the truth.

So, when we mask it, exaggerate it, or downright lie about it, we trade LinkedIn likes and impressions for integrity. And, the bank doesn't cash LinkedIn impressions. 

What makes you different is your advantage. Not your flaw to cover up.

I think the best cold email campaigns have 3 things in common. A campaign that drives ROI doesn't need all 3, but each one of these points drives significantly more replies. 

Ever since we started doing free tests for companies to work with us, we've launched quite possibly 3-5x more campaigns with different offers than we previously would. 

Before, I thought I could tell from one look if a campaign was going to work, now, I'm basically never surprised. I've tried to put my finger on what makes a great campaign versus others and this is what I've been thinking. 

1. Great campaigns communicate the promise to either help companies make more money, save 90% of time, save 90% of costs in a way that the recipient didn't know about with a next step that is easy to say yes to. 

The best type of offer to convert cold traffic is an offer that helps people make more money for sure. If you can, always lead with that. 

If you can't, the time savings / cost savings you can provide has to be orders of magnitude higher. 

When Instantly.ai first released a sequencer with unlimited inboxes where everyone else was charging per mailbox, the community went crazy. And that was maybe a 99% cost reduction depending on your scale. 

Save Time/Save Money offers have to be orders of magnitude better than what they are doing today. 

2. Great campaigns communicate a mechanism that the recipient didn't know existed. 

I think the increase in amount of outbound messages people are receiving is maybe responsible for 20% in the decrease in outbound effectiveness. (I'll make another post demonstrating this). 

The bigger driver of the decrease in outbound effectiveness is that prospects have access to more information than ever before. 

They know that performance outbound lead gen, bookkeeping, HR management, payroll automation, cyber security, recruiting, are all things they can get access to. And when they're ready they will find you. 

They don't know that 

- Trigify.io can find customers talking about their exact problem

- That negative google reviews can be removed with a proper appeal process 

- That Forbes is more pay to play than you might think

- That the Donut can target newsletter subscribers by income/interest

- That Starbridge can get them a list of governments that have open RFPs. 

So the second thing great outbound campaigns do is present a mechanism they didn't know was possible. 

3. The best outbound campaigns explain the value in taking the next step AND the next step is easy. 

It costs Young Dental $200-$300 to get a dentist to request a sample through Facebook ads. 

With us, it costs ~$40. 

Their campaigns if anything are a time saving / reducing risk of a bad patient experience type offer. Not make more money. And these dentists don't know that these products exist. 

But the call to action being to get a free sample set sent to their office is such a no brainer that they get tons of responses.

Is your Google ads CPA too high?

Here's how to fix it: 

1. Impression Share

→ If it's under 80%, you have a visibility problem. You aren't showing on enough of the searches you bid on. Go to 2.
→ If it's 80% or higher, go to 4.

2. IS Lost (Budget) vs IS Lost (Rank)

→ If budget is bigger, your budget runs out before the day ends. Raise the daily budget by the percentage you're losing, or cut target CPA so the same money buys more clicks. At 30% lost, cut tCPA 20-30%. At 50%, cut it 40-50%.
→ If rank is bigger, go to 3.

3. Quality Score components

→ If expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience all say Below Average, your Ad Rank is too low to enter the auction. Rewrite 2-3 RSAs per ad group and fix landing page relevance.
→ If they're average or better, nothing is broken. You're bidding into keywords further from your core intent, which is what rank loss looks like when you scale. Tighten match types and negatives for efficiency, leave it for volume.

4. CTR

→ If it's below what that campaign normally runs, you have an engagement problem. People see the ad and don't click. Go to 5.
→ If it's at or above, go to 7.

5. Absolute Top Impression Share

→ If it's low, you're sitting at the bottom of the page. Raise bids on the terms that convert.
→ If it's healthy, go to 6.

6. Search term report

→ If they aren't the queries you want, build negatives in three tiers: universal blockers, campaign filters, ad group sculpting. On a takeover that cut CPA 40% in 15 days, negatives were the fastest win.
→ If they're the right queries and nobody clicks, your ad is the problem. Rewrite the RSAs, stop pinning headlines, build out your ad assets. There are 11 and most accounts run 4.

7. Conversion Rate

→ If it's holding steady and CPA is high anyway, go to 8.
→ If it dropped, go to 9.

8. IS Lost (Budget), again

In audits, this is where a conversion problem turns out to be a budget problem.

→ If it's above 0% on tCPA or tROAS, budget loss is inflating your CPCs. $5,000 at a $5 CPC buys 1,000 clicks. At 10% conversion, 100 conversions at a $50 CPA. Halve the target CPA and the same $5,000 buys 2,000 clicks at $2.50. Same conversion rate, 200 conversions, $25 CPA.
→ If it's at 0%, go to 9.

9. Landing page rate, then lead quality

→ If the landing page rate fell, get a page test running and keep one running.
→ If it held and the leads are junk, you're feeding Google the wrong signal. Move your primary conversion down the funnel (qualified lead or booked call), pass it back with the GCLID, and retract spam within 24 hours.

“How did you go off on your own?" 

Here’s how I did it. It doesn't mean this is the “right” way. Just what worked for me. 

1 - Build Your Network Before You Need It

Be active on on social channels and communities where your future clients are. For me, some of those were LinkedIn, Sales Assembly, 30 Minutes to President’s Club, and Women in Sales. You don't need to post everyday. Engage with others' content, sincerely. Get comfy putting what you believe out there for the internet to rip apart. Doesn't have to be a post. Could be comments. You'll get some mean comments. That's ok. You're not for everyone. A lot of the feedback is helpful for pre-empting future client objections. You'll build a network of people who start associating your name with a problem you want your future business to solve. 

2 - Study Great Marketing 

Pay close attention to what stops your scroll. Pay even closer attention to copy that causes you to think differently about your own beliefs and assumptions. I'd argue that Marketing skills matter more than Sales skills when you launch a biz. Who cares if you can close, if you can't open? Study human psychology and perceptual curiosity. Those two things alone will help you avoid sounding like version 239 of companies that already exist. 

3 - Look Within Your Company 

Ever heard the term "intrapreneur"? It's someone who takes initiative to create and drive new ideas inside of their current org. I did this at Challenger when I pitched creating the Chief Evangelist role. It gave me the chance to speak at Sales Kickoffs under the Challenger brand. It helped build my decision confidence that this was something I wanted to do full-time. It was still scary to go off on my own, but less scary because it wasn't a complete unknown. 

4 - Don't Send Generic "Pick Your Brain" Requests to Other Solo Founders

If you want to tap the experience of others, lead with something specific you like that they'e done. Instead instead of asking to pick their brain (painful, not specific, who knows what you're walking into) - be ultra-specific about THE thing you want to more deeply understand. The more specific you are, the more you sound different from everyone else asking for time. It shows you've taken  initiative. Worst case - they say no to a call, but you made it easy for them to shoot you a few thoughts back over email/DM. 

5 - Do Stuff For Free Before You Do It For $$

I know we don't like this one. But, client testimonials and proof are your best friend. You'll work out the kinks in a much lower pressure environment. I did a LOT of stuff for free before I ever started charging. 

I love what I do. It’s hard, at times. I get a lot wrong. I still have a voice in my head that screams, “You’re going to be irrelevant in a year”. There are times when I wonder if I’m not thinking big enough. Usually, when I see others doing bigger, cooler things than I am. But, I’m proud of what I’ve built.

Rooting for you, no matter what path you choose!

What's the best Google ads bidding strategy?

Follow this flowchart:

1. Do you clear the 30-day minimum?

Conversions in the last 30 days, by campaign type:

→ Search: 15
→ Display: 15
→ Shopping: 15
→ PMax: 30
→ Demand Gen: 30-50
→ App: 300

Under the minimum: stop here. Stay on Max Conversions (or Max Conversion Value). Smart bidding has nothing to learn from at that volume. Nothing below this line applies to you yet.

Selling $100K-$1M deals? Manual CPC until you hit 50 conversions a month. High-ticket B2B accounts get wrecked here. They turn on tCPA at 8 conversions a month and wonder why CPA swings week to week.

Over the minimum: go to 2.

2. Do deal sizes vary by more than 3x?

→ No, they sit within about 20% of each other: tCPA. Every conversion is worth roughly the same, so cost per conversion is your metric.
→ Yes, 3x or more: go to 3.

3. Are you uploading dollar values?

→ Not yet: tCPA anyway. tROAS without dollar values is just tCPA with worse reporting.
→ Already uploading (E.g., MQL $50, SQL $250, Closed Deal $10,000 pushed back from the CRM): tROAS. Now Google can move spend toward the clicks that turn into the $10,000 deals.

Note, if you're launching something (influencer, PR, brand), skip the tree. Go manual and target 90% impression share. Coverage on every search the launch creates beats the efficiency you give up.

If you landed on tCPA, here's how to set the bid:
→ Pull your CPA over the last 4 weeks, excluding the last 3-7 days (conversion lag makes recent CPA look worse than it is).
→ Set the target at or above that number. Never below historical at the start. That's the mistake that costs accounts 40%+ of traffic overnight.
→ Want more volume, raise 5-10%. Want more efficiency, lower 5-10%.
→ Wait 1-2 conversion cycles between changes.

If you landed on tROAS, here's how to set the bid:
→ Pull "Conv. value/cost" over the last 4 weeks, excluding the last 3-7 days.
→ Set the target at or below that number.
→ Want more volume, lower 5-10%. Want more efficiency, raise 5-10%.
→ Wait 1-2 conversion cycles.

Note, always check Search Lost IS (Budget). If above 0%: your target is too tight. Your daily budget runs out mid-afternoon, CPCs inflate. Raise the target until lost-to-budget hits zero.

Cheatsheet:
- Deal sizes within 20%: tCPA. Vary 3x or more: tROAS.
- No dollar values flowing back from the CRM: tCPA.
- Raise tCPA to increase volume, and lower tROAS to increase volume
- Get Lost IS (Budget) to 0%

IM8 Health just took $1 billion in rev-share loan

To pay for 70% of their CAC:

- General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund (CVF) doesn't buy equity.
- GC gets no stock and no board seat, and IM8 doesn't dilute.

It's a revenue-share loan:

→ Finances up to 70% of IM8's customer acquisition cost
→ Repaid from "reference income" = revenue from those customers × a fixed gross-margin assumption
→ GC's share is capped, and once the cap is hit they stop getting paid.
→ IM8 scale acquisition without selling equity, and GC only earns if the customers they paid to acquire produce margin.
→ We don't know the covenants, so we can't see what happens if the LTV of a customer falls off

The whole thing is a bet on LTV. IM8's per-customer economics ($PRE, FY25):

→ CAC: $130 (GC will fund about $91 of that)
→ Blended AOV: $110 first order, $233 on the quarterly plan
→ Gross margin: 63% (60% in Q4)
→ Day-1 CAC recovery: ~55%, the rest paid back over the payback window, which now initially will be going to GC
→ Payback: 3.5 months, down from 3.9
→ 24-month LTV:CAC: ~3x
→ ~80% of new customers subscribe
→ FY25 revenue $60.1M, guiding to $180-200M in 2026

I'm sure IM8 will be pulling every LTV lever now to clear that cash even faster.

The way I break LTV down:

LTV = Initial Value + Returning Value

→ Initial Value = units bought × revenue per unit × margin
→ Returning Value = (revenue per unit × units per order × margin) × return rate % × purchase frequency

Most important metrics here are:

1. Return rate %

The share of customers who make purchase #2. IM8's ~80% subscription rate drives it, and that's what carries a break-even first order to a 3x LTV:CAC.

2. Purchase frequency

How often they reorder. It correlates with return rate, so fix one and you often fix both. Quarterly billing already pulls three months of orders forward.

Fascinating times!

Google ads CPC high?

That's a good thing!

I analyzed 4,000+ Google ads over 73 accounts

You pay higher CPCs for deeper conversion events:

- I pulled 73 Google ad accounts
- Grouped by the conversion the bid strategy optimizes to
- Plotted their CPCs
- Marked the median CPC as a bar

Results:
Shallow event (clicks, page views): $1.38
Leads event (forms, calls): $3.48
Deep events (qualified, revenue): $6.65
Here's what's going on:

1. Bid math

→ The most Google can pay for a click is your target CPA multiplied by the conversion rate to that event. Move the event deeper and that conversion rate falls, while the CPA you'll accept rises faster.
→ A $100 lead converting at 3% lets Google pay $3 a click. A $600 qualified lead converting at 1% lets it pay $6.
→ Nothing else about the account changed. You asked for a rarer, more valuable event, and the price of a click followed.

2. Cheap clicks leave the mix

→ At shallow signal Google buys anything that clicks, including the $0.40 clicks from people who will never speak to sales. They drag the median down.
→ Point it at a deep event and it stops entering those auctions. The cheap clicks leave your average, so CPC rises while cost per customer falls.

3. Deep intent is contested

→ The auctions where someone is ready to book, buy, or verify insurance are the ones every serious competitor is bidding on too. That's where the clearing price sits.

Quick caveats:
- This is a cross-section and not a before/after.
- Deep-signal accounts in our mix skew toward healthcare and B2B where CPCs run high regardless, and only 5 accounts sit in the shallow group

I've found the deeper conversion events I send back, the better the CPAs.

So high CPCs are not a bad thing.

I've audited 200+ ABM programs

The biggest predictor of ABM success isn't your ICP, messaging, or your team. 

It’s a financial issue

The first question I always ask:

“Walk me through the math. What are we actually buying here?”

Maybe 5 had a defensible answer.

The ABM programs that get renewed are decided before launch, not after.

Here’s how to set it up correctly:

STEP 1 // BUILD YOUR COST MODEL

Total ABM investment breaks into 3 buckets:

A. Media spend
↳ LinkedIn, CTV, programmatic, direct mail
↳ Budget $150-300 per target account per month for air cover
↳ 100 accounts = $15K-$30K/month minimum

B. Tech stack
↳ Intent data, ABM platform, enrichment tools
↳ Annualize and divide by # of programs

C. People cost
↳ % of SDR, marketing, ops time dedicated to ABM
↳ Burdened salary × time allocation

Add all three = Total Program Cost

STEP 2 // MODEL YOUR EXPECTED PIPELINE

Formula:
Target Accounts × Expected Engagement Rate × Meeting Conversion × Opp Conversion × Avg Deal Size = Expected Pipeline

Example with real math:
↳ 100 accounts
↳ 25% engagement rate (25 engaged accounts)
↳ 40% meeting conversion (10 meetings)
↳ 70% opp conversion (7 opportunities)
↳ $75K avg deal size
= $525K in pipeline

STEP 3 // CALCULATE PROGRAM ROI

Pipeline ROI = Expected Pipeline / Total Program Cost

If your program costs $50K and generates $525K in pipeline:
↳ Pipeline ROI = 10.5x

But leadership cares about closed revenue, not pipeline.

Revenue ROI = (Expected Pipeline × Historical Close Rate) / Total Program Cost

↳ $525K × 30% close rate = $157.5K expected revenue
↳ $157.5K / $50K = 3.15x revenue ROI

STEP 4 // BUILD THE SENSITIVITY TABLE

This is what separates amateurs from operators.

Show leadership 3 scenarios:
↳ Conservative: 20% engagement, 25% close rate
↳ Base case: 25% engagement, 30% close rate
↳ Aggressive: 35% engagement, 35% close rate

Map each scenario to pipeline and revenue ROI.

When leadership asks "what if it doesn't work?" you already have the answer.

STEP 5 // TIE TO EXISTING BENCHMARKS

Pull your historical data:
↳ What's your current cost-per-opportunity from other channels?
↳ What's your average CAC payback?
↳ What's your LTV:CAC ratio by segment?

Show how ABM compares. If your current CPO is $8K and ABM delivers at $7.1K, that's the story.

The pitch isn't "ABM is cool." The pitch is "ABM delivers pipeline at a lower CPO than our current mix."

Programs that launch with this model don't get cut at month 9.
They get expanded.

→ Freedom: "what would you do with an extra $40K/month?"
→ Status: "this is what 3x ROAS looks like at scale"
→ Triggers: ambition, envy, possibility

3. Social Proof
→ Testimony: "we switched from X and cut CPA by 34% in 2 weeks"
→ Authority: "10,000 DTC brands use this. here's why"
→ Relatability: "I was skeptical too. then I saw our Q4 numbers"
→ Triggers: trust, FOMO, validation

3x Formats:

1. Static
→ 60-70% of conversions for most brands I manage
→ Smartphone-quality beats studio 84% of the time in Stories
→ Fastest to produce, easiest to iterate. Test 10 statics in the time it takes to shoot 1 video
→ Use when the value is immediately visible (fashion, jewelry, food)

2. Video
→ First 3 seconds decide everything. I track hook rate (3-sec views / impressions) religiously
→ Below 25% hook rate? Kill it. 30-40% is good. Above 40%? Scale it
→ Partnership Ads (running from creator's handle) = 53% lower CAC
→ Use when the customer needs to believe it before they buy (skincare, supplements, transformations)
→ Quick rule: if they need to SEE IT, run statics. If they need to BELIEVE IT, run video.

3. Carousel
→ Best for education-heavy products and comparison selling
→ Card 1 hooks with a problem or question, not your product
→ Average swipe-through on a good carousel is 1.4x higher engagement than single image
→ Use when the buyer needs to understand WHY before they buy

(If Carousels don’t apply to your brand, insert animated statics, GIFs, or another format)

3x Funnel Levels

1. Top of Funnel (they don't know you)
→ Lead with a problem, bold claim, or pattern interrupt
→ 80% of your creative volume should live here

2. Mid Funnel (they've seen you, they're comparing)
→ Education, competitor comparisons, "why us" content
→ Carousels and founder stories work hardest here

3. Bottom Funnel (they're warm, they need a push)
→ Offers, urgency, risk removal, testimonials with CTA overlays
→ Bundles + Free gifts work really well here

And then you multiply them

TOF x Static x Pain Point = text graphic about a problem they have
MOF x Video x Social Proof = UGC testimonial walkthrough
BOF x Carousel x Desire = transformation story with offer on last card

That's 3 combinations there.

There are a total of 27.
- 3 angles x 3 formats x 3 funnels stages

I audited a Y Combinator startup's Google Ads

What I found & what you can steal:

1. Brand mixed with non-brand

→ Brand and generic keywords sat in the same campaign. Brand converts cheap because those people already know you, so it drags the average down and makes your non-brand CPA look better than it is.
→ Split brand into its own campaign from day one. Then you can see what new customers actually cost.

2. Cheap CPA on the wrong action

→ Cost per signup was ~$10. For B2B SaaS, that number is far too low. A qualified conversion in B2B SaaS should cost $100+.
→ Fire on the aha moment instead. E.g., a second use of the product, because the first one happens automatically at signup.
→ If you can't move the event, add friction to signup.

3. Broad match on new accounts

→ Broad match lets Google decide who sees your ads. Point that at a signup conversion and it goes and finds you more people who sign up and never buy.
→ The sequence: exact match only → build conversion volume → move the conversion action down funnel → open phrase → then broad.

4. Top-clicked keyword

→ One of the highest-click keywords was "free AI use". This doesn't make sense for a paid product.
→ Review search terms weekly. I have AI score every term 1 to 10 on relevance, then I review the low scores myself.
→ Don't add too many negatives as you'll restrict the account.

5. Ad group structure

→ Over 30+ keywords sat in one ad group, forcing the same ad copy to appear across completely different keywords and intent
→ Example: someone searching "landing page builder" wants something different than someone searching "website builder".
→ Group by intent, then write copy per group.

6. Ad copy at half strength

→ Google gives you 15 headlines and 4 descriptions. The account used a fraction of them.
→ Missing assets: business name, logo, callouts, structured snippets. Sitelinks were solid but had no descriptions.

You can boil all the above down to 2 bullets:
- Every fix was campaign structure, conversion action, or match type.
- Always optimize for the highest quality conversion signal possible

Is your bad Google ads rank increasing CPA?

I analyzed 441 campaigns across 68 accounts:

Every dot on the chart is one of 441 non-brand Search campaigns.

→ X axis = how much impression share each one loses to rank, from under 20% to over 60%
→ Y axis = its CPA, indexed to that account's own average, so 1.00 is a normal cost for that account
→ The black bar in each column is the group's median CPA

Results

→ Under 20% lost to rank: 1.00
→ 20 to 40%: 1.39
→ 40 to 60%: 1.27
→ Over 60%: 1.07

If losing rank was costing you, the over-60% group would be the most expensive.

This shows 'bad rank' = higher search lost to rank does NOT mean worse CPA.

And the standard advice is a high Search Lost IS (rank) means your bids are too low, so raise them to win those impressions back.

That's not completely true. This is what you should do instead:

1. Budget loss first
→ Search Lost IS (Budget) above 0% means your daily budget dies before the day ends. Fix that before rank, you already paid to win those auctions.
→ Rank loss while budget loss sits at 0% means you're holding auctions back to protect CPA, which is the point.

2. Index CPA to account
→ Divide each campaign's CPA by your account average. 1.00 is dead on typical. In my pull the over-60% rank-loss bucket landed at 1.07.
→ A campaign losing rank while converting at target is a scaling candidate. Raise budget or tCPA on purpose.

3. Read search terms
→ Pull the term report before buying rank. The impressions you're losing are usually broad, low-intent queries you don't want anyway.
→ Median CPA in the 20 to 40% bucket was 1.39, so the mid-rank-loss campaigns cost the most, above even the worst-rank bucket.

4. Split Exact vs broad IS
→ Compare Search Exact Match IS to overall IS. Exact at 90% while overall sits at 40% means your money keywords already win.
→ The gap is broad-match volume you can negative out instead of bidding up.

5. Raise bids on purpose
→ Only lift bids when a campaign converts under target and budget loss is 0%. Then the lost rank is real headroom.
→ Move in 20 to 30% steps and watch CPA hold before the next push.

Rank loss when you're scaling is normal.

Budget loss is the one that actually costs you.

Want higher converting Google ads?

How to get high intent clicks:

Low-quality clicks come from two places:
- Who you let into the auction
- What signal you train Google on

Follow this order to fix both:

1. Negative keywords

→ A negative keyword blocks your ad from any search containing that word.
→ Example, we want to exclude terms with words like "free," "jobs," "login," "DIY," "template" etc.
→ Pull the search term report 2-3x a week. Score every term 0-10 for relevance and block the 0-2s. Add campaign-specific junk at ad group level and universal junk at MCC level (high-spend accounts run 30,000+ negatives).
→ We run this with AI. It flags 500-700 terms a run against the 20 you would catch by hand.

2. Match type discipline

→ Exact match first. Phrase once Exact clears 15+ conversions a month. Broad only after Smart Bidding is mature and tracking is clean.
→ Google gives you two impression share numbers. Search IS covers every auction it made you eligible for, loose broad matches included. Exact Match IS covers only the searches that match your keywords.
→ Read them together for example: if Search IS 40%, Exact Match IS 90%. Your keywords are solid. The gap is broad-match junk, so negative it out instead of raising budget to chase it.

3. Location set to Presence

→ Switch location targeting from "presence or interest" to "presence" only.
→ Otherwise you pay for people who searched about your city even though they're not there

4. Suppression audiences

→ Exclude the people who cannot buy from you. Existing customers, out-of-area, ineligible insurance, self-serve searchers on an enterprise offer.
→ On rehab accounts, insurance and level-of-care qualifiers cut unqualified volume 30-40%.
→ These exclusions are for people who literally cannot buy. Everywhere else, stay in observation mode and let Google find the buyers.

5. Conversion signal

→ If Google is optimizing for form fills, it sources cheap form fills. The auction gives you exactly what you asked for.
→ Move your primary conversion as far down funnel as you can while holding 30-50 conversions a month. Qualified lead or booked call, passed back through GCLID.

→ Retract spam and disqualified leads within 24 hours.

Hope this helps

When should you give free shipping?

How to decide:

1. Weights & cutoffs

→ Carriers price in weight steps, and the step is where your margin gets eaten.
→ Example: shipping jumps from $3 to $5.50 as you cross 0.99 lbs.
→ Naturally, selling heavier things requires more expensive shipping = higher thresholds

2. Contribution margin per order

→ First-order contribution = AOV - COGS - shipping - processing - CAC.
→ Also need to account for LTV and payback period and how much you want to lose in margin on the first order

3. What the customer already expects to pay

→ Someone buying 85lb of weights knows it costs money to ship
→ Someone buying a $30 supplement expects the box to show up free. Sweet spot there is $50-75.

With this you can engineer your free shipping tiers:

1. Histogram your AOVs. Plot them against your shipping provider's weight cutoffs.
2. Find where the cost spikes.
3. Engineer the lower-tier bundle to land just under that limit.
4. For the tier above, skip the weight that sits just over the line and design the bundle heavy enough that the added revenue absorbs the higher shipping cost, dropping shipping as a percentage of total revenue.
5. Set your threshold just above your average AOV so it pulls people into the optimized bundle.

Shipping is one of the few lines in a DTC P&L you can engineer down without touching CAC or COGS.

Hope this helps

In 2022 I started my own business. Within 9 months I was earning $10k+/mo. But my relationship with money suffered, because:

I started seeing money as a game.

I'd look at my Stripe numbers month to month and the number would be going up and up incrementally each month.

And I'd think "okay i beat last month, i can breath now".

This pretty much went on like this for the first 2-3 years of running my business. Fortunately, each month was getting better and better for 2 years. And by the end of 2023 I was doing anywhere between $30k - $50k every month. My business absolutely smashing it.

But then I started having months where it wasn't better than last.

And tbh, I struggled to handle that.

I thought I was doing something wrong or I was on a slippery slope. Obviously a business should be growing and I absolutely could've done more or better to make sure it continued growing. But that isn't how life goes for a small business like mine. I do this all myself and I love that, too.

So when the month before wasn't as good, I'd freak out a bit. I'd get all down etc. My wife would call me out on it often but I never really listened to her.

It took me a good year or two to get over this and realise that a business doesn't just grow and grow and grow, especially month to month. 

Yearly, yeah, sure. 

But even that, I'm not in a business model where my revenue needs to or should be growing year to year. My business is built around my life and it provides me the cash to go and live my life how I want to in a comfortable way. 

That's what's most important to me.

Nowadays, my months fluctuate a lot:

- $10k one month
- $40k another
- $25k the next

And I can happily say it doesn't bother me.

Because I know exactly what I can do to make more money and scale to $1M or $2M.

I'm just not prepared to do some of those things.

I'm not in the game of hyper scaling or hiring a team.

I'm in the game of getting clients I want to work with and love working with and working with them in a way that fits my life.

I'm not in the game of working 6am to 9pm. Or travelling to events just to do some brown nosing with people I don't know.

I'm in the game of watching my daughter grow up every single day and spending as much time as possible with my wife, that I chose to spend my life with.

My advice to new business owners out there:

You will have good months. You will have bad months.

It's part of the game.

Growth is not linear.

And most importantly:

Grow the business that serves YOU. Not someone else.

Does Meta always choose the best ad?

And how do you know when it's wrong?

- I analyzed 1702 ad sets.
- Each ad set had 5+ ads
- Meta predicts the best ad, begins spending, but doesn't always stick with it

Results (from day 1 to day 4)
- No. 1 ad continues to be top ad 64% of the time
- No. 4 ad continues to be fourth ad 60% of the time
- No. 2 and 3. ad have roughly the same chance, X%, of becoming top ad

This helps you make more informed decisions (with of course some level of risk)

Deciding on day 1 data

→ You can turn ads on / off change budgets, but it's low confidence
→ Only act on big outliers, or make small adjustments (10-15% budget max)
→ Fold in pacing from the current day (call it day 1.5) before you touch anything

Holding for day 2 and 3

→ Hold most changes for here unless there's an extreme outlier
→ This is where the eventual winner separates from the pack
→ Let Meta finish sorting before you scale or cut

What counts as an extreme outlier:

1. Flip signal

→ Top ad doing very poorly, a lower-budget ad crushing it
→ A strong sign the ad set is about to flip
→ Force it early instead of waiting on Meta

2. Dead ad set

→ Top ad poor and the whole ad set poor (e.g. 5x CPA, 0 conversions)
→ Nothing in here is going to turn around
→ Start trimming budget now

Most of the time the answer is to wait for more data to come in.

Is your email agency doing a good job?

Ask for these metrics weekly:

1. Revenue per signup
→ Total lifecycle revenue divided by active signups, month over month.
→ Up means the program is compounding. Down while signups grow means the newer signups aren't buying.

2. Welcome flow
→ Conversion rate, revenue, and opens on the last email in the flow.
→ Opens holding on that last email means people are still reading. Revenue up but opens down means promos got added to hit the number.

3. Win-back and retention
→ Repeat purchase rate and revenue per recipient, 60 days post purchase.
→ Repeat rate climbing means retention is working. Flat while sends go up means you're over-mailing for the same revenue.

4. Replenishment
→ Reorder rate and time to reorder.
→ Shorter time to reorder and a higher reorder rate means the timing is right.

5. Campaign mix
→ Number of sends, promo vs non-promo split, and revenue per campaign as a percent of total.
→ 100% promo is the warning sign. Watch the non-promo share.

6. List health
→ Engaged vs unengaged counts, the 90-day repeat-opener pattern, bounces and complaints.
→ If this month's openers are a shrinking slice of last month's, engagement is declining. Fix it before revenue drops.

This will only give you a high level view.

How to maximize Google ads testing velocity

With 100s of AI-landing pages:

→ Every keyword carries a specific intent. When the page headline answers that intent, conversion rate goes up and CPA comes down.
→ Quality Score reads landing page experience, so a congruent page lowers CPCs
→ Goal is to create bespoke landing pages per keyword intent to lower CPA

1. Account structure first

→ Split campaigns into Brand, Competitor and Non-Brand. Brand under 20%, Competitor around 10-20%, Non-Brand takes the rest
→ Build ad groups around one keyword theme each. A page can't align to an ad group carrying 40 unrelated keywords.
→ Move the primary conversion action as deep as possible, ideally qualified lead or booked call, passed back with the GCLID.

2. Diagnose congruency

→ Pull every ad group by spend and put its top keyword next to the headline of the page it lands on. Compare and evaluate how closely they match intent
→ Read the Landing Page Experience column in Google Ads. "Below average" is Google's diagnostic that the page doesn't match the query
→ Compare conversion rate by ad group. If you see a wide conversion rate range and you know the keywords have intent, then it's likely you need to break the pages out

3. Connect Ploy to Google Ads

→ OAuth into the account, pick the workspace scope, turn it on.
→ Ploy reads cost-per-conversion back from Google Ads, so it ranks which pages need work
→ It flags message-match gaps between the ad copy and the page, then rewrites the page.
→ Tags and UTMs stay consistent across every page it ships, so reporting doesn't break mid-test.

4. One lander per ad group

Point it at the keyword clusters and it builds a page per ad group

→ Headline mirrors the keyword theme.
→ Add trust block near the fold: testimonials, certifications, team bios.
→ Add location-specific elements wherever delivery is geo-based.
→ Add relevant features / benefits and objection handling blocks that match the query

What it bought us:
- Enrolled clients get 2-5x more landing page tests than before
- Cost to spin up new landing pages down by 80%
- Higher testing velocity

Can you have a 6.0 MER & be failing?

Yes. And it's more common than you think...

Look at these two metrics:
- aMER = new customer revenue / total marketing spend
- nCAC = total marketing spend / new customers

Four brand types I see again and again:

1. Retention coasters

Metrics
- $120M revenue, $20M spend
- MER 6.0, aMER 1.3, nCAC $182
- 78% of revenue is repeat

→ Diagnose: big gap between MER and aMER, repeat revenue above 70%, new customer count flat or falling.
→ What's happening: returning customers are carrying revenue.
→ Fix: rebuild prospecting. New hooks for cold traffic, an aMER floor you don't drop below, and a lower blended MER for a quarter.

2. Leaky bucket

Metrics
- $14M revenue, $6M spend
- MER 2.3, aMER 2.1, nCAC $41
- 10% of revenue is repeat

→ Diagnose: MER barely above aMER, 90-day repeat rate near zero, email and SMS revenue share near zero.
→ What's happening: customers buy once and never come back.
→ Fix: retention before scale. Post-purchase flows, a subscription offer, a second-order bundle. Email should be doing 25-40% of revenue.

3. Too efficient to grow

Metrics
- $38M revenue, $4.5M spend
- MER 8.4, aMER 4.6, nCAC $32
- Marketing is 12% of revenue

→ Diagnose: flat revenue with rising MER, spend only 12% of revenue, marginal CAC far below breakeven.
→ What's happening: the brand can afford far more customers than it's buying.
→ Fix: spend into it. Raise budgets until marginal aMER hits breakeven, and judge the account on new customer volume and total profit not just profit margin.

4. Scaling past breakeven

Metrics

- $150M revenue, $95M spend
- MER 1.6, aMER 0.9, nCAC $238
- 45% of revenue is repeat

→ Diagnose: MER below 2, aMER below 1, first-order contribution negative, payback past 12 months.
→ What's happening: the brand is buying customers it can't afford.
→ Fix: cut the worst 20-30% of spend, reset to the efficient core, then rebuild scale through creative testing.

MER measures efficiency.
aMER and nCAC measure whether you're acquiring anyone.

- MER high, aMER low = living off the existing customer base
- MER and aMER almost identical = no repeat business to live off
- Both high with flat revenue = underspending
- aMER under 1 = buying customers at a loss

I looked at over 2,196 email campaigns to try to define what a "cold traffic offer" really is. 

Everyone says you need a "cold traffic offer" to make outbound work, but what does that actually mean? 

It's a great suggestion but defining it as just "an offer that converts cold traffic" is difficult to wrap your head around. 

So I looked at every campaign in our Smartlead account to try to define it so we could have a framework to work from. 

Please challenge me on this as I'm trying to clarify the meaning of this in public. 

Every campaign that crushed had a mix of 5 pillars. Some had all 5 some only had 1 but they all had some kind of mix. 

1) Offers come in 6 shapes 

Raise Status -> (B2C)
Live Longer -> (B2C)
Reduce Risk -> for some reason no one cares cold

Make More Money -> the king of all cold offers

Save Money/Save Time -> these two can work but they must be orders of magnitudes of savings. Think a verifiable 90% saving. 

Guarantees help here and I debate making that it's own category vs. just being in the offer.

2) Unique Mechanism

I think the biggest reason outbound is working less and less isn't the amount of volume in people's inboxes. It's that they have so much more access to great knowledge. They know what exists.  

We ran a LinkedIn event with a loophole that got us 4,000 registrants in a week. Before the loophole closed, we sold it as a playbook we would implement.

We used that to pitch and say we could help them book calls just like we did. Nothing special in the offer at all. Just the fact we did it using a strategy they hadn't heard of before is what hooked them. 

3) Next Steps are Easy/Valuable

Lead magnets can go here but even just an explanation of why is a call worth their time or an easy next step for them to follow like a free trial sign up. 

We have some campaigns that don't even have the full offer of the company and are just sending out free samples of B2B physical products and our campaigns crush their facebook ads cost. 

We are just asking if they want a free sample sent their way and then the sales team follows up 7 days after shipment to discuss the product. 

4) Well Researched Segmentation

It would be like selling refrigerators door to door if you emailed companies and ask if they needed their parking lots redone. 

But using AI to estimate the ones that are old based on color/how much splitting/potholes are in the lot. 

Credit to Jordan Crawford for the work here

5) Relevant Social Proof 

I could just email martech cos, "I built Clay's first outbound channel and set up the initial playbook for content marketing. Do you want to talk?"

Here's the key though. Tell that to someone in Public Relations and it completely falls flat.

In 2020, I met my wife living in the UK. But 12 months later, we moved to Cyprus. Here's what I got wrong about living in another country:

I met my wife around September 2020.

We went on some dates and very quickly moved in with each other.

Around March 2021, we both started talking about how we'd love to move abroad and live in another country.

It was random. 

We just found it out about each other.

I'd always had this idea in my head that I'd be retired and living in Spain somewhere by the time I was 40 or 50. For some reason I'd had that in my head since I was young.

Turns out she had a very similar thing.

Then it became apparent her mum had a flat in Cyprus that was empty. No one was living in it. She said we could go and use it.

Off we popped for a 2 week holiday in July.

We came back and we loved it.

Handed in our notices in August. Moved there by October.

When I told my parents it was a mixed reaction. Happy for us, because it sounded exciting. Apprehensive, because I was quitting my job and they're my parents and they worry about my security.

I'm not even sure they thought we'd stay. 

I think they had it in their head that we'd go and see what it was like, realise we don't actually like not living in England and come back.

But here's what I got wrong about living in another country:

I assumed anywhere else you lived, it'd just be like living on a holiday.

It's not. 

- You wake up
- have your breakfast
- do some work
- watch some TV
- go for a coffee
- go for lunch

You're doing pretty much the same stuff you'd do anywhere else, just in a different location.

The beach, the bar overlooking the sea, the piña colada, that's your spare time. That's a few hours.

You are really just the same no matter where you live.

So it's the day-to-day stuff that matters most.

What makes this feel like home isn't anything to do with being back home. It's the little things.

I can walk in the morning under a bright blue sky and it's not freezing. I don't have to push myself out the door because it's grey and raining.

I can park wherever I want, right outside the front door, for as long as I want, and I'm very unlikely to get a ticket.

A sunbed on the beach is €2.50. Somewhere else it's €30.

Less going on in my head, every day. 

That's what makes somewhere home.

I use this McKinsey & Company framework to run ads

It's how you can diagnose any high CPA:

It's called MECE. 
- MECE = Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive
- McKinsey built it to break any problem into a tree.
- Mutually exclusive: every branch is separate, so no cause gets counted twice.
- Collectively exhaustive: the branches cover everything, so no cause can hide outside the tree.

In an ad account, the tree is your funnel. CPA sits at the bottom and every node above it feeds in. 

1. Forecast every node

→ CPC, CTR, click-to-cart CVR, cart-to-purchase CVR, CAC, AOV, ROAS. Write the number you expect for each one before you spend a dollar.
→ Do it per channel. Google non-brand, Google brand, PMax, Meta prospecting, retargeting. 

2. Pace actuals against forecast

→ You forecast CPC at $5 and it comes in at $10. That gap is your constraint.
→ The first node that diverges is the problem. Everything downstream of it is a symptom.
→ If there's no forecast on the account, run the same funnel across the last 18 months and find the week the trend broke.

3. Walk up node by node

Example: 

→ An ad account we run had cost per checkout initiated sitting around $10 for months, then it doubled inside a single week and stayed there.
→ Cost per app install jumped on the same date, roughly $2.50 up to $4
→ One node further up, CPC spiked and CTR tanked, same week again
→ Budget was flat and the change log showed no edits that month

4. Rule out until one survives

→ Hypotheses on the table: new creative, a targeting change, creative fatigue, brand fatigue, a landing page edit, a price drop
→ A price drop doesn't move CTR or CPC, so that's out
→ No edits in the change log rules out targeting and landing page
→ CTR falling on its own leaves creative fatigue as the most likely problem

5. Fix one node

→ You now have the node, the date it broke, and the cause. 
→ If the node recovers, the diagnosis was right. If it doesn't, you've eliminated a branch and you go again.

Cheatsheet:
- Forecast the full funnel per channel before you launch
- The first gap between forecast and actual is your constraint
- Diagnose upward, one node at a time
- Change one thing, then read the same node again

Are your ads lumpy?

They should be to scale:

Account A

→ 40 ads, $200k/month, 1 concept
→ Every ad collapses into a single spike on the similarity curve
→ If ad #1 fatigues, the whole account dies off

Account B

→ 40 ads, $200k/month, 5 angles across 3 formats
→ Four separate lumps on the same curve
→ Top ad might fatigue, but the other three lumps keep spending

Real recent consulting client story:
- Had a high spend ad running at a normal ROAS.
- It was driving new customer awareness, and it very clearly lifted every other row of the account.
- That ad suddenly and very quickly fatigued
- Then every other ad fatigued with it

How to check your ad similarity:

- Pull your last 90 days of ads and read the first 3 seconds of each transcript
- Count how many distinct selling points you actually have (at $200k/month you want 5+)
- Count your formats and your hook variations
- If your top 5 ads share an angle then you're in risky territory

- Make your ads more lumpy

I'm using AI on $70M+ of Google Ads:

There are 3 ways to correctly delegate:

1. Fully autonomous

→ The task is well-defined and the answer comes straight from the data.
→ Human judgment changes nothing at execution.

Example:
→ RSA ad copy. The agent writes 15 headlines off the search terms report. We’re very close to this becoming fully autonomous (just fixing some edge cases)

2. Agent-primary, human-closing

→ Agent does all the work
→ Human steps in for final review and alterations

Example:
→ Negative keyword mining. Our AI tool found 2,500 negatives on one account and cost $2.40 to run. Reviewing all 2,500 manually takes days and delays results.

3. Agent-amplified judgment

→ The human owns the decision.
→ The agent surfaces the signals and risks.

Example:
→ Flags. The agent flagged spend jumping from $7k to $30k in a day with no changes made, and showed me where the overspend was going. I decide what action to take.

Cheatsheet for which one to use:

→ Fully autonomous → low stakes, easy decision making
→ Agent-primary, human-closing → high volume to produce, but final decision needs review
→ Agent-amplified judgment → decision / judgment is nuanced and has higher stakes

I got anxious that we were leaving data on the table, so we ran six approaches against each other to find local business owners.

Smartlead Email Finder. Prospeo. Blitz API. Exa. Parallel.ai. And an open source website scrape with HTML2Text, validated by Gemma 4 running locally on my own machine.

The winner was the boring one. Scrape the site, scrape Google, let a local model read both.

Which makes sense when you think about what you would tell a human to do. If you handed an intern a list of 100 plumbing companies and said go find who owns each one, they would open the website and they would Google it. We just automated exactly that.

The order we actually run it in:

1. Check Blitz and Prospeo first. If somebody states on LinkedIn that they own this business and links this website, that fidelity is worth paying for and you should not give it up.
2. If those miss, scrape the site. HTML2Text converts the page to text, then Gemma 4 crawls the about, team, contact, and footer pages looking for an owner name and any on page email. This leg is free because the model runs locally.
3. If that misses, search "who owns [business] in [city]" through OpenWeb Ninja, including the AI overview, and parse it with Gemma again.

To be clear about cost, because "free" gets thrown around too easily. The website scrape leg is genuinely free. OpenWebNinja is paid, and it is cheap. The LinkedIn based providers are paid. We spend $6M/mo on Google Ads.

Here's our Demand Gen checklist:

1. Consolidate for Data Density, Segment by Audience. Do not split Ad Groups by placement (YouTube vs. Discover). Demand Gen is designed to be cross-channel; forcing a placement "chokes" the AI’s ability to find the cheapest conversion across the ecosystem. Instead, use Ad Groups to segment by Audience Theme (e.g., Top 25 Search Terms vs. 2% Lookalikes). This keeps your data signals concentrated in one place while allowing you to see which buyer persona is actually biting.

2. Check image AND video asset quantity. Ads & assets > Assets. You need variety in both formats. We've seen 20% more conversions running image and video together vs video only.

3. Check headline and description variety. Campaigns > Demand Gen > Ads > Headlines and descriptions. Demand Gen serves across YouTube, Gmail, and Discover. Each placement renders differently. You need variety.

4. Check view-through conversion tracking. Demand Gen drives view-throughs that Search doesn't. We value them at ~30% of click-through. If you're not tracking them, you're undervaluing the entire campaign.

5. Segment device performance. Campaigns > Demand Gen > Segment > Device. Demand Gen skews mobile because of Gmail and Discover. I've seen mobile CPA run 3x worse than desktop. And other times where mobile significantly outperforms.

6. Review your bid strategy. Settings > Campaign settings > Columns > Bid strategy. For Demand Gen, start target CPA at 2x your Search CPA. CPCs are cheap ($0.09 vs $7+ on Search) but conversion rates are lower. Give the algorithm room to learn.

7. If running product ads, check feed health. Google Merchant Center > Products > Diagnostics. Disapproved products mean your ads don't serve for those items.

8. Set your budget for a "Conversion Floor." While the "15x tCPA" rule is great for rapid scaling, it’s often unrealistic for high-CPA accounts. At a minimum, aim for a daily budget that supports 1–2 conversions per day. If your Target CPA is $200, a $300–$400 daily budget is your "efficiency floor." It will take longer to exit the "Learning Phase" than a $3,000/day budget, but it prevents the algorithm from overspending on low-quality placements while it searches for a baseline.

9. Build custom segments from your top 25 converting Search terms. Audiences > Audience manager > Segments. You're reaching people before they search. That's the whole point of Demand Gen.

10. Confirm auto-tagging is on. Settings > Account settings > Auto-tagging. Without it you lose conversion and view-through data between Ads and Analytics.

11. Retract bad leads within 24 hours. This matters more on Demand Gen because the audience pool is broader.

This is 11 out of 31 items we check on every Demand Gen launch.

One wrong setting can burn thousands before you catch it.

You should spend past your marginal break-even ROAS

This is why:

- Take a 60% contribution margin account.
- Break-even ROAS = 1 / 0.60 = 1.67x.

Your ROAS drops as you spend more:
→ $50k/month at 3.0x = $150k revenue
→ $200k/month at 2.5x = $500k revenue
→ $500k/month at 2.0x = $1M revenue

Go from $200k to $500k. You spend $300k more and get $500k back. That extra spend ran at 1.67x.

Your blended ROAS reads 2.0x. Your last dollar (marginal) ran at 1.67x. That dollar broke even.

On this account, 2.0x blended is the break-even point despite 2.0 being profitable.

I still spend past it. Notes 2/3 people often skip.

1. LTV
→ On this account a customer costs $33 to acquire ($55 AOV × 60% margin at break-even).
→ At 3:1 LTV:CAC that $33 buys $100 of lifetime value, with sub-3-month payback.
→ Moving subscription rate 30% → 40% and churn 10% → 7% lifts that LTV ~90%, to $190.

2. Learnings
→ Every dollar past break-even funds a test.
→ Only 10-15% of ads beat target and only top 1-2% end up driving 50% of spend.
→ You find those winners by running more tests, which happens faster when past break even.
→ Every winner fatigues in 45-60 days. You need new tests running to replace it.

3. Impressions
→ 99% of impressions don't convert in a conversion window when you pay for them.
→ Strong ads build awareness. Those viewers come back and buy at 30, 60 and 90 days.
→ We've seen strong top funnel, converting ads on client accounts hold up the rest of the account and increase ROAS for everything else.
→ Scaling bast marginal profit today means more impressions on strong ads that build awareness for next week/month/year.

4. Tracking
→ Marginal ROAS is a great number to understand but practically impossible to track
→ It changes daily and so yesterdays data is helpful to know but not necessarily predictive

Summary:
- The blended ROAS you actually break even at is higher than your break even ROAS
- Dollars past that point buy LTV, test winners and delayed revenue
- Only spend them if your cash can carry it (and you have the LTV to support it)
- Otherwise, try to understand your marginal ROAS and underspend breakeven ROAS to maximize Profit in the short term.

How to max out your AOV:

It all starts with the initial price of your product.

Example: $5 Toothpaste

1. Premium pricing

→ In a commodity category you can charge a premium
→ The realistic ceiling is about 4-5x the category average
→ So your $5 toothpaste becomes a $20 product.

2. The multi-pack limit

→ You can sell more than one unit
→ In practice that's 3 to 5 units per order
→ 5 units x $20 = $100. Push past that and conversion rate will likely drop off

3. The upsell

→ Bolt on one complementary product or a discounted gift
→ Expect roughly half your buyers to take it, for another $10-30
→ Call it +$20 blended across the whole order

So for a $5 product, your max AOV is likely:
→ ($20 x 5 units) + $20 upsell = $120

Once you're near that number, squeezing AOV harder is wasted effort.

The better lever is retention.

Cheatsheet:
→ Note your category's average price
→ Calculate / find your category's premium price
→ Determine your total multi-pack limit
→ Add an upsell amount
→ Calculate your max AOV
→ Get as close as possible
→ Then move all of your focus to keeping the customer

How to manage cost/bid cap Meta campaigns

You need to stay right side of the slope:

You have two dials to achieve high scale and low CPA.
- Moving budget up or down
- Moving bid up or down

If you're under budget:
→ Want better performance? Bid down, budget flat.
→ Want more scale? Bid up, budget the same.
→ Want to scale hard? Push both.

The moment you ARE hitting your budget, the bid is how you protect efficiency:
→ Performance meh? Budget up, bid down.
→ Performance good? Budget up, increase the bid a bit.
→ Performance strong? Budget up, bid up. Let it rip.

When making local business lead lists, once you have the owner's name, you don't need a fancy email finder to find their email most of the time.

Many email finders are doing the same thing under the hood. They take a name and a domain and runs permutations. john@, johnsmith@, jsmith@, john.smith@.

So if you already know the owner is John Smith and the site is johnsplumbing.com, you can just run the permutation yourself and check whether the mailbox exists.

And when you cannot get a personal address, use the generic email on the site. 

If we found the owner's name but no personal address, we email info@ and open with "Hey John." Depending on the size of the business, they'll be reading it. 

If we could not even find the name, we email info@ and open with "Hey there." That still works for us. Not as well, but well enough to keep in the sequence.

I know there is a reflex that info@ is a dead end and it goes to a black hole. For local businesses that is mostly not true. At a plumbing company or a dental office, the person reading info@ is frequently the owner, their spouse, or the one office manager who will walk it over to them.

We are running this exact process right now for a company targeting dentists. Over 100 leads in one month.

For local lead gen targeting, the generic inbox is one of the most underrated assets you have

If you scrape Google Maps for "funeral homes" you'll actually will miss most of the funeral homes you're looking to collect.

This is the part of local list building that breaks everyone's list and I almost never see it talked about.

Google Maps businesses are found by their category, and the category is chosen by the business, not by you. So a funeral home might list itself as a funeral home. Or it might list itself as a memorial park. Or a cremation service, or a mortuary, or a cemetery.

Search one category and you get a slice. You will think you have the market. You have maybe a third of it.

Same thing with restaurants. There is no useful "restaurant" category. There is American restaurant, Mediterranean restaurant, French restaurant, Chinese restaurant, and on and on.

Same with HVAC. Half of them call themselves general contractors. Some are under heating. Some are under air conditioning. Plenty do both and picked one.

When you're building local business databases, Open Maps, look up 10 businesses you know are in your market, and write down what each one actually calls itself. 

Then run every category search across every zip code.

And then clean it, because "memorial park" will absolutely return actual parks. We pull the homepage with HTML2Text and have a local model read it to confirm the company is the kind of company we wanted. That part runs on my own computer and costs nothing.

This will significantly increase the TAM you can reach out to. 

I have a full list of google maps data in my cold outbound skills repo if anyone wants it as well.

Just analyzed 3,900 Google ads across 65 accounts.

Ad Strength is NOT correlated with CPA:

- Ad Strength = Google's Poor to Excellent on responsive search ads
- Grades headline volume, keyword relevance, asset uniqueness & pinning

For every ad:
- Measured its CPA against the account
- 1.0 = best CPA in account
- 0.5 = average
- Then grouped by Ad Strength and looked at the average rank

→ Poor: 0.48 average (n=492 ads)
→ Average: 0.51 (n=684 ads)
→ Good: 0.51 (n=1,503 ads)
→ Excellent: 0.49 (n=1,221 ads)

Correlation between Ad Strength & CPA = +0.002

Which means a Poor ad has the same CPA as an Excellent ad.

I'm not surprised, but it's good to see it in real data.

Here's how we fixed inboxes running a 40% sender bounce rate.

Not a bounce because the address was bad. The addresses were validated. Google was refusing to let us send the email at all.

The first time I saw this, I couldn't wrap my mind around what was happening because the lead list was validated. 

We revalidated it again and it was still happening. 

After a bunch of trial and error, we found the Google had fingerprinted the text we were sending and wasn't letting the message even get sent. 

We spintaxed the subject line and the unsubscribe language with over 20 variations. We already had a little spintax in the body.

The sender bounces went away immediately.

I want to be honest that a year ago I was the guy telling people spintax didn't matter. 

We were using so much AI in the message that I figured the variation was already there. I was wrong about that.

What changed my mind is that the fix worked in isolation. Same domains. Same inboxes. Same offer. Same list. Only the subject line and unsubscribe language changed, and a 40% sender bounce went to zero.

What we do now internally, and what I would tell anyone running real volume:

20 variations in the subject line. 20 in the unsubscribe language. Variations in the signature block. Three or four versions of the overall body, and three or four options every five words or so.

We have Claude skills that write all of it, because writing 20 subject line variants by hand is miserable.

If you are reading this thinking "his big tip was spintax," I know. 

But the amount of spintax you think you need should 5-10x for the health of your domains.

Are your new creatives actually diverse?

How to tell:

1. Download every active ad including ad spend, headline, body, script, on-screen text
2. Transcribe every single ad with timestamps
3. AI tag every ad with format, angle, hook style, creator and core selling point
4. Vectorize every ad so it has a data point on an n-dimensional space
5. Flag the near-duplicates by measuring cosine similarity of >0.95
6. Cluster into concepts by grouping the vectors
7. Measure concentration with Herfindahl index (economists use this to measure market monopolies)

If you have too much concentration your account is at risk from fatigue. One idea gets tired, and the whole account goes with it.

Summary:
- AI tag every ad you run for analysis
- Vectorize and measure concentration to go deeper

I've launched 30+ SKUs for 9-figure DTCs

Easy framework to launch winning ads fast:

THINK

1. Decide the job of the new SKU. Is it to acquire new customers, or to pull more revenue from the ones you already have? Each needs a different budget, audience and creative.

2. Back the budget out of inventory: (Units x AOV) / MER gives you the number to spend. A 2,000-unit run at a $50 AOV is $100k of inventory. At a 2.0 MER that's a $50k launch budget, and at $15 COGS you still clear $20k in first-order profit if you hit it.

3. Hold 700-1,000 units in reserve, another $35-50k of stock, so you can scale if a creative starts performing well. We don't want to sell out once we've found winning creatives, thats where the profit is. 

RESEARCH

4. Read reviews before you create any ads. Reddit, Trustpilot, your own. Cluster them into ICPs and weight each one. Those percentages are your budget allocation: four ICPs at 40/30/20/10 splits the $50k into $20k, $15k, $10k and $5k.

5. Find the universal objection. It's the one thing 70% raise regardless of persona. Every ad has to clear this objection before it goes live.

6. Grade the market's sophistication. Stage 1, you name the product and win. Stage 4, they've heard every claim and you need a mechanism to prove it.

7. Scrape the competitor library, then ignore the longest-running ads. Check for new creative velocity and duplication instead.

LAUNCH

8. Pick 4 angles to launch with, one per ICP. Don't spread your budget across too many angles, else nothing will get enough spend to prove out.

9. Build 5 concepts minimum, 3-4 variations each. That's around 18 ads. You don't know the winning angle, persona or format yet. You need volume to find this out.

10. Aim to budget $2-4k behind each ad. Across 18 ads that's your $50k. It won't split evenly. Your top 2-3 ads take half the spend.

11. Match the page to the awareness level. Problem-aware traffic gets an advertorial. Product-aware gets a PDP. Test both against the same ad so you learn what converts best.

12. Run the new SKU as a separate campaign. Exclude past purchasers to see how it performs on cold, new traffic. You want 70%+ of orders from first-time customers, otherwise the SKU is cannibalizing your hero product instead of driving incremental growth.

ANALYZE

13. A new product for a cold audience (i.e., not a new flavor or color) will convert worse at first. Since each ad is doing more work, it will also be worse optimized, since you won't know the angles, landing pages, and CRM flows to best capture the audience. Set your target lower and analyze against that lower target. 

14. Track LTV against different offers and variants to ensure that you're selling the one that people are most excited about and also they can repurchase the most. 

15. Scale!

The age of your domain when you start sending is a lever almost nobody pulls.

Here is the normal way it goes. You want to start outreach. You buy domains. You warm them for two weeks. You start sending on a domain that is two weeks old.

Normal tried and true. 

We have now seen a lot of success buying the domains we need to start sending in 2 weeks and then buying more and just sitting on them. 

We have to pay the one time domain cost but we don't put inboxes on them, we just let them sit. 

Then, when we need the domains because the others have started to lose their reply rate effectiveness, we use these domains that have aged for 3 or 4 months instead of completely fresh ones. 

Still needs warmup. You can rush a 1 week warmup but we try to do 2 weeks still. 

Those domains perform better. Consistently enough that we changed how we buy.

If you are doing consistent cold outreach, buy some domains you know are going to sit around for a bit and see if they perform better than 2 week old domains when you need them!

How I get high intent Google Ads clicks:

With disqualification ads.

Accounts chasing perfect Ad Strength scores are paying MORE per click from people who will never buy.

Your ad copy should push bad fits away on purpose.

Headlines that disqualify:

→ "Starting at $25K/mo" (budget shoppers leave)
→ "For Teams of 50+" (solopreneurs scroll past)
→ "SOC2 Certified Platform" (filters non-enterprise)

Descriptions that add friction:

→ State pricing minimums
→ List requirements upfront
→ Include certifications and compliance

This will hurt your CTR.

That's the point.

When your ICP is a fraction of total search volume, every unqualified click is wasted budget.

We did this on a B2B SaaS account:

→ CAC was 75% above target
→ Added disqualifying ad copy and pricing on the landing page
→ Negated self-serve search terms ("free," "DIY," "tool," "template")
→ CAC dropped to 1% below target

We didn't increase budget or launch new campaigns. We just changed what the ads said.

Your ad copy is a filter.

Use it like one.

Last year, I was the "First Bathroom Stall" speaker. This year, I was the "Dead Fish" speaker. Many of my workshop attendees associate me with the "Wee-Wee Problem". Before your mind joins mine in the gutter, why do I enjoy collecting these undesirable nicknames? 

First, there's no one way to be an effective speaker. It's what makes the job so interesting. Half the fun of attending events is studying the brilliance of other speakers. I love learning from speakers with different styles from mine. 

But, there's one element I incorporate into all of my workshops and talks. 

It's the unexpected inside joke. 

A central "you had to be there" component that connects me with the audience in the room. It's relevant to the subject matter, but feels slightly inappropriate, unexpected, or unusual. And, as a result, the audience is much more likely to remember - and talk about - the key teaching point. 

Here's an example from a conference keynote I gave this week. 

The conference was held in Jackson, where Nick and I were married. 

I opened the talk with that. Then, pivoted into how we met. Bumble. 

Then, I asked the audience if they could guess the pattern my friends and I observed across all of the men's Bumble photos. 

"They're all holding a fish!" (--Emily Pick, nailed it) 

Pulled up this slide and joked about the origin of this behavior. Maybe it's men wanting to signal to women that they're a provider. 

But, because it's so common, it's lost its meaning. We can't tell if the dude actually fishes, or if he just snapped a pic on a bachelor party and decided to make it his Bumble personality. 

I named it the Dead Fish problem. 

Then, asked the audience to consider how it's the exact same problem we're facing in Sales & Marketing today. 

Every pitch deck, website, and 1-pager is touting the same dead fish. 

"Powered by agentic AI, trusted by industry leaders." It used to mean something. So, we jumped on the bandwagon. And, as a result, every message has started to sound unforgettably the same. Which is why we have to pivot towards better enabling sellers to tell customer stories, instead of continuing to drone on about features for the sake of being AI-forward. The central point of my talk. 

I share this because I think there every great speaker has something unique that makes them memorable. Does every audience member love it? Of course not. 

But, I think a lot of great ideas go to die in perfectly polished talks. 

Public speaking is nerve-wracking for everyone.  No matter how many times you step on stage. But, a laugh softens a room. It softens the pressure. 

(I don't write as often about public speaking - but if this subject matter is interesting, I can share ideas here more often)

Does Meta's quality, engagement or conversion rankings predict your ROAS? I analyzed $30M in ad spend to find out:

Meta scores every ad into three rankings on ads manager

→ Quality ranking: perceived quality vs competing ads
→ Engagement rate ranking: expected engagement vs competing ads
→ Conversion rate ranking: expected conversion vs ads chasing the same optimization goal

Each one lands in a tier after 500 impressions
- Above average,
- Average
- Below average (bottom 35%, 20%, or 10%).

Columns → Customize Columns → search "ranking" → add all three.

Here's what the data showed.

1. Quality ranking

→ Across the accounts we manage, it barely tracks ROAS or CPA.
→ Sometimes it inverts. Below-average quality ads beat above-average ones.
→ A low quality score is not a reason to cut an ad.

2. Engagement rate ranking

→ Predicts how much people will like, comment, share and click.
→ Same story as quality. Weak correlation with what the ad returns.
→ Hook rate and engagement rate feel like the metrics that matter.

3. Conversion rate ranking

→ Predicts conversion against ads chasing the same optimization goal.
→ This is the one that does track ROAS.
→ Kind of makes sense as Meta serves ads it predicts will convert.

Summary:
- Quality and engagement rankings show low correlation with performance, and sometimes invert.
- Conversion rate ranking predicts CPA in most accounts to small degree

We spend $72M/year on Google Ads

How to run advanced competitor brand campaigns:

1. Cherry pick easiest target
List every competitor in a Google sheet and create a matrix of every dimension you compete on. E.g. pricing, features, support, use cases. Cherry pick the competitors where you have an obvious and clear advantage and you look different. There’s no point trying to compete against a big incumbent who is likely to outprice and/or out-product you. The more selective you are here, the better. We found a huge range in CPAs depending on the competitor we go after.

2. Build dedicated landing pages
Build dedicated pages that directly address "why us vs. them" for each major competitor. List their pain points. Show your advantages. Make the comparison obvious. Conversion rates go up because you're meeting the searcher exactly where they are. It’s important to be as factually correct on this page as possible. There’s no point lying or bending the truth to convert a lead that ultimately doesn’t have the right expectations, and then ultimately churns and has a low LTV. We found a 30% reduction in CPL just with dedicated landing pages.

3. Segment LTV by competitor
This is where most competitor campaigns fall apart. You need GCLID and UTM parameters flowing all the way through to your CRM, tied to the specific competitor keyword that brought them in. And then from there, you track win rates by competitor, not just leads. You track LTV by competitor. Some competitor traffic converts at lower rates but higher deal sizes. Some converts faster but churns.

4. Improve Keyword Intent
Not everyone searching a competitor name is in-market. Some are job seekers looking to work there. Some are existing customers searching for support or login pages. We aggressively remove terms from the start, things like "careers," "jobs," "login," "support," "help desk." (You should already have these in your NKL anyways!) Otherwise you're paying for clicks that were never going to convert. It seems obvious, but we see this mistake in almost every competitor campaign audit we run. When budgets get large enough we use Negative Nancy. It’s our AI agent that runs every week on client accounts and ingests every keyword that drove clicks. If the intent of the keyword is poor, we add it to negative keywords inside Google ads (this by itself can lower CPLs by 30% in 24-48 hours).

SUMMARY:

→ Cherry pick weakest competitors
→ Build dedicated landers
→ Full funnel tracking from ad click to closed deal
→ Negative keywords

If you're running competitor campaigns and not seeing pipeline like this, the issue is usually one of these four things.

Meta's budgets are weird

Decreasing budgets can actually increase spend:

How Meta works:
- Meta can overspend on a single day.
- It does this because it thinks it can get you more conversions
- But over the next few days it pulls back spend to average out.

Example:
- Budget set to $1,000/day
- it might spend $2,000 on day one
- Then run lower the rest of the week until it lands at $7,000 total.
- Averaged to your $1,000/day.

But, if you lower the budget mid week, the pacing resets.

And if Meta is bullish on your ads, this can happen:
→ Day 1: $1,000 budget, spends $2,000. Running total $2,000
→ Day 2: cut to $900, spends $1,800. Running total $3,800
→ Day 3: cut to $800, spends $1,600. Running total $5,400
→ Day 4: cut to $700, spends $1,400. Running total $6,800
→ Day 5: cut to $600, spends $1,200. Running total $8,000
→ Day 6: cut to $500, spends $1,000. Running total $9,000
→ Day 7: cut to $400, spends $800. Running total $9,800

(Happened to us recently)

If you left it alone, you would have spent $7,000.

That's $2,800 more, 40% over budget, for trying to rein it in.

Two ways to handle an ad that consistently overspends:
- Make one big cut and hold it for the full 7 days, so the pacing clock resets a single time
- Or leave it and let Meta reallocate across the 7-day window, if that pacing fits your cash flow

Hope this helps.

There is MINIMAL category synergy.

FY25 P&L

R&D holds near 6% of sales, $249M to $368M, while revenue went $4.25B to $6.4B. Gross margin climbed to 49%.

Launching this much isn't clean. Obsolescence reserve tripled to $65.7M in two years. Inventory now sits at $1B.

Google is forcing DSAs to AI Max

How we're transitioning safely:

Example:
- Client is running two DSAs at $1-2k/day each
- Both are doing well and converting
- We don't want to put the business's results in jeopardy with a binary switch. So instead:

1. Harvest

→ Pull the search term report on each DSA campaign weekly
→ Flag every converting search term

2. Graduate

→ Launch those terms as keywords in normal Search campaigns
→ Set explicit match types and bidding

→ We ran the same play on PMax: the Search campaign built from harvested terms hit 0.7 ROAS vs the 0.45 PMax averaged

3. Shift

→ Move budget from DSA into those Search campaigns gradually
→ No hard cutover on Google's date

4. Wait

→ Let other advertisers test AI Max and let Google collect its data
→ Same posture we took with PMax. It took time to evolve
→ Google ran this migration play in 2022 too, forcing Smart Shopping into PMax before Q4

Two caveats:

- Check your actual deadline. Most DSAs now migrate Feb 2027, but campaigns using auto-created assets plus campaign-level broad match upgrade this September.
- Time the move around seasonality. If your strong months are before cut off, don't change any campaign structure until it passes. If it's just after cut off, you'll want to move early to stabilize

How many ads should you launch?

5 ways from simple to complicated

1. Capacity

→ How many ads can you make without dropping the quality of the strategy or the execution?
→ Quality here means the thinking and the concept not the camera.
→ Anyone under $50k/month should stop reading here. This is the answer, start here.

2. Spend per ad

→ Total ads = target spend / $3k.
→ $150k/month gets you 50 ads.
→ It falls apart the second someone cuts 40 hook variations off one concept. The count looks healthy and the account has one idea in it.

3. Spend per concept

→ Total concepts = target spend / $9k. Each concept gets 3 ads.
→ $150k/month gets you 17 concepts and the same 50 ads.
→ Better than method 2 because it stops you making lots of iterations

4. Calibrated to revenue

→ Revenue per ad = your ROAS x average spend per ad.
→ Revenue target / revenue per ad = ad count.
→ Use this on scaling accounts or unique ones where typical best practices don't apply

5. Churn replacement

→ Work out what share of spend churns each month. Call it 30% for a typical account.
→ Current revenue x churn rate = revenue you're losing. The delta between that and your target is what new ads have to cover.
→ Run that replacement revenue number back through method 4 and you get your ad count.

Where accounts tend to land:

- Under $50k/month ad spend: method 1
- $50k to $200k ad spend: method 2/3
- $200k+ ad spend or scaling hard: methods 4 and 5 together
