Stop being pedantic about ad naming conventions

Set the core right and then install this AI tagging system:

- Naming conventions are fragile
- They take up valuable time setting up the convention
- For qualitative tags, different people have different outputs
- Names have limits (litterally but also pragmatically)
- And often you want to ask something in retrospect that was in your tag name
- Or you want to ask something but only once.

There's a better way:

We set up our core naming convention for things that matter for media buying.

Then every ad runs through an AI model and gets tagged retrospectively.

→ Format (static, video, carousel)
→ Length
→ Co-branded (true/false)
→ Funnel stage
→ Hook type
→ Core problem the ad solves
→ Who's on screen (facial recognition tags the person)
→ Props in frame (e.g. I can pull every ad with product in it and compare against the ones without)
→ Full transcript and selling points
→ On-screen text (I can search every ad by the words on screen)
→ Comments and reviews on the ad
→ Semantic similarity (how close each ad's hook, transcript and angle are to the rest of the account)

Then you cross-reference the tags against spend.

High spend areas
- Which variables absorb the most budget across the account
- Example: filter by format and you see static testimonial images are eating most of your prospecting spend

High spend per ad
- The combinations that are efficient but low volume
- Example: a static image on one specific problem angle might be your best cost per ad, and you've only launched three of them

Competitor spend areas
- Scrape and tag your competitors' ads out of the Meta ad library
- Where are they concentrated that you've barely tested?
- Which formats and angles are they betting on that never show up in your account?
- We are currently working on automating this in-house for greater detail.

Important to know the top 1-2% of ads drive about 50% of your spend.

If you can't see what makes up that 1-2%, you're scaling blind.

You end up pouring production budget into the wrong ads, or never finding the right ones.

Paid search is boring (if you do it well)

Process we use to spend $70M+/yr 

1. Graduate PMax terms into Search

→ Pull the search term report from PMax
→ Launch the converting terms as keywords in your Search campaign
→ Search lets you match keyword to ad to landing page. PMax hands that to Google's algo

2. Negative keywords

→ Run search term reports 2-3x per week. Converting queries become keywords, irrelevant ones become negatives
→ E.g. Our AI workflow finds 2,500 negatives on one $100k/mo account. Cost $24 to run
→ We maintain master lists at the MCC level.
→ Negative count should rise with spend. It's one of the signals I use to judge whether a media buyer is doing the job

3. Dedicated landing pages

→ Dedicated pages convert at a 6.6% median vs 2.35% for general site pages (Unbounce data)
→ Keep one landing page test running at all times

4. Full-funnel conversion tracking

→ Fire conversion events at every stage: MQL, SQL, customer
→ Optimize Google for the down-funnel events so Google optimizes for buyers

5. Ad assets

→ Fill out sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets, images. Refresh monthly
→ Contributes at least 3-5% of performance every time they're in place
→ People set them once and forget them. Beware as Google's auto assets fill gaps with FAQ and blog sitelinks that don't convert

6. Bid strategy targets

→ Switch from max conversions to target CPA once conversion volume supports it, then tune the target in small increments (full decision tree in my bidding strategy post)

How to set up your DTC attribution

Based on ad spend from $50k/mo to $1M/mo+

1. $50k/mo

→ Server-side tracking (CAPI, Elevar) is non-negotiable. Post-iOS your pixel alone under-tracks by 20-30%, and CAPI feeds that back.
→ Read the platform dashboards for purchase velocity only. Compare 1-day vs 7-day vs 28-day windows to see how fast people convert after seeing an ad.
→ Steer by MER and new customer CAC. Every platform inflates its own numbers. MER can't.
→ Turn on a post-purchase survey. The highest-ROI thing you'll set up here.

2. $100k-200k/mo

Add a multi-touch attribution tool. Triple Whale or Northbeam, about $300-500/mo.

→ Now you validate attribution yourself instead of trusting Meta's dashboard.
→ Meta underreports by 20-40%. Google overreports by 30-50%. Stop making ad-level calls off either.
→ The MTA runs your daily decisions: which ad to scale, which to cut. Keep the budget call on blended MER and true CAC.

3. $200k-500k/mo

→ Point the MTA at new-customer acquisition.
→ Your top ads can look 50% different in Northbeam vs the platform. Facebook rewards recent, frequent conversions, so bottom-funnel wins in-platform while your best top-funnel ads look like they're failing.
→ Set the tool to new customer CPA with wider conversion windows.
→ Add cohort LTV by channel. A $40 Meta CPA with a $180 twelve-month LTV beats a $30 TikTok CPA with a $95 LTV. Your per-channel CPA targets come from here.

4. $500k-1M/mo

→ Run incrementality and geo-lift on the big questions.
→ Turn spend off in one region, hold the rest flat, measure the drop in sales.
→ Run these quarterly, for strategic questions like whether retargeting is real or retail spillover is real. Daily calls stay on the MTA.

5. $1M/mo+

→ Add MMM and triangulate.
→ MMM uses your historical spend and revenue. No user-level tracking, so iOS never touches it. It shows where you sit on the diminishing-returns curve for each channel.
→ Now you steer by all 3 of my favorites: MTA for which ads, surveys for which channels, MMM for direction.
→ When all three point the same way, I push budget. When they disagree, that's where I dig.

Summary:
- $50k: CAPI, MER, a free survey.
- $200k: add an MTA, stop trusting the dashboard.
- $500k: incrementality tests for the strategic questions.
- $1M: add MMM, triangulate all three.

The bigger you get, the less any single number means.

That's why you run three at once.

Is Meta sequencing your ads?

How to check:

We were running an ad that was performing well
- Against account average it was 1.2x on ROAS
- 1.8x on new customer rate
- 3.1x on net new website visits

So we kept pushing the ad and scaled to $14k/day

But then we then paused it on day 62 because the offer was over.

Guess what happened?

While the ad was running:
- Overall account spend, exc that ad: +28%
- Overall account ROAS, exc that ad +45%.

But when we paused it:
- Overall account spend -7%
- Overall account ROAS -24%.

It's clear that this ad was driving performance for the rest of the ad account

And was therefore probably being sequenced early in the journey

Hence why changing its spend seemed to influence the whole ad account

You might have one of these in your ad account:

1. Sort your account by new customer rate and net new visits.
2. Index the rest of the account to that ad's launch day.
3. Plot spend and ROAS together across the window.
4. If ROAS & spend both move in the same direction as the ad, you might have an influencing ad

If you have an example of an ads that was NOT performing well but had signs of sequencing I’d love to hear it. So far all examples I have are the two moving together.

Where does PMax actually spend?

Pulled 365 days of data from 53 accounts: 

1. Search

→ Median account: 61% of PMax spend goes to Search
→ The range across all 53: 2% to 99%
→ Above 90%, PMax is a glorified Search campaign (I audited one at 82% and Search had under 30 conversions a month)
→ On our accounts we pull converting search terms out of PMax into Search until the search portion drops below 10%

2. Search Partners

→ Median: 3% of spend
→ We launched one PMax campaign where it took 30% (it got calls, but no qualified leads)
→ No campaign-level toggle exists to turn it off. Keep an eye on this

3. YouTube and Display

→ Medians: 10% and 3%
→ Individual accounts push over 80% into YouTube
→ Google allocates from your assets, audience signals and conversion data
→ Repurpose your Meta ads into the asset groups to start (statics too, no re-edits). That's how we launch every client and performance holds
→ If YouTube CPA comes in near Search, that's your case to invest in proper YouTube creative

4. Gmail, Discover and Maps

→ Median: 0% across nearly all 53 accounts
→ One account has 84% of its PMax spend going to Maps

5. Why no benchmark exists

→ Google gives you no channel-level budget control (their own docs say to influence the mix through assets, signals and exclusions)
→ Channel reporting only rolled out to every PMax campaign in November 2025, and to MCC level in December

Summary

- 61% median Search share, with a 2% to 99% range
- High Search share means PMax is duplicating your Search campaign
- Search Partners needs a manual account-level exclusion
- Pull the channel report on your own account before assuming it's typical

Are your Google ads incremental?
Or just stealing paid social conversions?
How to check:

1. Ramp brand spend

→ Pull paid and organic brand clicks into one report before touching budgets
→ 3x the brand budget and read total clicks over 6 weeks, ignore in-platform CPA
→ We spent $40k testing this: 3x spend bought 2,500 more paid clicks and lost 5,000 organic ones
→ Watch when brand searches climb. If it lines up with your Meta spend, paid social created that demand

2. Geo holdout

→ Keep the channel live in half your markets, pause it in the other half
→ Compare total conversions across both, the gap is your lift

3. On/off pulse

→ Run the channel 1 week on, 1 week off, for 6+ weeks minimum
→ Use a 2x spend contrast so the swing is readable
→ Compare total conversions in on weeks against off weeks
→ eBay ran the extreme version in 2014. Turned brand ads off, traffic held.

4. PMax brand exclusions

→ Add brand exclusions to PMax and watch two numbers: PMax conversions and account conversions
→ If PMax drops but the account total holds, PMax was claiming demand that converted anyway
→ Same test works on Search Partners. One account had it taking 30% of PMax spend for calls that never became qualified leads

5. ABM list holdout

→ This is for B2B. Upload your prospect list and target half of it
→ Hold out the other half, compare conversion rates between the two
→ The gap between the halves is the incremental gain

6. Google's lift test

→ Google runs a randomized conversion lift study inside the platform
→ The spend threshold to run this dropped from $100k to $5k
→ It's Google measuring Google, so run it alongside your own tests

Use the following to make better decisions:

→ First touch answers budget allocation
→ Data-driven answers which ad wins inside Google
→ Holdout tests answer whether a channel drives new customers
→ Google's models can't measure their own incrementality because they don't see the other channels

How to get lower CPAs on Google

By improving expected CTR:

Your CPA = CPC / CVRv

Your CPC falls as your expected CTR increases (among other things)

To increase expected CTR:

1. Add negative keywords in bulk to strip the queries that were never going to click
2. Kill queries based on intent, even at 1 impression and 0 clicks
3. Grow your negative list as spend grows
4. Tighten match types on the terms that convert
5. Edit your ad text to make the offer more compelling
6. Match your ad copy to the intent of the keyword
7. Highlight a unique benefit, like free shipping
8. Experiment with different calls to action
9. Be more specific in your ad text

Are your Google ads being run well?

How to check:

1. Quality score

→ Pull it on your non-brand keywords.
→ We charted this across our accounts. Higher quality score tracked with lower CPA
→ WordStream's 2025 study of 15,666 accounts puts the median at 5 to 6. Only 22% score 7 or above
→ Then check the expected CTR component. Ad relevance and landing page experience are easy fixes (keyword in the copy, keyword on the page)
→ Expected CTR is the hardest metric to improve. If it's above average, your marketer likely knows what they're doing

2. Negative keyword count

→ Count negatives relative to spend.
→ The number should climb as spend climbs. More spend means more queries, and more junk to block
→ Go to Change History, last 90 days. If no negatives were added in 60+ days, nobody is reviewing the search terms and your marketer is not doing a good job
→ Accounts running negatives convert at 13% monthly vs 4.6% without (same WordStream study)

3. Ad copy change history

→ Filter Change History to ad edits.
→ You want a visible testing cadence. New RSAs launched, losing headlines swapped out
→ A flat history means nobody is testing
→ On a recent takeover, ad copy rewrites drove 5% of a 40% CPA drop in 15 days

4. RSA build-out

→ Open any ad and count what's filled in.
→ You need 15 headlines and 4 descriptions. Anything less cuts the combinations Google can test
→ Same for ad assets. There are 11 types and most accounts run 4
→ Google's own data says a second RSA per ad group lifts conversions 6.6% on average

Summary
- Quality score above average, especially expected CTR
- Negative count growing with spend
- Change history full of ad tests
- Every RSA fully built

Wild. Google lets you send negative conversions.

But hardly anyone does it.

You can retract bad leads from Google.

Essentially telling Google "this conversion was bad, stop finding people like this."

1. Set up offline conversion import

This only works if you're already passing conversion data back to Google (GCLIDs from your CRM).

2. Create a separate offline conversion import with a "RETRACT" column

When a sales rep marks a lead as spam, disqualified, duplicate, or a test submission in your CRM, that lead gets flagged for retraction. You upload it back to Google with the retraction tag. Google removes that conversion from its learning data.

3. Do it within 24 hours

The faster you retract, the less time Google spends optimizing toward that bad signal. We automate this through the CRM so it fires the same day the lead gets disqualified.

4. Observe post effects

The algorithm stops finding lookalikes of your junk leads. Your lead quality goes up without changing a single campaign setting, ad, or keyword.

This is especially important for PMax campaigns:

→ PMax has a broad audience pool
→ It's pulling from Search, Display, YouTube, Discover, Gmail.
→ PMax will happily keep expanding into audiences that look like your worst leads.

Easy way to shift dead stock

And increase your AOV:

Package dead stock as a Mystery Gift With Purchase.

1. Threshold above AOV
→ If your AOV is $80, gate the gift at $100+
→ "Spend $100 to unlock a limited-edition mystery item"
→ That $20 gap is AOV growth.

2. Fund it with dead stock
→ The gift is inventory you already wrote down
→ The cost sits in COGS, so your discount line never moves
→ Gross margin stays clean for the CFO

3. Price at perceived value
→ The customer sees $40 of free value, you clear $8 of dead stock
→ This doesn't train customers to wait for discounts as it's a free gift

4. Plug-and-play warehouse
→ Fulfillment packs whatever discontinued SKU is on hand
→ No SKU-specific picks, no bottleneck

Math breakout:
→ Base order: $80 at 30% COGS = $56 gross profit
→ The gift pulls it to $100, and the extra $20 adds $14 of margin
→ The mystery gift costs $8 in written-down stock
→ Gross profit lands at $62, up from $56
→ That's 25% more AOV and $6 more contribution per order

NEVER analyze a losing ad

Unless:

Firstly, why we don't analyze losing ads:

1. The math doesn't work
- I can take an ad doing a 0.5 ROAS and maybe get it to a 1.
- Or I can turn it off and take an ad doing a 2 and push it to a 3. This is a higher leverage activity.

2. You'll learn the wrong lessons
- There are so many reasons an ad can fail. Persona. Camera quality. Audio. Loading speed. Music in the background. The way someone delivers a line.
- We had an ad we thought bombed because of the filming location. Analyzed it, made that call, recorded the ad. Guess what? Still was bad performance.

But, in case of the following I MAY iterate on a losing ad:
- There's a glaring user experience issue such as poor text overlay which is hard to read (@Dara Denney raised this exact example in the comments last time I posted this)
- It is a 'good' losing ad (just below average) with incredible body retention and a horrendous hook rate

So what do I do instead?

Spend 100% of creative energy branching the winners and testing new ideas from the ground up.

If Ad A works, build off that root:

→ Same angle, new format (UGC to static)
→ Same angle, new visual (talking head to challenge)
→ Same angle, new persona
→ Same angle, new hook

(Notice how it's not swapping a CTA, changing music or captions. These are low impact changes and not worth your time, unless there is a user experience issue)

The only exception (nuance is important)
- If you've tested an angle multiple times / angles / and formats and it bombs consistently then that is the time to cut it.

Learn from individual wins / learn from aggregate losses

It will help reduce noise in your decision making.

Are you spending your next marketing dollar efficiently?

How to check:

→ Your next dollar isn't worth your last one.
→ Allocating on average ROAS is the mistake.
→ Spend on marginal ROAS: what the next dollar returns.

1. Platform ROAS is lying to you.

→ Every platform has a directional under/overreporting.
→ Example: Meta underreports 20-40%. Google overreports 30-50%. TikTok underreports 30-50%. (Changes by brand and sales channel mix)
→ And most reported conversions aren't incremental. Prospecting is around 60-80%, retargeting 15-30%, brand search 10-30%.

Example:
→ One brand showed me 5x ROAS on retargeting. We turned it off for two weeks. Revenue stayed flat. Only 12.5% of those conversions were incremental, so true ROAS was 0.62x. (Profit loss even with LTV)

Platform ROAS tells you which ad to scale inside a channel. It can't tell you which channel deserves the next dollar.

2. Anchor on blended MER.

→ Blended MER = Total revenue divided by total marketing spend.
→ This is not double-counted across platforms.
→ If you add $50k to Meta and blended MER barely moves, the channel is not driving incremental sales
→ That next dollar is buying sales you'd have gotten anyway.

3. Quick tests to evaluate

→ Holdout: turn a channel off for two weeks and watch blended revenue. If no change = not incremental (or long conversion window, validate with post-purchase questions FIRST). If you ever have a platform go dark accidentally definitely run this test when it does.
→ Geo test: spend heavy in one region, hold another flat, compare the lift.
→ Check post purchase survey. Aim for 30% response on the first question "How did you hear about us". If you're seeing survey, blended MER and platform data agree then you have an incremental channel you should spend into

4. Follow marginal ROAS down to profitable CPA.

→ Keep feeding the channel while the next dollar clears your profitable CPA (lower than target CPA)
→ The marginal dollar only has to clear profitability, or push your average back over target.

How to solve any ads problem

6 steps:

1. Pick one number

→ Choose the metric the account is judged on: ROAS, CAC, or cost per qualified lead
→ Write its target next to it

2. Date the drop

→ Pull the trend and find the exact day it turned
→ Check the change log against that date. Example, a consulting client had zero changes, spend flat but still a drop.
→ A clean change log means the cause is outside your settings

3. Split the blended number

→ Segment by device, campaign, geo, and ad
→ Example: A healthcare account I audited had a spike in CPA. We then segmented by device and found it ran a $1,375 desktop CPA and a $7,355 mobile CPA.

4. Find the constraint

→ Keep segmenting until you can point at one thing
→ In the example account, CTR and conversion rate were falling while CPC got more expensive, all starting from that date
→ Creative fatigue was the only explanation left.

5. Fix one thing

→ For the fatigued account: pump out new creative as fast as possible
→ Don't touch offers or landing pages until the constraint clears

6. Prove the fix worked

→ Set forecast vs actual pacing and watch the metric daily
→ Account for conversion lag

Summary

- Define the number
- Date the drop
- Segment past the blend
- Isolate the constraint
- Fix that one thing
- Prove it moved

How to scale your Google ad account

Look at impression share metrics:

There are 6: 

→ Search IS. Impressions you got, over impressions Google estimates you were eligible for.
→ Lost IS (Budget). How often you didn't show because the budget ran out.
→ Lost IS (Rank). How often you didn't show because Ad Rank was too low.
→ Exact Match IS. Impressions you got over impressions you were eligible for on exact match search terms
→ Top IS. Impressions among the top ads, over impressions you were eligible for among top ads.
→ Abs. Top IS. Impressions in the very first ad slot, over that same top-ads eligible pool.

How and when to read them: 

1. Budget loss first

→ Lost IS (Budget) above 0% means there are more impressions you are eligible for BUT your budget is too low. 
→ At 30% lost to budget, raising your daily budget 30% unlocks 30% more auction volume (in simple terms). 
→ If you don't want to spend more budget, lower your target CPA instead. Your budget lasts longer through the day, you buy cheaper clicks, and if conversion rates hold your CPA drops too.
→ Note on tCPA or tROAS, budget loss under-delivers volume and also inflates your CPCs.
→ Eliminate Lost IS (Budget) in the campaigns you already run before you open new keyword themes or service lines. Expanding sideways while you leave profitable auctions on the table wastes the budget you just added.

2. Exact vs broad

→ Compare Exact Match IS against overall Search IS.
→ Example 1: If Exact 90%, overall 40%. You’re appearing for your money keywords 
→ Example 2: If Exact 40%, overall 40%. Now you're probably losing the searches you want. 
→ Caveat - I do not like to optimize towards these metrics blindly. They’re more steers on auction dyanmics to help explain any changes in performance 

3. Rank loss is not always a bad thing

→ Spend more and you buy your way into auctions further from your core keywords. Those searches are less relevant, so your rank on them is worse, and Lost IS (Rank) climbs. 
→ We took one account from $268K to $786K a month. Search lost to rank went from 74% to 85%. The ads never changed. We were bidding into looser keywords. This is not a bad thing. 
→ Rank loss is only an ads problem when Quality Score backs it up. High Lost IS (Rank) with expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience all reading Below Average is the one case where you rewrite.

4. Ceiling math

→ Impressions divided by Search IS gives you the eligible pool. 50,000 impressions at 40% IS = 125,000.
→ Treat that as roughly your market search volume. 
→ Don't chase 100% impression share. It gets way too expensive, and most of what you buy on the way there is broad-match traffic you'd rather block.
→ The exception is launches. On influencer campaigns, PR or brand pushes, go manual and target 90% impression share.

Hope this helps

YouTube ads are crushing right now

There are actually 6 types

1. Skippable in-stream

→ Plays before or during videos. Viewer can skip after 5 seconds.
→ You only pay when someone watches 30 seconds or clicks. Our blended CPV across the MCC is $0.07.
→ Converts better mid-funnel than any other format we run. This is where the direct response budget goes.
→ Con: only 24% of impressions ever turn into a paid view. Three in four never reach 30 seconds, so the first 3 seconds decide everything.
→ Use it for: demand capture and remarketing where you need the conversion.

2. Non-skippable in-stream

→ 7-15 seconds, no skip button, priced on CPM. Longer variants run on connected TV.
→ Guarantees the full message gets delivered.
→ Con: you pay for every impression, including people who would have skipped. CPMs run higher than skippable, and no skip button doesn't mean anyone watched.
→ Use it for: brand messages where message control matters more than efficiency.

3. Bumpers

→ 6 seconds or less, non-skippable, CPM-priced.
→ Cheap frequency. You can repeat one line across a remarketing pool for very little spend.
→ Con: 6 seconds fits one claim max, so it can't explain anything new.
→ Use it for: retargeting and reinforcing a message your other campaigns already introduced.

4. In-feed

→ Thumbnail plus text in search results, home feed, and watch next. The viewer chooses to click.
→ Mostly opt-in viewing, so intent is the highest of any format here. Autoplay views count too, so the number flatters itself slightly.
→ Con: inventory is limited, so it caps out fast as a spend line.
→ Use it for: B2B and considered purchases, with bumpers behind it for frequency.

5. Shorts

→ Vertical ads inside the Shorts feed.
→ Our blended CPM is $6.09. Cheaper than long-form on paper.
→ Con: the swipe-away is instant and view quality is lower than in-stream.
→ Use it for: top-of-funnel volume and creative testing, judged on downstream quality rather than CPM.

6. Masthead

→ YouTube homepage takeover, reserved through Google Ads Reservation, Programmatic Guaranteed, or a Google rep instead of the auction.
→ Biggest single-day reach YouTube sells.
→ Con: fixed CPM or cost-per-hour commitment, no smart bidding toward conversions.
→ Use it for: launches and moments where one day of mass reach matters.

(Technically there's a 7th, outstream, but it serves on Google video partners rather than YouTube itself.)

Our spend split: 
- Skippable in-stream: 48%
- In-feed: 26%
- Shorts: 25%
- Bumpers + non-skippable: under 1%

Got lots of negative comments for your DTC?

Steal this ad format to bait skeptics:

1. Find the haters
→ Read the comments on your videos and your competitors' ads
→ Collate everything they're complaining about: e.g. "there's no proof" or "it's overpriced"

2. Write the negative hook
→ Frame your own product like a scandal: "BRAND is CAUGHT OUT. Finally [COMPLAINT] revealed"
→ This blends controversy and intrigue and creates drama
→ The skeptics click to feed into the negativity

3. Pivot
→ Cut straight from the hook to the positive proof
→ Example: "Results reveal 90% of users saw BENEFIT"
→ Your proof needs to be as rock solid as possible

Why it works:

1. CPM drops as controversy gets high engagement
2. Conversion rate holds as the proof matches the promise. If you see high CTR and low CVR it's because you were overpromising
3. Cheaper CPM and stable conversion rate results in lower CPA

Good luck & go find your worst comment

Getting cheap Google ads clicks?

That's not always a good thing

Reviewed an account selling a $3,500 product:

→ 18,000 clicks.
→ 255 checkouts started.
→ $0.40 CPC 

Problem is, we all know an audience who can afford a $3,500 product and has intent to purchase is a lot more expensive than $0.40 click 

The price got that low for a few reasons.

→ Targeting was set as broad as it goes.
→ Purchase volume was too thin to train the bid strategy on buyers.
→ So the algorithm optimized on the only signal it had enough of, which was clicks.

How to get high intent clicks instead:

1. Exact match first

→ Start every keyword on exact. You decide which searches enter the auction. 
→ Expand to phrase once exact clears 15+ conversions a month.
→ Google gives you two impression share numbers. Search IS covers every auction it made you eligible for, loose matches included. Exact Match IS covers only the searches that match your keywords.

2. Negative keywords

→ A negative keyword blocks your ad from any search containing that word.
→ Pull the search term report 2-3x a week. Score every term 0-10 for relevance and block the 0-2s.
→ Campaign-specific junk goes at ad group level and universal junk at MCC level. High-spend accounts run 30,000+ negatives.
→ We run this flow with a bespoke multi-step AI workflow. 

3. Location set to Presence

→ Switch location targeting from "presence or interest" to "presence" only.
→ Otherwise you pay for people who searched about your city while sitting somewhere else.

4. Suppression audiences

→ Exclude the people who cannot buy from you. Existing customers, out-of-area, ineligible insurance, self-serve searchers on an enterprise offer.
→ Everywhere else, stay in observation mode and let Google find the buyers.

5. Conversion signal

→ If Google is optimizing for form fills, it sources cheap form fills. The auction gives you exactly what you asked for.
→ Move your primary conversion as far down funnel as you can while holding 30-50 conversions a month. 
→ Retract spam and disqualified leads within 24 hours.

Hope this helps

How to attribute the right way:

We audited podcast and creator spend for a brand
- On last-touch, the numbers looked awful.
- CPA hit over 10x target on some placements based on coupon codes.
- Half of the creators’ placements drove nothing tracked in the affiliate portal.
- A ROAS-brained media-buyer would mark this as a failed channel

Here's why those tracking models are wrong for this:
- Users listen to podcasts driving, or at the gym.
- But then they search your brand on Google three days later and buy.
- Last-touch credits that sale to organic search. The podcast gets nothing.
- Promo codes and vanity URLs catch about 21% of podcast conversions (Podscribe, 66k campaigns).

Instead:
- Run post purchase surveys PPS and ask "where did you hear about us"
- Measure responses and calculate PPS CAC
- On this audit, PPS CAC came in at $25
- That was very strong (target around $28 in this case).

Takeaway = be very careful using last touch CAC for top funnel marketing activities

What Meta ads bid strategy is best?

Full breakdown:

1. Highest Volume

→ You choose the budget. Meta spends it all.
→ Your CPA will vary to ensure the full spend.

2. Cost per Result Goal

→ You lock in a cost target.
→ A cost target rejects expensive conversions. And if cheap conversions aren't possible then you'll spend less money.
→ Set the target below your recent CPA and Meta stops bidding.
→ Meta notes: "Adherence to cost per result goal limits is not guaranteed."
→ Set it 10-20% above recent CPA and control budget by moving the cost target up and down.

3. Bid Cap

→ You lock the bid in every auction.
→ Your spend varies to whatever it takes to meet that bid.
→ This is useful when you know your exact break-even to the dollar and you're fine spending varying budgets as a result.
→ Meta notes it "does not control for the CPA that you see in reporting." You control the bid. The reported CPA is whatever the auctions produce.

How I use bidding strategies

- Highest Volume until I have a baseline CPA.
- Test a cost target after that, to steer budget and bids in and out of the right ads. Compare on performance.
- Almost never bid cap.

How to scale your Google ads when it takes 60 to 180 days to collect cash:

- Most accounts get scaled on ROAS and CPA.
- But even if you're running at a 5x ROAS you can fail if it takes 135 days to liquidate the ad spend

Before you sign off on a budget increase, run this Google ads cash flow model:

1. Media inputs

→ Monthly ad spend. Where you are today, before any increase.
→ Monthly spend increase. Your ramp rate. 10% a month is moderate.
→ Cost per click. Blended across Search, PMax and Demand Gen over the last 90 days.
→ Landing page conversion rate. Share of clicks that become a lead.

2. Funnel rates

→ Lead to qualified.
→ Qualified to proposal.
→ Proposal to close.
→ Average deal value. What you collect per deal after discounts and early cancellations.

3. Three lags

→ Deal cycle length. Days from lead to signed contract.
→ Invoice terms. Days from signature to the invoice going out.
→ Payment terms. Net 30, 60 or 90. Pull off your aged receivables.
→ Deal cycle + invoice terms + payment terms = cash conversion cycle.

4. Collection split

→ Model out your collection time split. Example:
- Paid on time. Around 70% in most B2B books.
- Paid 30 days late. 20%.
- Paid 60 days late. 10%.

5. Costs and margins

→ Delivery cost as a share of revenue.
→ Fixed monthly overheads.
→ Target net margin.
→ Reinvestment rate. This is share of net profit that goes back into ads.

Then check:

→ Revenue booked against cash collected.
→ Uncollected receivables.
→ Closing cash balance. Any month that is negative means you're scaling your ads faster than cash balance (fine if you have a marketing war chest)
→ Cash ROAS against booked ROAS. Booked can read 5x while cash reads under 1 for the first four months.

Here's the deliverability test we run that catches domains going to spam that are passing every other check.

Everybody talks about warmup reputation and seed inbox tests. A couple people are testing the actually reply rate counting real out of offices / human replies. 

The problem is an inbox can sit at 100% warmup reputation and still be landing in spam, and you would have no idea if it's the luck of the draw or it's really going to spam.

And the seed inboxes you send into have never marked an email as spam in their life. That is not human behavior. Directional at best.

So here's what we do.

We keep every reply we get for every customer. A lot of them are automated responses that say this inbox is no longer monitored and the email won't be forwarded, nobody reads this address.

We save all of those. Internally we have about 10,000+ now.

Which means we have a list of real addresses at real companies that will bounce something back at us if the message actually arrives.

Send to them and you should get about 80% coming back. It is never 100% because inbox detection is messy and some of those auto responses take a while to fire.

Anything under 80% I would kill.

What this catches is the domain that passes warmup, passes the seed test, looks ambiguous on reply rate, and then gets nothing forwarded back at all. 

Use Claude to read your replies and start saving these. It costs nothing and the list builds itself over time.

Then you can even run split tests to see what versions of your copy get the most responses back and which get the least etc. 

Make sure to manually check that it's a true auto response no one will read otherwise you're going to spam for sure bothering people.

Hack to become a DTC CFO's best friend

Show them this data:

1. Retargeting holdout

→ Turn retargeting off for two weeks, track total revenue.
→ Incremental conversions ÷ platform-reported conversions = your incrementality rate.
→ Platform ROAS × that rate = true ROAS.
→ One brand reported 5x on retargeting. Revenue stayed flat with it off. 12.5% of those conversions were incremental, so true ROAS was 0.63x.
→ The number finance gets: discount platform retargeting revenue by 87.5%.

2. Geo holdout

→ Spend heavily in a few selected regions, hold the rest flat, measure the lift.
→ Test region revenue growth minus control region growth = your lift.
→ Extra spend in the test region ÷ incremental conversions = incremental CPA.
→ Incremental CPA ÷ platform-reported CPA = the adjustment factor for that channel.
→ Cross-check that lift against your post-purchase survey for the same window.
→ Scale only where that incremental CPA clears your break-even CPA.

3. Account-wide lift test

→ From the day a high-scaling top-of-funnel ad launches, ignore net-new launches and track aggregate ROAS of the ads already running.
→ Baseline that cohort's ROAS for the 30 days before launch. It should decline softly.
→ Cohort ROAS during the scaling window minus that baseline trend = the halo the ad is generating.
→ Example, one TOF ad: ROAS on everything else rose 45% while it ran, down 24% when paused.

4. MER and contribution margin

→ Lead the weekly report with contribution margin split across your highest value ads, sat next to revenue.
→ MER = total revenue ÷ total marketing spend.
→ Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin. At 60% margin that is 1.67x.
→ Report every channel against that line.

5. Survey vs last click

→ Compare your post purchase survey responses to last click UTM.
→ Survey share of a channel ÷ last click share of that channel = your adjustment multiplier.
→ If the survey shows 1.5x what Meta reports, Meta's number gets multiplied by 1.5.
→ Hand over one multiplier per channel, with the response count it came from.

6. Conversion window

→ Click attribution overvalues lower funnel by up to 250%. (Haus has shared great data here)
→ Top of funnel drives 13x more incremental acquisitions than bottom of funnel.
→ Days 20-40 is the biggest repurchase window, so a 1 day view window grades your best ads before they have done anything.
→ Same ad on a 7 day click window ÷ that ad on a 1 day view window = what your reporting window is costing top of funnel.
→ Apply a window multiplier to every top of funnel ad

How to test a new Google Ads conversion goal without breaking smart bidding

- Changing conversion action forces the Google algorithm to reoptimize
- Reoptimization is worth it if you're able to drive higher quality leads
- Google docs state you need around 1-2 conversion cycles for reoptimization

But, you also need to do this too:

1. Measure every potential event

Pull each event in your funnel and score it two ways.
a) How well reaching it correlates with a purchase
b) Whether it passes Google's minimum conversion event volume

→ Search: 15 conversions in 30 days
→ PMax: 30 a month
→ Demand Gen: 50 a month

2. Add it as a secondary

Secondary conversion actions are observation only. Google doesn't feed them to the bid strategy, so the new event builds history in All conversions while your bidding carries on untouched. Added benefit it gets the conversion event measured and ready for an eventual switch.

3. Set budget before you switch

Set it to what you intend to spend, then leave it. Google's guidance is to avoid large scale budget moves for 4-6 weeks after a conversion change.

4. Adjust targets for the new funnel stage

Your tCPA is different for a form fill vs a booked call. Reprice the target to the CPA you expect at the new stage (apply conversion event data you have to make that assumption)

CAUTION: Do this incrementally. Do not go to the new CPA number at once, the algo takes some time to adjust. I like to update the tCPA target every 1-2 days.

5. Freeze other changes

Then assume 1-2 conversion cycles for reoptimization, and 2-3 conversion cycles for measurement. For these 3-5 weeks do not make any other changes (e.g. adding keywords, new campaigns). We want to see if the change in conversion action improves performance.

6. Account for conversion lag

Example. An account had 51% of conversions land on day one and another 29% arrive after day 12. If your business has a conversion lag you need to wait longer for the CAC to stabilize until you can make an informed decision.

Cheatsheet:
- Score every candidate event on correlation and volume
- Run the new event as a secondary before promoting it
- Reprice the target for the deeper stage
- 1-2 cycles to reoptimize, 2-3 to measure

I ran GTM at a $23M SaaS

We grew 43% when we measured sales and marketing against the same metric:

Pipeline Velocity = (Qualified Opps × Win % × ACV) / Sales Cycle Length

Constraint ownership:
↳ Qualified opp volume drops → Marketing owns the 7-day fix
↳ Win rate drops → Sales diagnosis
↳ ACV drops → Check discounting first. Discounts up = Sales. Discounts flat, smaller logos = Marketing is sourcing the wrong segment
↳ Cycle length stretches → Sales analyzes stage by stage (pre-meeting = Marketing)
↳ Everything drops at once → ICP mismatch (joint war room)

Here is the exact RevOps architecture we used to scale from $16M to $23M ARR in 16 months:

1 // The CRM Object Model: Fit + Signal Tiers

Most CRMs are graveyards of unworked leads with no account context. We restructured the account object into 3 operational tiers and rolled every lead up to it:

↳ Tier 1 (Active Demand): Full ICP fit + 2 verified buying triggers in last 30 days. Routed directly to SDRs who reached out within 1hr
↳ Tier 2 (Fit, Low Signal): enrolled in stage-matched ABM air cover and nurture tracks
↳ Tier 3 (Signal, Poor Fit). auto-DQ to preserve SDR capacity

We required two fields on every target account:
↳ Committee Coverage Score: number of buying roles mapped out of the total for that segment. No deal moves past discovery with fewer than 3, and a single-threaded deal in Stage 3+ triggers a manager review.
↳ Trigger Timestamp (hiring surges, new tech install, leadership change)

2 // Routing & Speed-to-Lead Automation

↳ Inbound speed-to-lead: in our data, leads touched in <1 hour converted 2.8x better than leads touched after 24 hours
↳ Outbound rules: SDRs never reach out off cold lists. They sequence only when the account is Tier 1 and trigger is under 72 hours old
↳ Pre-call enrichment: Clay auto-populates the likely economic buyer and technical evaluator onto the account ahead of disco call, so the AE knows who to multi-thread toward.

3 // The Monday 9am Operating Cadence

Every Monday morning, leadership received 3 dashboards:

Report 1: GTM Efficiency
↳ Magic Number: annualized net new ARR ÷ prior-quarter S&M spend. 
↳ CAC Payback by segment: Mid-Market came down from 15 to 11 months. 
↳ LTV:CAC by channel: scale at 3:1, breakeven is 2:1, kill anything that stays under 2:1 for two quarters.

Report 2: Funnel Health
↳ Pipeline coverage by segment: 3x SMB, 4x Enterprise, reviewed against next-quarter quota↳ Deal aging: automated alert when an opportunity exceeds 2x average stage duration↳ Concentration risk: flag when 1 deal represents >25% of total pipeline
Report 3: Forecast Accuracy
↳ MAPE score by segment
↳ Bias detection: identifies consistent sandbagging vs optimistic forecasting
↳ Slippage risk: deals with no champion touch in the last 14 days.

This meant leadership walked into Monday knowing the 2-3 pipeline constraints to solve asap

1 formula, simple system architecture and 3 reports will steady the ship through Q4.

My real benchmark for how smart a model is: does it finish the work. Here's the loop I run it on every day.

Every day I round up everything that has to get done and all of it goes into ClickUp. Then I open each task and dictate the plan straight into it with Wispr Flow. It is the exact same planning prompt I would write if I were about to sit down and do that task myself.

Then I say one thing. Read all the open tasks in ClickUp, they all have plans inside them, write one gigantic plan with finish conditions on every part of it, hand them out to sub agents, and go do the work. Ask me any clarifying questions you need.

That is my whole day. It is my favorite thing to do with AI and I wish it was easier to show you.

With Opus 4.8 and the models before it, we would get 90% of the way there and the last 10% was a grueling battle every single time.

Fable 5 was the first model that got everything across the line. It listened to the run conditions and the finish conditions the best and it needed the least oversight from me of anything I have run.

Then I looked at my usage. One day of this and Fable had burned 85% of my account and I had to move over to Codex.

I ran the same work on Opus 5 this week. All of it finished, on 8% of my usage.

That is my own run on my own tasks, so take it as one data point and not a benchmark.

The reason the plan lives in ClickUp and not in a chat window is that the task is already where I write down what done looks like. The model gets the goal and the finish condition in the same place every time, and I never re-explain it.

I've advised over 100 founders on their content marketing strategy. The first thing I tell them is to write from their lived experience. Here's what I ACTUALLY mean by that:

- Start with a thing that happened, ideally in the last 7 days 

- Say when it happened and who it happened with

- Prioritise being specific and factual over impressive and interesting. e.g. writing about a client call from last Tuesday will build more trust than writing about your best ever year in business

- Share lessons, not advice. Advice is telling people what to do but a lesson is what you found out by doing it. Always write lessons.

- Frame, frame, frame. Show what most people in your market assume, THEN show what you found. 

- If anyone else in your industry could have written it, then it's not worth posting.

- Write it in your own clumsy way. The way you process thought and communicate is unique to you and that is way better than overly polished PC crap.

- If the actual writing part is blocking you from writing, voice note it. Use Wispr Flow to get it all out, then rewrite whatever comes back in your own words.

- Your niche is never too niche. There is an audience for everything. You just need to understand your TAM and reign expectations in accordingly.

None of this requires an impressive result. 

It just requires something to have happened and everyone has something happening to them, especially founders who are juggling business, health, family, relationships etc.

People tell me cold email doesn't work and then I ask how many emails they sent. 300.

Here's the threshold we actually use.

We don't call a campaign successful or unsuccessful until it has sent 1,000 emails.

If it sends 1,000 and gets one positive response, we let it run to 3,000 before we decide anything. Sometimes you just get unlucky, sometimes it is a bad week.

If it sends 1,000 and gets zero positives, we shut it off.

My full belief is that campaigns work quickly or they don't work.

You might have heard Alex Hormozi say he thought he could get outbound implemented in six months and it took a year. Fine, that is true of all of outbound. But that is the booking, the no shows, whether it is the right ICP, the sales process for a cold lead versus a warm one. Everything up to the positive response should show up fast.

So when you hit 1,000 and it is dead, before you rewrite the first line again, go check the two things that are a hard science.

Deliverability. Warmup at 100, the seed list came back clean, reply rate above 1%, the auto responder inboxes coming back over 80%, and whatever campaign you run that always works is still behaving normally.

The list. Have Claude read the whole thing and tell you whether these are actually the people you meant to email, then go look at a hundred of them yourself.

If both of those check out, stop editing the copy. Your problem is the offer, or the framing of it.

That is also why we will just run a free campaign for a company that wants to work with us. Either it works or it doesn't, and if it doesn't, you most likely need to radically change the offer.

"we hit 90% impression share & max'd Google ads"

I checked. It's not true.

I see at least 10x more Search growth. Here's how:

→ Impression share = impressions you got divided by impressions you were eligible to get.
→ 90% Impression share means you're appearing for 90% of what you were eligible for
→ But the account runs exact match only,

So 90% impression share means they win 90% of the auctions their exact match keywords enter.

Anyone can get to 90%, by only entering auctions that have the highest intent

But you can still grow your Google ads revenue by:

1. Match type split

→ Pull Search Exact Match Impression Share and compare it to overall Search Impression Share.
→ Both sitting at 90% means you're not bidding into the wider query space.
→ Exact at 90% with overall at 40% is the opposite problem.

2. Layer by theme

→ Exact match first, one theme per ad group.
→ Add Phrase once Exact hits 15 conversions a month.
→ Broad only with Smart Bidding running and a negative list already built.
→ Negatives are the guardrail on Broad match.

3. Impression share falls

→ Wider match types create more eligible impressions
→ This is normal and not a bad thing, we're not entering into more auctions
→ You need to then look through all the auctions you're entering and remove the keywords that aren't relevant

4. Max Search TAM

→ Triangulate volume. Search Volume = Impressions ÷ Search IS. Cross-check against the Google Ads forecasting tool (build a campaign, don't launch it, set max CPC high, read Impressions) and a keyword planner like SEMrush or Ahrefs. Average the three.
→ Max Potential Revenue = Volume × CTR × CVR × Rev/Conv.
→ Max Efficient Spend = Max Revenue ÷ Target ROAS.

For example, imagine a hypothetical account:

- Their exact match universe reads 100,000 searches a month (90,000 impressions ÷ 90%).
- Triangulated across the full theme, it's 1,000,000.
- 1,000,000 × 5% CTR × 8% CVR × $3,000 per conversion = $12M a month.
- The 100,000 they can see = $1.2M a month.
- At a 4x target ROAS, max efficient spend is $3M a month.

Cheatsheet:
- Impression share measures how much of your own keyword list you win
- Match type sets the size of the keyword list
- Widening match types drops the percentage and raises the revenue
- You can calculate your Google ads Search revenue ceiling

How to know which ads to kill or scale

1. Take every ad you're running
2. Plot it on a graph
3. Y axis = CPA
4. X axis = Spend (log)
5. Choose your target CPA
6. Define your kill CPA (typically 2-3x tCPA)
7. Draw those lines horizontally

Now you have three types of ads:

Scale = Green
→ CPA below your target line, with spend already behind them
→ Expect about 1% of your ads here. They'll drive 50% of revenue
→ Move budget 20% at a time so you don't trigger relearning

Test = Yellow
→ CPA sits between your target and kill line
→ This is most of your account, usually 65%+ of ads
→ Push more budget and watch where it lands. Drops toward target you scale, climbs past kill you cut

Kill = Red
→ CPA above your kill line with enough spend behind it
→ Enough data to be 90% confident it never hits target
→ Ideally you have zero here. If an ad got this far, you cut too slow

How are you deciding what to cut in your accounts?

Yesterday, I lost a 3000-person January SKO workshop deal. Here's exactly what I did to lose it (and how you can lose deals, too). 

First, am I bummed? Of course. It would've been an awesome logo. It had all the markings of a deal that should close. Former client introduced me. On a texting basis with the champion. Champion looped me in with her boss + peers for conversations. She, personally, wanted it to happen. Clear COI against a '27 CEO business objective. 

But, these are exactly the type of deals that used to stay in my pipeline for months. Because I didn't want to hear bad news. So, I didn't make it easy for prospects to give it to me. So, I'd stall until I got desperate for an answer at EOQ.  As a result, I'd leave myself no time to fill my pipeline gap. And, I'd frustrate my manager when my forecast would bottom out 2 days before EOQ. 

One of the great things about my business now is that I HAVE to be better at disqualifying. If I hold a January SKO date, and the customer gives me a no in November, it's unlikely I'll book another one for that day. 

So, here are the two things I did to lose the deal early (that any seller can copy): 

1. In the discovery call, I asked a direct question: "I hope I've earned the right for you to be transparent with me. What, in your opinion, are the most likely reasons your CRO would say no to our idea?". She gave me 2 reasons. 

2. When I didn't hear from her for a couple days, I sent her a text. "Hi! If you hit a sticking point, or heard bad news, you can tell me." Other times, I'll use "Did we hit an unexpected roadblock?". Or, "Did REASON end up happening?". 

The key is that YOU are the one to label the bad news. If you did #1 in discovery, you already know the likely deal threats. Be the one to throw one out in the open, first. If we're wrong, they'll correct us. 

This is especially true if you have good rapport with your prospect. In general, humans don't like the way they feel about themselves when they tell someone they like, "no". Be the one to put the bad news out there, first. 

I got a reply right away that reason #1 was it. "I've been holding out hope that we can keep pushing, but unfortunately.....". 

Of course, it's a bummer to lose a deal. But a GREAT seller has a 30% win rate. That means they lose 7 deals and win 3. 

We can't be afraid to hear bad news. It's part of the job. It's WHEN we hear the bad news that makes the difference. Your time is your most precious commodity.  

Lastly - I sent a note to the leaders I spoke with, thanking them for the opportunity and wishing them a successful SKO. Sales is a long game. How we show grace after a loss matters.

I have been hired 9 times to fix a revenue number that was missing target. The candidate who presents well and the operator who steadies the ship are not the same person. 

Most exec teams find that out in month 6.

Here is what actually separates an experienced operator from someone who interviews well:

1 // They do not need domain expertise to move the needle
Helpful, not required. Pattern recognition travels. Category knowledge can be bought in 60 days.

2 // They evaluate fast, then decide
Short diagnostic window, then calls. Not a 90 day listening tour that produces a deck.

3 // Their early calls are better than 80% right
You will know by day 45. Write the decisions down. Score them.

4 // When they do not know, they have the confidence to see it through
The tell is not certainty. It is what happens when they are wrong in week 6 and still have it fixed by week 10.

Anyone can be good in month one. The job is months 3, 6 and 9.

And here is what most exec teams are not seeing.

You are watching revenue miss. That part is easy to see, it shows up on a slide.

What does not show up is the confidence draining out of the team. Quarter after quarter of leadership not knowing how to fix it, until the org quietly stops believing anyone will.

Missed targets are recoverable. Distrust compounds.

Keep the wrong leader in the seat, or hire the fourth replacement in three years, and entire departments go into a spiral you cannot hire your way out of.

Question for the operators here:

What was the earliest real signal you got that a leadership hire was wrong?

For one of our customers we're getting 80 to 100 positive responses a day and I don't touch the account. A Grok bot does four jobs on a cron.

Here's what has to stay true every day or a campaign like this dies.

1. Enough leads in the campaign.

Every day Grok Bot checks how many leads are not started. If it's ever under 100,000 it pulls from our Supabase, which tracks who we emailed in the last 60 days, who we re-reached in the last 30, and what month we last touched them, so nobody gets hit more than once a quarter. Then it fires them at a Clay webhook and the Clay CLI workflow does the cleanup, the enrichment, and the AI content.

2. Volume actually going out.

At noon it checks how many emails went out that day. If something locked up and we're under-sending, it rechecks the campaigns and refills them itself.

3. Daily Deliverability check

It reads our inbox table in Supabase every morning. If a domain was replying at 1.5% and drops to 0.2% day over day, it pulls that domain out, cancels the subscription, and swaps another one in.

4. The Friday inbox destroyer

Every Friday it looks for domains that have sent over 200 emails with under a 0.7% reply rate overall. Those get scheduled for cancellation and pulled out of the campaigns. Then it tells me how many domains we need to buy to replace them. I audit that, make the correction, and put the order in at Hypertide.

The reason it's Grok Bot and not the other agent harnesses is boring. The cron job actually fires. I have set one up in Hermes, then checked in three times wondering why it never ran. 

Codex or Claude schedules can totally do this too but if my computer is off it won't run.

IM8 Health launched 10,000 ads since June.

Isn't that WAY too many???

→ Launched in June, already running 10,000 ads
→ A chunk of the output, in my opinion, is AI slop
→ Their last reported quarter put $22.2M of marketing against $23.3M of gross profit

So why 10,000 ads?

Heres my take:

1. Marketing eats gross profit

→ Q1 revenue $36M, gross profit $23.3M on a 65% margin
→ Selling and marketing came in at $22.2M, so 95% of gross profit went straight back out to acquisition
→ Loss from operations $8.9M, and adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $5.6M from $4.5M a year earlier
→ Net loss reads $23.1M, but $17.8M of that is non-cash marks on digital assets and warrants
→ Revenue grew 6x YoY and the cost base scaled right along with it

2. Orders went backwards

→ Q1 orders came in at 220,000, down from 230,000+ in Q4
→ Revenue climbed 23% QoQ anyway, on $240 new customer AOV and ~79% of new customers subscribing
→ So the growth came out of order value while the customer count fell

3. Someone else funds 70% of CAC

→ General Catalyst's $1B CVF finances up to 70% of IM8's customer acquisition cost
→ It books as a financial liability, repaid out of revenue from those customers
→ The return sits below operating income as interest expense, so it never touches gross margin
→ 100% of the marketing keeps landing in S&M, which is why that line looks so heavy

Payback is ~3.5 months and 70% of the CAC is financed.

Volume is the obvious lever to pull.

But this invites natural failure points
→ Too many low-quality ads
→ Too many ads carrying legal risk
→ Too many near-identical ads splitting the same audience
→ Brand consistency begins to slip

Worth saying those numbers cover January to March. The blitz started in June, so none of it has hit a reported quarter yet. Q2 is guided to $46-48M and May alone did $16.7M.

I'm very curious how the next 12 months pans out...

I've been getting a lot of questions about Google AI Max. Here's common questions and my answers. Hope it helps:

Q1: Is it going to be the default?
- The forcing is only for certain campaign setups. Campaign-level broad match and auto-created assets get upgraded in September. Dynamic search ads follow in February 2027. Outside of those setups you aren't being forced at all. Google documents no opt-out for the ones that are.

Q2: Is it going to work for my business?
- We're testing it on a few accounts at one campaign each. No findings worth sharing so far.

Q3: How many conversions do I need per month?
- Google says there's no minimum. But Search Term Matching won't run on manual CPC at all. I won't open broad expansion under 30 conversions a month (ideally 50). That's 30-50 across the account. Per campaign is a myth.

Q4: What businesses does it work for?
- Ecommerce and retail, the same as DSA before it. Google always starts with retail because that's where they make the most of their money, so retail benefits first. I expect B2B SaaS, Healthcare, etc to follow suit.

Q5: Do I need to do anything to the ad copy?
- Text Customization writes the copy for you. There's no manual override. Turn on Text Customization and Final URL Expansion together and Google stops respecting your pinned RSA assets.

Q6: Do I need to do anything to the landing pages?
- Final URL Expansion picks whichever page on your domain it predicts will convert best. Constrain the expansion with URL exclusions in the Rules tab, or URL inclusions at ad group level.

Q7: Do I need to do anything to the keywords?
- Build the negative list before it turns on. Run in-depth search term reports in the weeks before your migration date so you go in with a strong keyword list. Once AI Max is live, stay close to the search term report and add as many negatives as you can. That's the best way to counteract it.

Q8: How do I optimize it over time?
- Google says wait two weeks after enabling before you change anything. Then pull the search term report every 2-3 days until the query set looks clean for 10 days.

Q9: How do I evaluate performance?
- Filter Match type to AI Max in the search terms report. Run the native experiment rather than a before/after read. Reconcile attribution yourself so AI Max doesn't grade itself.

Q10: Will my results fall or improve?

You need to stay right side of the slope:

You have two dials to achieve high scale and low CPA.
- Moving budget up or down
- Moving bid up or down

If you're under budget:
→ Want better performance? Bid down, budget down.
→ Want more scale? Bid up, budget the same.
→ Want to scale hard? Push both.

The moment you ARE hitting your budget, the bid is how you protect efficiency:
→ Performance just okay? Budget up, bid down.
→ Performance good? Budget up, leave the bid.
→ Performance strong? Budget up, bid up. Let it rip.

Don't let Meta pick your winning ads

Without doing this:

I recently ran an analysis for a brand with two products.

They were judging their ads on in-platform day-one or 7-day click CPA.

Product A
→ Converted great on day one
→ Tapered off fast after that
→ Lower AOV product
→ Easy decision for the consumer to buy

Product B
→ Looked worse on day-one and 7-day click
→ Longer consideration cycle, higher AOV
→ Ended up the best product after we waited 15+ days
→ Won by even more once we layered in incrementality

Follow Meta's in-platform metrics and we kill Product B. Meta was losing the conversion event proven by incrementality testing, and it is what we have been told to blindly trust.

But there is more to attribution than what Meta reports.

1. Compare 1, 7 and 28-day windows. (Start with in platform then move to incrementality testing)
→ That gap is your purchase velocity. Promos convert inside the 1-day window. Awareness ads show up at 28.
→ A high-AOV ad that looks dead at day 7 could still climbing at day 28.

2. Judge new-customer CPA in your MTA.
→ Triple Whale or Northbeam shows who bought and where they came from first.
→ Meta may miss the ad that opened the consideration cycle. And they report all customers not just new.

3. Give high-AOV ads 30 days before you cut.
→ Days 20-40 is where the repurchases land.
→ Cut at day 7 to look efficient and you never see them.

Day-one CPA tells you which ad converts fastest.
It tells you nothing about which one drives your LTV.

P.S. This isn’t sponsored but Churney has a cool free tool to see how much impact LTV has and if this should be a concern in your account. It isn’t always an issue. Just look up “churney growth predictability test”

I asked Claude & ChatGPT a Google ads question

Both got it HORRENDOUSLY wrong

Q: "How do I increase ROAS while scaling spend?"

I pointed it at a live account and let it pull everything. Campaigns, keywords, search terms, quality scores, conversion lag, geo, dayparts.

The audit came back detailed, but some key errors:

1. PMax

→ It said don't run PMax, and cited the last test's blended CPA as proof it fails on this account.
→ I asked whether the algorithm had moved on since then.
→ It split the campaign by network. The Search slice was running at about a third of the blended number, cheaper than the main non-brand Search campaign. Most of the spend had been sitting on Search Partners, Display and YouTube.
→ Wrong. It wrote off a channel on a blended average while 80% of the spend sat outside the part that was working. The old test had also run on a budget too small to exit learning, so there was nothing to conclude either way.

2. Landing page experience

→ It said fixing landing page experience would buy 10-20% CPC relief, and put a monthly dollar figure on the saving.
→ I asked whether I should update the page now and whether it would hit the live ads.
→ It went and tested the account. Keywords rated below average on landing page experience were taking cheaper clicks and a better CPA than the ones rated average.
→ Wrong, and it withdrew the number. The saving came off general benchmarks and the account pointed the other way. What it said next was right. Don't swap URLs mid-test, because editing an ad's final URL replaces the ad and resets its history.

3. Reading the data too early

→ It said one of the revenue mix metrics had dropped under the client's floor.
→ I told it I was worried about the drop.
→ It re-pulled the metric by cohort maturity. Most conversions land same day, and same-day cohorts read lowest on that metric. Across the weeks old enough to read, the number sat comfortably above the floor.
→ Wrong, and it caught the reason itself. It had written the rule earlier in the same audit that nothing inside 14 days should be read, then read two weeks that were four days old.

Before you act on an AI audit, check three things.
- Whether the number is blended or sliced.
- How mature the reporting window is.
- And where the claim came from, the account or a benchmark.

VP of Sales: "We're losing to competitors"

So I read all 35,000 of their closed lost deals.

Not one was tagged competitor.

When a revenue number misses, the default suspects are always product, lead gen, or the competition.

Then you open the CRM activity logs.

On their largest deals, over 18 months:
↳ The median won deal took 13 contact attempts
↳ The median lost deal stopped at 5
↳ The median disqualified deal stopped at 3

But here's the part that actually matters.

With the same deals and size band, the only variable was who owned them:
↳ Top rep: 34% win rate
↳ Team average: 19%
↳ Shared inbound queue: 5%
↳ No owner assigned: 0%

The deal didn't decide. The routing did.

55 of those deals were worth $694k combined and were never assigned to anyone. Median contact attempts: zero. They won none of them.

And the ones that die don't get closed out.

A deal they win closes in 36 days. A deal they lose sits open for 165 days before anyone marks it dead.

So reps spend months staring at bloated pipeline, convincing themselves coverage is fine, working deals that died last quarter.

Here's the fix:

1 // Fix routing before you fix reps

↳ Kill the shared inbound queue for anything above your ACV threshold & assign it to a human on arrival.
↳ Audit unowned pipeline weekly. Zero is the only acceptable number.
↳ Reassign books held by departed reps within 48 hours, not "eventually."

2 // Enforce persistence thresholds

Deals we invested in closed at roughly 10x the rate of deals we didn't. Some of that is that good deals attract effort. Some of it isn't.
↳ Validation rules so opportunities can't be marked closed-lost below a minimum touch count.
↳ Multi-channel, not single-channel bursts.
↳ Track average contact attempts per opportunity by rep, and coach on the gap.

3 // Age out the rot

When dead pipeline sits open for 165 days, forecast accuracy is fiction.
↳ Alert the moment a deal exceeds 2x average cycle time.
↳ Stage duration limits: advance it or disqualify it.
↳ Route abandoned accounts back to nurture instead of letting them decay in open pipeline.

You don't need more top-of-funnel to hit the number.

You need the pipeline you already have to reach a human and a minimum # of touch points per deal.

Scaling a B2B lead gen account to $300k/mo

Levers we're working through right now

- Funnel runs lead, booked call, qualified proposal, closed won
- Multi-location, one page template across all
- Tracking runs through HubSpot
- Google rep pushing AI Max on every call

What we're doing:

1. AI Max stays off
→ Google is auto-upgrading some search campaigns to AI Max.
→ Teams panic and migrate a working account early. The upgrade only hits campaigns on broad match at the campaign level, or dynamic search ads. Check those two settings before you assume you're moving.
→ Google ships every product for retail first, because retail is where the money is. Lead gen gets the version that works several releases later.
→ So AI Max stays off. We're pulling search term reports weekly and building the negative list now, ready for if the account does get moved.

2. HubSpot connector troubleshooting
→ We push closed-won deals from HubSpot into Google as offline conversions, so bidding chases deals instead of form fills.
→ Some deals arrive with gaps. Every missing deal is a buyer Google never learns from, so it keeps buying leads that look like form fills.
→ The connector gives you no error log, so there's nothing to debug against.
→ Build a throwaway test conversion action in Google, wait four hours for it to activate, then manually CSV upload those same deals.
→ The manual upload returns an error per row. Now you can see whether the timestamp, the click ID, or the HubSpot filter is at fault.

3. Second conversion goal
→ The account bids on booked calls today. Good volume, but a booked call includes people who were never going to buy, and Google buys more of whatever you count.
→ We're adding qualified proposals as a second conversion action. The account runs about 60 a month, and you want 30 or more before a secondary carries enough signal.
→ Google doesn't rank the two conversion types. Smart Bidding optimizes the combined count, so the deeper event pulls spend toward the people who reach it.
→ Cost per conversion will look close to 10% worse for a few weeks, because proposals take longer to land than calls.

4. Quiz funnel replaces long form
→ Every location page ends in one long form asking for everything up front. This is high friction.
→ Instead, opting for a quiz that asks one easy question first, shows the rest of the offer as they move through it, then expands into the full form. The buyer self-selects on the way in.

A campaign with a low reply rate and a campaign whose reply rate fell off a cliff are two different problems, and here's how we tell them apart before touching the copy.

We pull reply rate per domain and per inbox on a 7 day and a 14 day window. That part is normal.

The part I would add for you is a separate alarm that fires on the size of the drop, not the level.

An inbox that was at a 1.5% reply rate and comes back at 0.2% gets looked at that day. It is still technically sending. Nothing in the dashboard is red.

Because a rate that was always bad is a list problem or an offer problem. A rate that was fine last week and is dead this week is almost always mechanical, and there are two things I check.

First, did we email a spam trap. If a trap address got into the list in the last day, those domains need to come out immediately, they are going to get tanked either way. This is worth moving to a more premium validation provider over, one that actually screens for traps. I always forget which ones do it, so ask around before you buy.

Second, content fingerprinting. Same text going out enough times that Google recognizes it.

Small thing on that second one. If you ask Claude to spintax an email, it will often just swap one word per sentence and call it done. Tell it you want word level spintax and you get real variation, and check that your signature and your unsubscribe language got spintaxed too, because most people only do the body.

Ask Claude or Codex to build the alarm against your sending tool's API. Mine is a scheduled job that just tells me which inboxes moved the most since last week.

Clay is ruining cold email. Take it from someone who spent 4 years sending 300+ outbound emails every single day. Outbound used to be about finding what resonated. You tested a core pain point, measured the response, and refined the message.

Today, I watch outbound teams build massive Clay tables to hyper-personalize

They scrape every detail they can find on a prospect, generate custom copy for every lead, and hit send.

Then the campaign falls flat, and they have no idea why.

Start with the offer. Then personalize.

Here is the cold outbound testing hierarchy that books me consistent 3.7% positive replies:

1// Test the offer first
Find an offer that pulls before writing custom copy.

↳ Keep copy standardized across the test cohort
↳ Zero deep personalization beyond basic account fields
↳ Test distinct value propositions against each other
↳ Run each offer until you establish a clean baseline

Target: ~1% baseline positive reply rate on a standardized email.

If an audience will not respond to the core offer with standard copy, personalizing the first sentence will not save it.

Example: “Would you be interested if I built you a contact list of your past clients who just changed jobs and aren't working with you yet?”

2// Hyper-personalization testing
Personalization does work, but it needs to be standardized and tested thoroughly. 

If you run offer testing against 100+ daily sends, pair it down to 10 per day. This will give you the ability to hyper-customize.

↳ Do a ton of research on the person, a little nugget about them and mention it to them in email, super casual.↳ Then find them on all social platforms possible (Instagram, LinkedIn, X, Facebook)↳ Message them on all those platforms to give you a higher probability of being seen.↳ This takes 10 outreaches per day and 3-4x’s it. ↳ Copy and paste the same message and say “btw I reached out to you via email also”

This is how you hit 25% reply rate on a small list. Same impact as 100+ emails per day.

2// Personalization + Offer = Scale

↳ Keep the winning offer and call to action identical
↳ Your manual personalization work will help you ID the 2-3 types of customized messages that work. Wrap them around a specific pain or buying trigger (Clay is great for this part!)

Target: scale reply rates up to 3-5%.With buying triggers I see positive replies above 6%.

Testing constraints:

1 // Cohorts
↳ 1 industry
↳ 1 buyer committee role
↳ 300 contacts per test cohort
↳ 2 emails per contact

2 // Send limits
↳ Never hit the same contact with more than 1 offer per month
↳ Tag every record with the offer version and cohort outcome

This testing system means:
- You know exactly which offer generates pipeline
- Personalization scales a working message instead of hiding a weak one

This is the rigor that outbound teams need.

There are only 3 ways to scale Meta ads

Increasing budget is the worst one. 

You find some winning ads and started increasing budgets

But eventually it loses effectiveness because:

-> The same people start seeing your ad 5, 6, 7 times
-> Cost per customer goes up 
-> Your winner ads burn out
-> The Meta algorithm runs out of new people to find

You can combat against this. 

There are 3 ways to scale:

(1) Vertical - increase spend on what's working. This is the default and the first to break. Use it until frequency starts climbing, then stop.

(2) Horizontal - change the message angle to increase creative diversity. The way I like to think of this is "motivator mapping". Different people have different motivations. For instance, if you’re running an efficiency angle ("Save 10 hours a week"), it’ll only reach efficiency buyers. Status buyers will scroll past no matter how much you spend. So, launch a status angle ("Look like a genius to your boss") or an enemy angle ("Stop letting [Competitor] win") and you reach a different segment. You can spend $50K/month on each without them competing.

The best way to test an email validator is on emails you already know are real.

Not a sample file. Not the vendor's demo list. Your own interested replies from last week.

Somebody who wrote back "yes, I'm interested" has proven their address is a live inbox with a human reading it. So if a validator grades that address catch-all or invalid, you caught it being wrong, and you can count how often.

1. export everyone who gave you a positive reply in the last week or two. that's your answer key.

2. run those through the validator you use today. anything that comes back catch-all or invalid is a miss you can prove.

3. do the same thing on a fresh pull from a provider like Prospeo, then watch the actual bounce rate in production. that's the other half of the picture and it's the half people skip.

4. cost-benefit it for your own volume.

I ran ours against Lead Magic, 500 addresses, about a day and a half of positive responses. 14.6% of them graded catch-all, and we throw catch-all in the garbage, so that whole slice would have been deleted off a normal list. Lead Magic validated them.

Most validator comparisons are people arguing about brand. This one is just a number you can check, and the answer key is already sitting in your replies folder.

Ugly YouTube ads work

Just hit a 4x ROAS

→ No need to pay for any additional creatives
→ Or make anything bespoke for Youtube 
→ And can be done with existing Meta ads 

We’re now spending ~$700k/mo across accounts profitably

This is the playbook: 

1. Ads
- Grab your highest performing social Ads. If you aren't running social, just make some simple animated text-based ads in 16x9, 9x16, and 1x1
- Launch into a PMax / DemandGen campaign 
- Avoid early traps of over-segmenting into YouTube-only campaigns. Let Google figure it out here. 
- Dedicate enough spend for 50 conversions per month (base CPA off search historicals)

We’ve found that production value isn’t a deal breaker for Youtube to work.

Ugly ads have high performance if they follow this structure: 
 - First 5 seconds must create pattern interrupt. 
- Then acknowledge the problem directly, mirror what viewers already know. 
- Finally, present simple resolution with clear next steps. 

Ugly = anything you already have motion graphics, founder talking heads, static-to-video conversions, basic screen recordings.

2. Scale on CPA
- Don’t compare Youtube to Meta. Instead, compare it to Search. If using Demand Gen, look at the "platform comparable" columns.
- Scaling = CPA within 20-30% of search + consistent conversion volume 
- Keep an eye on brand search volume, it’s likely Youtube will generate demand that Search will take attribution for. 

3. Creative Upgrade
- Ideally, you’re seeing positive returns from Youtube 
- Now you've earned better production
- YouTube users have longer attention spans and expect education or entertainment. 
- Think mini-documentaries, content series and informative assets 
- We bucket creative into 3 different lengths. Length 1 (20% of assets) = 30-60 seconds for fast validation, Length 2 (70% of assets) = 60-120 seconds for core performance, Length 3 (10% of assets) 2-5 minutes for education and high trust. 

It’s a simple playbook 
1. Validate cheaply (ugly ads)
2. Prove economics (CPA vs Search)
3. Upgrade creatives (structured creative)
