Are you underpricing your DTC product?

Quick check:

I mapped 21 DTC categories by price.

There are five zones on the curve in my opinion.

1. Impulse. $5 to $30.
→ Low purchase prices means minimal risk to the buyer
→ Sell dissatisfaction with what they already own.

2. Low consideration. $22 to $70.
→ They'll likely make a purchase given proof
→ Run problem solution ads with clear proof

3. Considered. $55 to $165.
→ Several sessions before they buy.
→ You'll want to argue why this product is better than another
→ If you're cheaper than competitors then show this

4. Deliberated. $140 to $560.
→ They now begin asking what happens if this is a bad purchase.
→ More heavily looking at refund policies, and asking what if questions
→ Risk reversals do well here

5. Major purchase. $460 and up.
→ They don't convert from a cold ad.
→ You need several touch points to show proof, build goodwill
→ You'll find only a small percentage of people would ever buy your product

Your price dictates how your customers act

Note some categories are sensitive (health / care of others) far more than price would imply and have long purchase cycles.

And where you sit between zones and your competitors dictates your marketing angles. 

Know if you are on the high end or low end of your own category but also against all potential purchases. 

Definitely worth running this exercise against all the other brands in your competitive category.

Here's how & when I run geo-lift tests:

HOW:

→ Start with one business question. Pick the single tactic you want to isolate ("is our top-of-funnel spend actually driving new customers?").
→ Split into matched regions. Balanced treatment and control groups on population, spend history and seasonality.
→ Turn the ads off in control.
→ Measure the lift. Spend heavily in the test region, hold control flat, measure the drop in sales.
→ Then cross-check it. Confirm against your post-purchase survey and follow marginal ROAS down to a profitable CPA.

WHEN:

→ You're spending $500K-1M a month. Below that, the operational cost isn't worth it. Above it, run one quarterly on your biggest budget questions.
→ You're making a reallocation decision and you don't fully trust existing data.
→ A channel looks too good on last-click.

WHY:

→ You're measuring incrementality. Click attribution rewards whatever converts last, so promos and retargeting look like your best performers. A geo-lift tells you what the spend actually caused.
→ You calibrate your MTA reporting to the causal read. Your top ads can look 50% different in Northbeam versus the platform. The geo-lift gives you the true number, so you adjust your MTA figure to it.
→ You allocate off the calibrated number. Spend goes to what's proven incremental.

Cheatsheet:
- Run one at $500K-1M/mo spend, quarterly.
- One region on, one region off. Measure the gap.
- Calibrate MTA to the causal number, then reallocate.

Helping a $500k/mo Google ads client run a geo holdout test. Here's everything that we're considering (so when you run one, you do it right):

CONTEXT:
- Last 12 months had great Google growth
- Next 12 months we're pushing more into Meta, TikTok, TV & Programmatic
- We want to know how those new channels working together will impact the business

1. Avoiding expensive tooling
→ You can measure new channel impact with multi-touch attribution, but it reads off the same click and UTM data you already collect. If that data has gaps, so does the tool. Plus it’s cumbersome to setup.
→ Media mix modeling runs $10-15k/mo. The client didn't want to spend into that.
→ A geo holdout needs none of that tracking to work. You measure it on total customers per geo.
→ Objectively easier and faster to set up

2. Calculate test size and timeline
→ Decide on what significant number of conversions look like for your business to have confidence in the end CAC number. For example, you might want to see 200 conversions.
→ Check your conversion lag, you might see that it takes 30 days for a click to result in an end customer and have a fully baked out CAC.
→ Assume a $150 CPA and that's $24k of new spend. If you spend that all on day 1 it would convert by day 30, but likely we'll spend that $500 daily in these new markets. That would take 48 days to spend. We then add 30 days to the last day which takes us to 78 days, which would be the length of our test
→ We can spend more daily, it'll make the test shorter and give less time for in-test optimizations. The more confident we are on the assets / creatives and channels performing out the gate, the faster we would spend

3. Answer in two phases
→ Phase one, put every new channel into a specific geo and compare against everything that isn't those geos. Measure impact on total customers
→ Splitting channels across separate geos at this stage can reduce budget too far and increase test time more than you'd like - but if you have the budget, you can do it
→ Phase two, once you have the combined lift, separate the channels to identify if it's Meta or Connected TV that has a bigger impact.

Note: a geo holdout won't tell you which creative drove the lowest funnel action.

Imagine you're working with a prospect who likes your solution. But, they can't make the decision to buy it on their own. I used to ask: "Who else should we involve in a demo?”

Prospect: "Well, let me socialize this with the group first. I'll get back to you." 

I'd follow up. 
And follow up. 
And follow up. 

Until, I realized the problem was what I was asking for and how I was asking for it. 

I was asking them to put their political capital at risk. I was asking for their permission to sell to people who didn't express interest in being sold to. I was dumping the hardest job in their lap. 

So, here's what I ask now, before asking "who should be involved": 

--> “Who is most likely to be skeptical of prioritizing this business problem? Why? What else would they prioritize above it?” 

--> “Who is most likely to be pro-status quo? Why?”

--> “We agreed the problem is ACME’s 22% customer churn rate. Who is likely to have a different opinion of the problem ACME should be solving? Why?”

--> “What other organizational priorities are we competing against for time/attention/budget?”

These indirect questions tell me who SHOULD be involved in a group meeting. I can take those answers and make a prescriptive recommendation to my champion. 

Because companies won’t reach consensus on a solution, if they can’t reach consensus on whether the problem is worth solving, and worth solving now.

Google Demand Gen ROAS falling?

It might be creative fatigue.

How to check (and what to do)

One of our big Google Ads accounts had Demand Gen performing well, then it stopped a few months ago.

Our diagnostics:

1. Check the change log first

→ Change History overlays edits against impressions, clicks, conversions, cost and CTR. If there are no bid, budget or targeting edits in the window, creative is the only thing that changed. (I run this through AI to make it easier)

2. Read rolling pacing 7 14 30 60

→ Break spend out by source and read last 7, 14, 30 and 60 day pacing plus CPC on a rolling basis.
→ The fatigue pattern is flat spend, no account changes, CTR down, CPC up, CVR down.

3. Compare actuals against forecast

→ Forecast every node. CPC, CTR, CVR, CAC, ROAS. Pace actuals against it. The first node that diverges is the problem. Everything downstream of it is a symptom.
→ ROAS is the last node in the chain, so diagnosing off ROAS tells you nothing about what caused the issue.

4. Open the asset level report

→ Demand Gen reports clicks, CTR, impressions and conversion value for every headline, description, image, video and logo, refreshed daily. That isolates which asset stopped performing.
→ Google publishes no fatigue score and no decay threshold here. Their only guidance is to replace an asset that gets zero impressions for several weeks.

5. Rule out the August target enforcement

→ On August 17 Google started enforcing tCPA and tROAS on budget-limited campaigns. A campaign converting at $48 against an $80 target gets pushed back toward $80. CPA rises, ROAS falls while the creative is untouched. This might look like creative fatigue, but is actually incorrect media buying.
→ This applies to Search, Shopping, Performance Max, Demand Gen and Travel. Check your targets before you assume it's creative fatigue.

6. Rebuild from what already worked

→ Audit what performed historically against what fatigued, build three new concepts off that, relaunch. On our account it returned to full performance plus around 10% incremental conversions.

- Forecast the full funnel before you need it, so you can spot the divergence the day after it happens.
- When fatigue is confirmed, produce new creative as fast as you can.

Dwight Schrute gave one of the best lessons I've ever seen re: how to defeat a bigger competitor in your category. Here's what he did + 2 real examples where I've seen this approach work in B2B. 

In Season 3, Episode 12 of The Office, Jim and Dwight meet a prospect who decides to buy from their big box competitor, because their prices are lower. 

At first, Jim does what what most of us do.

He rambles on about discounts and custom work in an attempt to increase the perceived value.

Meanwhile, Dwight uses the prospect's phone to call customer service at their big box competitor. 

Jim: "How important is customer service to you?"

Prospect: "Very important."

At that moment, the competitor's automated customer service line says, "Your call is very important to us...please hold...".

Dwight hangs up and calls their own customer service line. Kelly picks up immediately.

Here's why I love this scene. 

We don't win competitive deals when we try to compete on areas where our competitors clearly outperform us. 

We win competitive deals when we reframe the customer's decision-making criteria in our favor. 

Jim and Dwight can't compete with a big box retailer's pricing, without destroying their margin. 

So, they reframe the prospect's decision-making criteria from price to service. 

But, best of all, they don't TELL the prospect they're "better" at service. Every rep claims that. 

They SHOW him. They give the prospect the information he needs to realize it for himself. 

Now, while most of us can't copy exactly what Jim and Dwight did, we can absolutely make this work in real-life.

Step 1 - Identify what makes your solution different (not better).
Step 2 - Identify how NOT having that difference impacts your customer's business.
Step 3 - Give them a way to do the math on their own to see the implications of it.

Examples I've seen in real-life:

1 - Small manufacturer vs. bigger competitor. Bigger meant more layers of approval for change orders. Waiting for change orders = more downtime. Downtime carried a significant cost. Helped the buyer do the math on cost of avoidable downtime.

2- Diagnostic product that gave more accurate patient results, but was slower. Kept losing b/c buyers valued faster results. Helped the buyer realize the downstream costs/implications of inaccurate patient results.

DTC creative benchmarks I follow:

1. Testing split

→ 50% iterations. Take a proven winner and tweak one thing.
→ 40% adjacent. Same selling angle, new format.
→ 10% big swings. Net new wildcard concepts.

2. Monthly creative churn

→ 27-35% of spend churns to new ads every month in high volume accounts.
→ You replace a third of your winners to stay flat.

3. Hit rate

→ 10-15% of new ads hitting your CPA threshold is healthy.
→ 70% of creatives get cut before week 2.

4. Spend concentration

→ Top 1-2% of ads drive around 50% of spend and revenue.
→ If they share one angle, they can fatigue together.

5. Kill or scale zones

→ Scale zone: about 1% of your ads. They drive 50% of revenue. Move budget onto them 20% at a time.
→ Test zone: 65%+ of your ads. Let them spend until they prove out or drop to kill.
→ Kill zone: enough spend to be 90% confident an ad never hits target. Turn it off.

6. Creative vs copy

→ Creative is about 10x more impactful than primary text.
→ Copy is worth testing anyway. Two primary texts on the same creative: $350 CPA vs $200 CPA.

7. Testing budget

→ Target 1 new concept per $10k in monthly spend.
→ Each new ad should get around $3k in spend

8. Hook rate

→ Median across 50+ DTC brands I've tracked: 32%.
→ Target 35%+. The top 25% of brands run 42%+.

9. Winner lifespan

→ Average winner lasts 45-60 days. Top performers run 90+.
→ Keep the creative pipeline 30 days ahead so replacements are live before decline.

Hope this helps

I let AI audit a live Google Ads account.

It got 3 things right and 3 things wrong.

I told it to check this account for disapproved ads and then have a general look around.

What it got right:

1. Identified constraint
→ Search lost impression share due to budget was 90%.
→ That is the correct constraint in this account. A limited budget stopped us from being eligible to show in 9/10 auctions. It's unlikely better ads will make a difference if we're not appearing for searches.

2. Match type progression
→ Every active keyword was exact match after a restructure we launched the previous Friday.
→ It confirmed exact was right for now and asked "When should we change the match type?"
→ That's a good question. Although it is an obvious answer in Google documentation: you open into broad match once those exact keywords hold a stable CPA, you've got conversion data in and you want to expand your universe of keywords to enter more auctions.

3. Search term negatives
→ It pulled the search term report and returned a clean list of junk queries.
→ They were generally the correct terms, albeit with some small manual cleaning required.

What it got wrong:

1. Answered a non-question
→ I asked about disapproved ads. It came back recommending I rebuild the conversion strategy.
→ We set that conversion strategy deliberately. It had no idea that decision was already made.

2. Dollar values with no volume
→ It flagged that every enabled campaign had four biddable goal categories treated equally.
→ Its fix was Google's standard recommendation to assign a dollar value to each goal, or pick one and drop the rest.
→ However, two of the goals it wanted me to add values for had 5 conversions and 9 conversions in the last 30 days.
→ Google's own published minimum for Target ROAS is at least 15 conversions in the past 30 days.
→ We don't want to add value goals this early because the conversion volume is too low.

3. No memory of the day before
→ It flagged the 90% budget constraint.
→ It also saw I changed target CPAs the day before.
→ It never connected the target CPA change to the budget ceiling. That bid change was already addressing the exact constraint it had just flagged.

So all in all... not bad - but not great either.

Idea generation is a beginner problem. Idea distillation is an expert problem. They are completely different things. I'll explain why:

Idea generation = not knowing what to write.

Idea distillation = not knowing HOW to write it.

Beginners:

- haven't got experience to know what people care about yet
- question their own thoughts
- wonder if the thing is even worth saying

Experts have the opposite problem.

For experts:

- Ideas coming out your ears
- Notes app full of thoughts
- Strong opinions earned from 15 years doing the work

You don't need someone to hand you a list of ideas.

You need someone to show you how to say the thing you already think, in a way that lands on a person who isn't you.

Which is why the people selling an automation that emails you 10 content ideas every Monday is useless to an expert.

It's solving a problem you don't have.

TL;DR:

You don't need more ideas.

You need a path from the idea in your head to the person on the other side of the screen.

So, if you're experienced and an expert:

Don't hire someone in the idea generation game.

Hire someone in the idea distillation game.

3 years ago an agency owner hired me to train up his new ghostwriter. But it didn't quite go as planned. Here's why:

The ghostwriter he hired was young, hungry, ready to live and breathe his brand. The agency owner, in his words, wanted: 

"someone who can pump out more volume than I ever could while running the business"

Made COMPLETE sense.

He'd just started the agency after walking away from the company he built from the ground up. He had no hours left. And buying hours is what you do when you've run out of them.

Our engagement lasted a few months.

But 2 years later we're on another call and he says almost word for word the same thing he said the first time:

"I've got these strong points I need to get across to the people I want as clients and I have no idea where to go from there."

The ghostwriter had given him volume, the structure and drafts ready to go every week.

But what the ghostwriter couldn't give him was WAY more important:

They couldn't tell him which of his opinions were worth writing about or how to distill them correctly for his ICP.

They hadn't spent the 15 years earning the opinions like the agency owner had, so of course they couldn't.

And that is the bit no hired ghostwriter ever gets to.

If you're considering hiring a ghostwriter, just think about this:

You can't hand that job to someone else, but you can't do it on your own either because you're stood too close to it.

Everything you know feels obvious to you.

Which is exactly why it never makes it onto the page.

So if you're sat there thinking the answer is more hands:

It isn't.

The answer: someone to think against.

Should you increase spend or new creatives?

How to know which, and when:

Push spend when:
→ You've got a winner holding its CPA below your scale line with confidence of it potentially scaling
→ You increase 5-15% at a time (optimize for smaller, more frequent changes)
→ You're running a sale and you need to drive more revenue now. You don't have time to wait for creative production.
→ You have a wide variety of ads in your account already. 10-15 ads carrying 50% of spend, so a single fatigue doesn't take the account down
→ You have a higher max-CPA, either because your LTV increased or you're just comfortable with less profitable growth
→ Auction got cheaper and you want to buy demand. Q2 and Q3 CPMs run 15-25% below Q4, and January drops 30%.

Launch creative when:
→ 1% of your ads are driving 70% of spend (I've seen this exact split on a brand's account). One fatigue and the account falls over
→ Your hit rate is under 10-15% and you're propping up the number with a handful of winners
→ Your spend per ad launched is over $15,000. Take the last 30 days of spend, divide by new ads launched. I aim for $3,000 per ad. About 30% of ads churn every month, so part of that batch only replaces what died before it funds any growth
→ You hit a high unique ad count, but it's from hook variations off a single concept. Instead, for example, at $200k+/month I want 5+ angles, 3+ formats, 10+ creators, 20+ hook variations live
→ Pushing more budget is pushing your blended CAC up above acceptable limits

Fundamental rule = prove the testing CPA before you touch the scaling CPA.

Easy way to lower CPAs without touching a single ad

Any DTC brand can do this:

1. List fears and desires

→ What your customer worries about ("the last 3 I tried didn't work")
→ What they want ("sleep through the night")

2. Name a page after one

Turn every fear or desire into a niche publisher page:

→ "The Supplement Report" (fear: nothing works)
→ "Rested Daily" (desire: real sleep)
→ "Honest Skin Reviews" (fear: wasting money on skincare)

→ Profile photo and add a few posts
→ Low lift internally

4. Match ad to page

→ Review-style ad runs from "The Supplement Report"
→ Soft lifestyle ad runs from "Rested Daily"
→ The angle has to fit the page it comes from

5. Run and cut

→ Push ads through the matched pages, watch CPA
→ Build 15, find the 2 or 3 that improve performance
→ Keep those, drop the rest

Meta treats the new ad-page combination as a function of the auction entry.

And when the page name matches what your customer is scared of or wants, the CPC tends to fall

Fascinating. Changing a conversion event on PMax shifted spend from 95% YouTube to 97% search. Here's what's going on:

Before:
→ Conversion event was a GTM tag firing lead event on site
→ Search inventory sat at 5.4% of PMax spend
→ Display and YouTube took about 95%
→ Blended PMax CPC ran about $1.55

After:
→ Conversion event was a new paid trial recorded in CRM
→ Search inventory jumped to 97% of PMax spend
→ Display and YouTube dropped to 2.6%
→ Search CPC inside PMax went from about $9 to about $45

This is what's going on:
→ Target CPA bidding buys the cheapest inventory it believes can produce the event you point it at
→ A new lead fire was a 'cheap' event
→ A new paid trial is a rarer event. Someone has to arrive with intent to sign up and pull out their credit card
→ Display and YouTube could produce the upper event, but Google made a decision it would struggle to produce a paid trial
→ So bidding moved off Display and YouTube and into Search

Worth checking how placements change whenever you adjust conversion events

What does a mature DTC brand look like in 2027?

1. They do not lead with ROAS. The CFO watches contribution margin per new customer and CAC payback in months. Median DTC payback went from 6.2 months in 2025 to 7.8 in 2026.

2. They know their incremental breakeven. At 45% contribution margin, first-order breakeven is ~2.2x incremental ROAS. Above it you profit on the first order. Below it, LTV carries the math.

3. MMM sets channel budget. Geo lift and holdout tests calibrate the MMM. MTA (Northbeam, Triple Whale) picks creative and campaign. Mature teams never use one to answer another's question.

4. Avoids overindexing on last click. Brands accidentally kill their best top-of-funnel concept this way.

5. Creative is the targeting layer, and they build for it. Andromeda went global across most objectives by October 2025, default in ecom by early 2026. Audience settings are a weak lever now.

6. They count concepts. Similar ads cluster into one entity, so 200 variations compete as one. Mature accounts run 8-12 genuinely different concepts.

7. They know their hit rate. 10-20% of new concepts scale. That number sets your production plan.

8. The bottleneck moved from production to approval. The constraint now is brand review, legal, claim substantiation.

9. Regulated brands run a pre-cleared claims library. But the best brands always are looking for novel ways to speak to their customers while staying compliant.

10. Fatigue windows collapsed, so the pipeline runs ahead by default. Creative fatigue went from 6+ weeks to 2-3. A 30-day forward pipeline is the floor to hold spend flat.

11. They measure time to kill. Cut losers at $500 ad-spend instead of $5,000, winners scaled inside 72 hours. Good and great accounts are separated by days.

12. Structure is consolidated and boring. Advantage+ as the core engine, one lean testing campaign, small retargeting.

13. Signal quality is infrastructure. Pixel and CAPI together, Event Match Quality above 7, dedup verified, server-side tagging owned by someone.

14. A meaningful share of spend runs through creator handles. Allowlisting and partnership ads have their own briefs, usage rights, and renewal calendar.

15. Landing pages are used to increase diversity of reach and customers.

16. Mature brands track new-customer ROAS and MER by market.

STOP wasting money on LTV prediction models

Run this simple test:

1. Take every customer who first bought 90+ days ago
2. Rank them by revenue at day 3
3. Rank the same customers by revenue at day 90
4. Correlate the two rankings

Answer tells you how well day 3 revenue predicts day 90 revenue in your account.

Around 70%:
→ You have a big optimization opportunity
→ Early revenue is not tracking long term value
→ You're probably overbidding on the customers who have low LTV
→ And likely underbidding the slow burn high LTV customers who take a full 90 days to materialize

85% or higher:
→ Leave it alone
→ Day 3 revenue is a good predictor of your LTV

Note - be careful with averages.
- Look for outliers.
- Two brands can post an identical average day 90 revenue and get opposite answers on this test.

Feel free to adjust the day depending on when your repeat purchases occur

How predictive are your early numbers?

Has anyone run this on their own account?

Running Google ads?

DON'T look at your last 30 days results. Instead:

Problem with last 30 days:
→ A click from four weeks ago has had a month to convert. But a click from yesterday has had a day, so the recent clicks drag the average down.

So instead, use cohorted results:
→ Group clicks by the week they happened. Now you can evaluate each week on its own, once that week has had time to convert.

How to build it and read it:

1. Export the raw data

→ In Google Ads, set the date range to the last 30 days and segment by week. Download clicks, cost, and conversions.
→ Google attributes each conversion to the click date, so every conversion sits in the week the click happened.
→ From your CRM, export leads, consults held, and signed deals with the GCLID or lead date on each row.

2. Build the cohort table

→ One row per click week. Columns for clicks, cost, leads, consults, signed, cost per consult, cost per signed.
→ Match each CRM record back to its click week using the GCLID or lead date.
→ Add a column for cohort age in days, counted from the last day of that week.

3. Pull the lag curve and project

→ In Google Ads, segment the same report by days to conversion. Turn the daily share into a running total so you have the share of conversions landed by day 7, 14, and 21.
→ Projected mature conversions = observed conversions ÷ the running total at that cohort's age.
→ Projected mature cost per conversion = cohort cost ÷ projected mature conversions.
→ The curve depends on your ad account. For example, on one account we manage about half the conversions land day 1 and another 29% land after day 12, so a day-old cohort there ends up at roughly half its day-1 cost.

4. Read only the matured cohorts

→ A cohort is mature when the running total from step 3 flattens, so almost no new conversions arrive for that week. Add one reporting day for offline conversions to sync. Mark anything younger as maturing.
→ The window depends on your ad account. For example, one account we manage matures at 21 days, so the August cohort gets read on September 22. Another takes 40 to 45 days.
→ Compare each matured cohort against the account's own history, which also depends on your ad account. For example, a lead-gen account we took on a month ago read 10 to 11% in-contact to signed on the blended window, and that account's history says early cohorts mature to 17 to 20%.

Hope this helps

Mistakes to avoid when scaling your Google ads account from $50k/mo to $500k/mo ad spend:

1. Impression Share Loss

→ Keep pushing Lost IS (Budget) toward 0% on the campaigns you already run. Raise the daily budget, or lower tCPA so the budget lasts longer through the day and buys cheaper clicks.
→ E.g. at 30% lost to budget, a 30% budget increase unlocks roughly 30% more auction eligibility. Clear that before you open new keyword themes.
→ As spend grows you'll also see Lost IS (Rank) go up. Two possible reasons.
→ a) Ad quality. Sometimes true. Check expected CTR, ad relevance and landing page experience, and only rewrite if all three read Below Average.
→ b) You're entering broader auctions further from your core keywords, where your rank is naturally worse. This is normal behavior and the most likely reason. Keep an eye on it.

2. Target Adjustments

→ Revisit tCPA and tROAS targets at every budget step as spend and conversions grow.
→ Before August 17, a budget-limited $100 tCPA campaign that ran out of budget early only bought the cheapest conversions, so it reported a $70 CPA.
→ Since August 17, Google spends toward the literal target on budget-constrained Search, Shopping, PMax and Demand Gen campaigns. The same campaign drifts up to $100 and buys more volume.
→ E.g. if you're beating a $100 target at $70, set the target to $75 to hold efficiency, or leave it at $100 and expect more volume at a higher CPA.

3. Conversion Lag

→ Judge a new spend tier on conversion data that has fully matured.
→ Google reports conversions by click date, so recent days understate performance until the lag closes.
→ E.g. if 29% of your conversions land after day 12, a day 7 CPA is missing almost a third of the result. Wait for the day 12 conversions before judging the number.

4. Campaign Sequencing

→ Start with Search. Keep Brand under 20% of budget, Competitors around 10%, and put the rest into Non-Brand.
→ Launch PMax once Non-Brand Search is producing 30 quality conversions a month.
→ Launch Demand Gen once PMax is producing 50 quality conversions a month, with a daily budget of about 15x your CPA.

→ E.g. if Non-Brand Search is at 15 quality conversions a month, keep adding budget to Search until it clears 30, then open PMax.

Summary:

→ Push Lost IS (Budget) to 0%. Rising Lost IS (Rank) is normal as you enter broader auctions.
→ Re-set tCPA and tROAS at every budget step, since Google now holds you to the literal number.
→ Read CPA only once the conversion lag has closed.
→ Launch PMax after 30 Search conversions a month, and Demand Gen after 50 from PMax.

Hope this helps

Are your new creatives actually diverse?

How to tell:

1. Download every active ad including ad spend, headline, body, script, on-screen text
2. Transcribe every single ad with timestamps
3. AI tag every ad with format, angle, hook style, creator and core selling point
4. Vectorize every ad so it has a data point on an n-dimensional space
5. Flag the near-duplicates by measuring cosine similarity of >0.95
6. Cluster into concepts by grouping the vectors
7. Measure concentration with Herfindahl index (economists use this to measure market monopolies)

If you have too much concentration your account is at risk from fatigue. One idea gets tired, and the whole account goes with it.

Summary:

- AI tag every ad you run for analysis
- Vectorize and measure concentration to go deeper

Where does PMax actually spend?

Pulled 365 days of data from 53 accounts: 

1. Search

→ Median account: 61% of PMax spend goes to Search
→ The range across all 53: 2% to 99%
→ Above 90%, PMax is a glorified Search campaign (I audited one at 82% and Search had under 30 conversions a month)
→ On our accounts we pull converting search terms out of PMax into Search until the search portion drops below 10%

2. Search Partners

→ Median: 3% of spend
→ We launched one PMax campaign where it took 30% (it got calls, but no qualified leads)
→ No campaign-level toggle exists to turn it off. Keep an eye on this

3. YouTube and Display

→ Medians: 10% and 3%
→ Individual accounts push over 80% into YouTube
→ Google allocates from your assets, audience signals and conversion data
→ Repurpose your Meta ads into the asset groups to start (statics too, no re-edits). That's how we launch every client and performance holds
→ If YouTube CPA comes in near Search, that's your case to invest in proper YouTube creative

4. Gmail, Discover and Maps

→ Median: 0% across nearly all 53 accounts
→ One account has 84% of its PMax spend going to Maps

5. Why no benchmark exists

→ Google gives you no channel-level budget control (their own docs say to influence the mix through assets, signals and exclusions)
→ Channel reporting only rolled out to every PMax campaign in November 2025, and to MCC level in December

Summary

- 61% median Search share, with a 2% to 99% range
- High Search share means PMax is duplicating your Search campaign
- Search Partners needs a manual account-level exclusion
- Pull the channel report on your own account before assuming it's typical

We ran a direct mail campaign that generated 4,600 leads and 450 opportunities for a $1,500 offer. How you can too

Results:
→ Roughly 375,000 mail pieces sent over the program
→ About 4,600 leads
→ About 450 campaign-attributed opportunities, roughly 1 in 10 leads
→ Roughly $1M in influenced pipeline

1. Audiences

→ We split the list into four audiences, the house file, previous responders, competitor audiences, and intent-based prospect lists.
→ Each audience got its own drop and its own campaign in Salesforce so we could compare cost per opportunity head to head.
→ House file and previous responders came in cheaper per opportunity than the broad prospect lists.
→ A previous responder had already replied to the brand once, so the piece read as a follow-up.

2. Tracking

→ Every piece carried a mailer-specific URL, a QR code, and UTM tags.
→ Salesforce logged the campaign attribution on every lead that came through a mailer link.
→ We matched back CRM records for responders who came in through another channel after the piece landed.
→ A QR scan alone does not tell you whether a piece acquired a customer profitably, so every audience was judged on cost per opportunity after the same maturation window.

3. Mailer creative and offer

→ We send a handwritten style letter for a B2B offer as we tend to see higher conversion rates versus a postcard.
→ We adjust copy by segment. For example, a previous responder gets a reminder of what they looked at before, and a competitor list audience member gets a switching offer.
→ Every piece carries one offer and one call to action. The reader scans the QR code or types the short URL.

Summary:
→ Split the list by audience type and track each one on its own campaign.
→ Put a URL, QR code, and UTM on every piece and matchback the rest.
→ Judge audiences on cost per opportunity after the same window.
→ Put one offer and one call to action on a letter written to the segment.

I've run 20,000 ads and spent $150M on Meta.

Benchmarks I've found over 6 years:

1. 1 new creative concept per $10k in monthly spend. At $500k/month that's 50 concepts (~3 ads per concept, more for static-heavy). 

2. At $100k/mo, aim for 70% new concepts and 30% variations. As you scale past $1m/mo, max out at 50/50. But never drop below 50% new. 

3. 70% of your creatives should be cut before week 2. Only 10-20% will ever hit your performance threshold. If you're keeping most of your ads alive, you're probably losing money. 

4. Your top 1-2% of ads should drive 50% of total spend. If they don't, you haven't found real winners yet or you haven't utilized them well enough.

5. Big swings have lower hit rates (5-10%) but higher total potential. These are the ads that can scale to $1m+ in spend.

6. 70% video, 30% static for most ecom brands. New brands need more video (more education, less BOF audience). Clothing should lean heavier static (lots of SKUs to show).

7. 15-20% of budget goes to testing. Under 10% and your creative pipeline dries up. Over 25% and you're burning cash without enough scale behind winners.

8. When you 2x spend, expect 20-30% ROAS decline. A $30 CPA at $50k/month might become $40 at $200k. Scale requires better ads, better optimization, better structure, or lower targets.

9. Limit bid and budget changes to 25% max. For 90% of changes, smaller and more frequent changes outperform bigger ones. 

10. Meta always targets returning customers. Aim to keep returning conversions under 15-20%. Accept it and plan around it.

11. Ad copy can improve performance up to 50%. But a great ad outperforms by 500%. Copy matters, but the creative itself is where the real leverage is.

12. A great media buyer improves ROAS 100%+ vs a bad one. Creative strategists make better decisions when they're working off clean data and with better media buyers, because the scaled ads are actual winners.

Most brands running Meta traffic to Amazon are optimizing for the wrong person.

You can't fire a purchase event from Amazon back to Meta. So the campaign optimizes on the last thing it can see: the outbound click. Meta gets very good at finding people who click Amazon links. It has no idea which of them ever bought.

I've managed $150M+ in Meta spend and this is the worst signal environment I deal with.

Was talking through this with the founders at Jurni, who was willing to share some data on their learnings. Jurni's fix is a "Pre-retail landing experience" sitting between the ad and the PDP.

What the page has to do:

1. Continue the ad, don't restart it. Same hook, same visual, same claim. If the page reintroduces the brand, you've reset the sale.
2. Handle the objection the PDP can't. On Amazon you're one tile in a grid of 40 competitors. The page is the only place you control the comparison.
3. One exit. No nav, no footer, no second offer. One button, deep linked to the right variant and pack size.

Across their beauty and CPG customer set:

- CPA down ~19%
- ROAS up ~26%
- 22% of ad traffic never clicks through to Amazon

That third number is the one people react badly to. A fifth of your traffic dies on the page.

That's the point though. That's low intent traffic getting filtered before it costs you an Amazon session. And now you have two segments you never had: people who clicked through, and people who didn't. Fire the first as your optimization event.

Then it compounds. Higher-intent traffic on the PDP lifts conversion rate, and Amazon's ranking rewards conversion rate. You buy better traffic, and the algorithm hands you cheaper organic placement for it.

Worth noting-  these pages Jurni builds are AI-generated per-audience/per-ad variant, not one static page. That's part of why the objection-handling can be this specific: each version is built to match the exact ad it's continuing, and they're tracking performance per variant, not just in aggregate

Caveat: this is their data across their customers, not mine, and CPA is in-platform. I'd want to see it hold in a geo test before I called it incremental.

Google ads over holidays periods can suck.

How to forecast performance & adjust bids in advance.

1. Holidays carry CVR risk

→ Traffic changes over holiday periods. B2B search volume thins out over Thanksgiving week and between Christmas and New Year because buyers are off work. Retail volume spikes into Black Friday and Cyber Monday, then drops off.
→ Volume on its own doesn't hurt CPA, since you pay per click and Google bids per auction. People keep clicking but delay the purchase, so the drop lands in conversion rate first.
→ Smart Bidding sets each bid from auction signals and accounts for conversion delay. A sharp CVR drop over a few days can land before bids catch up, and you pay pre-holiday prices for holiday clicks.
→ E.g. a hypothetical account at a $10 CPC and 5% CVR runs a $200 CPA. If CVR slips to 4% over a 4-day holiday weekend and CPC holds, CPA comes in at $250 for those 4 days.
→ Holding a $200 CPA on a 4% CVR takes an $8 CPC. A -20% conversion rate adjustment pushes bids toward that $8 but doesn't guarantee a 20% lower CPC. Set the change ahead of the window, through the seasonality adjustment in step 2 or a manual bid cut on campaigns that don't use Smart Bidding.

2. Seasonality adjustments for short windows

→ A seasonality adjustment tells Smart Bidding ahead of time that conversion rates will move over a set date range.
→ Don't set a seasonality adjustment for every holiday. Smart Bidding already accounts for normal seasonality. Use the adjustment for a significant, short-lived CVR change you have a reason to expect.
→ Find it under the Tools icon, then Budgets and bidding, then Adjustments, then the Seasonal tab. Hit the plus button and pick Conversion rate.
→ Set the start and end dates, choose which campaigns it covers, and enter the conversion rate change you expect. For the hypothetical 5% to 4% drop above, enter -20%.
→ Keep the adjustment to events of 1 to 7 days. Google says seasonality adjustments may be less effective over longer periods.
→ The adjustment reverts automatically once the end date passes.

3. Read lag before reacting

→ Conversion lag is the gap between the click you pay for and the conversion Google reports against it. A form fill lands the same day. A signed deal can take weeks.
→ Holidays stretch that gap. People click on the Wednesday and buy after the long weekend. B2B buyers click before the break and convert once the office reopens.
→ E.g. the 4% CVR in the hypothetical above can be understated. Conversions from holiday clicks get reported after the weekend and the 4% climbs.
→ Pull your time-to-conversion report before the window (Goals, then Measurement, then Attribution) so you know how long your lag runs.
→ Wait out that lag before judging the holiday week.

Hope this helps.

6 weeks ago, Google changed how bidding works

I checked 120 accounts to see what happened:

CONTEXT
- Before August 17, a budget-limited campaign with a $100 target CPA always tried to find the cheapest conversions. So if it ran out of budget it might have a CPA of $70.
- Since August 17, Google bids up to the target CPA. So even if you run out of budget, you'll hit $100 CPA.
- Target ROAS works the same way. A campaign beating its ROAS target gets pulled back down to the target.
- Note: some of these 120 ad accounts we manage, some we don't.

I split every campaign into three groups and compared 28 days before against 28 days after:

1. Budget-limited and beating target CPA
2. Budget-limited but already at target CPA
3. No target or no budget limit

The campaigns that were budget-limited and beating target CPA

- CPA up 63%
- CPC up 20%
- Conversions down 22%

Campaigns that were budget-limited but already at target CPA:

- CPA down 6%
- CPC up 1%
- Conversions down 1%

The control group barely moved either:

- CPC up 3%
- CPA up 3%
- Conversions down 1%

What this means:

If you're not actively managing your account, and ensuring you minimize Search Lost IS (Budget) by adjusting budgets and target CPA / ROAS, you will overpay for your conversions. (None of our client fit into this bucket)

I run a Meta/Google ads agency exclusively for (high) 8 & 9-figure brands. I'll be the first to say AEO is IMPORTANT. A quick 101 guide in case you haven't made any changes:

1. Map the buying decisions

→ A buying decision is anything a shopper settles before they buy, across discovery, comparison, objections, fit and care.
→ Pull 20-30 questions from support tickets, reviews, site search and post-purchase surveys, in the shopper's wording.
→ Example: "best polarized sunglasses for driving" (discovery), "[brand] vs [competitor]" (comparison), "is [brand] worth the price" (objection), "will [frames] fit a wide face" (fit), "how to clean [lenses]" (care).
→ Each question is a prompt. Type each prompt word for word into ChatGPT and Google AI Mode more than once. Log the answer, whether you were mentioned or cited, and which sources it pulled.

2. Fix eligibility

→ OpenAI runs 3 crawlers. GPTBot is training, OAI-SearchBot is search inclusion, ChatGPT-User is user-triggered fetches.
→ OpenAI will commit a felony (Hugging Face hack) for training; they may ignore your bots.txt, but I don’t risk it. A broad WAF rule or a wildcard disallow should in theory stop these bots which you don’t want.
→ Robots.txt changes take roughly 24 hours to register on OpenAI's side.

3. Build a product truth layer

→ Put price, availability, variants, shipping and returns in visible HTML. Keep your Merchant Center feed matching the page.
→ Same problem as a Meta catalog throwing disapprovals when the feed and the PDP disagree on price. Same fix, wider blast radius.

4. Publish data only you have

→ Publish return reasons, support questions, product tests and sizing failures.
→ This is the single most underused asset in DTC. Use it for AEO, but also for creative.

5. Answer the follow-up questions

→ AI Mode queries average 3x the length of a traditional search.
→ One decision page should cover the answer, trade-offs, edge cases and next step.

6. Write an honest comparison page

→ Own "X vs Y" with a dated methodology, named criteria, and who shouldn't buy your product.

7. Keep product names consistent

→ Use the same brand, model and variant names everywhere. Otherwise the engine reads your old reviews, new listing and current SKU as 3 unrelated things.

8. Earn corroboration

→ Fix wrong facts on the review sites and forum threads already showing up in your answers from move 1.

9. Land citations on the right page

→ Deep-link citations to the relevant PDP or guide. A great ad pointed at a generic homepage underperforms a mediocre ad pointed at the right page.

10. Measure

→ Track AI visibility in Search Console, AI referrals in analytics, and citation rates on your question set, dated before and after.
→ Add an AI option to your post-purchase survey. When someone asks an assistant and walks straight to your site, there's no click to capture.

Shout out to Lorea Lastiri for this playbook.

Is one Google ad group taking ALL the spend?
And NOT testing your other keywords?
How to kickstart starved ad groups:

1. Rank and budget 

Search Lost IS (Rank):
→ If it's high, bids and quality score are the constraint. Fix those first.
→ If it's low, the starved ad group wins the auctions it enters.

Search Lost IS (Budget):
→ If it's high, the campaign is capped. Raise the cap and the extra budget still flows to the dominant ad group.
→ If it's low, the campaign was never capped, and the starvation sits in how budget splits between ad groups.

Either way, every ad group inherits the campaign's target CPA, and shared budget typically concentrates on the ad group with the deepest conversion history.

2. Fix the bid strategy first

→ Confirm the campaign runs Target CPA. Maximize Conversions gives no ad-group-level lever.
→ Raise the target CPA on the starved ad group. The override gives Smart Bidding permission to enter more auctions there, above the shared campaign default.
→ Raise the campaign budget cap next, so the ad group you unlocked doesn't get re-capped the moment it spends.

3. Overshoot the target CPA on purpose

→ On a low-spend ad group, set the target CPA above what you want, buying more auctions and more signal on what converts.
→ Pull the search term report while the overshoot runs and add negatives aggressively, or the spend lands on queries you don't want.

Summary:
→ Check rank loss and budget loss together first
→ Switch the campaign to Target CPA
→ Raise the target on the starved ad group
→ Raise the campaign budget cap straight after
→ Add negatives while the overshoot runs

A shared budget typically concentrates on the deepest conversion history by default.

A target CPA override is how you move that budget somewhere else.

More connection requests, more profile views, more DMs etc.

There are 4 types of incrementality studies you can run with them

Brand Lift:
→ Survey-based test that measures whether the ad moved recall, awareness, consideration, favorability, or purchase intent
→ Runs on YouTube Video and Demand Gen campaigns
→ Needs $10,000 in spend over a 10-day window

Search Lift:
→ Measures whether people searched for your brand after seeing the ad
→ Runs on the same Video and Demand Gen campaigns as Brand Lift
→ Rides alongside a Brand Lift study at no extra budget

Conversion Lift based on users:
→ Splits your audience into people who saw the ad and a holdout who didn't
→ Native on Video and Demand Gen, needs a Google rep to set up on Search, Shopping, Display, or PMax
→ Gives directional results from $5,000 in spend and 1,000 conversions
→ Relies mostly on opt-in traffic, which brings its own measurement gaps

Conversion Lift based on geography:
→ Splits regions on and off instead of individual users
→ Counts both online and offline conversions
→ Spans Search, Shopping, PMax, Video, Display, Demand Gen, and App
→ Needs a Google rep, and the geo split is noisier with no demographic breakdown

Got $10,000 and 10 days? Run Brand Lift and Search Lift together.
Got $5,000 and 1,000 conversions? Run Conversion Lift based on users.
Need offline conversions counted? Run Conversion Lift based on geography.

Note- a Google lift study is Google measuring Google. Pair the result with a holdout test of your own for greater impartiality.

Hope this helps.

Can you scale on Meta ads?

Plot your aMER versus your blended MER.

Blended MER (bMER) = total revenue divided by total marketing spend.
Acquisition MER (aMER) = new-customer revenue divided by acquisition spend.

Two lines to plot against:
→ Sitting on the bMER = aMER diagonal means no repeat revenue to average in
→ Falling below aMER = 1 means you're buying customers at a loss

Plot yourself and you land in one of four spots.

Low bMER, low aMER
→ E.g. 1.6 bMER vs 0.9 aMER, nCAC $238, below the loss line
→ This is the brand scaling past breakeven. Every new customer costs you more than they're worth right now, and payback stretches past a year
→ Cut the worst 20-30% of spend, reset to the efficient core, rebuild through creative testing

Low bMER, mid aMER
→ E.g. 2.3 bMER vs 2.1 aMER, 10% repeat customers, right on the bMER = aMER line
→ This is the leaky bucket. There's no repeat business to average in, so bMER barely clears aMER
→ Fix retention before you scale spend

High bMER, low aMER
→ E.g. 6.0 bMER vs 1.3 aMER, 78% repeat customers
→ Left alone, Meta harvests the cheapest conversions available, and those conversions are people who were buying anyway
→ Rebuild prospecting with hooks written for cold traffic, accept a lower bMER for a quarter

High bMER, high aMER
→ E.g. 8.4 bMER vs 4.6 aMER, marketing at 12% of revenue
→ This is the brand that's growing too efficiently. You need to spend more!
→ Keep spending until marginal aMER hits your LTV:CAC goal to grow quicker.

Last week, I heard the craziest thing. An agency had BANNED its ghostwriters from using AI. I geddit… story time: 

I’ve had 200+ applicants for our $100k/y ghostwriter role. 

And I want a ghostwriter that actively uses AI… but they also have to be capable of doing 2 very important things. 

Which if you cannot do… you’re better off NOT using AI. 

1: IDENTIFICATION

One must be able to identify clear AI tells. They take 2 sub forms:

A) AI isms in writing. Classic ones include “It’s not X. It’s Y”. But also slightly less obvious ones, e.g “Statement. Negative of Statement.” 

B) Overfitting. This is where the AI output overfits to the language of the source material. But that language only works if it has the context of the source material. The AI output ends up having artifacts of that language and doesn’t make sense standalone. 

2. PRIORITIZATION

Unless you’ve built a really good AI writing system, it’s likely an output struggles with choosing the right things to talk about.

It’ll either include weak points (which your post would do better off without) or it’ll exclude the best points - because it thought they sucked

So back to the story…

If a writer can’t identify or prioritize - I get why banning AI might be considered

But it’s a pretty bad response to what actually is an education / skills problem

Eight variables make up a winning ad.

Ranked here from least important to most:

1. Audio quality / lighting
→ Phone-shot creator ads beat studio about 80-90% of the time.
→ Polish pays off in luxury, complex demos and some fashion. Everywhere else, shoot on an iPhone in natural light.

2. Ad length / CTA
→ Runtime and CTA wording barely move a result. 15-30 seconds wins most DTC tests.
→ Go long when trust has to come before the product. Founder stories hold the product back until 40-50 seconds, documentary-style testimonials run long, and a proven concept can stretch to 2-5 minutes with more proof. Saw a 13-minute ad at the top of an ad account once.

3. Filming location
→ Location tells the viewer when and where the product gets used. Keep the use case the same and a new setting is a low-impact change.
→ Change the location to go after a different use case. The same product in the kitchen, the bathroom and on the sofa pitches 3 different use cases.
→ If you want to try to drive CPMs down you can pick a weird location to film something, it can work but is a risk.

4. Key selling points
→ The selling point is the reason to buy your product over the one next to it.
→ Find the one USP no competitor claims, then show it visually. A static built on a striking visual of one USP has taken $2M+ on a single ad for one of our clients

5. Offer
→ An offer change hits every impression at once. A strong offer is behind almost every account I've seen scale 2x in a month.
→ Sequence offer tests. An A+ offer can jump this whole list.

6. Creator
→ In my tests only around 20% of creators are compelling, which makes creator one of the biggest swings in any test.
→ If you're testing a new creator, give them 1-2 top ads to remake so the creator is the only new variable. If you're testing anything else, use a top creator who reliably performs.

7. Angle
→ The top 1-2% of ads drive around 50% of spend. If they share an angle, they can fatigue together.
→ Spin a winning angle into 15-20 variations. Keep any one angle under 40% of active spend.

8. Product
→ A new product can change who the ad goes to entirely. And the product is what people spend their money on, so it outweighs everything else on this list.

Easy AI way to run Meta creative analysis

1. Copy the image of this post (and copy text)
2. Export csv of Meta ads data (Breakdown: Daily)
3. Paste it all into Claude (ChatGPT if you must, sorry not sorry)
4. Look at the 3 charts it generates

This is what you should see:

Chart 1: Creative churn
→ Each color band is a month of ad launches, oldest sitting at the bottom
→ The band's height over time shows how fast that month's creative churns out
→ Monthly churn normally runs 20-30% across the accounts we manage
→ A cohort still carrying 30%+ of spend two months after launch means you're not producing enough to replace it

Chart 2: Production vs hit rate
→ Light bars are ads produced each week. Dark bars are hits
→ A hit crosses $3,500 in lifetime spend
→ Compare the weekly hit rate to your trailing 6-month average. We aim for 10-15%
→ Hits dropping while production stays flat means creative quality is slipping

Chart 3: Reliance on old creative
→ Stacked bars show daily spend split by ad age, 0-7 days out to 180+ days
→ Darker bars are newer creative, lighter bars are older
→ Track what percentage of spend is coming from ads under 30 days old
→ Strong performance sitting on old creative means the churn hasn't hit yet

These 3 charts give you a 1-2 month head start before performance dips.

How to predict when your Meta ads stop working: 

1. Get every active ad
2. Look at how many days it's been running. 
3. Weight each ad's age by its share of total spend.

The result is a single number:

The spend-weighted average age of your creative portfolio.

E.g. 3 active ads:

→ Ad A: 5 days old, $30,000 spend (60% of total)
→ Ad B: 30 days old, $15,000 spend (30%)
→ Ad C: 45 days old, $5,000 spend (10%)

(5 x 0.60) + (30 x 0.30) + (45 x 0.10) = 16.5 days

In this case, $50k is being spent on 16.5 day old creative. 

Is spend-weighted average age = 15: 
→ Account is looking healthy 

Is spend-weighted average age = 60
→ Most budget is being spent on 'old ads'

And if you launched new ads recently but your number is still high, it means those new ads aren't getting spend.

So they're either not promising or they're not getting testing budget. 

This number should be relatively stable in a well-managed account. 

Check the image: 
- The blue line below shows creative age across the account.
- If it's trending upward month over month you're falling behind
- Increase creative production because fatigue is building.

(One caveat: if you have poor media buying this metric won't work right - you might just be spending on new bad ads or missing new good ads).

3 ways to FORCE Google ads to acquire NEW customers and NOT waste budget on existing:

1. Build an exclusion list

Pull an all-time list of everyone who has ever bought from you.

→ Email
→ Phone number
→ Zip code
→ Country code
→ First name
→ Last name

Upload the CSV under Tools, Audience manager, then the plus button and Customer list. Apply the list as an exclusion at campaign level under Audiences. Note needs to be > 1,000 matched members.

2. Suppress conversion actions

Stop passing conversion actions to Google when the buyer is a repeat customer. This stops rewarding the algorithm for repeat customer conversions.

Add the new_customer parameter to your purchase tag. Send true for a first-time buyer and false for a repeat one. If your purchases arrive by offline import, leave repeat buyers out of the upload.

3. Change your customer lifecycle goal

There are three types of goals:
→ New Customer Value. Bids higher for new customers but keeps bidding on existing ones. Requires value-based bidding (tROAS / Max conv value) and a purchase conversion goal
→ High-value new customer. Adds a tier for new customers who look like your best ones. Same requirements as New Customer Value
→ New Customer Only. Bids only for new customers, works on any bid strategy.

Pick New Customer Only.
→ Goals, then Summary, then Set up on the Customer acquisition panel.

It knows who's new vs existing by:
→ Auto-detection. On by default, built from up to 540 days of tracked purchases. It's cookie based
→ Your Customer Match list. The all-time list from point 1, loaded as the existing customer definition.
→ The new_customer parameter from point 2.

Hope this helps!

Which Google ad test should you run next?

How to decide:

Decision value:
→ How much budget or margin actually moves if you know the answer
→ How much uncertainty you're sitting on right now
→ Whether you can act on what the test tells you

Test feasibility:
→ How much control you have over the setup
→ Whether the data will give you a precise answer
→ The effort and downside if the test goes wrong

Score both 1 to 5. Decision value is the vertical axis, feasibility the horizontal. A 3 or higher counts as high.

Top right
→ Decision value 3 or higher, feasibility 3 or higher.
→ Validate the design and run the readiness checks before you launch.

Top left
→ Decision value 3 or higher, feasibility 1 or 2.
→ The answer matters but the test can't give it cleanly yet. Improve the design first.

Bottom right
→ Decision value 1 or 2, feasibility 3 or higher.
→ Easy to answer with less at stake. Run it when you have spare capacity.

Bottom left
→ Decision value 1 or 2, feasibility 1 or 2.
→ Park it. Revisit once the decision or the design changes.

Loving YouTube Shorts ads right now.

There are 6 ways to run Youtube Shorts campaigns:

1. Demand Gen

→ Serves across YouTube, Discover, Gmail and Google video partners
→ Creative Preferences lets you pin a specific video asset to serve on Shorts
→ The call to action button appears at 3 seconds.
→ You cannot buy Shorts placements on their own inside a Demand Gen campaign.

2. Video view

→ You add Shorts by checking the Shorts option under multi-format ad settings.
→ Opting out of every other format at the campaign level gives you a Shorts-only Video view campaign.
→ A view counts as billed once someone watches 10 seconds, though the public view count starts ticking the moment the Short begins playing.

3. Video reach

→ Shorts ads only run on Video reach campaigns using the Efficient reach goal.
→ Video reach optimizes for the lowest cost per unique person reached.
→ You segment the report by ad format to pull Shorts numbers on their own, otherwise every format's metrics blend together as one sum and average.

4. YouTube reservation

→ You can buy Shorts inventory through YouTube Select Shorts, a set of premium lineups like Trending Music or Sports, booked through your Google Ads rep.
→ First Position serving on YouTube Select Shorts puts your ad as the first thing a viewer sees on YouTube.

5. Performance Max

→ Performance Max automatically includes Shorts placements.
→ You cannot buy Shorts placements as a separate line item inside Performance Max.
→ There is no unique reporting for Shorts inventory inside a Performance Max campaign.
→ The call to action button appears at 3 seconds.

6. App campaigns

→ App Install and App Re-engagement campaigns cannot buy Shorts placements on their own either.
→ Reporting gives you the same blind spot as Performance Max, with no unique numbers for what ran on Shorts.
→ The call to action button appears at 3 seconds.

Which one you use depends on your goals and the level of control you want.

DON'T set up DTC partnership ads wrong

There’s actually a RIGHT way: 

Meta gives every partnership ad up-to two identity slots.

Default puts your brand in slot one and the creator in slot two.
→ E.g. Ad header: "YourBrand with @Creator"

We then tested, with dynamic identity turned on (where Meta decides whether to show one identity or both), whether the creator tag in slot one performs better
→ E.g. Ad header: "@Creator with YourBrand"

It did…

Roughly 30% improvement on this test. 

Difference between scaling and cutting the ad. 

Why?
→ Dynamic identity can serve the first identity only
→ With the default setup, your creator ad renders as a brand ad
→ Creator in slot one gets you creator-led framing

When you set up partnership ads the FIRST slot defaults to your page, dont make the mistake of leaving it like that. 

If you don’t have a plan it will it often set up brand first and you lose a lot of the value. 

Creator ad performance:
- Partnership ads running from the creator's handle have driven 53% lower CAC in accounts we've seen
- Meta's own reporting has them at 19% lower CPA than standard brand ads.

Do it on your next partnership build.

Yesterday, I opened my inbox to see this email from a past client. I spend a lot of time thinking about how to make my Sales kickoffs keynotes and workshops stick, long after I leave. There are some obvious things I think most presenters focus on (clear ideas, audience engagement, supporting tools, manager coaching guidance, etc.). Here are 5 less obvious things I think about to engage an audience and make the content memorable: 

1. I don't start my Sales kickoff keynotes or workshops with a bio slide. For the same reason i don't start a pitch deck with an "About Us" slide. Sellers judge my credibility in the first 5 mins by how well-versed I am in their sale, not my resume. 

2. When speaking about problems, I rarely (if, ever) use "you" language. I use "we" language.  (Ex: one of the mistakes we make when doing discovery with CXOs is....). You're already on an elevated stage, looking down. "You" language feels like a wagging finger. Sellers tune out when they feel like their parents are scolding them. 

3. I don't do rah-rah stuff. I didn't grow up in Sales with rah-rah leaders. I had leaders who gave me tough feedback. IMO, the best way to motivate a rep is to be honest about what's hurting their results + teach them a new way + build their confidence by trying it on a real account. This is why most of my SKOs are workshops. I take the time to review team's work in advance, so I'm not making assumptions or generalizations. 

4. I throw myself under the bus. I speak about my mistakes more than my wins. Losses are a better teacher. Every single tactic I teach was born out of me getting it wrong, first. I aim for relatability. Not for 'expert'. This builds trust. 

5. I don't memorize my talks. This is a personal preference. I grew up watching speakers who spoke like normal people. They didn't sound performative. I liked that. So, I mirrored that. It helps me stay present, engage with the audience, and keep it fun. 

I've got a fun lineup of SKOs in January in cities like Cancun, Vancouver, Austin, Chicago, and Salt Lake City. If you're still looking for a keynote or workshop, let's chat! If I'm not the right person, I can make a referral to one of the great speakers I've watched on a client's SKO stage across the last 6 years.

Is your new ad concept reaching net new audience?

How to find out: 

1. Pull your account's total reach
→ Note the reach number for your whole ad account over the period you're checking.

2. Filter to the new concept
→ Filter ad name contains "Product A"
→ Note the reach number when filtered to Product A alone.

3. Flip the filter
→ Switch to ad name does not contain "Product A"
→ Note the reach number without the new concept.

4. Run the math
→ Subtract the does-not-contain reach (step 3) from the total reach to get net new reach
→ Divide net new reach by the new concept's own reach to get your incremental percentage

Say your account reached 5.6M people this month.
Filtered to Product A alone, the reach is 1.3M.
Filtered to everything except Product A, the reach is 5.3M.
5.6M minus 5.3M is 300,000 net new people.
300,000 divided by 1.3M is 23% incremental.

How to think about the results:
- A lower ROAS ad at 80% incremental is good. That ad is opening the account to an audience it wasn't reaching before.
- A high ROAS ad at 23% incremental is mostly re-serving the audience the account already had.

Judge a new product by how many new people it reaches! 

That said, be careful about running this for individual ads. Note that any brand-new launch tends to go to the same people first and then expand out later. That's just the way Meta works. 

Last, you can’t tell which direction this goes. (i.e. did they see the new or old product first). So the best bet is to calibrate vs others in the account in the same timeframe for comparison.

We're scaling a Google Ads campaign to $100k/week. It has a $1,300 CAC, but our target was $800. We've never turned it. This is why:

This account spends ~$100k/week and day 7 CAC is ~$1,300

BUT, as we extend over more time, we see something interesting happen:
→ Day 21 CAC ~$900
→ Day 40-45 CAC ~$715

We're confident to keep scaling because we run a conversion lag report to measure day 45 CAC on the day 1 click.

Here's how:

1. Set window to full maturity
→ Open Goals → Conversions → Summary → Edit settings
→ The click-through window defaults to 30 days and maxes out at 90
→ Set the window to cover full maturity, 45 days on this account, so a 30-day default stops hiding conversions you already paid for
→ Switch attribution to first interaction under Goals → Measurement → Attribution, then pick the conversion action that maps to revenue

2. Pull days to conversion
→ Go to the Campaigns page and hit Segment → Conversions → Days to conversion, then download the segment
→ This account averages 14 days, with 51% of conversions landing on day 1, 5% on day 2, and another 29% arriving after day 12
→ Given 51% conversions land on day 1, we can roughly double the conversion count on day 1 to assume the CAC roughly halves
→ Or optimize toward an upper-funnel action like leads (90% fire day 1)

3. Forecast from your CRM
→ Pull your historical lead→customer rate (this account runs 6%, currently dipped to 3%)
→ Multiply current leads by that rate to project customers and true CAC
→ Run a lookback every month comparing your forecast to actuals
→ Tighten the rate each month as the real conversions mature

Summary
- Set your click-through window to the 90 day maximum
- Pull the days to conversion segment before you judge any campaign
- Double your day 1 cost per customer to estimate the mature number
- Check your lead to customer rate when CAC spikes and cost per lead holds

Our competitor in a deal is almost never, ever "do nothing."

Let's say you’re a working parent and your mattress is shot. Your back hurts when you wake up every morning. It’s been months since you had a solid night’s sleep. 

Maybe you flip it. Or, you buy a mattress topper. Or, you keep sleeping on it and pop Advil every morning. Or, go to the chiropractor. 

All of those are alternative solutions to solve the problem (bad sleep). Even the Advil. 

You’re doing SOMETHING to solve the problem. 

That’s your status quo.

But, the objection sounds like price/budget. “A new mattress is too expensive.”

So, feature-based ROI messaging does little to change your mind. You already know a new mattress would be better. 

Cost of Inaction (COI) illuminates an underappreciated negative consequence of status quo. 

So, instead of this:

"Introducing the CloudRest Pro! 7 layers of cooling memory foam, edge-to-edge support, and a 10-year warranty. Wake up refreshed and sleep up to 30% better. Upgrade your sleep today!"

It’s more like this:

“Another morning of bad sleep and an achy back.

Because mattress shopping is miserable, and $2,000 is a lot of money to spend on a new one. 

So, you flipped the mattress. You bought the topper. A half-empty bottle Advil sits on your nightstand. Weekly visits to the chiropractor. 

But, it’s another day of foggy meetings. Or snapping at your kids before 8am because you slept like garbage. And, feeling regretful about it. Again.

How much is that bad night’s sleep actually costing you?”

*cue the GIF of Milhouse from the Simpson’s playing frisbee by himself*

It’s not really the cost of the chiropractor and mattress toppers. Sure, that adds up. But, it’s not the big driver.

It’s the foggy meetings and snapping at your kids. Most parents don’t want to see themselves that way. That’s an emotional trigger.

Sometimes, COI can be a rational, financial cost. Sometimes, it’s more emotional, like above.

But, either way, it should feel like holding up a mirror to the prospect. You give your prospect a way to size the negative consequence of status quo. They decide if the cost is big enough to warrant change. 

But, it’s delivered with empathy.

And, it’s agnostic of your product. It’s about their current state. Not a future state with your product. 

Does it always work? No. Nothing in sales always works or never works. Some prospects literally don’t have $2000 to buy your mattress. They aren’t your buyers, though. 

If someone is going to buy a solution, first, they must decide the problem is worth solving and solving now. 

COI is a way to get them thinking about cost of the problem differently. That’s why it’s most effective early in a sales process (outbound + discovery), when the goal is to give them a reason to reconsider status quo.

Interestingly, they have 5 definitions of watched:

0 seconds:
→ This triggers a public view counter as soon as an ad begins playing

2 seconds:
→ An impression counts as viewable once 50% of the ad sits on screen for 2 continuous seconds
→ vCPM bidding pays out on the viewable impression

5 seconds:
→ Shorts logs an engaged view conversion when someone watches 5 seconds or taps the call to action
→ The skip button shows up at 5 seconds

10 seconds:
→ Engagement counts kick in once someone watches 10 seconds
→ Skippable in-stream logs an engaged view conversion at 10 seconds
→ In-feed and Shorts ads running target CPV bidding get billed at the 10 second mark

30 seconds:
→ A skippable in-stream ad becomes a TrueView view once someone watches 30 seconds or the ad ends, whichever comes first
→ Target CPV bidding on skippable in-stream pays out here

Bumper and non-skippable ads:
→ Bumper and non-skippable ads never count a TrueView view because viewers can't skip them
→ Google bills both formats on CPM

Landing page tests might kill your acquisition

Be careful how you measure:

- I've seen an account launch ~60 'ads' a week
- And still somehow lose 35% of new customer acquisition

How? Their reporting dashboard:
- Brand was running landing page tests for a week
- They reused an existing winning ad and pointed it at a new URL.
- That creates a new ad ID
- Which under their reporting dashboard, counts as a "new ad launched."
- But actual new creative fell from ~70% of launches to 30%.
- New customers stayed flat for 2 weeks after the collapse started, so nothing looked wrong until it was 6 weeks deep.

There are two reasons this is a common issue
1. Marketing people get pulled into both creative and landing pages, they can easily get distracted if you aren’t careful when you launch a new “landing page initiative”
2. Test spend is limited, you can’t test everything well with a ton of creative and landing pages at the same time. 
3. Most people track launches by new ad name and swap ad name with landing page. Track by core name instead. (Or they dont track at all) 

How to avoid:

Sort every launch into three buckets:
1. New creative
2. Small variations
3. New landing pages
4. Pull new customers per week
5. Measure Frequency, CPC and CPA

Plot all at the same time so you can see all your creative inputs in one place

1. When to run pLTV

- pLTV is predicted life time value
- If day-1 AOV has zero to little correlation to who becomes a whale, first purchase won't tell you who's valuable. In this case you should send pLTV to accurately tell Meta what that customer is worth
- If your day-1 AOV does predict 12-month LTV, then that signal is good enough and acts as the LTV signal. You don't need to do it

2. How to calculate and send it

- Build a model on your historical cohorts: take the signals you already know on day one (first product, AOV, discount used, acquisition source, first-order margin) and predict each customer's ~12-month value
- Score every new customer with that model right after they purchase
- Send that predicted score to Meta as the conversion value via the Conversions API, instead of the first-purchase revenue

3. High-LTV trap

- Don't just send the raw value back into Meta if that raw value is highly skewed
- For example, if your SKU is $200 and you predict a $10k LTV
- It's easy for algorithms to over-index on extreme values
- Instead, cap extreme values and compress the range so no single amount dominates and reads as an outlier

4. Test optimization signals

- Meta has two performance goals: maximize conversions or maximize value
- The lever is which event you optimize toward. Run three campaigns:
→ Maximize value, with your pLTV score as the value
→ Maximize conversions on a custom high-quality event
→ Maximize conversions on the standard purchase event
- See which one correlates with higher LTV and if you're happy with that payback period.

3 charts to track new creative velocity:

Chart 1: Launches vs spend

- Track total spend against how many ads you've launched, net-new concepts included.
- Divide spend by launches to get spend per launch.
- I'm targeting about $3,000 per launch.

Chart 2: Launches by audience segment

- Tag every ad's key persona with AI, or manually in the ad name.
- Track what percent of spend goes to each segment.
- If 50 of your launches target female audiences and they're only pulling 20% of spend, change the targeting or the strategy for that audience.

Chart 3: Spend in testing

- Testing means creatives under 14 days old or under $1,000 spent. Under 7 days and $500 works too if your account runs a lower CPA. Pick one rule and stay consistent.
- This shows the real cost of testing, and whether the assets you're producing get spend.
- Flip it by hook strategy, hook type, visual setting, offer focus, and influencer vs product to check your splits.

Most underused YouTube ad features

1. Sitelinks

→ Extra links under the video that send someone straight to a specific page. Mobile only.
→ Need at least 2 to appear, up to 4 will show.
→ Add sitelink assets at the campaign level

2. Product feed

→ Pulls products straight from your Merchant Center feed, minimum 4 products required.
→ If your account has assets attached, products show first, unless the campaign goal is Leads, then lead form assets show first instead.
→ You can attach five different assets to one ad and only one of them ever shows.

3. Companion banner

→ A 300x60 banner that sits beside the video after it plays. Desktop only.
→ A click on the banner counts as a view, even if nobody watched 30 seconds of the ad itself.

4. Related videos

→ Lists 2 to 5 of your other videos underneath the ad. YouTube mobile app only, and each linked video has to be Public or Unlisted.

5. Target frequency

→ Not a frequency cap. It's a fixed range you set, 2 to 7 times a week across most formats.
→ Google's own guidance is to add at least as many creatives as the number you set.
→ Breaks the moment you add shared budgets, video partner inventory, or pause the campaign mid-flight.
